Interdisciplinary modelling in support of people-centred transitions: Forecasting citizen adoption of rooftop PV systems under alternative sociopolitical future-world evolutions
papers.abstract: Rooftop photovoltaic (PV) systems are central to decentralised solar transitions in Europe, yet their diffusion depends on more than technical potential, technology costs, or the formal design of support schemes. As Member States move from guaranteed remuneration mechanisms towards more market-reflective compensation, rooftop PV adoption increasingly depends on how citizens perceive policy credibility, profitability, social influence, and uncertainty. This article investigates citizen adoption of rooftop PV systems in the Greek residential sector by 2030 under three alternative sociopolitical storylines representing citizen-driven, government-directed, and market-driven future-world evolutions. We operationalise an interdisciplinary modelling framework that sequentially couples sociopolitical storyline development with agent-based technology adoption modelling. The framework is applied to assess the recently introduced net billing scheme, both as a standalone policy and in combination with battery energy storage system subsidisation, and to benchmark its performance against former feed-in tariff and net metering designs. Results show that the former net metering scheme remains the most effective design by 2030, while net billing ranks second and remains comparatively robust when combined with storage. However, none of the analysed schemes is sufficient, on its own, to achieve the national target of 1 GW of residential rooftop PV capacity by 2030. Adoption outcomes vary across storylines and behavioural profiles, indicating that policy effectiveness is shaped by perceived profitability, policy maturity, social learning, investment resistance, and trust in the stability of the support framework. The study shows how compensation mechanisms translate into adoption trajectories under behavioural and sociopolitical uncertainty, supporting more adaptive and citizen-centred policy designs.

papers.title: How the social capital of influencers drives social media engagement?
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine the impact of the influencer-follower relationship on engagement, integrating social capital theory and consistency theories to assess how social capital affects user engagement. Design/methodology/approach This study collected publicly available data on the TikTok platform, including 278 target posts and 5,722 past posts. Based on these data, the authors measured bonding, bridging, contributing, creating and post frequency and examined the relationships among them. Findings Bonding social capital is positively related to contributing and creating engagement, whereas bridging social capital is negatively related to both. Post frequency mitigates the positive effects of bonding and the negative effects of bridging. Research limitations/implications This study discussed the relationship between social capital and user engagement from the influencer’s perspective and revealed the double-edged effect of post frequency, providing valuable insights for influencer marketing strategies. Future research could further consider psychological factors to complement the role of social capital in the context of influencer marketing. Practical implications Influencers can strategically control their posting frequency based on their social network relationships to boost user engagement. Originality/value By measuring social capital using online metrics, this study examines the relationship between social capital and user engagement from an influencer’s perspective. This study provides a comprehensive understanding of social capital in influencer marketing.

papers.title: When Co-Branding breaks down: strategic misalignment, symbolic rupture, and consumer resistance
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how and under what conditions co-branding in collaboration-saturated markets is associated with negative consumer responses. Moving beyond fit- and synergy-based explanations, it theorizes consumer negative agency (CNA) as agentic, tactic-focused resistance toward co-branding episodes. Design/methodology/approach A sequential, multi-method design is used. Study 1 applies grounded, Gioia-based analysis to walking interviews (n = 55), in-depth interviews (n = 12) and netnographic materials (n = 186) from young Chinese consumers in a high-frequency co-branding environment. Study 2 constructs 29 co-branding episode cases and applies fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis and necessary condition analysis to identify degree-based bottlenecks and sufficient configurations associated with high CNA. Findings Study 1 reveals four dimensions underpinning resistance: strategic misalignment, identity and cultural disconnect, emotional and cognitive strain and CNA. Study 2 identifies equifinal, largely conjunctural configurations associated with high CNA: resistance is organized around distinct configurations labeled practical value distortion, conflict of meaning interpretation and emotional experience split, with image erosion also exhibiting a standalone sufficient set relationship with high CNA in one pathway. Research limitations/implications The study reconceptualizes co-branding breakdown as a consumer-interpreted collaboration stream in which governance, pacing, symbolic legitimacy and experiential costs shape resistance. It introduces CNA and provides a configurational framework explaining when co-branding shifts from engagement to backlash, offering actionable guidance for collaboration governance, symbolic coherence and experience design. Practical implications Three operational priorities follow from the configuration logic: brand managers could strengthen collaboration governance with explicit partner screening, reputational due diligence and a documented rationale; implement symbolic legitimacy checks by auditing meaning coherence and image erosion risk before launch; and reduce experiential strain by controlling release density, simplifying menu/interface presentation and aligning promotional claims with product experience. Originality/value The study reframes co-branding breakdown as a consumer-interpreted collaboration stream in which governance, pacing, symbolic legitimacy and experiential costs shape resistance. It conceptualizes CNA as a context-specific form of tactic-focused resistance and provides a configurational framework explaining when co-branding shifts from engagement to backlash, offering evidence-informed guidance for collaboration governance, symbolic coherence and experience design.

papers.title: Coordinating the Frontlines: An Interdisciplinary Agenda for Extending Organizational Frontlines Research
papers.abstract: Organizational frontlines research (OFR) has generated significant insights into the interactions between organizations and customers, the service interfaces through which these interactions occur, and how they unfold over time. However, less attention has been directed toward the mechanisms through which organizations coordinate these frontline dimensions. Building on Schneider and Bowen’s three-tier view of service organizations, we extend the OFR literature with a specific focus on the coordination tier, which consists of mechanisms responsible for integrating the boundary tier with the customer tier. Drawing on industry benchmarking survey data from senior service leaders and mapping these findings to established and emerging service research priorities, we identify six coordination-tier domains. These domains relate to the management of customer experience, service innovation, new technology exploration, service operations, culture and climate, and talent. By delineating key coordination challenges and a set of future research directions for each domain, we offer an integrated research agenda to advance interdisciplinary OFR scholarship. Additionally, we highlight the role of managers in coordinating resources and processes to deliver value across multiple touchpoints.

papers.title: Tourist Safety Intelligence: Scale Development, Validation, and Prediction
papers.abstract: Safety intelligence is critical for navigating security challenges but remains unexplored in tourism. This study conceptualizes the structure of tourist safety intelligence, develops a measurement scale, and investigates its behavioral influence mechanisms. Study 1 confirmed a triarchic structure of analytical, practical, and creative intelligence based on Sternberg’s Successful Intelligence Theory and validated a scale with adequate fit for both first-order and second-order models. Study 2 revealed that analytical intelligence positively predicts safety compliance but negatively predicts safety participation, while practical and creative intelligence both positively predict safety participation. Analytical and practical intelligence also indirectly influence both behaviors through sequential mediation of social and personal norms. Practically, these findings enable tourism authorities to design targeted training programs enhancing specific intelligence dimensions, develop tailored safety communication strategies based on tourists’ cognitive profiles, and implement differentiated interventions to promote both safety compliance and participation.

papers.title: Reply to Kettl: Public Administration and the Shifting Competing Forces of Accountability
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT The accountability context for how public administrators operate has shifted markedly and has become much more volatile. This shift has placed new and some conflicting demands on public administrators to demonstrate their accountability to various competing governmental actors and has complicated policy and program implementation. The changed context, its causes, and the resultant challenges are analyzed and discussed. Questions are presented for public administration research to help public administrators deal with the challenges.

papers.title: Independent Agencies, Regulation‐Compliant Citizens? Evidence From a Survey Experiment on Vaccine Authorization in the EU
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT The effectiveness of regulatory policy in many areas is contingent on citizens adhering to the scientific advice of regulatory bodies. This in turn depends on whether they perceive this advice as credible . One of the biggest threats to regulatory credibility is the concern that regulatory policy can be tainted by short‐term political interests. Consequently, regulation literature points to agency independence as a crucial resource to securing regulatory credibility, which in turn fosters citizen compliance. We test this assumption both observationally and experimentally in the case of the European Medicines Agency's (EMA) risk assessment for the first COVID‐19 vaccine—a prime example of reliance on credibility in regulation under conditions of controversy and concerns over political interference. We conducted a pre‐registered survey experiment with 4000 EU citizens from four countries timed shortly after the vaccine's approval and before its mass distribution. The results provide partial support that independence is beneficial to regulatory credibility and by extension, to regulatory compliance. Citizens who perceive the EMA as more independent found its risk assessment to be more credible and were more willing to take the vaccine. However, our experimental evidence is less conclusive. Thus, while independence might not in and of itself be a “silver bullet” to ensure regulatory credibility and compliance, it does play an important role, and its real‐life substantive significance would scale up considerably at population levels.

papers.title: Executive Aggrandizement: Understanding the Silent Erosion of Democratic Constraints
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Studies of executive aggrandizement face a double measurement problem. Measures of aggrandizement may include institutions that constitute liberal democracy, while broad composites may treat substantively different executive practices as interchangeable. This article develops a measurement‐oriented classification that reduces direct overlap with the V‐Dem Liberal Democracy Index and compares distinct practices under common analytical rules. Using V‐Dem v15 data and a common sample of 17,404 country‐years across 179 countries from 1901 to 2024, country‐ and year‐fixed‐effects models estimate conditional within‐country associations for five lagged practices. Patronal‐distributive allocation, judicial purges, and personalist/mobilizational legitimation are negatively associated with liberal democracy. Executive corruption is consistently imprecise, whereas politicized administrative appointments are negative only in some specifications. Item‐level, restricted‐period, timing, and first‐difference analyses document practice heterogeneity but also show exceptional persistence; negative future‐lead estimates prevent a causal or sequential reading. The primary contribution is a bounded measurement and modeling strategy that preserves comparability while reducing, rather than claiming to eliminate, outcome overlap. Its linked theoretical contribution is a practice‐family account of executive aggrandizement: politically coordinated practices may coexist and remain interdependent without becoming interchangeable indicators or stages in a common causal sequence.

papers.title: Regulatory Learning or Regulatory Privilege? How Sandbox Design Shapes the Governance Value of Experimental Regulation
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Regulatory sandboxes are controlled, time‐limited environments in which selected innovations are tested under regulatory supervision. This article asks how sandbox design can make selective experimentation capable of generating public regulatory value rather than regulatory privilege. It develops regulatory learning asymmetry to distinguish private, supervisory, and public regulatory learning and unequal distributions of access, information, learning, and benefits. A structured reading of public documents from five deliberately diverse FinTech and artificial intelligence cases illustrates a six‐element operational framework. The case material is not used to infer private or supervisory learning; it records only publication, generalization mechanisms, and documented uptake. The framework identifies a public‐learning configuration, a supervisory‐learning configuration that public documents cannot verify, and a regulatory‐privilege risk configuration. Market signaling is treated as a cross‐cutting dynamic. The article offers a bounded diagnostic for assessing whether case‐specific experience becomes contestable and institutionally usable knowledge.

papers.title: Achievements amidst asymmetries: power dynamics in Swedish civil-military collaboration - an exploratory conceptualization
papers.abstract: This article examines how power dynamics are shaped and managed in day-to-day civil-military collaboration in Swedish total defence. Drawing on semi-structured interviews with key civilian and military actors involved in total defence planning, the article investigates the interplay of power asymmetries, the collaboration’s institutional and relational conditions and how collaborating actors perceive and manage asymmetries in practice. Using thematic analysis, we demonstrate that civil-military collaboration is characterized by imbalances in authority, resources and discursive legitimacy. The paper further sheds light on micro-level practices of power enactment and details how collaborating actors negotiate and manage power asymmetries. The main finding suggests that when the relatively more powerful actors engage in power moderating practices, which we conceptualize as Strategic Power Moderation (SPM), collaborations can perform productively despite asymmetrical relations. The results offer a nuanced understanding of how collaborations fare under conditions of power asymmetry and have implications for both research and practice.

papers.title: A Practical Guide to Conditional Mediation Analysis with GSCA: Method, Simulation, and Software
papers.abstract: Conditional mediation (CoMe) analysis integrates mediation and moderation to examine how an indirect effect transmitted through a mediator varies across levels of a moderator. In this tutorial, we show how to conduct CoMe analysis in generalized structured component analysis (GSCA), a component-based structural equation modeling approach. We first outline the technical foundations of GSCA-based CoMe analysis and then report a simulation study evaluating its performance relative to partial least squares path modeling, another component-based approach. We also present an empirical illustration that provides step-by-step guidance for implementing GSCA-based CoMe analysis using GSCA Pro, a free, user-friendly software package.
papers.journal_name: Structural Equation Modeling: A Multidisciplinary Journal

papers.title: From mobilization to diversion: a comparative study of wartime communication tactics of Ukrainian and Russian political elites on Telegram
papers.abstract: This study examines how Ukrainian and Russian political elites communicate on Telegram during the ongoing Russo-Ukrainian war. Using a dataset of Telegram public posts from 2019 to 2024, we analyze changes in communication volume, thematic content, and actor engagement before and after Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion. While the invasion triggered a massive spike in elites’ activity on Telegram in both countries—most notably among actors associated with Russia’s ruling pro-regime party—the focus of this communication diverged sharply. While Ukrainian elites initially prioritized war-related mobilization, this emphasis has declined over time. By contrast, Russian elites from the start adopted a tactic of strategic diversion, avoiding discussion of the war and shifting public attention to unrelated issues, such as crises in the West. Finally, we show that communication patterns are stratified by party size, with smaller parties specializing in narrow policy niches. These findings shed light on how political elites adapt their communication strategies in online environments during wartime.

papers.title: Data benefits? Attitudes and aspirations of recipients towards social security administrative data sharing
papers.abstract: This paper outlines benefit recipients’ views towards the sharing of data that is collected about them when they routinely interact with social security services. Sharing this administrative data between public bodies promises to transform the delivery and evaluation of social security. However, there remains a lack of research into public attitudes, understandings, and aspirations for the sharing of this data, particularly from those whose data would be shared. Drawing on discussions from deliberative focus groups with 41 individuals, we reflect on the scope for increased data sharing to deliver improvements for recipients.While participants were aware of how their data is currently shared and how increased data sharing might have advantages, they expressed strong distrust in government agencies to manage their data and concerns about being placed in a position of increased vulnerability. We argue individuals’ views towards data sharing cannot be separated from their lived experiences of data systems – their data realities – which are often markedly different from system designers. We conclude by offering considerations against data systems re-introducing paternalistic policy, unintentionally, via automation – which we term ‘automated paternalism’.

papers.title: Framework for integration of regional transportation model (RTM) with collision prediction model (CPM)
papers.abstract: Traditional road safety planning is largely reactive, while existing Collision Prediction Models (CPMs) often function as disconnected post-processing tools. However, a growing body of research has highlighted the need for proactive safety assessment at the transportation planning stage. Building on this research, the present study demonstrates a large-scale, automated framework that integrates CPMs with a calibrated, tour-based Regional Transportation Model (RTM), enabling travel demand and network-wide collision outcomes to be evaluated within a unified modelling workflow. Using the Calgary metropolitan region as a case study, Negative Binomial models were developed to estimate Fatal/Injury (FI) and Property-Damage-Only (PDO) collisions at mid-block segments and intersections. To ensure seamless operational integration, all explanatory variables used by the CPMs were derived exclusively from the RTM’s multimodal outputs, thereby eliminating the need for additional external data collection . Validation against independent historical data from 2017 to 2019 demonstrated robust predictive accuracy at both the aggregate network level and the individual facility level. The framework was then applied to a 2028 planning horizon to evaluate twelve demand-side policy scenarios involving changes in fuel prices, parking costs, and transit fares. The results revealed a consistent, monotonic dose–response relationship across all interventions. Increases in fuel prices produced the largest network-wide reductions in collision, while lower transit fare and higher parking costs generated more targeted safety benefits. Intersections were particularly sensitive, especially with respect to FI collisions under the transit fare scenarios. By generating severity-stratified safety estimates alongside conventional demand outputs, without requiring additional data inputs or manual post-processing, the framework enables planners to evaluate mobility and safety trade-offs for proactive, data-informed long-range transportation planning.

papers.title: Why does the medical staff remain silent? Preventing child abuse begins with reporting: A cross-sectional study
papers.abstract: Background Despite mandatory reporting laws, discrepancies between the estimated prevalence of child maltreatment and official reports may reflect both under-identification and failure to report recognized concerns. Healthcare professionals face emotional, cognitive, and institutional barriers that may influence reporting willingness. Methods This cross-sectional study examined sociodemographic, professional, cognitive, emotional, perceptual, and institutional factors associated with healthcare professionals' self-reported willingness to report suspected child maltreatment. The sample included 272 healthcare professionals caring for children (44% physicians, 43% nurses). Data were collected using a validated anonymous questionnaire. Results Years of experience were positively associated with identification ability ( r = 0.24, p < .001). Women reported higher willingness to report than men (M = 20.97 vs. 18.77, p < .001). Hospital-based staff demonstrated higher self-reported willingness to report than community-based staff (M = 20.74 vs. 18.95, p < .001), and managerial staff demonstrated higher self-reported willingness to report than non-managerial staff (M = 20.96 vs. 20.18, p = .03). Anger toward the child's family was the most common emotional response (44%). More positive perceptions and attitudes, together with greater emotional readiness, were associated with greater self-reported willingness to report suspected child maltreatment. Conclusions Female healthcare professionals, professionals with greater clinical experience, hospital-based healthcare professionals, and those in managerial roles reported greater willingness to report suspected child maltreatment. Targeted training incorporating clinical exposure, emotional processing, and ethical decision-making is recommended, particularly for community-based and male professionals. Stronger leadership and organizational support may enhance reporting willingness.

papers.title: From silence to sharing: A six-month prospective study on adult disclosure of childhood sexual abuse
papers.abstract: Background Disclosure of childhood sexual abuse (CSA) is often assumed to be beneficial. However, prospective research examining outcomes associated with disclosure remains scarce, limiting evidence-based guidance for adults considering disclosure. Objective The primary aim was to examine changes in posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) symptoms following first-time disclosure of CSA to personal contacts and to test whether perceived supportiveness of confidants' responses moderated these changes. The secondary aim was to explore characteristics of CSA disclosure. Methods Forty adults with a history of CSA who had not previously disclosed the abuse to personal contacts completed two assessments, at baseline and at follow-up six months later. Participants who disclosed their CSA to a personal contact during the follow-up period were classified as disclosers, whereas those who did not were classified as non-disclosers. Results During the follow-up period, 60% ( n = 24) disclosed for the first time to personal contacts, after on average 31.5 years ( SD = 16.2), most often to friends (47%). Disclosers showed a clinically relevant, greater reduction in PTSD symptoms than non-disclosers. Perceived supportiveness of confidants' responses was moderate to high but did not significantly moderate changes in PTSD symptoms. Conclusions First-time disclosure of CSA in adulthood to personal contacts was associated with a clinically relevant reduction in PTSD symptoms. Nevertheless, individual differences in symptom change indicate that outcomes following disclosure vary. Guidance should therefore move beyond the question of whether to disclose and consider when, under what circumstances, and for whom disclosure may be beneficial.

papers.title: Screening for suspected child physical abuse in a Colombian pediatric emergency department: Clinical characteristics and performance of SPUTOVAMO-R
papers.abstract: Background Physical abuse causes morbidity and mortality in young children, yet Latin American emergency data are scarce. Objective To describe characteristics associated with a multidisciplinary child-protection panel's classification and estimate SPUTOVAMO-R sensitivity relative to ICD-10 coding and panel classification. Participants and Setting Children aged 1 month–18 years with emergency department records at a pediatric referral hospital in Bogotá, Colombia (2015–2017), coded with physical-abuse ICD-10 diagnoses. Methods Retrospective cross-sectional study. High- and low-probability classifications were compared using Fisher's exact test and odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Results Of 322 coded children, 59 (18.3%) were classified as high probability. An internally inconsistent account (OR 34.7, 95% CI 12.0–124.0), history inconsistent with injury (OR 18.0, 8.3–40.7), and disclosure by the child (OR 56.1, 12.7–516.7) were strongly associated with high-probability classification. Absence of an adult witness was not associated among children aged 0–4 years and was associated with low-probability classification in older children (OR 0.08, 0.00–0.58). All four high-probability children with high-specificity fractures, and none of three low-probability children, had a history inconsistent with injury. SPUTOVAMO-R sensitivity was 34.2% (110/322; 95% CI 29.0–39.6) relative to ICD-10 coding and 91.5% (54/59; 81.3–97.2) relative to the panel. Conclusions ICD-10 abuse coding corresponded poorly with panel classification. Panel classification was most strongly associated with history coherence. SPUTOVAMO-R was negative in two-thirds of coded children and should be evaluated in unselected populations.
authors: Diana Carolina De la Hoz-Díaz Granados

papers.title: Towards a nutrition-enhancing and water-conserving diet: insights from China
Evidence and knowledge gaps on pumpkin in sub-Saharan African food systems: a scoping review
papers.abstract: Abstract Pumpkin holds significant potential to improve food security, nutrition, and economic development in sub-Saharan Africa, yet is one of many neglected and underutilized crop species which has received limited attention from researchers and policymakers. This scoping review synthesizes findings from 44 peer-reviewed and grey literature sources across multiple disciplines to appraise the state of research on pumpkin within sub-Saharan African food systems. It explores value chain dynamics, dimensions of the food environment, consumer behaviour, and policy factors, alongside outcomes for nutrition, health, economic development, environmental sustainability, and social equity. The evidence base is geographically concentrated – with 41 studies (93%) having a single-country focus and the majority conducted in Ethiopia, Kenya, and South Africa—and shows limited methodological diversity, with 33 (75%) employing cross-sectional observational designs. Fifteen documents examined value chain activities, 18 focused on consumer behaviour, and 37 provided insights into external and personal dimensions of the food environment – although none explicitly applied a food environment framework. Most studies centred on consumers and the use of pumpkin leaves and fruit. Production was the most frequently analysed value chain component, with other areas significantly underexplored. Insights on vendors, processors, and policymakers were largely absent, as were urban and peri-urban contexts. Of food environment dimensions, findings on availability, product properties, and desirability were most common. Evidence on outcomes of pumpkin production, value chain participation, and consumption remains limited: with a primary focus on social equity and food and nutrition security. Our review identifies the need for an interdisciplinary, systems-oriented approach in future research, covering the entire value chain and incorporating gender, market, and policy dimensions. Collated evidence supports the need for targeted interventions to improve processing, enhance food safety, shift cultural perceptions, and strengthen governance mechanisms, for pumpkin to contribute more substantially to resilient, equitable African food systems.

papers.title: Who Is Afraid of ChatGPT? A Natural Experiment on the Effect of ChatGPT Release on Labour-Market Concerns
papers.abstract: The public release of ChatGPT on November 30th, 2022 revived the public debate on technological change and, particularly, on its impact on the labour market. Despite the sudden growth in AI salience after the launch of the new chatbot, to our knowledge, no empirical investigation has assessed the impact of this technological breakthrough on citizens’ first concerns. By means of a unique survey fielded between November and December 2022 in five European countries, we use an Unexpected Event During Survey (UEDS) design to causally test the effect of ChatGPT’s launch on individual perception of unemployment risk. We rely on statistical matching techniques, combined with regression analyses to explore heterogeneity in responses between socioeconomic groups. We show that the release of the new chatbot mildly but significantly increased unemployment concerns in advanced industrial democracies, particularly among individuals with low and middling levels of income and education, as well as poorly exposed to AI. By capturing reactions before informational framings consolidate and widespread adoption occurs, this study provides a rare window into citizens’ genuine response to technological change, indicating that its socioeconomic consequences are perceived as immediately salient.

papers.title: Managed Multiplicity: The Political Versatility of Assisted Reproductive Technologies in Singapore’s National Imaginary
papers.abstract: This article presents a discourse analysis of reproductive policy in Singapore, a small Southeast Asian country with ultra-low fertility rates. Focusing on assisted reproduction between the 1980s and 2024, it shows how egg freezing and in vitro fertilization emerged as “politically versatile technologies” that are simultaneously associated with women’s reproductive choice and patriarchal pronatalism. It theorizes that such versatility arises through shifting and stratified policy provisions, the interplay of different policy domains, and discursive processes conditioned by the political regime. Enmeshed with foreign policy goals, social policies and regulatory approaches to assisted reproduction are justified via an increasingly global interpretation of competing gender ideologies. Furthermore, media policy supports the naturalization of heteronormative and patriarchal “family values,” as state-regulated media deploy emotional frames while spotlighting the connections between assisted reproductive technologies, egalitarianism, and pronatalist social policies that selectively benefit heterosexual or married women. By demonstrating how the ideological versatility of assisted reproductive technologies is discursively maintained by state-regulated media and government actors amid policy change, this article advances the concept of “managed multiplicity” to characterize the patriarchal state’s organization of gendered meanings across policy tools, domains, actors, and broader projects concerning national and international legitimacy.

papers.title: Who speaks up? Voice and community belonging in Australian local government
papers.abstract: Much has been written about the value of responding to community voice, yet we know far less about who expresses that voice. Using a nationally representative dataset of 65,336 observations, we analyse the association between direct local political voice and individual characteristics, distinguishing occasional from frequent engagement. Occasional voice is relatively common, but sustained participation is rare. Consistent with theory, educational attainment and community belonging are positively associated with speaking up. Unemployment is also positively associated with voice, while gender differences emerge across the models. We further observe a marked reduction in voice in 2022, a period marked by COVID-19. Overall, around one-third of citizens voice opinions, but participation is concentrated among specific groups. These patterns matter because many promised benefits of participation depend not merely on whether citizens speak, but on who speaks. We conclude by outlining implications for practitioners seeking broader and more equitable engagement.

papers.title: Screening-based siting and metocean-aware O&M routing for floating offshore wind farms
Unlocking the green power of the North Sea: Identifying key energy infrastructure synergies for 2030 and 2040
papers.abstract: The North Sea will play a key role in providing clean and secure energy for Europe. This not only requires the development of new offshore wind farms, but also their successful integration into the onshore system. In this work we analyze and compare three key integration options and their preferred siting (onshore vs. offshore): grid expansions, electricity storage, and the production, storage and transport of low-carbon hydrogen. We focus on their potential to reduce emissions and energy system costs – individually and in combination with each other. Additionally, we study the consequences of constraints on their implementation. We analyze the years 2030 and 2040, starting from the projections of installed energy infrastructure and demand from the Ten Year Network Development Plan (TYNDP) 2022 of the European Network of Transmission System Operators (ENTSO-E). Results show that cross-border electricity grid expansions across the North Sea are a no-regret measure, resulting in significant reductions in system costs and emissions compared to national grid expansions. By comparison, the production, storage and transport of hydrogen have a lower cost and emission reduction potential. In both the short and long term (2030 and 2040), electricity storage can help to reduce emissions, but it is not cost competitive unless emission reduction targets are enforced. Combining the three integration measures at optimal capacities provides additional benefits. Overall, the highest emission reductions can be achieved by combining electricity storage with an expansion of the grid, while the highest economic benefits can be achieved with a combination of grid expansions and hydrogen production for direct use in industry.

papers.title: Steering profitability: How electricity balancing regulations drive V2G feasibility in Germany
Morocco's nuclear option readiness (2026–2050): A governance-first approach aligned with the IAEA milestones framework
Mechanisms and pathways for the integrated development of coal power and renewable energy under the coupling of electricity, carbon, and green certificate markets
Institutional risk, finance, and the limits of techno-economic optimality in green hydrogen deployment
papers.abstract: Green hydrogen is widely positioned as a key option for deep decarbonization, yet large-scale deployment remains limited despite growing techno-economic potential. This review examines how non-technical conditions influence the feasibility of green hydrogen business models, using the Netherlands as an illustrative case. A review-driven mixed-methods framework integrates evidence from a systematic literature review, semi-structured expert interviews, and an established hourly-resolved techno-economic optimization model to examine how policy design, investment risk, infrastructure constraints, and demand formation influence both the levelized cost of hydrogen (LCOH) and deployment feasibility. A multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA) is employed to synthesize qualitative and quantitative evidence and prioritize the principal drivers and barriers identified across the different sources. The synthesized evidence, supported by the illustrative techno-economic analysis, indicates that LCOH values below €6 kg −1 are attainable under favorable assumptions, including low renewable electricity prices, reduced weighted average cost of capital (WACC), and access to underground hydrogen storage. However, regulatory fragmentation, grid congestion, weak demand coordination, and limited institutional legitimacy substantially constrain the realization of such conditions in practice. The findings demonstrate that techno-economic assessments alone may overestimate the deployability of green hydrogen when institutional risk and market coordination challenges are not explicitly considered. The proposed integrative framework provides a structured approach for assessing hydrogen market readiness in early-stage European contexts and supports the alignment of techno-economic competitiveness with governance capacity, investment conditions, and social acceptance.

papers.title: Pathways for fulfilling global extended producer responsibility: a data-driven optimization for sustainable and circular electric vehicle battery supply chains
papers.abstract: As electric vehicle (EV) adoption accelerates, managing end-of-life (EOL) batteries is critical for EPR implementation. This study optimizes recovery networks for China's exported EV batteries across 172 destinations. We develop a bi-objective MILP framework with Weibull-based forecasting, processing capacities from 156 Chinese recyclers and CAPEX of 24 automakers (2025–2060). Evaluating Ship Back, Local Plant, and Formal Outsource, results show cumulative EOL demand of 57.96 Mt over 2025–2060 and demand of 4.78 Mt in 2060. Domestic capacity constraints force profit-driven systems toward localized overseas recycling. Relative to PROFIT_MAX, CARBON_MIN advances local investment by ten years, raises local processing by 11.2 percentage points, and improves net GHG mitigation by 16.3%, but reduces NPV by 54.4%. PARETO_KNEE captures 66.7% of additional mitigation with a 13.2% NPV loss. CARBON_MIN yields the highest Li, Co, and Ni recovery, revealing synergy between environmental optimisation and resource circularity.

papers.title: Soil Protists Consume Viruses to Drive Microbial Nutrient Cycling: Overlooked Trophic Pathways in Soil Food Web
papers.abstract: Abstract Soil viruses are traditional top-down regulators that redistribute organic matter through host lysis and the viral shunt, implicitly positioning them as terminal sinks rather than active trophic components. Here, we show, for the first time, that soil viruses can also be direct prey for protists, establishing an overlooked pathway for the transfer of viral-derived nutrients and energy within soil food webs. In controlled cocultures, the ciliate Tetrahymena pyriformis actively ingested the soil bacteriophage HRZ04p, with viral abundance declining by 0.66-log within 24 h at a virus-to-protist ratio of 5:1. Under high viral availability (104:1), viral consumption enhanced protist population growth by 2.24-fold relative to virus-free controls. Viral grazing altered nutrient dynamics, characterized by ammonium peaking at 1,206 μg L–1 (a 92% increase compared with protists alone) and coordinated shifts in nitrogen-metabolizing enzymes. Untargeted metabolomics revealed extensive metabolic reprogramming, with amino acid catabolic pathways upregulated. In contrast, amino acid biosynthesis and aminoacyl-tRNA biosynthesis were simultaneously activated, reflecting recycling of viral-derived substrates into new protein synthesis. These findings confirm the existence of a soil “viral consumption” pathway, reposition viruses as active nodes within microbial food webs, and provide a mechanistic and conceptual foundation for incorporating virus-mediated nutrient fluxes into soil biogeochemical models.

papers.title: A short-stroke, low-stepping-resistance inverted-V electromagnetic energy harvesting floor: design, output performance and biomechanical evaluation
Public stockpiling, offtake, and the value of domestic rare earth midstream capacity: A calibrated policy valuation for South Korea
papers.abstract: For import-dependent manufacturing economies, the policy value of domestic rare earth midstream readiness depends on whether it can provide useable supply that reduces shortages remaining after external supply and public stockpiles have been used. This study evaluates that condition for South Korea by comparing a BASELINE of external supply and a common public stockpile with an ENHANCED state that adds a pre-established joint neodymium–praseodymium (NdPr)–Dy 2 O 3 separation/refining pathway, domestic operating inventory, and public offtake. A 20-year monthly material-flow and inventory model is evaluated under a deterministic disruption and 10,000 stress-test paths, using 0.5 t/year of joint oxide output as a functional scale anchor. Under the deterministic full-usability benchmark, ENHANCED reduces the 2466.18 t BASELINE residual priority-demand shortage by 1.375 t (0.056%), with USD 9.584 million in incremental real-resource cost and a required USD 8974.7/kg break-even value, not an estimated economic benefit. Public offtake improves facility finance, but facility net present value remains negative under all three contracts, including OT-3 at −USD 1.478 million, while government fiscal burden reaches USD 8.913 million. At the same break-even unit value, economic net value is non-negative in 81.58% of full-usability paths, 59.27% of partial-usability paths, and 0% under pathway failure. These are conditional stress-test outcomes, not probabilities of policy success. Taken together, these diagnostics identify a bounded role for public offtake in improving the financial conditions for maintaining readiness, while downstream usability remains necessary for shortage reduction; they do not establish facility viability or economic justification.

papers.title: Spatial trajectories and land-use potential of China's utility-scale photovoltaic expansion toward 2035
papers.abstract: China aims to reach 3600 GW of combined wind and solar capacity by 2035, requiring substantial expansion of utility-scale photovoltaic (PV) deployment. Quantifying the geospatial footprint of this expansion is essential for sustainable land-use planning and ecological protection. This study develops a nationwide assessment framework that integrates multi-source remote sensing observations, Random Forest (RF) suitability modeling, SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) for model interpretation, and scenario-based spatial allocation. Historical PV data from 2000 to 2025 show that China's utility-scale PV farms expanded to 13,800 km 2 , with growth concentrated in northwestern mega-bases and emerging decentralized installations in central-eastern regions, indicating a dual-track spatial trajectory. Scenario projections suggest that Scenario B (NDC Update-Aligned Pathway) requires an additional 21,420 km 2 , whereas Scenario C (Wind-Slowdown Compensation) increases land demand moderately to 24,405 km 2 . Scenario A (Business as Usual) could require up to 63,990 km 2 and would disproportionately affect croplands and forests. However, China retains more than 206,000 km 2 of high-potential land, indicating that ecological conflicts are driven mainly by spatial mismatch rather than absolute land scarcity. These findings underscore the need for integrated spatial governance, optimized ultra-high-voltage (UHV) transmission, and distributed PV deployment. By linking observed spatial trajectories, interpretable suitability modeling, and capacity-to-land translation, this study provides a transferable framework for assessing the land-use potential of utility-scale PV expansion toward 2035.

papers.title: Practical application of a global biodiversity framework indicator for species protection in national policy
Bridging the cultural divide to improve drinking water security, sustainability and resilience in first nations communities: A case study from Australia
Mechanisms of circularity: How epistemic, financial and material flows construct new waste geographies
papers.abstract: Circular Economy (CE) initiatives originate predominantly in the Global North, yet their material, epistemic, and financial effects increasingly manifest in Global South contexts. Using Dutch–Kenya waste relations as a critical case study, this article examines how CE interventions transform waste materials into a marketized commodity through three interconnected variables: an epistemic variable, reframing waste and circularity through market-oriented knowledge systems; a financial, channelling investment towards formalized circular infrastructure that excludes informal and community-based actors; and a material variable, establishing new waste geographies that concentrate processing activity in the Global South. Kenya's dual position as a destination for Dutch waste exports and a recipient of Dutch CE development funding, makes it a relevant site for observing how these variables operate and interact. Drawing on interviews with Dutch and Kenyan government, donor, and civil society actors, the article argues that CE interventions restructure the governance of existing waste markets not through Dutch influence alone, but through negotiated convergence between Dutch donor priorities and the Kenyan state's own regulatory capacity constraints and economic interests. This restructuring concentrates control over the terms of participation among formal, internationally connected, and resourced actors, while progressively marginalizing informal workers who have long managed waste through community-based practices. Through an environmental justice lens drawing on Schlosberg's (2007) tripartite framework of distribution, recognition, and participation, the article demonstrates that the critical question is not only who governs the new waste geographies and on whose terms material recovery proceeds, but how donor and recipient-state interests jointly produce the exclusion of informal actors from that governance. The article contributes an integrated analytical framework for studying the shift from conventional waste trade to circular trade in North–South relations, and positions this contribution within political ecology and critical CE scholarship.

papers.title: Selective nostalgia: development through ‘shared heritage’ diplomacy in post-colonial Sri Lanka
papers.abstract: Developing nations are increasingly inscribing urban heritage sites to UNESCO’s World Heritage List for global recognition, political legitimization, and economic development. Sri Lanka’s ‘Old Town of Galle’ is a colonial-era site inscribed to the List as an outstanding example of a fortified city built by Europeans in Asia. Although Galle Fort’s colonial-era heritage is attributed to three European traditions – Portuguese, Dutch, and British – its Dutch ancestry is prioritized by experts, the State and its residents. This “selective nostalgia” in the parsing of layered colonial pasts through heritage conservation reveals how heritage operates as a medium for pursuing diplomatic relations and developmental agendas. Using evidence from interviews, observational data, and documents, I show that through its production as World Heritage, colonial-era heritage is reinterpreted as a shared heritage to serve diverging diplomatic and developmental agendas. For the Dutch, the construction of a shared heritage narrative neutralizes this past by boosting colonial accomplishments while underemphasizing colonial exploitations. For Sri Lanka, Dutch-aided conservation of Galle Fort provides a marketable commodity that is a magnet for global tourism. However, the cultivation of ‘shared heritage’ is also restructuring the Fort’s socio-spatial fabric with rampant gentrification and touristification marginalizing the local community of this living heritage site.
papers.journal_name: Environment and Planning C: Politics and Space

papers.title: An agenda for plastics crisis research in the synthetic age
From Green Culture to Sustainability Performance: Unpacking a Sequential Capability Pathway Through Environmental Leadership and Circular Economy Practices
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Although green organizational culture has been associated with sustainability outcomes, less is understood about the mechanisms through which sustainability‐oriented cultural values are translated into organizational action and performance. Drawing on the Natural Resource–Based View (NRBV) theory, this study examines how environmental leadership and circular economy practices independently and sequentially transmit the effects of green organizational culture to sustainability performance. Using a quantitative explanatory design, survey data were collected from 1209 employees across Ghana's oil and gas, power generation, transmission and distribution, and regulatory segments and analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS‐SEM), supplemented by cluster‐robust sensitivity analyses. The findings show that green organizational culture positively influences sustainability performance and environmental leadership. Environmental leadership, in turn, enhances circular economy practices and sustainability performance, while circular economy practices positively influence sustainability performance. However, circular economy practices do not independently mediate the green organizational culture–sustainability performance nexus. Instead, significant indirect effects operate through environmental leadership and sequentially through environmental leadership and circular economy practices, while the direct effect remains significant. These findings extend the NRBV by revealing how sustainability‐oriented culture translates into performance through interconnected leadership and operational capabilities rather than through cultural orientation alone. The study provides large‐sample evidence from an under‐researched emerging‐economy energy context and demonstrates the practical importance of aligning green organizational culture, environmental leadership, and circular economy implementation to enhance sustainability performance.

papers.title: Sustainable Building Operation and Maintenance as a Strategic Environmental Capability in Net‐Zero Office‐Type Buildings: A Web of Science–Based Bibliometric–Systematic Review (2009–2025)
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Sustainable building operation and maintenance (O&M) is increasingly supported by digital technologies; however, research remains fragmented across technical, organisational and behavioural domains, limiting understanding of how performance gains are sustained in net zero energy (NZE) office‐type buildings. This study maps, critically synthesises and theorises this interdisciplinary evidence base. An integrated bibliometric–systematic literature review combined descriptive bibliometric analysis and science mapping of 137 Web of Science records with a systematic qualitative synthesis of 30 purposively selected studies, supported by search‐sensitivity and cross‐database robustness checks. The analysis identified 17 bibliographic clusters that were consolidated into eight research streams and four higher‐order socio‐technical themes. The findings indicate that sustained performance depends on the recursive integration of technological sensing, organisational interpretation and governance, behavioural–operational enactment, verification and learning. Building on these insights, the study develops the dynamic socio‐technical capability (DSTC) framework, offering an integrative and empirically testable explanation of sustainable building O&M as a strategic environmental capability, defined here at the building operational level.

papers.title: Trust in algorithms biased appraisal and boosted affect in online dating
A latent profile analysis of child maltreatment and its psychosocial correlates in a sample of school-aged adolescents
How experiential knowledge becomes evidence in lawmaking through consultations with incarcerated people
papers.abstract: Experiential knowledge, grounded in lived experience, is increasingly recognized as an important source of evidence in policy making and legislative drafting. Yet questions remain about how knowledge derived from consultations with affected individuals can legitimately inform broader lawmaking. This article examines how experiential knowledge from targeted consultations with incarcerated individuals is transformed into context-specific legislative knowledge through the interplay of propositional system knowledge, procedural knowledge of navigating the prison system, and implicit analogical reasoning. Drawing on consultation memoranda and a draft Bill produced during the reform of the Finnish Imprisonment Act, we analyse consultations concerning incarcerated individuals’ use of communication technologies to manage essential practical matters beyond prison under conditions of administrative burden. We first construct a narrative from the consultees’ propositional and procedural experiential knowledge and then examine how this knowledge was incorporated into legislative arguments alongside official expert knowledge. Our analysis shows that the draft Bill employed implicit analogical reasoning to transform procedural knowledge of navigating the prison system into propositional claims applicable to broader prison populations sharing similar contexts, institutional routines, and practical needs. By demonstrating how analogical reasoning links propositional and procedural knowledge to generate context-specific generalizations, the article offers a novel conceptual framework for understanding how experiential knowledge can become legitimate evidence in lawmaking. We suggest that this approach is applicable to other institutional settings characterized by standardized living conditions, shared procedures, and common systems of navigation.

papers.title: Identification of territorial spatial conflict and its influencing factors from a cross-scale and multi-dimensional perspective: A case study of the Three Gorges Reservoir area, China
Selection and optimization of phase change materials for active-passive coupled battery thermal management system matching thermal shock loads
Prospective life cycle sustainability assessment and decision support for solar electricity and industrial heat under uncertainty: a service-specific evaluation of PV, CSP, and CST
Multilayer stacked thermoelectric generator with temperature-window-matched materials for waste heat recovery in series-hybrid electric vehicles

Desert dust storm, ambient temperature, and pulmonary function among children with asthma in the Eastern Mediterranean
papers.abstract: Background Climate change has contributed to increased dust events and rising ambient temperature, posing potential health risk for susceptible populations including children with asthma. The study aims to examine associations between exposure to desert dust storm (DDS) and higher ambient temperature with pulmonary function indicators, including forced expiratory volume in 1s (FEV 1 ), forced vital capacity (FVC) and FEV 1 /FVC% among asthmatic children during the dust season in the Eastern Mediterranean. Methods We conducted exploratory secondary analyses of repeated pulmonary function measurements from schoolchildren with asthma in Cyprus and Crete, Greece during spring of 2019 and 2021. Dust exposure was defined using short-term (at least one DDS day on the assessment day or during the preceding 7 days) and cumulative days (over the spring season) metrics based on site-specific DDS classifications as well as ambient temperature assessed from the nearest meteorological station. Associations were examined using linear mixed-effect models. Results Among the 135 children included, short-term DDS exposure was associated with a non-significant decrement in FEV 1 (-20.46 mL, 95% CI: -50.38, 9.46) and FVC (-27.21 mL, 95% CI: -59.45, 5.02). Cumulative dust exposure was associated with -3.52 mL (95% CI: -5.90, -1.14) difference in FEV 1 per DDS day. Ambient temperature averaged over 0-7 days before assessment was inversely associated with FEV 1 (-19.77 mL; 95% CI: -37.91, -1.63 per 5°C increase) and FEV 1 /FVC% (-0.81; 95% CI: -1.36, -0.25 per 5 °C increase), with no statistical evidence of effect modification by short-term DDS exposure. Conclusions This exploratory secondary analysis demonstrated inverse associations of cumulative DDS exposure and ambient temperature with pulmonary function among children with asthma, while short-term DDS associations were not statistically significant. These findings may inform the management of children with asthma during desert dust seasons, but confirmation in larger studies is required.

papers.title: Ecological responses and reduced estimated dietary cancer risk in PAH-contaminated soil following dual-oxidant remediation
Intensifying compound drought–heatwave events weaken ecosystem water-use efficiency in the Nile River Basin
papers.abstract: Climate warming has intensified compound drought–heatwave (CDHW) events worldwide, posing growing threats to ecosystem carbon–water dynamics. However, the impacts of CDHWs on ecosystem water-use efficiency (WUE), particularly event sequencing, drought memory, and climatic heterogeneity, remain poorly understood at large river-basin scales. This study investigated the spatiotemporal evolution of CDHW events and their impacts on ecosystem functioning across the Nile River Basin (NRB) during 2000–2025 using SPEI, heatwave detection, harmonized MODIS-derived GPP and ET, phase-space trajectory analysis, and machine-learning approaches. CDHW frequency, duration, severity, and spatial extent generally increased across the basin, with heatwave-leading events showing a 29.5% increase in spatial extent compared with 12.9% for drought-leading events. A chronological Pettitt test identified 2014 as a significant change point in CDHW frequency. Although basin-wide GPP and ET increased, WUE declined across 58.6% of valid WUE grid cells, indicating substantial spatial heterogeneity in ecosystem carbon–water coupling. CDHWs were generally associated with stronger reductions in GPP and ET than individual drought or heatwave conditions, while WUE commonly increased at the event scale because ET declined proportionally more than GPP. WUE responses varied across SPEI accumulation timescales, with longer antecedent timescales prevalent across much of the basin. Precipitation contributed most in arid and semi-arid regions, whereas temperature, radiation, and VPD contributed relatively more in wetter environments. These findings provide a comprehensive basin-scale assessment of ecosystem WUE responses to CDHWs in the NRB, highlighting spatial heterogeneity, event-scale impacts, and antecedent hydroclimatic associations, and inform ecosystem management under a changing climate.

From source to sink: Multimedia fate, seasonal drivers, and priority control of synthetic phenolic antioxidants in typical bays of the Bohai Sea and the Yellow Sea, China
papers.abstract: Synthetic phenolic antioxidants (SPAs) are emerging contaminants of concern in coastal environments, yet their multimedia distribution and integrated risks remain insufficiently characterized. We investigated 10 SPAs in seawater, suspended particulate matter (SPM), sediment, and Ruditapes philippinarum at 10 sites in three bays during May and August 2025. Total operationally dissolved concentrations ranged from 948 to 9851 ng/L in May to 19,585-42311 ng/L in August, and the across-site arithmetic mean was 6.35-fold higher in August. Sediment and clam concentrations across both campaigns ranged from 26,190 to 126425 and 28,666-117083 ng/g dry weight, respectively. Structural equation modeling indicated season-dependent associations between SPA concentrations and hydrochemical and nutrient variables. Positive matrix factorization resolved four factors tentatively associated with plastics, rubber, personal care products, and petroleum/lubricants. Biomarker associations in field-collected clams indicated co-occurring physiological stress but did not establish SPA-specific causation. In the provisional weight-of-evidence screen, BHT was classified as major in both campaigns, whereas AO1010 was classified as major in May and severe in August based on the sediment partitioning parameters, dietary exposure assumptions, and toxicological screening benchmarks. The integrated assessment supports targeted monitoring of BHT and AO1010 and investigation of their probable product-related inputs, with quantitative risk prioritization conditional on these methodological uncertainties.

Quality Regulation and Competition: Evidence from Pharmaceutical Markets
papers.abstract: Abstract Quality regulation seeks to ensure quality and foster competition by reducing vertical differentiation, but it may also have adverse effects on market structure. We study this trade-off in the context of pharmaceutical bioequivalence, which is the primary quality standard for generic drugs. By exploiting the introduction of bioequivalence in Chile, we find that stronger regulation reduced the number of drugs in the market by 18% and increased average paid prices by 13%. We estimate a model of drug entry, certification, and demand to study how drug quality, aversion to generics, and certification costs shape the equilibrium effects of quality regulation. We find that quality regulation increased demand for generic drugs by resolving asymmetric information and reducing aversion to unbranded generics, which induced the entry of high-quality drugs in place of low-quality drugs. Consumer welfare increased despite higher prices and a lower number of firms. We compare minimum quality standards with alternative designs of quality regulation, including quality disclosure.

papers.title: Too little too late? Nationwide carbon trading in China
papers.abstract: China launched a nationwide, rate-based carbon market in 2021. Covering the world’s top CO₂ emitter, compliance depends on the intensity of carbon emissions rather than an absolute cap. We draw on the theoretical literature of rate-based systems to provide the first empirical evidence on an early adopter. Using plant-level data from satellite imagery and machine learning methods, we find that high-efficiency power plants increased electricity generation and CO₂ emissions by approximately 5% relative to low-efficiency plants. Because its carbon market regulates nearly all coal plants in China, we focus on the differential responses by plant efficiency, finding no evidence of a differential reduction in emission intensity (though these estimates are imprecise). Relative to coal plants in Indonesia and the Philippines, which had no carbon market, China’s high-efficiency plants also increased emissions, while the estimate for its low-efficiency plants is small and insignificant. This pattern of responses suggests that emissions increases of high-efficiency plants exceeded substitution away from low-efficiency plants. Underscoring the production stimulus to more efficient Chinese plants, air quality worsened downwind of high efficiency plants relative to low-efficiency plants, compromising air quality in relatively clean areas of China. To curb the level of China’s carbon emissions and thereby slow climate change, benchmarks need to be tightened within the existing system or an alternative system adopted that does not simultaneously incentivize electricity production.

papers.title: The unseen pain of the Vietnam War: long-term effects of Agent Orange on labor market outcomes
papers.abstract: Abstract We examine the long-term labor market consequences of exposure to Agent Orange during the Vietnam War, focusing on cohorts whose childhoods overlapped the spraying period. Exploiting district-level variation in herbicide exposure intensity, we find exposed individuals attain lower levels of schooling and reduce their labor supply by 7% relative to the mean. Among individuals who remain in their birth provinces, labor income is reduced by 26.7%. We show that cognitive and physical health impairments do not fully explain the effects. Exposure also reduced household income and pushed individuals toward primary industries, away from wage employment. We further document intergenerational effects, as children of exposed parents exhibit lower educational attainment and reduced labor supply. These findings highlight the lasting and multigenerational economic costs of wartime chemical exposure.

papers.title: A Century and a Quarter of Stock Market Liquidity and Trading Costs
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT A widely cited working paper from the 2000s, now published (Jones, 2026), documents a substantial decline in trading costs and a positive relation between bid–ask spreads and excess returns from 1900 to 2000. We update the analysis and find that over the next quarter century, turnover surges, spreads decline sharply and subsequently cluster near zero, and excess returns become negatively related to spreads. Additional analysis attributes the reversal of the excess returns relation to distortions in the time‐series analysis created by the sudden reduction and clustering of spreads. We find similar distortions using the Amihud illiquidity measure and in simple cross‐sectional analyses, which suggest the effects we highlight might be pervasive.

papers.title: Consumer sophistication and firm strategy when social feedback is untrustworthy
Biodiversity risk premium
papers.abstract: We identify a biodiversity risk premium (BRP) in investment strategies designed to mitigate biodiversity risks. To capture this premium, we construct optimised portfolios by reweighting approximately 3,000 constituents of the MSCI All Country World Index, using their MSCI biodiversity risk scores as a key screening criterion. Analysing data from 2013 to 2023, we find that biodiversity-screened portfolios exhibit lower risk-adjusted returns compared to randomly selected portfolios. This suggests the presence of a biodiversity risk premium: screening at three different intensities reduces the maximum attainable Sharpe ratio by 1.19 % to 4.14 %, a return loss of 16 to 60 basis points per year, of which 1, 5, and 11 basis points per year are attributable to the biodiversity criterion itself rather than to the reduced universe size. Our findings provide valuable insights into the pricing dynamics of biodiversity risk, enhancing the understanding of how natural capital considerations impact financial markets and investment strategies.

papers.title: To Acquire or to Ally? Foreign Competition and Firm Boundary
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines how foreign competition influences firms’ external growth strategies. Exploiting staggered US import tariff reductions as a quasi‐natural experiment, we find that heightened competition leads firms to expand their use of strategic alliances. This pattern is more pronounced for firms with limited financial or operational flexibility, weaker competitive positions, and firms operating in low‐entry‐barrier industries. Under competitive pressure, firms predominantly form alliances with partners in the same industry, as well as with firms in high‐tech, business‐to‐consumer (B2C), and product‐differentiated sectors. In the long term, alliance‐active firms exhibit higher R&D intensity and patent outputs. Overall, the study highlights how domestic firms reshape their external growth choices, partner selection, and long‐term innovation outcomes in response to global competition shocks.

papers.title: Rhetorical Contests Over Environmental and Social Proposals in Proxy Statements
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Activists push firms to improve their environmental and social (ES) performance using shareholder proposals. These ES proposals threaten managerial legitimacy and control, so management argues against activists to deflect their threat. We quantitatively examine how activists and management use rhetorical strategies in proxy statements to persuade shareholders to vote for or against ES proposals. Drawing on Aristotle's On Rhetoric , we study how appeals to ethos , logos , and pathos persuade proxy advisors and shareholders. We utilize natural language processing to develop replicable measures for each type of appeal, which we use to examine 1708 ES shareholder proposals in 1055 proxy statements from 2007 to 2021. Management at firms with higher levels of insider control and block ownership uses less persuasive rhetoric. Rhetorical strategies by activists and management are associated with proxy advisor recommendations and shareholder votes that support their respective sides. Activist and management rhetoric affect votes incrementally to proxy advisors’ recommendations, suggesting that the contesting parties are able to influence individual investors through their rhetoric.

papers.title: Random Disclosure Costs: A Unified Theory of Disclosure
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT We propose a unified framework for a class of evidence games in which a sender, seeking to increase posterior expectations (e.g., a market price), chooses whether to reveal or withhold her information. Our model nests several classic models, including type‐dependent disclosure costs or benefits, uncertain information endowment, and the market for lemons. Frictions are captured as random disclosure costs that are privately known to the sender and noisily inferred by the receiver. We derive a simple characterization of the equilibrium and show that it features increasing disclosure for lower frictions or greater fundamental uncertainty. Further, with high uncertainty or low frictions, greater uncertainty about disclosure costs decreases the likelihood of disclosure. Positive costs do not necessarily rule out unraveling to full disclosure, especially when outcomes have heavy tails or when disclosure costs are not constant. Finally, we demonstrate that the model can be estimated with a simple probit, suggesting that cost uncertainty is descriptive of real‐world behavior.

papers.title: The Bank for International Settlements innovation hub: infrastructural power or innovation theatre?
papers.abstract: Financial technology (FinTech) is disruptive not only for banks and payment providers, but also for public authorities. Although the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) has produced extensive research on FinTech since 2000, it took on an experimental new role in 2019 with the launch of the BIS Innovation Hub. This hub brings together multidisciplinary teams of economists, computer scientists and design thinkers in seven centres across the world to develop FinTech prototypes, products and public goods. This article contributes to debates about the legitimacy of international financial institutions and the global governance of FinTech by asking why the BIS has reimagined itself as an innovator despite its limited experience of innovation. Through a mixed methods study, which includes a thematic analysis of 50 hub projects and case studies of Projects Nexus, mBridge and Genesis 1.0, it finds that the BIS has become an innovator to bolster its legitimacy and reassert greater public control over money and payments systems in the era of FinTech disruption. Even though its projects have struggled to achieve scale, the BIS has avoided the risk of innovation theatre and put itself at the centre of debates about infrastructural power in an era of rapid technological change.

papers.title: Competing Digital Money
papers.abstract: Abstract We study competition between two payment instruments: bank deposits and digital platform tokens. Using a Hotelling model that integrates the theory of two-sided markets and payment economics, we assess how this competition is affected by a public payment infrastructure that makes private payment instruments interoperable. We show that interoperability, whether implemented as a fast payment system (FPS) or a central bank digital currency (CBDC), may eliminate payment access exclusion and increase trade volumes and social welfare, but at the cost of some disintermediation. When new payment service providers (PSPs) enter and compete for consumers, they soften competition for merchants: incumbent intermediaries then charge merchants higher fees and earn higher profits. This contrasts with entry of PSPs on the merchant side, which disciplines incumbent fees instead.

papers.title: EXPRESS: The Collecting Mindset: Viewing Purchasing as Collecting Enhances Acquisition Experience and Product Desirability
papers.abstract: Abstract Managers often struggle to make acquisition processes engaging. While the dominant approach to reducing search costs has been to streamline the acquisition process, seven preregistered studies plus one supplemental study (N = 3,306) reveal an alternative pathway: Prompting consumers to view purchasing as “collecting” by positioning products as additions to their own collections, rather than as ad hoc purchases, improves consumers’ acquisition experience and increases product desirability. The authors demonstrate that activating such a collecting mindset shifts consumers’ psychological focus of the shopping process from securing a standalone product to instead investing in advancing their collection, thereby making them derive positive experience utility from the process, and in turn, elevating the desirability of the sought products. This research also offers practical guidance on how marketers can maximize the effectiveness of activating a collecting mindset: (i) encouraging active engagement in search, (ii) ensuring that search yields products that meaningfully advance the collection, and (iii) aligning the collection with an identity consumers value, as the effect may otherwise attenuate or reverse. These findings advance theory on everyday collecting and consumer search, and show how retailers and brands can strategically turn purchasing into a more positive acquisition experience that enhances product desirability.
