EXPRESS: Lifestage Bias: How the Visual Representation of Product Lifespan Shapes Replacement Timing
papers.abstract: To guide consumers’ decisions regarding when to replace products such as water filters, printer ink cartridges, and engine oil, companies often provide visualizations of the product’s lifespan. We document a lifestage bias in which representing a product’s lifespan with more (vs. fewer) visually distinct stages increases replacement intentions even when the product’s actual usage is the same. The effect emerges because a greater number of visually distinct stages leads consumers to mentally simulate previous use, thus enhancing the perception that a product has progressed through its lifespan and encouraging product replacement. Ten studies document lifestage bias and provide support (via mediation and moderation) for the underlying usage simulation mechanism. Notably, lifestage bias is eliminated when stages are represented non-visually or when stages are not visually distinct. Furthermore, lifestage bias is attenuated when product deterioration can be observed directly. These findings provide important insights into how consumers make product replacement timing decisions. Adjusting the number of distinct stages in product replacement guides offers firms and policymakers a practical tool to influence replacement timing—accelerating it when timely replacement is necessary for health, safety, or regulatory reasons (thus improving consumer welfare), or delaying it when items can be safely used for longer (thus reducing waste).

papers.title: So similar, yet so different: comparing the US GAAP and IFRS experience at eliciting greater transparency on pension asset disclosures
papers.abstract: Abstract We exploit two regulatory changes, one under US GAAP and the other under IFRS, that mandate improved disclosure of pension asset allocation. While the changes are otherwise similar, US GAAP retains the expected rate of return (“ERR”) on pension assets, which preparers can more easily manipulate if asset allocation remains opaque, while IFRS eliminates the ERR. We find that the IFRS standard improves pension asset transparency more than the US standard, which only mandates higher-quality disclosure without changing recognition or measurement and hence leaves unchanged preparers’ incentives to obfuscate. The US standard elicits a mixed response that reduces transparency in some respects. We isolate the relative deterioration in US firms’ transparency to firms with stronger incentives to inflate ERRs. Overall, our study highlights the potential for standard setters to learn from each other by comparing their regulatory experience on a specific accounting topic with clearly identifiable managerial incentives.

papers.title: Digital Inclusion in Corporate ESG Communication: A Text‐Mining Analysis of Global AI Companies
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT As digital platforms increasingly mediate nearly all human activities, artificial intelligence (AI) exhibits dual potential: It can enhance digital inclusion or intensify the exclusion and inequality faced by digitally vulnerable populations. This study examines digital inclusion and accessibility in the ESG reports of eight AI technology companies representing diverse business models. By applying a text‐mining method to analyze reports from these eight companies covering 2019–2024, we found that ESG disclosures are dominated by environmental topics. The coverage of digital inclusion and accessibility increased alongside major regulatory developments, suggesting a temporal alignment between disclosure practices and the evolving regulatory environment. Moreover, a comparative analysis with the WBA Digital Inclusion Score revealed selective disclosure and divergences between disclosure emphasis and external benchmark assessments across business models. This study recommends institutionalizing digital inclusion and accessibility as measurable ESG metrics to support practical assessment and industry‐level governance.

papers.title: Water as a Strategic Design Variable for Climate‐Resilient Urban Farming: Reconfiguring Sustainable Business Models Through the Water‐Enabled Resource Architecture Framework
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines how water sourcing and management can be embedded within urban farming business models to enhance environmental sustainability, climate resilience, and economic viability. It introduces the water‐enabled resource architecture (WERA) framework, which conceptualizes water as a strategic design variable capable of reshaping value proposition, governance arrangements, value capture logic, feasibility conditions, and performance indicators. The framework is illustrated through a comparative case study of an urban aquaponics installation in which two structurally equivalent systems operate under closely aligned conditions and different water sourcing strategies: centralized potable water supply and rainwater harvesting. Within the analyzed case, the decentralized configuration is associated with greater water autonomy and estimated operating‐cost reductions, while also redistributing organizational responsibilities and requiring additional infrastructure, treatment, and monitoring routines. WERA therefore provides an analytical lens for examining how water choices reshape governance, stakeholder value, cost‐risk mechanisms, and resource resilience within urban farming business models. It also clarifies how water choices reshape governance, stakeholder value, and cost‐risk mechanisms in urban systems.

papers.title: Sustainable Corporate Loans: A Systematic Literature Review and Future Research Agenda
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT This paper presents a systematic literature review of sustainable corporate loans (SCLs), including green loans and sustainability‐linked loans, to synthesise current academic knowledge and outline future research directions. Using a PRISMA protocol and a bibliometric analysis of 102 peer‐reviewed articles published in AJG‐ranked journals (3 and above) between January 2009 and May 2025, the review examines publication trends, theoretical perspectives, methodological approaches, thematic patterns and research gaps. The literature shows rapid growth after 2020, with substantial regional concentration in China, the United States and Europe. Stakeholder theory is the most frequently invoked explicit theoretical lens, although many studies do not anchor their analysis in a clearly stated theory. Quantitative designs prevail, but longitudinal, mixed‐method and experimental approaches remain scarce. Four main themes emerge: borrower ESG and financial outcomes, lender incentives and risk management, loan contract features, and macroeconomic implications. Key gaps relate to causal identification, ESG metric standardisation and borrower–lender dynamics in emerging markets.

papers.title: How Complementarities Affect Technological Innovation Within Platform‐Based Innovation Ecosystems: The Role of Orchestrators' Platform Capability and Interorganizational Trust
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Complementarities in Platform‐based Innovation Ecosystems (PIEs) are crucial for collaborative technological innovation (TECI), yet how they influence TECI remains underexplored. Therefore, by integrating Resource Dependence Theory and Dynamic Capabilities Theory, this study empirically examined the relationships between two key complementarities (supermodular and unique) and TECI. With a sample of 203 technology firms, this study demonstrates that: (a) supermodular complementarities are more strongly positively associated with TECI than unique ones; (b) orchestrators' platform capabilities and interorganizational trust significantly moderate these complementarities–TECI links, with moderating effects varying by complementarity type. Theoretically, this study advances literature on complementarities–TECI relationships in PIEs. Managerially, it provides practical insights into effectively managing complementarities for TECI performance.

papers.title: Promotion and prevention regulatory focus in equity crowdfunding reinvestment decisions
An integrative theoretical framework of strategic marketing solutions for resolving social dilemmas
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how marketing can help resolve firm-level social dilemmas. The authors synthesize insights from sociology, psychology, economics, political science, management and marketing to conceptualize firm-level marketing social dilemmas, organize marketing solution levers into an integrative taxonomy and develop a testable framework with antecedents, marketing solutions, boundary conditions, consequences and propositions. Design/methodology/approach The authors conduct a systematic review to identify core social-dilemma constructs and diagnostic attributes (e.g. observability, externality dispersion/reversibility, coordination/free-rider risk, short–long payoff gap). Building on this base, the authors propose an integrative taxonomy of marketing solutions − communication and norm activation, regulation, group-structure and governance and strategic marketing − and illustrate generalizability with four cases: climate change, pandemic, data privacy and DEI. The authors then develop an integrative framework and associated propositions. Findings The authors offer a firm-level conceptualization of social dilemmas that links diagnostic dilemma attributes to matched marketing solution bundles and specifies boundary conditions that shape effectiveness. The framework explains how marketing efforts translate antecedents into firm-level outcomes, while positioning employee-, consumer- and society-level consequences as broader downstream implications of firms’ efforts to resolve social dilemmas, yielding clear, mechanism-based propositions for explanation and prediction. Research limitations/implications Future research could expand on this research by empirically testing the proposed framework and exploring marketing solutions for resolving different social dilemmas. Practical implications This study offers actionable strategies for marketers and marketing to address social dilemmas, foster stakeholder relationships, enhance organizational outcomes and benefit society. Social implications Addressing firm-level social dilemmas through marketing activities fosters long-term societal benefits while enhancing firm performance. Originality/value This research advances the understanding of social dilemmas within the marketing domain through a novel framework and a taxonomy of marketing solutions that address firm-specific challenges. By bridging gaps across disciplines, it contributes foundations for innovative marketing strategies that can resolve complex social dilemmas.

papers.title: Public Interest Capacity: The Case of Direct File
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT This article describes the conditions for creating and undermining public interest capacity, that is, the ability of the state to generate public goods with widely distributed benefits. The creation and elimination of Direct File, a free, online public tax reporting system in the United States, offers an instrumental case. The creation of Direct File depended upon political commitment sufficient to overcome private interests: both the traditional dependence on private contractors to produce digital products, and the opposition of the private tax preparation industry which saw Direct File as a competitor. Political will was not enough: creating internal capacity in the form of skilled government tech teams who could build a quality digital product was also necessary. But without this political commitment in the Trump administration, which instead pursued downsizing and was receptive to the tax preparation industry arguments, both Direct File and the team that built it were eliminated.

papers.title: Partisan composition and public spending on adult education: An event study analysis using German county-level data (2008–2022)
papers.abstract: Political parties vary in their education policy preferences, with public spending on education serving as one indicator of these policy priorities. We hypothesise that centre-left parties in local government increase public spending on adult education. To test this, we analyse public data on expenditures for adult education at the local level and data on party participation in county and city councils in Germany (n = 390; N = 5534). Using the seat share and party affiliation of the head of the administration as measures of partisan influence, we employ two-way fixed-effects models and heterogeneity-robust difference-in-differences estimators to account for variation in treatment timing and duration of parties’ local government participation. The investigation covers the period from 2008 to 2022. For counties where centre-left parties hold a majority of seats, we observe a statistically significant positive effect, whereas where they have the head of administration the effect is not significant.

Unlocking the potential of nanocellulose: Promising substrate materials for electrocatalysts
papers.abstract: Nanocellulose as substrate materials have garnered considerable interest for developing high-performance carbon-based electrocatalysts toward hydrogen evolution and oxygen evolution/reduction reactions, due to their many advantages including unique fibrous nanoarchitecture, mass production capacity, environmental benignity, cost effectiveness and sustainability. However, the intricate relationships between structure, design and catalytic activity in nanocellulose-based electrocatalysts have yet to be comprehensively discussed and deciphered, which hinders their practical application and further development of nanocellulose-based electrocatalysts. Therefore, this review summarizes and analyzes the latest development for electrocatalysts integrated on nanocellulose substrate. Herein, the design and application of nanocellulose as substrate materials for electrocatalysts closely related to its structure characteristics and chemical properties are fully discussed, highlighting the unique merits of nanocellulose substrate in the field of electrocatalysis. Simultaneously, the commonality and individuality of nanocellulose categorized into three types with diverse structure properties are analyzed. Moreover, the viable optimization strategies for enhancing catalytic activity have been systematically explored based on the coupling of nanocellulose substrate and active sites, focusing on the core structure-performance relationship. Centering on these topics, the future research challenges and prospects for designing high-performance nanocellulose-based electrocatalysts is presented, aiming to pave the way for new research directions of this attractive field.

When heat hits: Short-run saving and withdrawal behavior among microfinance clients in Benin
papers.abstract: Increased access to finance is widely viewed as a key driver to increase adaptive capacity in response to climate change. However, apart from limited studies on borrowing behavior, little is known about how exposure to extreme heat impacts microfinance clients’ financial behavior. This study addresses this gap by investigating the short-run effects of unusual heat on microfinance clients’ saving and withdrawal behavior. In a case study, it combines geo-located temperature data with a unique dataset of around 50,000 clients of a leading Microfinance Institution (MFI) in Benin. Applying two-way fixed effects, seemingly unrelated regression, and ordinary least square models, the study finds that exposure to extreme heat is heterogeneously associated with microfinance clients’ financial behavior. Specifically, non-agricultural clients show suggestive evidence for the accumulation of precautionary savings after extreme heat days in the precedent quarter, while agricultural clients statistically significantly reduce their savings following exposure to extreme heat in the precedent quarter. Microfinance clients increase their withdrawals when exposed to extreme heat within the precedent quarter, but the association is not robust to agricultural clients’ withdrawals in response to an increase in annual extreme heat days. Addressing the heterogeneous financial responses across different clients to extreme heat consequently requires explicit policy attention. Our findings contribute to a better understanding of the impact of extreme weather events on individual economic outcomes, how financial behavior relates to weather risk, and how microfinance clients respond to shocks.

papers.title: Can green innovations enhance competitive advantage?
papers.abstract: Abstract Sustainable New Product Introductions (SNPIs) enable firms to meet consumers’ increasing demand for sustainable options while addressing rising expectations for corporate environmental responsibility. This study demonstrates that SNPIs can also strengthen brands by enhancing brand equity. Drawing on signaling theory, we propose that SNPIs serve as product-based sustainability signals that enhance brand equity by generating social goodwill. A staggered event study of the initial launch of a sustainable product line by a major laundry detergent brand shows that SNPIs can increase parent-brand equity. A complementary analysis of subsequent SNPIs across 15 leading brands in 12 retail chains reveals that this effect is moderated by parent firms' ethical reputation and retail chains' sustainable assortment share. These findings advance our understanding of whether and under what conditions sustainable products serve as credible signals of environmental responsibility and enhance brand equity.

Semantic–geography integrated spatiotemporal safety mapping for urban low-altitude airspace environments
papers.abstract: Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) safety is becoming increasingly critical as UAV operations are integrated into urban service and transportation systems, creating an urgent need for risk representations that can support refined low-altitude airspace management. Existing urban safety maps are still mainly expressed as two-dimensional or height stratified representations, which cannot capture the continuous variation of risk with altitude and therefore remain inadequate for continuous low-altitude flight scenarios. This paper develops a continuous three-dimensional spatiotemporal safety mapping framework for urban low-altitude environments. The framework integrates semantic information, digital surface model (DSM) and digital terrain model (DTM) derived morphology, pedestrian related exposure, and meteorological conditions within a unified geo-referenced support. A vertical continuous interpolation function is introduced to transform discrete risk representations into a continuous three-dimensional spatiotemporal risk field, thereby enabling continuous risk analysis across space, altitude, and time. Experiments in a real urban scene show that risk values vary significantly across different regions, time periods, and scene conditions, and that the resulting field reveals clear vertical differentiation and temporal redistribution patterns that conventional planar safety maps cannot represent consistently. These findings show that the proposed reusable continuous three-dimensional and time varying risk model offers a practical basis for refined low-altitude airspace management and has the potential to support future high density UAV operations.

papers.title: Balancing adversariality and naturalness in autonomous vehicle testing scenario generation via multi-objective reinforcement learning
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL)-based adversarial scenario generation through dynamic agent–environment interactions has emerged as a promising approach for accelerating autonomous vehicle (AV) testing. However, existing RL approaches struggle to balance adversariality and naturalness because naturalistic driving behaviors avoid risk whereas adversarial behaviors intentionally induce it. The reward-driven nature of RL can further lead to objective polarization under linearly weighted rewards, resulting in scenarios biased toward a limited range of adversariality–naturalness trade-offs. This study proposes a preference-conditioned safety–critical scenario generation framework based on multi-policy multi-objective reinforcement learning (MORL), which models adversariality and naturalness as separate components of a vectorized reward and jointly optimizes them across the preference space. The adversariality reward incorporates risk–liability screening to filter two predefined invalid-risk patterns, while the naturalness penalty leverages a computationally efficient shadow-mode evaluation to provide real-time behavioral-deviation feedback relative to a reference driving policy. Envelope Q-learning is adopted to learn multiple preference-conditioned policies and is enhanced by a Kullback–Leibler divergence–based policy differentiation mechanism that mitigates policy mode collapse and encourages diverse behavioral evolution. Experiments in highway car-following and lane-changing environments show improvements in the evaluated scenario-quality and diversity metrics over the RL baselines. Compared with multi-round linearly weighted RL, the proposed method achieves 2.70 times the Pareto-front hypervolume, increases the valid safety–critical scenario success rate from 4.4% to 14.6%, and achieves 2.83 times the feature-space coverage volume. The results support the framework’s ability to generate diverse safety–critical scenarios across testing preferences within the studied highway operational design domain.

papers.title: Role-Playing as Immigrants for Learning to Trust: Constructing a Theory of Experiential Contact
papers.abstract: This research examined whether a computer-based role-playing game in which participants created immigrant characters from Mexico and took them through the process of naturalizing to the United States could be used to promote trust. A posttest-only experiment with a control group was conducted in Fall 2024 ( N = 98). Results indicate that participants who played the game had significantly higher levels of trust in immigrants in general, as well as those from Mexico, Central/South America, India, China, and the Middle East specifically, compared to the control condition. Parasocial connections to characters in game-based settings strengthened the effect of role-playing on trusting immigrants from Mexico. Half of the role-playing participants also saw a thank-you video from an outgroup representative, as a form of mediated indirect contact. The video condition appeared to drive the interaction between role-playing and sensing parasocial connections to characters in predicting Mexican immigrant trust. Results demonstrate the potential for role-playing games to foster trust between groups who may struggle to interact in person, along with the additive effect of mediated indirect contact at high levels of parasocial connection.

A broad review of metal/metal oxide based integrated thermal, biochemical and electrochemical systems for waste into hydrogen conversion
papers.abstract: Global efforts to turn waste into useful fuels have accelerated due to the growing demand for clean and sustainable energy, with hydrogen emerging as a vital energy carrier. Metals and metal oxides have shown remarkable promise as catalysts and functional elements in a variety of Waste-to-Hydrogen (WtH) pathways among the materials studied. The functions and mechanisms of metals and metal oxides in the three main processes of hydrogen generation via thermal, biochemical, and electrochemical conversion are critically examined in this review. Metal oxides aid in cracking, reforming, and tar reduction in thermal pathways like pyrolysis and gasification, increasing hydrogen yields and lowering carbon emissions. Metal oxide additives enhance microbial activity and electron transfer efficiency, which promotes the production of biohydrogen in biochemical processes, especially anaerobic digestion and dark fermentation. Metal and metal oxide-based catalysts are essential for enhancing electrocatalytic activity, stability, and overall system efficiency in electrochemical systems, such as water electrolysis and microbial electrolysis cells. Recent developments in hybrid catalyst systems, process integration techniques, and nanostructured and doped metal oxides are also covered in this review. The three WtH approaches are compared, with important considerations like economic viability, scalability, environmental impact, and energy efficiency assessed. Additionally, the incorporation of WtH technologies with carbon capture and circular economy principles is explored. By addressing current challenges and identifying future research directions, this review underscores the transformative potential of metal/metal oxides in advancing sustainable hydrogen production from waste resources.

papers.title: Comparative review of multi-energy systems modeling tools for scenario analysis toward climate neutrality: Case studies, achievements, and challenges
papers.abstract: Climate-neutrality planning requires modeling tools that connect long-term investment, multi-sector demand and emissions, power-system operation, and grid-security assessment. This structured review examines six widely used platforms such as PyPSA, Julia/JuMP, GAMS, TIMES, DIgSILENT PowerFactory, and LEAP for large-scale multi-energy-system analysis. Based on 100 cited sources, the platforms are qualitatively compared in terms of temporal and geographical resolution, optimization structure, data requirements, sector coverage, solver flexibility, and application domains. Kazakhstan's coal phase-down and renewable-energy expansion toward 2060 provide the practical context for discussing their suitability and complementarity. The review demonstrates that no single platform can fully represent all planning, operational, environmental, and engineering aspects of a climate-neutral energy system. TIMES and LEAP are particularly suitable for long-term demand, policy, and emissions scenarios; PyPSA, Julia/JuMP, and GAMS support investment and dispatch optimization with different levels of flexibility and transparency; and DIgSILENT PowerFactory provides detailed power-flow, contingency, protection, and dynamic-security analysis. The findings support a staged modeling workflow in which long-term transition pathways are linked to network-constrained optimization and subsequent engineering validation. This application-oriented comparison clarifies the respective strengths and limitations of the reviewed tools and provides guidance for selecting complementary platforms for large-scale energy-transition studies.

papers.title: Battery–hydrogen storage transition in a grid-connected PV prosumer: A self-sufficiency threshold analysis under weather variability and techno-economic sensitivity
The role of remoteness and competition on Australian mining costs
papers.abstract: Remoteness from major urban centers strongly correlates with increased costs in Australian construction projects and is a key consideration when estimating the cost of regional energy developments. This is a concern for mine planning as mining activities often occur in remote regions. However, key differences between mining and construction suggest that remoteness may not affect different industries in the same way. Mining has a long history of operations in regional Australia and practices adapted to these conditions, which may impact the costs of remote operations. In this paper, we consider what extent remoteness determines mining and processing costs for sites across Australia. The analysis reveals that while there may be some increase in on-site mining costs due to remoteness, these trends are substantially weaker than those observed in the construction industry, and are minor compared to other variations in costs. The analysis also fails to demonstrate a clear correlation between remoteness and on-site mineral processing costs. Instead, increased competition between mining companies for labor and equipment may be a greater determinant of regional variations in mining and processing costs. Conversely remoteness is found to correlate strongly with increased infrastructure and logistical requirements, such as transportation and power transmission. This points to a potential strategy to reduce the costs of remote operations through targeted development of supporting infrastructure.

papers.title: Adsorption-based compressed CO2 energy storage system using commercial adsorbent pellets: Experimental screening and thermodynamic-economic assessment
papers.abstract: Adsorption-based compressed CO 2 energy storage (AB-CCES) offers a promising route for compact low-pressure CO 2 storage, however, the selection of optimal adsorbents for practical applications remains uncertain and requires further investigation. This study systematically screened five commercial adsorbent pellets and evaluated the performance of the corresponding AB-CCES system by integrating material characterization, CO 2 adsorption-desorption experiments, ad-desorption kinetics, thermodynamic simulation, and techno-economic analysis. Zeolite 4A emerged as the most promising candidate because it combined high CO 2 uptake with favorable kinetics, regenerability, and cyclic stability under the special conditions of AB-CCES. The experimentally derived adsorption model was incorporated into the system simulation, demonstrating a substantial reduction in low-pressure tank volume and an approximately 36 times increase in volumetric energy density over conventional CCES while maintaining competitive energy and exergy efficiencies. Lower adsorption temperatures could reduce the storage-tank volume and increased energy density, whereas higher desorption temperatures enhance power output but reduce exergy efficiency. Further techno-economic analysis indicates that AB-CCES achieves lower equipment-related and land-related costs, resulting in a lower LCOE value of 0.1237 $/kWh and a dynamic payback period of approximately 11.2 years. Economic sensitivity analysis further suggests that the desorption temperature should be maintained at 200-250 °C to balance thermodynamic performance and cost-effectiveness.

papers.title: Pricing RMB Policy Risk: Evidence From Onshore and Offshore FX Option Markets
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT This paper examines how onshore and offshore RMB option markets price potential shifts in China's RMB exchange rate regime. We calibrate a regime‐switching option pricing model to USD/CNY and USD/CNH options to recover daily risk‐neutral parameters summarizing the pricing of regime‐switching risk, including the risk‐neutral switching probability, the size of a possible RMB realignment, and exchange‐rate volatility under a possible new regime. This allows us to quantify and compare policy‐related tail‐risk pricing embedded in option prices over the past decade. The results show that CNH options price larger potential RMB devaluations and higher exchange‐rate volatility under a possible new regime than CNY options, especially during stress periods, whereas CNY options imply higher risk‐neutral switching probabilities. An event study around the introduction of the countercyclical factor further shows that CNY and CNH option‐implied risk‐neutral distributions evolved differently before and after the policy announcement. These findings point to segmented risk‐neutral pricing of RMB policy‐related risk across onshore and offshore option markets.

papers.title: The Search for a Universal ESG–FDI Relationship: Why Development and Investment Context Matter
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT The empirical literature has not established a consistent relationship between environmental, social, and governance (ESG) performance and foreign direct investment (FDI). One reason may be that the association varies with countries' level of development and the structure of their investment flows. This study examines this possibility using a balanced panel of 10 upper‐middle‐income and 10 high‐income economies over the period 2002–2023. The baseline estimates are obtained from country fixed‐effects models with Driscoll–Kraay standard errors and are supplemented by lagged and dynamic specifications, pillar‐level analyses, nonlinear models, income–group interactions, and country‐level sensitivity checks. The results point to a negative and statistically significant association between ESG performance and FDI inflows in upper‐middle‐income economies, and this finding is relatively stable across alternative specifications. For high‐income economies, however, the estimates are considerably more sensitive to the composition of the sample. The ESG dimensions also exhibit distinct patterns across the two income groups, suggesting that the aggregate ESG measure masks important underlying heterogeneity. The interaction estimates provide further evidence of differences in the ESG–FDI slope across income groups, although both the magnitude and direction of this difference are sensitive to the inclusion of the Netherlands. Once the Netherlands is excluded, the estimated difference in slopes reverses, and the implied ESG coefficient for the high‐income group is no longer statistically significant. A similar sensitivity is observed in the linear and nonlinear specifications, indicating that the Netherlands plays an unusually influential role in the high‐income results, plausibly reflecting its position in international investment and financial‐routing networks. Taken as a whole, the findings suggest that the ESG–FDI relationship is better understood as context‐dependent rather than universal. They also underscore the importance of distinguishing robustness across model specifications from robustness to sample composition, particularly when aggregate FDI data include economies with substantial conduit investment activity.

papers.title: Circular Transformation in the Silk Sector: A Fuzzy Delphi–DEMATEL Analysis of Critical Factors
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT The circular transformation in the silk industry is crucial for enhancing resource efficiency and minimizing waste. Despite growing interest in circularity within the textile sector, the silk industry remains underexplored. This study addresses this gap by systematically assessing the barriers and enablers influencing circular economy adoption in silk. A two‐stage methodology was applied. First, a comprehensive literature review combined with expert input identified key factors, which were then validated using the fuzzy Delphi method (FDM) with 16 experts from industry and academia, resulting in nine barriers and 12 enablers. Next, the Decision‐Making Trial and Evaluation Laboratory (DEMATEL) technique examined the prominence and causal relationships among these factors. Results indicate that lack of policy support from fashion brands, ineffective planning, and inadequate communication are the most significant barriers, while limited consumer awareness and high technology costs strongly influence other barriers. Key enablers include upcycling business models, rediscovery of silk knowledge, and waste material recovery. Resource efficiency culture, design for longevity, and traditional expertise act as causal drivers. The study provides actionable guidance for managers, policymakers, and researchers, offering practical and theoretical insights to advance circularity in silk.

papers.title: How Does Entrepreneurial Alertness Lead to Green Product Innovation in Companies? The Roles of Organizational Unlearning and Diversity Climate
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Green product innovation is crucial for achieving a competitive edge during the transition toward carbon neutrality. Existing studies have extensively emphasized the roles of environmental regulations, customer demand, and leadership; however, the importance of entrepreneurial alertness in green opportunity identification remains underexplored. Drawing on information processing theory and the knowledge‐based view, this study examines the relationship between entrepreneurial alertness and green product innovation by developing a theoretical model that incorporates the mediating role of organizational unlearning and the moderating influence of diversity climate. Using a multisource survey design, we collected data from 339 firms in East China. The empirical findings indicate that entrepreneurial alertness is positively associated with green product innovation via organizational unlearning, and this indirect relationship is stronger when diversity climate is supportive. This study delineates the cognitive pathway and contextual contingencies that link entrepreneurial alertness to green product innovation, providing theoretical insights into how firms can leverage entrepreneurial alertness within a supportive diversity climate to foster eco‐innovation.

papers.title: Frugal Innovation as an Environmentally Oriented Business Strategy: The Roles of Servant Leadership and Organizational Learning Capability
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines how firms develop frugal innovation as an environmentally oriented business strategy that combines competitiveness with lower resource intensity. Drawing on sustainable business strategy research and using degrowth as an interpretive lens rather than a causal theory, we conceptualize frugal innovation as an organizational outcome centered on core functionalities, substantial cost reduction, and shared sustainable engagement. We test the roles of servant leadership and organizational learning capability using survey data from 450 manufacturing firms in Santa Catarina, Brazil. The results show that both servant leadership and organizational learning capability are positively associated with frugal innovation, with organizational learning capability exerting the stronger direct effect. Organizational learning capability also mediates the servant leadership–frugal innovation relationship, indicating that leadership also contributes to frugal innovation when relational conditions are translated into learning routines such as experimentation, dialogue, and participative decision‐making. Multi‐group analysis indicates that the structural relationships predicting frugal innovation are broadly stable across technological intensity levels, although the servant leadership–organizational learning capability link is stronger in medium to medium‐high technology firms. The study advances research on business strategy and the environment by empirically specifying organizational learning capability as a mediating mechanism linking servant leadership to frugal innovation. It also examines the stability of these relationships across technological intensity groups in an emerging‐economy manufacturing context.

papers.title: Strategic Environmental Sustainability Decisions Under a Digital Twin–Based Optimization Framework
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Increasing environmental requirements and the complexity of strategic decision‐making have challenged organizations to balance economic performance and environmental sustainability. This study presents an integrated framework based on digital twin and multi‐objective optimization, in which digital twin is directly integrated with the optimization model as a scenario‐based layer for generating and dynamically updating decision‐making conditions. The research data were extracted from real information of a manufacturing organization and, after refining and calibration, were supplemented with scenarios generated in the digital twin environment to enable the analysis of strategic decisions under different conditions. The results showed that with the increase in the intensity of environmental policies, the optimal level of green investment increased from 0.32 to 0.61, and at the same time, the environmental impact decreased from 61.7 to 35.2. Also, scenario‐based analyses, sensitivity analysis, temporal stability assessment, and statistical validation showed that the proposed framework is capable of extracting balanced, stable, and reliable solutions for strategic decision‐making. The main innovation of the research is in transforming the digital twin from a purely operational and simulation tool to an active mechanism for supporting scenario‐based strategic decision‐making; an approach that can strengthen the link between advanced quantitative analytics and sustainable decision‐making in industrial environments.

papers.title: Co‐Creating Circular Pathways in the Fashion Industry: A Participatory System Dynamics Perspective
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Circular economy transitions in the fashion industry are frequently constrained not by a lack of reinforcing drivers but by endogenous feedback structures that limit growth as systems expand. Focusing on the Brazil context, this study identifies the dominant feedback archetypes governing circular transitions across four distinct socio‐technical contexts, namely, fashion brands, consumers, micro‐businesses, and digital circular platforms and offers an explanation, grounded in a participatory system dynamics approach, for why circular initiatives stall or progress. A participatory approach was adopted, combining co‐created causal loop diagrams, group model building, and backcasting workshops targeting a shared 2030 circular economy scenario, actively engaging 20 heterogeneous stakeholders including fashion brands, waste picker cooperatives, local government officials, and academics. Four causal loop diagrams were developed and validated through recorded and transcribed stakeholder interviews. The results identify a dominant limits to growth archetype across all four contexts, each driven by a distinct limiting mechanism: margin erosion in fashion brands, price‐mediated adoption constraints in consumer markets, infrastructure and workforce deficits in micro‐business recycling systems, and a dual operational and financial constraint in digital circular platforms. By structurally mapping reinforcing drivers, limiting feedbacks, and generic solutions onto four empirically grounded causal loop diagrams, this study contributes to the understanding of circular economy transitions as feedback‐driven processes and offers context‐specific leverage points for firms, cooperatives, and policymakers seeking to design more durable and coordinated circular strategies in comparable settings.

Board sustainability expertise: how shareholder and employee representatives shape supervisory board practice in codetermined German firms
papers.abstract: Purpose This paper asks how sustainability expertise is constructed, distributed across shareholder and employee representatives and translated into influence through the governance channels of parity codetermined supervisory boards in German listed corporations, as European sustainability regulation and scrutiny intensify. Design/methodology/approach Thirty-six semi-structured interviews with supervisory board members in parity codetermined listed corporations are analysed abductively through an integrated resource dependence and resource-based perspective. The analysis treats the two theories as jointly explaining how externally oriented resource dependencies and internally grounded capabilities are combined within board processes, tracing how directors construct sustainability expertise, how it is allocated across shareholder and employee benches, and how it becomes consequential through formal and informal governance channels. Findings Sustainability expertise is constructed less as an individual credential than as a collectively developed board capability combining regulatory literacy with operational understanding. Shareholder representatives tend to supply externally oriented regulatory and capital-market knowledge, whereas employee representatives contribute firm- and workforce-grounded implementation insight and longer time horizons. Codetermination thereby broadens the board's resource base but holds these logics in productive tension. Expertise becomes influential only when channelled through committee mandates, agenda-setting authority and informal cross-bench coordination. Boards vary, however, in whether these channels confine expertise to defensible compliance or open it to strategic integration. Research limitations/implications The study is context-specific to large German parity codetermined listed corporations with a mandatory two-tier system. Because strategic sustainability integration unfolds over longer time horizons than a single interview phase can capture, future longitudinal research could trace how the governance channels identified here shape integration over time and across corporate governance regimes. Originality/value This paper opens the boardroom black box by theorising sustainability expertise as a dynamic, collective board capability and by specifying the mechanisms through which it is constructed, reconciled across competing resource logics and mobilised into influence. It shows how codetermination, by combining distinct shareholder and employee resource bases, conditions whose expertise counts and how it is converted into influence.

papers.title: Reply to Kettl: The Field of Public Administration in America and an Unpreparedness of Its Own Making?
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT This Reply suggests the sub‐field of U.S.‐specific public administration is under‐prepared to address democratic deconsolidation given its multi‐decade distance from the disciplines of comparative politics and political economy and from the sub‐fields of comparative and development public administration. The narrowness of what is understand as “good” public administration by U.S.‐based scholars has largely excluded cross‐disciplinary and non‐U.S. intellectual histories which, if understood, would have deepened sub‐field intellectual depth and breadth but also, better prepared the sub‐field for America's current administrative state. This Reply suggests the value of drawing upon post‐WWII administration‐linked trends in other disciplines and upon links between administration and prior democratic deconsolidations (the U.S. is not unique). This includes the sub‐field's historical reluctance to research existential insecurity, intolerance (beyond social inequity), the role of democratic restraint, the role of crisis (or lack of) in democratic deconsolidation, and theories of democracy‐to‐autocracy and autocracy‐to‐democracy.

papers.title: From Judicial Regulation to Judicial Governance: Locating the Courts on the Map of Social Ordering
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Courts have long been recognized as venues of social control and policymaking. The rise of regulatory capitalism suggests reconsidering the judiciary in regulatory terms, notably through work that casts courts as regulators. This article argues, however, that styling courts as regulators is both analytically and normatively deficient: it obscures the distinctive function of courts and their contribution to social ordering. At the same time, judicial decision‐making plainly exhibits a regulatory dimension. Yet rather than stretching the concept of regulation, this article proposes to capture this dimension through governance theory. On this theoretical foundation, the article outlines a model of judicial governance that elucidates how social ordering emerges from adjudication and how it unfolds over time. In particular, the model highlights the implications of judicial decision‐making for private ordering and draws attention to processes of intermediation through lawyers, media, and advanced digital technologies. It thus opens a set of analytically structured research questions and complements them with a methodological framework to orient future work on judicial governance.

papers.title: Linkage as Leverage: OECD Accession as an Informal and Indirect Graduation Mechanism in the International Climate Regime
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT As global power is shifting, international institutions face a challenge: established powers will often request that rising powers no longer continue to benefit from their status as “developing countries”. Yet only a few institutions have formal rules in place to organize this transition. As a result, tracing the informal pathways through which change occurs becomes relevant. In this article, we study one such mechanism in the international climate regime. In that regime, the so‐called Annex I countries agreed “to take the lead” in reducing greenhouse gas emissions while developing countries remained exempt from a similar obligation. Because Annex I was hard to amend, the regime has frequently been said to lack a graduation mechanism. Yet, once we take the interaction between the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) and its broader institutional environment into account, the process of acceding to the Organization for Economic Co‐operation and Development (OECD) comes into view as an indirect and informal graduation mechanism. We examine the effects and limitations of this mechanism in relation to the accession processes of Mexico (1994), South Korea (1996), and Chile (2010). Our analysis leads to two main results. First, we show that a graduation mechanism based on “linkage as leverage” existed. Second, we sketch three distinct causal pathways that lead to different degrees of graduation in each case. Overall, our study suggests that graduation based on “linkage as leverage” depends on three conditions. First, states needed to activate the mechanism in each case. Second, domestic support was required to sustain graduation. And third, major emitters had to develop an interest in joining a club organization that could exercise leverage.

Citizen science-based mapping of radiofrequency electromagnetic field exposure in Europe: A proof-of-concept validation study
papers.abstract: Characterising population-level radiofrequency electromagnetic field (RF-EMF) exposure from mobile telecommunications networks at fine spatial resolution has been limited by the cost and scale of conventional measurement methods. The ETAIN 5G Scientist app, developed within the ETAIN (Exposure To electromAgnetic fIelds and plaNetary health) project uses citizen science smartphone data to produce calibrated RF-EMF exposure maps for 4G/5G networks at 25 x 25 m 2 spatial resolution across Europe. As of 2026, the app had collected over 19 million measurements globally. We conducted a proof-of-concept validation of these exposure maps in two European cities with contrasting urban and network characteristics: Utrecht (Netherlands) and Basel (Switzerland). Walking measurement campaigns used the ETAIN app installed on smartphones and the ExpoM-RF4 reference exposimeter carried simultaneously in a backpack. App-derived exposure estimates were compared with spatiotemporally matched reference measurements at the grid-cell level. Validation was performed separately for 4G Long-Term Evolution (LTE) and combined 4G LTE and 5G New Radio (NR) environmental exposure estimates. 4G LTE exposure estimates correlated strongly with measured exposure in both Utrecht ( r s = 0.87, 95% CI: 0.80-0.91, N = 127) and Basel ( r s = 0.71, 95% CI: 0.63-0.78, N = 214; both p < 0.001). The combined 4G LTE and 5G NR exposure estimates correlated strongly in Utrecht ( r s = 0.88, 95% CI: 0.81-0.92; 19.7% of grid cells with 5G NR detection) but showed moderate correlation in Basel ( r s = 0.41, 95% CI: 0.29-0.53; 45.3% of grid cells with 5G NR detection). Sensitivity analyses showed map reliability stabilised at five or more observations per grid cell and improved when data from two network operators were combined. These results demonstrate that the ETAIN 5G Scientist application can produce validated, spatially continuous RF-EMF exposure maps at scale. The approach is well suited for characterising exposure trends as mobile networks continue to evolve.

papers.title: Plant growth improvement and microbial community reorganization are decoupled during restoration of trampled urban forest soil
papers.abstract: A key question in trampled urban forests is whether improved understory plant growth is accompanied by corresponding changes in the belowground microbial community. We compared ploughing, Bacillus thuringiensis NL-11 inoculation, biochar addition, and NL-11 plus biochar co-application to determine whether improved plant growth was accompanied by parallel bacterial and fungal responses in a trampled Ophiopogon japonicus system. At the one-year sampling, NL-11 and co-application both showed improved plant growth, but their soil and microbial responses differed. NL-11 increased nitrate nitrogen and urease activity. Co-application increased sucrase and urease activities but reduced available phosphorus, available potassium, and average root diameter, showing that improved plant growth under co-application was not accompanied by uniformly greater soil nutrient availability. Relative to ploughing, NL-11 and co-application reduced bacterial richness and Shannon diversity, whereas fungal ACE, Chao1, and Shannon indices did not differ significantly among treatments. Bacterial and fungal community composition differed overall among treatments. Network and assembly analyses showed clear bacterial-fungal asymmetry. Among the restoration treatments, the NL-11 bacterial network descriptively had the largest number of edges and the highest average degree and density, and the NL-11 fungal network descriptively had the largest numbers of nodes and edges. Relative to the ploughing procedural control, NL-11 showed higher bacterial and fungal positive cohesion, whereas biochar showed lower bacterial positive cohesion. iCAMP showed that homogeneous selection was the largest observed bacterial assembly component across all five groups, whereas drift or undominated processes were the largest fungal component; the focused NL-11-versus-ploughing bacterial contrasts did not remain significant after multiple-testing correction. NL-11 and co-application improved O. japonicus growth one year after transplanting, with distinct changes in soil nutrient availability and bacterial and fungal communities.

papers.title: From flood hazard to governable climate risk: An integrated framework for adaptive flood governance and the Flood Resilience and Sustainability Index (FRSI)
papers.abstract: Climate change, urban expansion and ecosystem degradation are intensifying flood-risk management challenges worldwide. However, mitigation and recovery approaches remain fragmented across engineering, community adaptation, technology, governance and finance, limiting integrated assessment of resilience and sustainability. This study examines the reported effectiveness and implementation constraints of flood mitigation and recovery strategies, their integration of sustainability principles, and their implications for adaptive governance. A PRISMA-guided systematic review of 62 studies combines thematic synthesis, comparative framework analysis and semi-quantitative evidence mapping. Strategies are compared across cases using reported effectiveness, implementation cost and complexity, scalability, and sustainability contributions. Standardised evidence-mapping scores support contextual interpretation rather than pooled effect estimates or universal rankings. The synthesis identifies three recurring patterns. First, hybrid approaches combine engineered protection, ecological buffering, early warning and community preparedness, with outcomes dependent on local conditions, maintenance and institutional capacity. Second, fragmented responsibilities, weak enforcement, financing constraints and limited community participation impede implementation and recovery. Third, existing assessment frameworks provide incomplete integration of physical, social, ecological, technological, institutional and financial dimensions. These findings inform the proposed Flood Resilience and Sustainability Index (FRSI), a conceptual framework comprising seven domains: hazard and exposure, vulnerability and equity, infrastructure resilience, ecological and nature-based resilience, governance capacity, technological readiness, and recovery-financial capacity. Its contribution lies in organizing these interdependent domains within a common structure for future resilience assessment and policy prioritization; operationalisation and empirical validation remain necessary. The synthesis supports coordinated institutional responsibilities, enforceable risk-sensitive land-use planning, sustained investment in complementary structural and nature-based measures, and equitable access to preparedness and recovery finance. These priorities connect flood-risk reduction with inclusive recovery and long-term adaptation.

papers.title: Comparative study on carbon emissions based on scenario uncertainty analysis: A case of asphalt and composite pavements construction in south China
papers.abstract: To improve the accuracy of carbon emission accounting results during the construction of asphalt pavement and composite pavement, and clarify the differences in their carbon emission levels during the construction stage, this study developed a comparative life cycle assessment model based on scenario uncertainty analysis. The model identifies influential inputs through sensitivity analysis and evaluates them using a Pedigree Matrix to obtain data quality scores. It quantifies the uncertainty of influential inputs by combining the transformation relationship between quality scores and distribution functions. Based on Monte Carlo simulation, uncertainties are propagated from influential inputs to random results. Meanwhile, the impact of model uncertainties caused by different transformation relationships and distribution function selections on random results is considered. Taking a highway construction project in South China, this study verifies the proposed model. Comprehensive analysis of extensive simulation results across all scenarios shows that the carbon emission level of asphalt pavement construction is relatively lower: the average global warming potential of composite pavement is approximately 1.65 times that of asphalt pavement, with a maximum global warming potential ranging from 1.84 to 2.13 times that of asphalt pavement. Additionally, the global warming potential uncertainty of composite pavement is relatively higher. This work further establishes selection criteria of transformation methods and distribution functions for diverse data quality conditions. The research findings provide a comprehensive theoretical basis for improving the quality of accounting results, and provide methodological support for pavement life cycle assessment uncertainty analysis amid data scarcity. The model proposed in this study can also be applied to compare the carbon emission levels of other pavement systems.

papers.title: Variable response in riverine nitrogen exports to long-term temporal changes in watershed inputs
papers.abstract: Aquatic nitrogen (N) pollution is a global problem, and understanding where best to implement mitigation strategies to reduce transfers from land to water is becoming increasingly urgent. Watershed nutrient budgets, using commonly available census data, can successfully predict riverine export spatially, albeit with variation related to fractional export. Furthermore, when using long-term data, watershed input-export trajectories vary and can be decoupled. Quantifying which drivers influence fractional export among trajectory types has yet to be explored. Here, we quantified the input-export trajectories of 33 subwatersheds (>25 years) in the St. Lawrence River, Québec, Canada, and assessed how fractional export was associated with land use, climate, and landscape features per trajectory type. Fractional N export ranged from 0.12 to 0.77 (median 0.29) and increased in many subwatersheds with higher input intensities. Annual runoff was associated with fractional export in watersheds with tracking input-export trajectories, and in those where N inputs decreased then increased overtime (nonlinear) while export was stable or increasing. However, shifts in N input components were also associated with fractional export, including in watersheds with decreasing input-increasing export trajectories often associated with legacy N. Higher fractional export was also associated with the runoff ratio in some trajectories likely through increased hydroconnectivity whereas lentification by lakes and dams reduced it in others. Our results suggest that beyond reducing total N inputs, understanding shifts toward leakier N input components as well as considering individual watershed features that govern N transport and retention are also required to minimise aquatic pollution.

papers.title: Challenges and strategies for dredged sediment decision management in Venice lagoon (Italy)
papers.abstract: This study presents the results of extensive sediment characterization campaigns conducted in 2024-2025 on more than 400 sediment cores collected across the Venice Lagoon, yielding approximately 1400 samples analyzed for chemical contamination and ecotoxicity. Investigated sediments presented exceedances of the protective screening values defined by the Italian legislation for metals (in particular Cd, Hg and Zn) and for HCB, PCDD/F and PCB; embryotoxicity test (P. lividus) showed a more widespread and extensive toxicity than the bioassays evaluating effects on bioluminescence (A. fischeri) and on algal growth (P. tricornutum) and represented therefore the main driver in the overall sediment classification. The dataset was used to test and calibrate the new classification tools recently set (2023) by the Italian legislation to regulate dredged sediment management in the Venice lagoon, with the aims of i) improving the balance between chemical and ecotoxicological evidence, through calibration of the ecotoxicological index for the lagoon context, ii) deriving alternative threshold values, specifically set for the Venice lagoon on the basis of the new dataset, and iii) identifying refinements and possible changes to criteria set by legislation for the integration of chemical and ecotoxicological results and sediment classification. Overall results are meant to support the appropriate reuse of dredged sediment for morphological restoration while optimizing the costs and resources in dredging operations.

papers.title: Plant litter promotes nitrate–sulfate co-removal in constructed wetlands: DOM dynamics and metagenomic insights into carbon, nitrogen, and sulfur transformations
papers.abstract: Plant litter is a low-cost carbon source for constructed wetlands (CWs), but its effectiveness and associated microbial mechanisms in nitrate–sulfate co-contaminated wastewater remains insufficiently understood. This study evaluated cattail and reed litters as in situ carbon sources by integrating substrate characterization, dissolved organic matter (DOM) spectroscopy, microbial community analysis, and metagenomic annotation. Both litter-amended systems effectively promoted simultaneous nitrogen and sulfate removal. The cattail-amended system achieved total nitrogen (TN) removal efficiencies of 73.48%–93.82% and a maximum SO 4 2− removal efficiency of 58.27%, while the reed-amended system achieved 61.10%–91.73% TN removal and 52.90% maximum SO 4 2− removal. DOM optical indices and PARAFAC analysis showed a gradual shift from protein-like to microbial humic-like fluorescence in the cattail-amended system, whereas microbial humic-like fluorescence dominated earlier in the reed-amended system. Metagenomic analysis revealed differences in carbon, nitrogen, and sulfur metabolic potentials. The cattail-amended system showed higher abundances of PPP-related genes associated with NADPH-generating reactions and several denitrification- and sulfur-oxidation-related genes, including narGHI , nirS/K , nosZ , sox , sqr , and fccA/B . The reed-amended system showed higher abundances of selected EMP- and TCA-associated genes and several reductive sulfur genes, including dsr , phs , and ttrABC . The detection of doxD and ttrABC further suggested potential thiosulfate–tetrathionate transformation. Overall, plant litter amendment effectively supported nitrate–sulfate co-removal, while integrated DOM, microbial, and metagenomic analyses revealed different metabolic potentials under cattail and reed amendment.

papers.title: Development and evaluation of biopolymer–fly ash amended sand for improved water holding capacity, abrasion resistance, and plant growth in desert ecosystem
papers.abstract: Desert sand, although mineral-rich, is unsuitable for agriculture due to its low water holding capacity and weak particle cohesion. In this study, a sustainable sand amendment approach was developed using Fly ash (FA) in combination with biopolymers, such as Guar gum (GG), Xanthan gum (XG), and Carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC), to enhance water retention and support plant growth in desert ecosystem. Sand and FA were blended at ratios of 90:10, 75:25, and 60:40, followed by the addition of 0.1% of biopolymer solution. The amended systems were evaluated for water holding capacity (WHC), evaporation rate (ER), and plant survival efficiency etc. Among the tested formulations, GG-amended sand-FA mixtures (60:40 and 90:10) exhibited 70% WHC that was equivalent to a 25% increase when compared with unamended sand. Evaporation losses were significantly reduced in all amended systems, with the lowest evaporation rates observed in the 90:10 sand-FA mixture treated with XG (48.68%), followed by CMC (53.16%) and GG (59.2%), compared to unamended sand (95%). The WHC-to-ER ratio, an indicator of effective water availability, was highest for XG and GG sand-FA amendments. SEM micrographs also revealed that GG and XG sand-FA amendments demonstrated superior performance due to their continuous, homogeneous matrix and strong inter-particle adhesion. Plant survival efficiency studies using a two-layer model demonstrated the 90:10 sand-FA amendment of GG and XG exhibited 61.9 and 57% plant survival efficiency. Overall, the findings demonstrate the potential of GG Sand -FA amendments as sustainable strategy for transforming desert sand into arable soil-like structure.

papers.title: A hybrid electrocoagulation–Solvay reactor for coupled CO2 mineralization and selective brine desalination via ion recovery and solid precipitation
papers.abstract: This study presents the design and performance of a novel hybrid reactor that integrates electrocoagulation (EC) with Solvay-based chemical treatment to enable simultaneous carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) capture and hypersaline brine desalination. The system features a temperature-controlled vertical chamber where direct CO 2 gas injection into brine promotes carbonate formation and CO 2 mineralization. Uniform mixing is achieved via mechanical stirring, while vertically oriented aluminum electrodes (1–4 V) induce electrochemical coagulation and facilitate solid recovery. The reactor operates within a controlled temperature range (22–50°C) to optimize reaction kinetics. A combination of chemical additives calcium oxide (CaO), ammonium bicarbonate (NH 4 HCO 3 ), and ammonia solution (NH 4 OH) was tested for enhanced selective precipitation. Maximum efficiency was observed with all three additives, achieving ∼85% calcium, 100% potassium, 99% magnesium, and 61% sodium removal, along with ∼97.5% sulfate reduction. Solid-phase characterization confirmed the recovery of valuable precipitates, including sodium bicarbonate, calcium sulfate, calcium carbonate, and magnesium hydroxide. The integrated system demonstrated a high CO 2 uptake of ∼16.49 g CO 2 /L of treated brine, illustrating its dual capability for carbon capture and resource recovery. This reactor platform introduces a scalable and sustainable route for environmental remediation, brine valorization, and carbon management in saline waste streams.

papers.title: Soil carbon and inundation regimes jointly regulate denitrification potential in restored riverine floodplains
papers.abstract: Denitrification plays a key role in nitrogen removal in restored floodplains, yet the relative importance of inundation regimes, hydrogeomorphic setting, and soil properties remains uncertain. In this study, we evaluated the environmental controls on denitrification potential across four restored sites using a combination of machine learning, structural equation modeling (SEM), and Copula-based analysis. Among the tested models, Random Forest provided the best predictive performance and explained 71% of the variance. Variable importance and partial dependence results identified total carbon (TC), soil moisture content (MC), and bulk density (BD) as the most influential predictors of denitrification potential. Specifically, a threshold in TC between 3% and 5% was associated with a sharp increase in denitrification potential. SEM results indicated that hydrological variables primarily influence denitrification indirectly through their effects on soil moisture and carbon accumulation, accounting for up to 44.4% of the variance at the site level. Copula analysis further quantified the joint probability of elevated denitrification enzyme activity (DEA) under combinations of favorable hydrologic conditions and sufficient carbon availability. Based on these patterns, the sites were grouped into three functional regimes: hydrology-carbon coupled regulation, carbon-limited regulation, and substrate-driven regulation with hydrological enhancement. Together, these results indicate that carbon availability establishes the biogeochemical potential for denitrification, whereas hydrological and physical conditions regulate its expression, with the relative importance of these controls varying among sites. The findings highlight the need for site-specific restoration strategies, including rebuilding soil carbon in degraded agricultural areas and maintaining appropriate inundation regimes while preserving favorable soil conditions in carbon-rich systems to enhance nitrogen removal.

papers.title: Scale-dependent bias in methane inventories: Satellite observations reveal overestimation from large coal mines in China
papers.abstract: Accurate quantification of China's coal mine methane (CMM) emissions is important for methane mitigation, yet bottom-up inventories remain subject to substantial uncertainty. Using TROPOMI observations from 2020 to 2024 and the Integrated Methane Inversion (IMI) framework, we performed annual inversions of regional methane emissions in Shanxi, a major coal-producing region of China, and integrated Global Energy Monitor (GEM) mine data to examine statistical relationships between mine attributes and posterior emission adjustments. Posterior methane emissions were estimated at 6.02-6.45 Tg yr −1 , averaging approximately 52% lower than the HEMCO-based prior, and exhibited pronounced spatial heterogeneity, with approximately 10% of grid cells contributing about 80% of total posterior emissions. After accounting for spatial differences in observational sensitivity using averaging kernel sensitivity (AKS), coal mine capacity remained the most stable GEM statistical explanatory variable for grid-scale posterior emission variability. Higher-capacity grids generally exhibited lower scaling correction factors (SCF) and stronger downward posterior adjustments, although the statistical significance of this relationship varied among years. Residual analyses further showed generally positive associations between the fraction of high-gas mines and local SCF deviations, whereas other mine attributes showed weaker cross-year consistency. These results suggest that conventional inventories may exhibit scale-related differences in required corrections across grids with different coal mine capacities, while local emission heterogeneity may also be associated with mine gas characteristics. This study provides observational constraints for evaluating and improving coal mine methane inventories and for supporting more targeted methane mitigation management in China's coal sector.

papers.title: Native plant effects on soil multifunctionality are mediated by microbial network reorganization in a subalpine spoil dump
papers.abstract: Engineering activities have led to a worldwide increase in spoil dumps, posing severe challenges to ecological restoration, particularly in vulnerable ecological regions. Identifying suitable restoration strategies is critical for the rapidly re-establishment soil multifunctionality to prevent secondary degradation and geohazards. In this study, we established a revegetation field experiment at a spoil dump on the eastern Tibetan Plateau, using four plant species with divergent functional traits, including Artemisia dubia , Melilotus suaveolens , Piptanthus nepalensis , and Rumex nepalensis . After two growing seasons, rhizosphere soils of the targeted species were collected and compared with bulk soils as controls. Soil multifunctionality was used as an integrated index to evaluate the restoration effectiveness. Our results showed that the rhizosphere of A. dubia (dense fine roots) supported significantly higher bacterial Shannon diversity and Pielou evenness than other treatments. Microbial co-occurrence networks were generally simplified in the rhizosphere compared to bulk soils. Soil functions related to C and N cycling, and overall soil multifunctionality were significantly enhanced in the rhizosphere across all species compared to bulk soils, but inter-species differences in these functions were limited. R. nepalensis (well-developed taproot) exerted the strongest positive effect on soil multifunctionality. Structural equation modeling revealed that plant traits shaped soil multifunctionality primarily through indirect pathways by alleviating nutrient imbalances and altering microbial attributes. Our findings highlight that the rapid improvement of soil multifunctionality is driven by the reorganization of microbial co-occurrence networks mediated by plant functional traits, rather than by microbial diversity. This work provides novel insights into plant-soil-microbe interactions in engineered-disturbed ecosystems, and underscores that trait-based configuration of native species represents a promising strategy for restoring the belowground functions of vulnerable alpine spoil dumps.

papers.title: Production activity and resulting pollution, not depth, driven microbial community structure, function, and assembly mechanisms in an aged petroleum hydrocarbon contaminated soil
papers.abstract: The degradation activity of soil microorganisms remains a crucial pathway for the reduction of petroleum hydrocarbons (PHs) pollutants in industrial site soils. Stimulating the metabolic activity of indigenous soil microorganisms to achieve pollutant removal is a promising remediation strategy in remediation practice. A vertical and horizontal investigation covering four production areas, four pollution levels, and five sampling depths at a PHs contaminated site from a long-term coking plant was launched to study soil PHs and bacterial community structure, function potential, and assembly. The results showed that both surface and subsurface soils (up to 6 m deep) at the contaminated site exhibit PHs contamination, with the most severe levels found between 4.5 and 5 m below the surface. The total petroleum hydrocarbon (TPH) concentrations in the soil ranged from 20 to 34,000 mg/kg. Potential PHs degrading bacteria, specifically the phylum Proteobacteria and the genera Pseudomonas and Sphingomonas, demonstrated positive correlations with TPH levels. Non-metric multidimensional scaling (NMDS) results showed that microbial community structure significantly differed among different production area and TPH pollution level. Redundancy analysis (RDA) results indicated that total nitrogen, moisture content, and available potassium in the soil exert the most substantial influence on the microbial community, while TPH, pH, soil organic carbon (SOC), sulfate content, and available phosphorus have comparatively minor effects. Analysis of community assembly mechanisms revealed that, with the exception of soils at the crude benzene, cooling tower (LQT), and L3 pollution levels-which were predominantly shaped by stochastic processes-most soil microbial communities were primarily influenced by deterministic factors such as environmental conditions and biotic interactions. Thus, production activity and the resulting pollution overwhelmed soil depth in shaping the structure, function potential, and assembly mechanisms of the microbial community in the aged, PHs polluted soil of the coking plant site. The relevant research results can provide theoretical support for the decision-making of PHs contaminated site remediation technologies and the regulation of remediation projects.
