papers.title: Intron retention regulates STAT2 function and associates with immunotherapy response in lung cancer
papers.abstract: Immunotherapy with checkpoint inhibitors has revolutionized cancer therapy and enabled considerable therapeutic advances for treating various diseases, including lung cancer. However, the molecular determinants of variable patient outcomes remain unclear. Using long-read RNA sequencing, we mapped the landscape of alternative RNA splicing in human primary lung adenocarcinomas. We identified more than 149,000 full-length messenger RNA (mRNA) isoforms, more than half of which were unannotated and many that occurred in immune-related genes, particularly within the type I interferon response pathway. We functionally characterized retained introns in the STAT2 gene that produced altered protein isoforms that regulated immune signaling and interferon responses and correlated with patient survival after anti–programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) immunotherapy. These findings position alternative splicing as a regulator of tumor immune responses and reveal intron retention in STAT2 as an interferon regulatory axis that correlates with PD-L1 checkpoint inhibitor response.

papers.title: Late Holocene reexpansion of the Laurentide Ice Sheet
papers.abstract: During interglaciations, the Laurentide Ice Sheet (LIS), which is the largest of the Pleistocene ice sheets, retreats to Arctic Canada, where it achieves a minimum configuration. The reexpansion of the LIS following this minimum marks the start of the next glaciation. Here, we show that the last remaining remnant of the most recent LIS, Barnes Ice Cap (Baffin Island, Canada), achieved its minimum interglacial dimensions after ~3.6 thousand years ago, before reexpanding ~2000 years ago, marking the onset of the next glaciation. The new LIS reached maximum dimensions in ~1960 CE, after which anthropogenic summer warming resulted in a negative mass balance, ice margin recession, and the termination of the next glaciation. The demise of the next glaciation, despite the ongoing decline in summer insolation, illustrates the influence of anomalous greenhouse gas forcing on climate.

papers.title: Decoupled self-assembled monolayer and perovskite deposition for efficient flexible solar modules
papers.abstract: The power conversion efficiency (PCE) and stability of flexible perovskite solar modules (PSMs) are less than those of their rigid devices because surface hydroxyls desorption on flexible substrates, which disrupts self-assembled monolayer (SAM) anchoring and perovskite crystallization. We developed a decoupled SAM-perovskite codeposition strategy that accelerates SAM anchoring by reducing the SAM-perovskite interaction and ameliorates perovskite crystallization. The certified PCE with phenethylammonium iodide as the passivation molecule was 20.2% on PSMs with device areas of 750 cm 2 . With 1,3-diaminopropane dihydroiodide as the passivator, the PCE of 22.0% for a device area of 14.55 cm 2 decreased by 8% after 1044 hours under maximum power point tracking at 85°C and 65% relative humidity. The devices pass all sequences of an international commercialization assessment standard for flexible portable PSMs.

papers.title: Electronic bound states in the continuum in a two-dimensional metal
papers.abstract: Bound states in the continuum (BICs) are quantum states that remain localized despite lying within a continuum of extended, delocalized states. Whereas optical BICs have been realized in photonic systems, achieving electronic bound states embedded in a metallic background remains an ongoing challenge. In this study, we used scanning tunneling microscopy to identify two defect-induced electronic states that remain localized within the metallic continuum of Pd 5 AlI 2 , a two-dimensional van der Waals metal. Our calculations suggest that electron-hopping interference on the decorated checkerboard lattice of Pd 5 AlI 2 gives rise to a (quasi) flat band built from spatially localized eigenstates that are orthogonal to the dispersive continuum. Atomic defects within this frustrated lattice shift the associated flat-band localized states into the metallic continuum, forming robust, symmetry-protected BICs.

papers.title: Dynamic functionality–enabled fast and selective transport in nanochannels
papers.abstract: Nanochannels capable of fast and selective mass transport are central to applications in energy, resources, biomedicine, and the environment. However, extreme nanoscale confinement, often coupled with rigid channel environments, imposes substantial frictional and adhesive barriers, causing sluggish transport and constrained selectivity. We identified nanochannel dynamics as a key to addressing these challenges by harnessing the intrinsic mobility (e.g., self-rotation) of confined functionalities to enhance molecular transport. Through a combination of experiments and simulations, we demonstrated that such dynamics reshape transport by promoting kinetic energy transfer and enabling more efficient molecular relays, thereby improving separation performance beyond current benchmarks. Our findings highlight the role of nanochannel dynamics in regulating mass transport under confinement and provide a framework for designing advanced nanochannel systems.

Natural product biosynthesis by guanidine prenyltransferases in plants and bacteria
papers.abstract: Guanidine exists almost exclusively as a resonance-stabilized cation, making its direct enzymatic functionalization challenging. We identified the cyanobacterial enzyme NosH, which catalyzes direct prenyl transfer to free guanidine. Structural and mechanistic analyses revealed guanidine activation by a two-aspartate clamp coupled to prenyl-donor binding through a distinct catalytic architecture. Guided by these features, we identified a large family of guanidine prenyltransferases across bacteria and plants. Plant enzymes produced guanidine alkaloids such as galegine in vitro and heterologous expression of a plant ortholog in Nicotiana benthamiana produced galegine in planta, providing a direct enzymatic link to plant-specialized metabolism.

papers.title: Imaging electron-hole asymmetry in the quantum melting of generalized Wigner crystals
papers.abstract: Two-dimensional moiré materials provide a versatile platform to explore phase transitions in strongly correlated systems. Using scanning tunneling microscopy, we imaged the density-driven melting of generalized Wigner crystals (GWCs) and Mott insulators (MIs) in electron-doped, near-60°–twisted molybdenum diselenide bilayers featuring a triangular moiré superlattice. We observed notable electron-hole asymmetry in GWC melting: Hole-doped GWCs yielded interaction-driven disordered states, whereas electron-doped GWCs melted into delocalized liquid-like states. This asymmetry arose from the broken particle-hole symmetry of the moiré superlattice, which produced electron and hole Fermi pockets with different momentum geometries upon GWC condensation. MI states melted without such asymmetry, consistent with the absence of a symmetry-breaking density modulation. This work provides direct visualization of the emergent phases that appear as GWCs undergo quantum melting transitions.

papers.title: Sequential diagnosis with language models
papers.abstract: We explored the capabilities of frontier language models in sequential diagnosis, a diagnostic paradigm that captures the iterative nature of clinical reasoning. Given a brief clinical presentation, clinicians selectively acquired information to reach a diagnosis, enabling assessment of diagnostic accuracy and workup cost. We developed an interactive benchmark and an artificial intelligence (AI) system that simulates a panel of physicians, continually revising the differential diagnosis and selecting cost-effective tests. Using this benchmark, the system achieved 83.2% accuracy on New England Journal of Medicine clinicopathological conference cases and 80.3% on MIMIC-IV-ED emergency department admissions, outperforming generalist physicians (36.1 and 46.8%, respectively). Although these findings were obtained in a controlled benchmark setting, they highlight the promise of language models for supporting more accurate, lower-cost diagnoses.

papers.title: Ultrarapid decision-making in an avian brain
papers.abstract: Perceptual decision-making is well studied in mammals, but its operation in other vertebrates remains unclear. We show that carrion crows ( Corvus corone ) make deliberate decisions in a classic visual motion discrimination task with unprecedented speed, reporting choices in approximately 235 milliseconds on average, which is roughly twice as fast as has been observed in monkeys or humans and without sacrificing accuracy. Recordings from the pallial endbrain reveal that direction-selective neurons encode the upcoming choice as early as about 70 milliseconds after stimulus onset and about 170 milliseconds before the response, with ramping activity scaling with sensory evidence and converging at response onset. These findings highlight the extraordinary efficiency of avian decision-making circuitry, possibly shaped by evolutionary pressures for rapid visuomotor control.

“We’re Not Handling Cases, We’re Shaping Lives”: How Lawyers Preserve Professional Authority and Advance Social Responsibility via Moral Identity-Based Client Persuasion
papers.abstract: Professionals are increasingly expected to deliver socially responsible services that protect vulnerable third parties, yet their authority may be threatened when such recommendations appear to conflict with clients’ perceived self-interests and desired end goals. Drawing on a qualitative study of 91 legal cases in China, we examine how lawyers navigate this tension when persuading initially resistant clients to accept socially responsible counsel. We develop a process model of “moral identity-based client persuasion,” a form of relational expertise that enables lawyers to preserve professional authority by reconstructing clients’ desired end goals to incorporate third-party welfare. The process begins with client moral identity discernment, through which lawyers determine whether a client’s moral identity is situationally salient. It unfolds through three linked practices: (1) articulating moral identity threats, (2) providing moral identity affirmations, and (3) legitimizing moral identity enactments. Together, these practices render socially responsible counsel both self-relevant and technically defensible to clients. We further identify three client-level inhibitors of success: insufficient moral identity salience, entangled decision locus, and limited emotional resilience. These findings augment research on professional work by identifying a novel form of relational expertise that mobilizes clients’ personal identities to secure compliance, and extend moral persuasion research into professional service contexts.

papers.title: Breaking the Silence: Developing an Organizational Mental Health Capability
papers.abstract: Organizations invest heavily in mental health resources, yet employee utilization remains strikingly low. This disconnect may signal low need but often masks latent demand: the unobserved gap between employees’ mental health needs and their expressed demand for support. Latent demand persists when organizational and individual barriers suppress recognition, access, and permission to seek help, confronting organizations with a capability-building challenge: the conditions sustaining latent demand also suppress the information needed to address it. Because this problem requires organizational adaptation, dynamic capabilities theory offers a starting point. Under latent demand, however, sensing can misread silence as sufficiency, seizing can leave resources unused, and transforming can learn from biased feedback. Integrating dynamic capabilities with positive organizational scholarship, we theorize how organizations develop an organizational mental health capability to recognize, act on, and adapt to employees’ observable and latent needs. We identify positive social capital as the bridging mechanism that scales relational micro-practices into organizational infrastructure through stage-contingent structural, relational, and cognitive pathways, each addressing a binding constraint. Our theory extends dynamic capabilities to contexts where information is suppressed rather than merely noisy, shows how positive organizational scholarship enables capability building under latent demand, and advances a macro-level perspective on workplace mental health.

Information Transparency, Choice Confidence, and Customer Retention: Field and Laboratory Evidence from Markets for Credence Goods
papers.abstract: How does information transparency affect customer retention in markets where quality is difficult to verify? Conventional wisdom suggests that transparency intensifies price competition and increases customer churn. We challenge this view by showing that acquisition-stage transparency can strengthen retention in markets for credence goods characterized by delayed feedback and persistent uncertainty, where customers revisit their decisions without clear quality signals. We develop a transparency-confidence-retention framework, in which transparency at acquisition builds choice confidence, a psychological switching cost that anchors customers to their initial decisions. Using 83,835 auto insurance contracts from a European insurer and multiple identification strategies, we find that customers acquired through transparent channels are 4.6%–11.8% less likely to churn than those acquired through less transparent channels. A randomized, controlled experiment with 1,515 participants shows that transparency reduces customer churn primarily by strengthening choice confidence rather than increasing conventional switching costs, such as brand trust or product fit. Decomposing transparency into attribute, comparative, and evaluative dimensions reveals that evaluative transparency exerts the strongest influence. Analyses of boundary conditions indicate that the retention effect of transparency is amplified when public and private signals remain congruent with earlier informational cues. These findings reconceptualize transparency as a relational mechanism that fosters decisional assurance and stabilizes retention under quality uncertainty. This paper was accepted by Anindya Ghose, information systems. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2020.02865 .

papers.title: From Bytes to Bites: Examining the Online and Offline Spillover Impacts of Online Food Delivery Platform Subscriptions
papers.abstract: With the rapid expansion of online food delivery (OFD) platforms, subscription models have emerged as a strategic tool to retain users and shape consumption behavior. Despite their growing prevalence, the broader impacts of these subscriptions—both within the OFD sector and across downstream consumer activities—remain underexplored. Leveraging a difference-in-differences approach and a large-scale individual-level transaction data set, we identify a significant shift in consumption from a competing platform to the focal platform following the introduction of a subscription service. This shift did not result in cannibalization; instead, overall food consumption within the OFD market increased. Geospatial analysis shows that subscribers were more likely to engage in offline spillovers, including increased local dining and activity in nearby noncompeting economic sectors. These patterns suggest that subscriptions in physical services, like OFD, not only reshape digital engagement, but also, they influence consumer mobility and stimulate localized economic ecosystems. Mechanistic testing supports the interpretation that these effects are driven by increased variety-seeking behavior for offline restaurants that predominantly serve non-OFD cuisines within a proximal location, suggesting that such behavior is constrained by transportation costs. Overall, this study offers novel insights into how subscription models in physical service platforms can expand market demand, foster crosschannel engagement, and generate positive spillovers in adjacent sectors. The findings offer actionable guidance for platform designers and policymakers to enhance consumer welfare and support local economic vitality. They also provide new evidence for restaurants that additional platform usage costs may be offset by latent economic benefits from heightened consumer engagement. This paper was accepted by D. J. Wu, information systems. Funding: F. J. Costello acknowledges funding by Fundação para a Ciência e a Tecnologia (UID/00124/2025, UID/ PRR/00124/2025, Nova School of Business and Economics DOI: https://doi.org/10.54499/UID/00124/2025 ), UID/PRR2/00124/2025: DOI: https://doi.org/10.54499/UID/PRR2/00124/2025 and LISBOA2030 (DataLab2030 - LISBOA2030-FEDER-01314200). Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.00954 .

papers.title: From Winning to Giving: The Effect of Gold Medals in Crowdsourcing Contests
papers.abstract: We examine how users respond to winning symbolic awards in online crowdsourcing contests. Our setting is a machine learning competition platform that grants symbolic medals to recognize participants’ contest achievements. Employing a regression discontinuity design, we find that gold medal winners participate less in subsequent contests but engage more in prosocial activities, evidenced by a greater volume and length of posts, as well as more substantial and frequent code contributions. In contrast, bronze and silver medals do not seem to exert a significant influence on recipients’ subsequent behaviors. Drawing on self-determination theory and the needs-as-motives hypothesis, we provide evidence that need-driven goal shifting plays an important role in driving the dual effects of gold medals—diminished contest participation but enhanced prosocial contributions. Further analyses reveal that winners with previous competition medals are more likely to favor contributing content over competing again, whereas winners with more prior contribution medals are less inclined to further increase contributions. Moreover, team winners exhibit a lower tendency than solo winners to shift their efforts from competition to contribution. We add to the symbolic awards literature by uncovering a novel goal-shifting effect induced by contest medals, where award receipt redirects user effort from the focal rewarded domain to other forms of platform engagement. This paper was accepted by D. J. Wu, information systems. Funding: Financial support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grants 72032006, W2611101, and 72371192] and the “Digital-Intelligent Operations Risk Management” Innovation and Entrepreneurship Team Project of the Sanqin Talent Special Support Program in Shaanxi Province [2025STD03] is gratefully acknowledged. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.07419 .

papers.title: Why Zoning Is Too Restrictive
papers.abstract: Economists estimate that zoning regulations raise house prices, lower productivity, and reduce aggregate welfare, yet regulations remain widespread. We develop and solve a model in which fragmented zoning authority leads to overly strict regulations: Homeowners impose stricter regulations to mitigate local congestion but fail to internalize the broader impact on metro-wide affordability. Empirically, the Herfindahl-Hirschman index of local governments explains 12% of the variation in zoning restrictiveness. Using an instrument based on 19th-century municipal fragmentation, we show that greater fragmentation leads to stricter zoning and higher housing costs. These findings suggest that centralizing zoning decisions could alleviate housing affordability challenges. This paper was accepted by Lukas Schmid, finance. Funding: This work was supported by the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada [Grant AWD-027881 SSHRC 2023]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.02844 .

papers.title: Women’s Approachability Premium in Sales: A Field Experiment Among Microentrepreneurs
papers.abstract: Female entrepreneurs consistently earn less than their male counterparts, a disparity that is particularly acute among microentrepreneurs in developing economies. Researchers often attribute this gap to structural constraints, but pay less attention to how social interactions shape earnings. This oversight is especially relevant in microentrepreneurship, where sales are contingent on customers approaching and interacting with sellers in the marketplace. Using an interactionist lens, we draw on social exchange theory and research on gender stereotypes to guide expectations. We anticipate that customers will more often approach female sellers, expecting warmer interactions, and that this higher volume will translate into higher earnings when business characteristics and selling behavior are held constant. Existing research hints at this dynamic, but methodological constraints have obscured it. To overcome these constraints and test our theory, we conducted a field experiment in two face-to-face markets in India. We trained confederate sellers to run identical, de novo microenterprises and follow standard protocols for customer engagement, thus isolating customer approach in response to sellers’ gender. Female sellers attracted 41% more customers, resulting in significantly higher sales than men, all else equal, in our experiment. Consistent with our theory, customers were more likely to talk with women about topics unrelated to the sale and attempt to bargain with women. This study advances research on gender dynamics in entrepreneurship, negotiation, and customer-facing work by identifying customer approach as a novel mechanism that can generate economic advantages for female microentrepreneurs and may shape gendered opportunities in other markets and organizations.

papers.title: The Fragmentation of Material Flows: Mapping Barriers to Circular Economy Adoption in Bangladesh's Ready‐Made Garment Sector
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT This paper provides an empirical diagnosis of the systemic challenges preventing the transition to a circular economy (CE) in Bangladesh's ready‐made garment (RMG) sector. Drawing on in‐depth interviews ( n = 13) with key industry stakeholders, the study characterises current waste flows and analyses the barriers to circularity. Findings reveal a predominantly linear material flow dominated by informal networks and constrained by a lack of traceability, limited recycling infrastructure and weak policy support. The study identifies power asymmetry between global brands and local manufacturers as one of four interacting ‘lock‐in’ mechanisms, alongside institutional voids, infrastructural and technological constraints and traceability failure, that together prevent the industry from moving beyond fragmented, linear practices. This structural governance failure actively inhibits progress toward Sustainable Development Goal 12, particularly Targets 12.5 and 12.6. Based on the multilevel perspective, supplemented by institutional theory and the resource‐based view, the analysis argues that the current linear production regime is maintained by institutional voids and internal resource constraints that must be addressed before prescriptive solutions can be operationalised. The empirical scope centres on postproduction and preconsumer waste governance; postconsumer textile waste is examined specifically as an import‐ and feedstock‐classification barrier rather than as an empirically traced material flow.

papers.title: Circular Economy Practices and Sustainable Performance: An Empirical Study
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines the extent to which basic and advanced circular economy practices are associated in different ways with the environmental, economic and social dimensions of sustainable performance at the firm level. Starting from the premise that the circular economy should not be treated as a homogeneous construct, the study distinguishes between more operational practices, geared towards efficiency and waste reduction, and more transformational practices, associated with redesign, value retention and the reconfiguration of value creation and capture models. Empirically, a quantitative, cross‐sectional, organisation‐level design is adopted, based on 255 companies operating in Portugal. The data were analysed using descriptive statistics, reliability tests, bivariate correlations and hierarchical ordinary least squares regressions. The results show that basic circular economy practices exhibit positive, robust and consistent associations with environmental performance and economic performance, emerging as the empirically strongest core of circular value creation. The environmental dimension proves to be the aspect of sustainable performance most directly sensitive to the adoption of these practices. In contrast, although advanced practices show positive associations in intermediate models, they do not demonstrate a robust incremental contribution to economic and social performance in the full models. The study contributes to the literature by emphasising the need to distinguish between different types of circular practices, by linking the debate on the circular economy to the literature on strategy and sustainability and by offering a more nuanced understanding of multidimensional sustainable performance. In practical terms, the findings suggest that organisations should not assume that more advanced circular practices automatically generate stronger performance outcomes and that the contribution of different forms of circularity should be assessed in relation to their specific organisational and performance context.

papers.title: Reframing Stakeholder Roles in Multistakeholder Partnerships: A Role Theory Approach to Collaborative Action on Food Waste
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Multistakeholder partnerships (MSPs) are promoted as collaborative arrangements to address food waste, yet most research focuses on core stakeholders directly involved in food production and consumption, leaving the roles of supporting stakeholders underexplored. This study redirects attention to these vital actors, such as governmental bodies, financial institutions, and industry associations, whose engagement can be important to initiating, stabilizing, and sustaining collaboration. Drawing on role theory, we examine the case of Food Waste Free United in the Netherlands through interviews and secondary data. We identify four dynamic role orientations enacted by supporting stakeholders: mediator, facilitator, supporter, and influencer. Each role embodies distinct practices, ranging from building trust and establishing data sharing arrangements to mobilizing networks, shaping policy, and strengthening capabilities, which can contribute to the stability and effectiveness of MSPs. Our analysis further reveals that motivations to engage extend beyond external pressure, encompassing a search for embeddedness within the partnership ecosystem and opportunities for learning. By applying role theory, we advance understanding of how supporting stakeholders enable MSPs to move beyond fragile arrangements toward sustained, systemic impact. These insights offer theoretical contributions to stakeholder and role theory that, in turn, inform practical guidance for designing partnerships that more effectively integrate diverse actors in the fight against food waste.

papers.title: Institutional technologies and the new frontiers of international marketing and global supply chain management
papers.abstract: Purpose This paper introduces the concept of institutional technologies as the socio-technical and interorganizational mechanisms and practices that enable the governance and coordination of economic exchange. We argue that emerging institutional technologies, such as digital platforms, distributed ledgers, smart contracts and digital traceability systems, are reshaping the foundations of international marketing and global supply chain management (SCM) by changing how firms create, substantiate and deliver value across borders. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on a conceptual and integrative approach, this paper examines how emerging institutional technologies alter the conditions under which firms create, substantiate and deliver value propositions and engage in economic exchange. We develop a framework that links institutional technologies to the governance, accountability and legitimacy processes that shape the international marketing–global SCM interface. Findings We argue that institutional technologies are reordering coordination, accountability, legitimacy and value capture across borders. We further suggest that the international marketing–global SCM interface has become a site of joint institutional work, where firms shape technology-enabled standards, proofs and governance arrangements that underpin contemporary cross-border exchange. Building on this perspective, this paper proposes five directions for future research: traceability as a market promise; platformization of international marketing; automation and smart contracts in relation to relational repair; algorithmic coordination as institutional technology; and the interplay between institutional technologies, regulation, geopolitics and infrastructures. We develop five propositions that link each cluster of institutional technologies to the forms of institutional work it performs, the outcomes it influences and the institutional conditions that shape these relationships. Originality/value This paper advances a more technologically grounded understanding of the interface between international marketing and global SCM. It offers a novel conceptual foundation for examining how the technological architectures and governance models of cross-border exchange are being fundamentally recast.

papers.title: Threat perception, issue knowledge, and citizen coproduction preferences: evidence from a national public survey on environmental health
papers.abstract: Building on the literature on citizen coproduction, this study examines how threat perception and issue knowledge influence individual citizens’ coproduction preferences in the issue domain of environmental health. Drawing on prior research, we propose a conceptual framework and derive theoretical expectations about the relationships between threat perception, issue knowledge, and citizens’ willingness to engage in coproduction. Empirically, we use data from a nationally representative public survey (N = 1,207) to test our hypotheses. Across multiple model specifications and robustness checks, the regression results consistently support our expectations: holding other factors constant, individuals who perceive greater threats and those who possess more issue knowledge tend to express stronger willingness to participate in co-planning and co-investment activities with public entities. In conclusion, we discuss the study’s key contributions, directions for future research, and practical implications for environmental health policy and management.

papers.abstract: While companies scramble to rebrand as AI companies, there is a parallel, but less visible, scramble to brand what ‘AI’ is and means. Firms such as Anthropic, Meta, and OpenAI are employing traditi...

papers.title: How does young children’s digital resilience operate within and across homes and communities? A thematic analysis of parents and early years educators’ experiences
papers.abstract: This paper examines how young children aged 0–5 years build digital resilience within interconnected home and community contexts. While playing, exploring, and socialising are central to early experiential learning, little is known about how parents/carers and educators support children to recognise, manage, and recover from mistakes in connected environments. Conceptualising digital resilience as a socio-ecological construct, the paper draws on findings from the TYKES project to address this gap. Using a multi-method qualitative design, the study thematically analyses semi-structured interviews with parents/carers (n = 17) and early years educators (n = 5), alongside focus groups with educators across two settings (n = 8), conducted using purposive sampling over a ten-month period (May 2024–February 2025). The paper argues that digital resilience is a relational and context-dependent process that unfolds across nested home and community environments, rather than solely within individual children or discrete settings. It highlights the importance of social capital and everyday interactions in shaping children’s emerging capacities to navigate online challenges. The paper contributes to the literature by demonstrating how parents/carers and educators actively cultivate digital resilience as an emergent capability, embedded in socio-ecological relations. The findings point to the need for more holistic and coordinated support across education systems, policymakers, industry, and governments to enable young children to thrive on the Internet.

papers.title: Effect heterogeneity of loneliness and social support on incident hypertension in older, normotensive populations
papers.abstract: Abstract Although social isolation is known to impact those with cardiovascular disease, its relationship with incident hypertension is unclear. In this retrospective cohort study, we used data from the All of Us research program. Participants were enrolled between May 2017-April 2023, aged 50+ years, and had at least 60-days of EHR data pre-index date. We identified incident hypertension during follow-up. Those classified as hypertensive at or prior to the index date were excluded. We defined low social support and loneliness as binary variables. Using causal forests, we estimated treatment effects as unweighted and overlap-weighted risk differences (RD). A total of 24,720 participants with a median follow-up of 2.6 years were included. While loneliness and social support were not significantly associated with incident hypertension in the overall population, causal forests revealed meaningful effect heterogeneity, with socially isolated male (RD: 0.038, 95% CI 0.002 to 0.075; overlap-weighted RD: 0.027, 95% CI -0.005 to 0.059) and Gay or Lesbian participants (RD: 0.108, 95% CI 0.011 to 0.205; overlap-weighted RD: 0.11, 95% CI 0.008 to 0.211) experiencing a significantly elevated risk. This illustrates how machine learning, when embedded within epidemiologic frameworks, can detect subgroup vulnerability that other approaches may obscure, enabling targeting of limited resources.

papers.title: Military-specific factors and incident melanoma diagnoses among active duty participants in the millennium cohort study, 2000 - 2021
papers.abstract: Service members experience unique occupational hazards that may increase their risk for melanoma. This longitudinal study aimed to determine associations between deployment status, environmental exposures, and solar exposures and incident melanoma among active duty service members. Millennium Cohort Study survey data (2001-2021) were linked with deployment and military health care records (2000-2021). Adjusted Cox proportional hazards models estimated effects of exposures and covariates on incident melanoma. Risk of melanoma diagnosis by age (early vs late onset) and anatomical site (sun-protected vs sun-exposed skin) were also estimated. Among 115,512 service members, 184 were diagnosed with melanoma during the study period (61% were <40 years old and 77% diagnosed on sun-protected skin). Melanoma risk by demographics was consistent with civilian studies. Among this military population, those who deployed (adjusted hazard ratio [AHR] 0.55 [95% CI 0.40, 0.75]) had reduced melanoma risk. Conversely, those who self-reported being exposed to occupational hazards (AHR 1.43 [95% CI 1.05, 1.95]) had elevated melanoma risk. Findings were consistent with the “healthy deployer effect,” while self-reported occupational hazards were associated with an increased risk of melanoma. Results may be informative for understanding melanoma etiology, risk counseling, and screening.

papers.title: The authors reply to ‘consistency and positivity are valuable for causal education and communication’ by lee Kennedy-Shaffer
Turning the Lens on Sexual Perpetration: Predictors of Acknowledging Sexual Perpetration
papers.abstract: Factors related to sexual perpetration acknowledgment are virtually unstudied, leaving a significant gap in the sexual violence literature. The current study explored (1) perpetration frequency and tactics and (2) acceptance of myths about sexual aggression (AMASA) as potential predictors of acknowledgment. In addition, post-traumatic stress and depressive symptoms were examined as possible correlates of perpetration acknowledgment. A secondary aim of this study was to provide descriptive data for the proportion of people who have sexually perpetrated and who also endorse being victimized (i.e. victim-perpetrator overlap in adulthood) as well as rates of perpetration acknowledgment in this sample. The data used were from a larger study of 1,177 participants recruited from Prolific, a university research pool, and snowball methods using a cross-sectional design. Of the 722 eligible participants, 305 (42.2%) endorsed perpetration and 302 (99.0%) of those endorsed victim-perpetrator overlap. Our results revealed positive associations between frequency and acknowledgment. Further, there were significant differences between the tactic used and acknowledgment. Finally, group differences based on acknowledgment were found when examining AMASA and psychological distress. The current study addressed critical gaps in the literature by examining factors related to perpetration acknowledgment, providing insights that can guide future research, develop theory, and inform interventions.

papers.title: Social Media Use and Openness to “Sugar Relationships”: Cultural Tightness–Looseness as a Moderator Across 22 Countries
papers.abstract: Abstract Social media use has been widely linked to sexual attitudes, yet it remains unclear whether its association with openness to sugar relationships is uniform across countries or contingent on country-level normative contexts. In the present study, we examined whether country-level cultural tightness–looseness moderated the relationship between social media use and openness to sugar relationships across 22 countries. Openness to sugar relationships was conceptualized as a manifestation of a broader orientation toward sexual–economic exchange. Using data from 22,292 adult women drawn from a large cross-national dataset, we tested this framework with Bayesian multilevel modeling. Measurement invariance of the openness construct was assessed, and alignment procedures were applied to address cross-country non-invariance prior to analysis. Cultural tightness–looseness was modeled as a country-level moderator of the individual-level association between social media use and openness to sugar relationships, while age was included as a control variable. Results revealed a positive association between social media use and openness to sugar relationships. In addition, this association was modestly stronger in countries characterized by lower normative constraint, suggesting that country-level norm strength may shape the attitudinal relevance of digital exposure. Models including this interaction outperformed alternative specifications that incorporated a range of theoretically plausible country-level covariates, including indicators of digital infrastructure, socioeconomic structure, and internet freedom. Although the interaction effect size was modest, the findings suggest that the attitudinal correlates of social media use vary systematically across countries and highlight the importance of country-level normative contexts in research on sexual–economic openness.

papers.title: Benefits and Harms of Adult Videos: A Sex Difference Social Representations Analysis Among Young Adults in Japan
papers.abstract: Pornhub Insights (2025) reported that Japan ranked 11th worldwide in total traffic, indicating widespread use of adult videos (AV). Existing research has primarily focused on AV-related harms from expert and Western perspectives. Few studies examine how Japanese young adults perceive these effects, particularly the benefits that sustain use, and sex differences remain underexplored. This study investigated the core social representations of AV benefits and harms and how they differ by sex. Data were collected from 251 Japanese participants, of whom 137 (54.6%) were male, with a mean age of 20.71 years. Most participants (81.3%) reported using AV, and most identified as heterosexual students. Data were analyzed using prototypical analysis to identify elements with high consensus. Five key observations emerged: (1) Both genders see “satisfaction,” “pleasure,” and “crime prevention” as key benefits of AV. (2) Sex differences appeared in describing benefits, with men mentioning “sex education” and women mentioning “stress relief.” (3) Both genders identified “incorrect knowledge” as a primary representation of AV-related harms. (4) Male respondents cited “addiction” as a harm, whereas female respondents were more likely to reference “encouraging sexual crime.” (5) More words or phrases were used to describe AV benefits than harms. These findings may inform targeted interventions and policy discussions.

papers.title: From atomic structure to catalytic function: Morphology engineering of MXene for Electrocatalytic energy conversion
Static reconfiguration techniques for PV under the corn canopy with deep reinforcement learning
papers.abstract: Valve integrated photovoltaic (PV) systems deployed in agricultural environments are prone to power mismatch caused by shading from maize canopies. To mitigate this issue, a static reconfiguration strategy based on shadow informed deep reinforcement learning is proposed. The method collects physically consistent irradiance information under maize canopy shading and constructs a deep reinforcement learning framework in which the average power loss rate is used as the optimization objective. This framework enables offline optimization of photovoltaic cell array layouts. The results demonstrate that the array configuration discovered by the proposed framework, which learns current mismatch mechanisms and applies a global trade off strategy, achieves an average maximum output power of 1.401 W. This performance significantly exceeds that of the conventional total cross-tied topology, which produces 1.057 W, and the Sudoku-based (SDK) method, which achieves 1.103 W. The corresponding relative improvements are 32.6% and 27.0%, respectively. In addition, the static reconfiguration matrix designed using this approach achieves an average maximum power loss rate of 42.31%. This study provides a new reference for the static reconfiguration of micro-photovoltaic arrays under shading conditions and confirms the effectiveness of physics guided, data driven optimization for reliable photovoltaic system design in complex natural environments.

papers.title: Optimizing biochar quality and economics across feedstocks and pyrolysis temperatures in a 50,000 t/year carbonization demonstration
papers.abstract: Biomass carbonization plays a critical role in industrial fuel substitution and efficient carbon sequestration, yet commercial-scale evidence linking biochar quality and economic performance based on actual operating data remains limited. Herein, based on an established biomass carbonization demonstration with an annual processing capacity of 50,000 t/year, 8 typical biomass feedstocks sourced within the collection radius (800 km) of the demonstration were selected as raw materials. Focusing on pyrolysis temperature, which is the key parameter governing biochar production, the quality and economic viability of biochar produced under the demonstration were systematically evaluated. Actual production data and economic parameters were analyzed using techno-economic assessment, correlation analysis, Random Forest prediction, Shapley interpretation, and Pareto optimization. At 500 °C, the fixed carbon contents and higher heating values of the 8 biochars ranged from 52.17% to 80.49% and from 5225 to 7525 kcal/kg, respectively. Only wood chips and bamboo chips exceeded 75% fixed carbon, reaching 75.85% and 80.49%, with corresponding higher heating values of 7373 and 7525 kcal/kg. The mixed biomass production line, using rice husk, sunflower seed shells, leafy firewood, pine branches, and green mountain wood, achieved the best economic performance, with an IRR of 8.19% and an NPV of 22.44 million Chinese yuan (CNY); in contrast, the bamboo-chip and wood-powder lines had negative NPVs and IRRs below the 2.5% discount rate. Pearson analysis linked Ash content, Volatiles matter content and temperature to heating value ( r = 0.77, 0.80, 0.31) and cost ( r = −0.55, 0.65, 0.38). Machine-learning-based Pareto optimization predicted an optimal trade-off for pine branches pyrolyzed at 375–425 °C, yielding 6821.60–6830.35 kcal/kg at 861.63–862.35 CNY. This work has developed an optimization strategy for industrial applications through experimental evaluation and machine learning feedback based on actual demonstration, thereby providing the theoretical foundation for the design and control of biochar production.

papers.title: A relational retrofitting void in the private rented sector: the Brighton and Hove ‘loop’
When do hydrogen technology patents improve ecological performance? Cross-country evidence on mediation and threshold effects in the load capacity factor
papers.abstract: This paper asks whether hydrogen technology patents improve ecological performance, and under what conditions. Using a balanced panel of 48 countries over 2000–2024 and a multidimensional patent value index, we estimate two-way fixed effects models for the load capacity factor (LCF), the ratio of biocapacity to the ecological footprint. We find that hydrogen patent value is positively associated with the LCF, with a level-dependent magnitude: a one-standard-deviation increase in transformed patent value is associated with an LCF 4.2% higher for an economy at ecological balance and 6.3% higher for one in ecological deficit. This gain comes mainly from a smaller ecological footprint and only marginally from greater biocapacity. The result holds under a shift-share instrument, heteroskedasticity-based identification, weak-instrument-robust inference, plausible-exogeneity analysis and dynamic panel estimation. Turning to mechanisms, a joint parallel-mediation model attributes 6.8% of the total effect to technical human capital and 7.2% to hydrogen production subsidy policy. The association is positive in both fossil-dependence groups, without a robust difference between them, but significant only in below-median-income economies. Panel threshold estimates show that it strengthens once institutional quality exceeds approximately 0.31 on a 0–1 index, turns from negative to positive once internet penetration passes about 92%, and becomes positive and statistically significant once a country operates three or more carbon capture, utilisation and storage (CCUS) facilities. For policy, hydrogen innovation is better assessed alongside absorptive capacity, digital infrastructure and operational carbon-management capacity than as a standalone environmental instrument.

papers.title: Advancing Environmental Justice Research within and beyond Science and Engineering
papers.abstract: Abstract Scientists and engineers have historically approached questions of environmental justice (EJ) differently from social scientists and humanists, from how they formulate problem scope to how they propose solutions. While scientists and engineers have assessed distributional injustices extensively, there are opportunities for deeper interdisciplinary collaboration with other EJ schools of thought. In this Perspective, we first present an EJ schematic for a science and engineering audience, where we trace epistemologies within EJ schools to show how EJ scholars conceptualize knowledge, how this relates to their methods, and how they present and publish work. We survey the EJ literature─mainly work related to the United States─across disciplines to determine major tensions within EJ and between EJ, science, and engineering scholarship. We also discuss possibilities for enabling interdisciplinary collaboration for scientists and engineers working on EJ-related questions by analyzing epistemological compatibilities. Next, we highlight opportunities to facilitate collaboration through an illustrative interdisciplinary case study. We conclude with takeaways for scientists and engineers moving forward, alongside some of the challenges accompanying interdisciplinary EJ research.

papers.title: Coupling 18F Radiotracer Imaging with Synchrotron Fe Speciation to Resolve Biogeochemical Dynamics in PHC-Contaminated Soils
papers.abstract: Abstract In petroleum hydrocarbon (PHC)-contaminated subsoils, iron bioavailability often is believed to constrain the degradation of PHC contaminants, but spatially resolved evidence linking microbial activity with Fe transformations is scarce. Here, we bridge this gap by integrating phosphor imaging using positron-emitting radiotracer [18F]fluorobenzene─a high-fidelity surrogate for benzene, toluene, ethylbenzene, and xylene (BTEX)─with synchrotron-based X-ray spectroscopy. This multimodal approach allows for targeted mineralogical fingerprinting, guided by direct visualization of microbial activity within PHC-contaminated soils. Bulk X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) showed little contrast, but microspectroscopy analysis revealed diffuse Fe at active zones and discrete Fe grains in inactive matrices, a pattern consistent with Fe(III) bioreduction to mobile Fe(II) and porewater transport before reprecipitation/reoxidation. Zones of high microbial activity were enriched in reactive phases (ferrihydrite, siderite, and green rust) comprising 27–71% of total Fe, whereas inactive matrices sequestered Fe mainly in Ca–Fe silicates with less than 25% reactive Fe. The recurring presence of green rust and vivianite aligns with phosphate-associated early-stage products under long-term tripolyphosphate biostimulation. We conclude that hydrocarbon degradation co-occurs spatially with Fe(III) bioreduction to mobile Fe(II), lateral transport in porewater, and phosphate-associated reoxidation/reprecipitation, processes that bulk methods often obscure but microscale mapping reveals. These insights support potential comanaging Fe and P amendments and targeted delivery of amendments to enhance PHC bioremediation in cold, calcareous soils.

papers.title: Purple Phototrophic Bacteria as a Novel Platform for Coenzyme Q10 Production from CO2, Syngas, and Sulfur Waste Byproducts
papers.abstract: Abstract The efficient conversion of CO2 and industrial waste streams into value-added products remains a critical challenge for sustainable microbial processes. Here, we present the first systematic demonstration of purple phototrophic bacteria (PPB) as platforms for the autotrophic valorization of CO2 and industrial off-gases or sulfur byproducts into valuable metabolites. Genome-guided screening combined with experimental validation identified strains capable of coupling photoautotrophic growth with the production of CoQ10 and carotenoid pigments. Among them, Rhodospirillum rubrum DSM 467 and DSM 107 exhibited the highest performance, maintaining stable CO2 and H2 consumption under semicontinuous operation and accumulating up to 9.6 ± 0.2 mgCoQ10 gbiomass–1 under CO2/ H2 conditions, comparable to engineered production systems. In addition, R. rubrum DSM 467 efficiently oxidized CO from syngas via the water–gas shift reaction, displaying hierarchical substrate utilization driven by energetic constraints. In contrast, Marichromatium purpuratum simultaneously oxidized H2 and thiosulfate (S2O32–), enabling parallel electron input into the photosynthetic electron transport chain and enhanced growth. Overall, these results establish PPB as robust and metabolically flexible biocatalysts for converting CO2 and industrial waste streams into high-value chemicals with direct applications in the pharmaceutical and nutraceutical industries.

papers.title: Unveiling the Hidden Load: High Flux and Deposition Dynamics of Atmospheric Microplastics in the North China Plain
papers.abstract: Abstract Atmospheric microplastics (MPs) play an important role in the transport of MPs across diverse environmental media, yet their annual deposition dynamics across heterogeneous urban–cropland regions remain poorly understood. We conducted a one-year field campaign at three contrasting sites in the North China Plain (NCP): Beijing (BJ, urban), Tianjin (TJ, industrial/coastal), and Handan (HD, agricultural). Atmospheric bulk-deposition samples were characterized for particle deposition rates, size, morphology, and polymer composition, with observations evaluated using meteorological and land-cover information. Deposition rates were significantly higher in BJ than in TJ (p < 0.05) and HD (p < 0.001). Median (interquartile range) deposition rates were 34640 (18703–90472), 14367 (6000–25810), and 6990 (3903–11790) items m–2 d–1 in BJ, TJ, and HD, respectively. Small particles (20–50 μm) dominated particle abundance (80.7%), whereas fragments dominated particle morphology (90.4%). Backward trajectories indicated seasonal differences in potential air-mass transport pathways. Integrating particle mass estimates with land-cover data yielded order-of-magnitude estimates of annual atmospheric MP inputs of approximately 6 Gg to urban areas and 17 Gg to cropland in the northern NCP. These results reveal pronounced spatiotemporal variability in atmospheric MP deposition and highlight the dominance of small MP fragments across urban and cropland ecosystems.

papers.title: Examining associations of urban green-space greenness and net primary productivity with water quality using interpretable machine learning
Projecting climate-driven changes in climatic suitability of Dacus ciliatus Loew, 1862 (Diptera: Tephritidae): Implications for agricultural biosecurity
Tracking the evolution of urban resilience: A systematic review of research themes and trends over two decades
Optimising resource management in data-scarce environments: A modelling approach for Greater Cairo
papers.abstract: Pressing environmental challenges present significant obstacles to cities’ sustainable development and underscore the need for effective resource management. However, resource management studies often overlook or oversimplify the spatial and social dimensions of resource use, limiting their ability to target interventions to specific population groups and integrate them into urban planning. Addressing this requires disaggregated data that capture spatial variation and interdependencies between socio-economic factors and resource consumption. Yet such data are often scarce in Global South contexts, where data limitations frequently hinder meaningful resource management research. This research develops a hybrid multi-scale analysis framework that integrates Spatial Microsimulation, Multi-Scale Geographically Weighted Regression (MGWR), and Geodemographic Classification to help researchers address data limitations and generate policy-relevant insights. The framework offers three contributions: methodological, empirical, and policy translation. The research provides the first systematic, household-level analysis of food-water-energy consumption patterns across Greater Cairo. Spatial microsimulation creates robust synthetic household datasets by integrating multiple surveys, while MGWR reveals spatially varying drivers of consumption. The geodemographic classification delivers the first empirically grounded typology of Greater Cairo households based on demographic, socio-economic, and consumption characteristics. Lastly, the applied probability-based allocation of clusters to neighbourhoods offers an indicative tool for exploring differentiated tariff structures and area-specific demand management, validated through expert workshops. By addressing Greater Cairo’s data limitations, the framework offers a replicable approach for other cities facing similar constraints, supporting the transition to evidence-based, spatially differentiated resource management in the Global South.

papers.title: Optimal Flood Insurance in a Second-Best World: Fiscal Spillovers, Reclassification Risk, and Moral Hazard
papers.abstract: Abstract Intensifying climate change makes protection against natural disaster risk – either through ex ante insurance or ex post aid – a first-order public policy issue. Flood risk protection in the U.S. traditionally featured ex post aid through FEMA and heavily subsidized insurance through the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP). In an effort to correct subsidy-induced overbuilding and under-mitigation in flood-prone areas, the NFIP recently moved to actuarially fair insurance premiums. But this change has two unintended consequences: a fiscal spillover onto FEMA disaster aid as insurance coverage declines in flood-prone areas, and household exposure to uninsurable reclassification risk from uncertain climate projections. We develop a model of optimal flood insurance that incorporates the static and dynamic tradeoffs of subsidizing premiums. We then use a variety of identification strategies and data to estimate the five key parameters needed to implement this model. We find that the fiscal spillover and reclassification risk protection benefits significantly outweigh the moral hazard costs, and that the optimal subsidy to flood insurance is 51%, comparable to the level of subsidization before the recent reform.

papers.title: How New Products Enter Markets: Social Networks, Consumer Imports, and Retailer Learning
papers.abstract: Abstract This paper studies how new varieties enter markets and become locally available. We provide causal evidence of demand externalities that operate in two steps. First, information about new varieties diffuses directly through real-world social ties among consumers. Second, early purchases generate an indirect spillover to firms: local retailers learn from “pioneer” consumers which new varieties are most likely to succeed and adjust their product offerings accordingly. We study this process in the context of direct-to-consumer imports. Using customs records on individuals’ purchases matched to population-wide social networks, international migrant links, and retailer catchment areas, we document economically meaningful demand externalities. Product-specific expenditure shocks abroad transmit through migrant networks and shift which varieties consumers purchase. Leveraging these shocks as a plausibly exogenous source of local demand variation, we show strong peer effects: prior purchases by close neighbors, coworkers, or friends increase an individual’s likelihood of purchasing the same variety, especially for premium and visible goods. We leverage this result to identify an indirect spillover from consumers to firms: retailers are more likely to add a variety to their assortment when it becomes popular among consumers in their catchment area. Combining the instrument with linked consumer–retailer data and a self-conducted retailer survey, we show that this response reflects learning about latent demand for varieties not yet stocked locally. Together, social diffusion and retailer learning generate demand multipliers that reshape local product availability and expand access to global variety.

papers.title: Cognitive ability, risk preferences and errors
papers.abstract: Abstract In this paper we examine the link between cognitive ability, risk preferences and the errors that people make. We build a unique dataset that contains almost 260,000 decisions made under risk in a variety of tasks by approximately 13,000 individuals, with each person having completed a test designed explicitly to measure their cognitive ability. Our analysis suggests that intelligence has (1) no impact on risk preferences and (2) a robust link to errors. Our results have implications for the development of theories that seek to explain the impact of cognitive ability on decision making.

papers.title: Europe at the crossroads: trading strategic autonomy for resilience under degrowth
Chinese and Russian nuclear energy companies in Europe’s geoeconomic turn: giving way to the Americans?
Natural resource management strategies of nature-based tourism firms
Biased by sustainability? How cognitive biases shape procurement decisions under information equivocality
papers.abstract: Purpose Climate change introduces new informational asymmetries across supply chains, increasing managers' need to process sustainability-related information in procurement decisions. Such information is equivocal, making its interpretation challenging and increasing decision-makers’ susceptibility to cognitive biases. Building on organizational information-processing theory and behavioral decision-making research, this study examines how cognitive biases shape procurement decisions involving sustainability information. Design/methodology/approach We developed hypotheses on cognitive biases emerging from three characteristics of sustainability information: structural properties (risky choice framing, attribute framing, numeracy and anchoring), inferential dynamics (halo effect) and social influences (herd effect). We tested these hypotheses through between-subject vignette-based experiments depicting individual, one-shot procurement decisions. The experiments were conducted in person with 475 participants, including managers and students. Findings We found that sustainability-oriented procurement decisions are vulnerable to cognitive biases. In particular, biases induced by the structural properties of information produced the strongest effects across both managers and students, followed by distortions emerging from inferential dynamics. In contrast, socially driven distortions emerged only among students, suggesting that professional experience mitigates reliance on peer behavior. Originality/value This study extends organizational information-processing theory-based sustainable supply chain management research by demonstrating that individual-level cognitive biases shape the interpretation of sustainability information. In doing so, we characterize the interpretation stage as being sensitive to information architecture, inferential reasoning and, under conditions of social influence, the professional experience of the decision-maker. Finally, we provide guidance for designing sustainability information and procurement decision processes that reduce susceptibility to cognitive biases.

Direct Evidence for Carbon Monoxide-to-Dioxin Conversion via Fly-Ash-Catalyzed Sequential Reactions in Incineration Flue Gas
papers.abstract: Abstract The formation of polychlorinated dibenzo-p-dioxins and dibenzofurans (PCDD/Fs) in industrial thermal processes is traditionally attributed to solid carbon precursors via de novo synthesis. Carbon monoxide (CO), despite serving as an operational indicator of incomplete combustion, has not been directly implicated as a molecular carbon source for dioxin generation. Here, we provide definitive experimental and mechanistic evidence that CO can be catalytically converted into dioxins and dioxin-like compounds through a sequential reaction network mediated by fly ash. Using fixed-bed reactors packed with real fly ash, we isolate CO, H2O, and HCl as minimal reactants to reconstruct flue-gas chemistry. Transition metal species (Cu, Fe) in fly ash catalyze CO conversion via a coupled water–gas shift and Fischer–Tropsch-type process, generating a wide spectrum of aliphatic and aromatic hydrocarbons. Concurrently, fly ash mediates HCl oxidation to active Cl2, enabling chlorination of these intermediates into chlorobenzenes and chlorophenols, which subsequently evolve into polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs), polychlorinated naphthalenes (PCNs), and ultimately PCDD/Fs. Notably, Cl4–8DD/F congeners account for >90% of the formed PCDD/Fs, consistent with de novo synthesis signatures. This work establishes a new mechanistic paradigm for dioxin generation and highlights CO emission control as a critical lever for mitigating toxic pollutant generation.

Human activities aggravate silicon limitation risks in floodplain lakes: Evidence from the sub-lakes of Poyang Lake
papers.abstract: The biogeochemical coupling of silicon (Si) and carbon (C) in floodplain lakes has been increasingly disrupted by human activities, yet the mechanisms and trajectories of this decoupling remain poorly constrained. Here we present well-dated sediment records of biogenic silica (BSi) and associated geochemical proxies spanning the past century from three sub-lakes of Poyang Lake to fill this knowledge gap. Despite divergent BSi-content trajectories shaped by the contrasting hydrological settings among these sub-lakes, BSi/TOC mass ratios consistently reveal a systematic transition from coupled Si-C cycling toward decoupling. This transition intensified following dam construction in the 1950s-1960s and the acceleration of anthropogenic nutrient loading from the 1980s onward. Random forest modeling further reveals that following damming and eutrophication, catchment erosion and nutrient enrichment ranked as the strongest positive and negative predictors of BSi/TOC variation, respectively, with these associations strengthening as hydrological connectivity to the main lake declined. Furthermore, the decreased BSi/TOC ratios during the decoupling phase indicate possible silicon limitation and are consistent with increased inputs of non-siliceous algae. Because dam-driven silica retention and nutrient enrichment co-occur in many regulated rivers and lakes elsewhere, the risk of Si-C decoupling merits evaluation well beyond Poyang Lake, with implications for freshwater carbon sink assessments.

papers.abstract: Abstract Since the 2000s, U.S. public pension funds have actively shifted their risky investments away from public equities and toward alternative assets like private equity and hedge funds—some much more than others. We explore a range of possible explanations for these trends and argue that beliefs about the risk-adjusted return of alternatives have played a central role. Pension beliefs are shaped by investment consultants, peers, and experience in the 1990s. Other demand-side channels related to risk-seeking motives, spending needs, and fund governance have weaker empirical support. We also consider supply-side factors and agency interpretations of the data. (JEL G11, G23, G41, H75)

Matching Function Equilibria with Partial Assignment: Existence, Uniqueness and Estimation
papers.abstract: We argue that models coming from a variety of fields, such as matching models and discrete choice models among others, share a common structure that we call matching function equilibria with partial assignment. This structure includes an aggregate matching function and a system of nonlinear equations. We provide a proof of existence and uniqueness of an equilibrium and propose an efficient algorithm to compute it. For a subclass of matching models, we also develop a new parameter-free approach for constructing the counterfactual matching equilibrium. It has the advantage of not requiring parametric estimation when computing counterfactuals. We use our procedure to analyze the impact of the elimination of the Social Security Student Benefit Program in 1982 on the marriage market in the United States. We estimate several candidate models from our general class of matching functions and select the best fitting model using information based criterion.

Crime and Prices:Thefts of expensive precious metals from cars
papers.abstract: Whether economic incentives matter for crime is studied in a novel way, from expensive precious metal thefts by thieves stealing catalytic converters from cars. Sharp and sizable variations in the prices of precious metals embedded in converters are combined with newly assembled U.S. crime data. Precipitously fast increases in precious metal prices generated a sizeable rise in auto-part thefts, while subsequent price declines and policy responses quickly reversed this pattern. The resulting boom-and-bust dynamics provide clean evidence that prices affect crime, and for these crimes that local resale infrastructure and target availability shape both the magnitude of this effect and the effectiveness of policy response.

Concentration and convergence: Regional productivity in Türkiye, 1950–2020
papers.abstract: Abstract This paper presents a comprehensive long‐run analysis of regional productivity convergence in Türkiye using a novel dataset combining newly compiled employment estimates with recent output estimates. The seven‐decade analysis reveals substantial productivity convergence driven by labour reallocation away from agriculture alongside within‐industry convergence. A distinctive pattern emerges: aggregate economic concentration proceeded together with productivity convergence, with distinct regional clusters forming. Furthermore, shift‐share decomposition shows industry‐mix effects persistently explain significant regional productivity variation, reflecting sustained agriculture‐other sectors productivity differences, with western regions enjoying both favourable sectoral composition and regional competitiveness advantages. From a policy perspective, agricultural productivity improvements offer significant potential for reducing regional disparities.

papers.title: The Effect of Red Scare Propaganda on U.S. Public Opinion: Evidence from the Newspapers of William Randolph Hearst
papers.abstract: Could anti-redistributive sentiment have long-run roots in Red Scare-era propaganda? In the 1930s and 40s, the media mogul William Randolph Hearst espoused vehement anti-communist rhetoric in his newspapers. Fears of socialism went head-to-head with FDR’s New Deal, the first wide-scale federal spending program. Using variation in newspaper penetration across U.S. counties, I show that an increase of 10 percentage points in Hearst circulation per capita decreased support for FDR by 2.1 percentage points. I also show evidence that these effects are long run, decreasing support for public healthcare and welfare programs through the late twentieth century.

papers.title: Borrowed plumes: the gender gap in claiming credit for teamwork
The impact of LLM-based recommendations on decisions under uncertainty
papers.abstract: Abstract We study how large language model (LLM) based recommendations affect evaluations of uncertainty. We elicit certainty equivalents for (i) lotteries that share the same reduced-form winning probability but vary in cognitive demands because they are compound, and (ii) an Ellsberg-style ambiguous lottery. Across all lottery types, valuations from participants who receive LLM-based recommendations before each valuation exhibit second-order stochastic dominance relative to valuations from participants who do not. Hence, LLM-based recommendations leave mean valuations unchanged but compress the distribution, reducing the incidence of extreme valuations. Consistent with this pattern, LLM-based recommendations reduce the intensity of risk, complexity, and ambiguity aversion, while leaving the fraction of participants classified as averse unchanged.

papers.title: The incidence and distributional effects of electric vehicle subsidies in China
Identifying the impact of exposure to armed conflict on individual preferences and field behavior: Evidence from Turkish draft Veterans
papers.abstract: Building on a population-level natural experiment, this study identifies the causal impact of exposure to armed conflict in a combatant role on risk, ambiguity and time preferences and related field behaviors for the average adult male randomly picked from the target population. Our setting allows us to analyze the difference in preferences without confoundment by community-level effects of conflict. Those exposed exhibit higher risk tolerance, ambiguity neutrality, patience and time consistency. We also find exposure leads to an increase in entrepreneurial activity but has no significant effect on risky health behaviors, and that elevated agency partially accounts for these shifts. Taken together, these patterns indicate that combat exposure alters preferences in ways that are not inherently positive or negative for economic welfare; what matters is how such preferences are expressed. Our results suggest agency as one potential channel through which exposure shapes this expression, making it more constructive than maladaptive in this setting.

papers.title: Financialization of Bitcoin: Spot ETFs and Futures Pricing Efficiency
papers.abstract: Does Bitcoin behave like a currency asset and is it becoming more integrated into financial markets? To answer this, we investigate whether financialization can be identified in the futures market around the introduction of exchange-traded funds (ETFs) using Markov switching models, Fama–French regression tests and structural break analysis. We conduct an event-based analysis of the implicit yield [r*]—an interest rate equivalent measure that includes the convenience yield and risk premiums specific to Bitcoin. Using data from December 11, 2017, to March 14, 2025, we study regulatory regime shifts around the launch of both futures and spot-based ETFs. We observe that ETFs impact volatility, information efficiency and institutional participation. While theory suggests that such instruments should improve market efficiency and reduce speculative frictions, our findings challenge this view. Our results, using Fama’s regression tests, showed weak forecasting power. This suggests an element of market inefficiency as well as that Bitcoin futures market prices are currently driven largely by speculative flows. That said, certain evidence shows that the introduction of ETFs marks the early stages of financialization.

papers.title: Globalised but divided: European corporations and the EU’s geoeconomic turn against China
papers.abstract: The European Union’s ‘geoeconomic turn’ against China is hotly debated among international political economy scholars, but the role of Europe’s leading corporations in this shift remains underexplored. This article focuses on the European Round Table for Industry, an elite forum of corporate executives tightly connected to the European Commission. The ERT played a key role in aligning European integration with corporate interests from the 1980s to 2000s. However, it has fallen out of step with the European Commission, whose posture has hardened since branding China a ‘systemic rival’. The disjuncture between the Commission’s assertive stance and the ERT’s more tentative approach to China prompts us to test and rethink what we know about state-business relations in a new geoeconomic age. Drawing on data under-used in IPE to chart ERT firms’ ‘territorial’ and ‘network integration’ with China, our analysis reveals a significant minority of firms deeply integrated into the Chinese market and supplier base, a small group of firms with minimal ties potentially receptive to the EU’s ‘geoeconomic turn’, and a large array of partially integrated companies in between these two positions. This uneasy balance of forces within the ERT explains why it is trailing rather than driving the EU’s stance.

papers.title: Corporate Tax Changes and Credit Costs
papers.abstract: Abstract We examine changes in the state corporate tax rate across the U.S. and their implications on the pricing and quantity of loans. We find that the cost of credit decreases by approximately 10 basis points following a tax cut. When we account for the magnitude of tax changes, a one‐percentage‐point tax cut (hike) is associated with a 10.5 (9.2) basis‐point decrease (increase) in loan spreads. Our findings mainly originate from the demand side: large firms are able to mitigate the effects of tax increases, while less profitable firms experience larger reductions in borrowing costs following tax cuts. The effect on the equilibrium loan amount is statistically and economically insignificant, consistent with a weak supply effect and an inelastic loan supply curve.

papers.title: The Economics of Data Unions: Optimal Data Sharing and Coordination
papers.abstract: Abstract We develop a model of data-driven competition in which product quality depends on users’ data contributions and firms’ investments in data infrastructure. Users’ inability to internalize the value generated by their data, together with firms’ strategic investment incentives, can lead to data underinvestment—limiting quality—or overinvestment—concentrating market power. We introduce a data union that coordinates users’ contributions and can be implemented through a data trust or intermediary that aggregates user data. By shaping data compensation, the union enables users to capture and internalize more of their data’s value, enhancing user welfare, especially when combined with data sharing among firms. We apply these insights to financial data, digital payments, and Open Finance. Our analysis shows that data portability can strengthen competition but, without coordination, may leave data investment too low or excessive.

papers.title: EXPRESS: The Dark Side of Competition for Market Share: Competitive Pressure May Trigger Corporate Misconduct
papers.abstract: There is an ongoing debate about the role of market share and market share–based competition in shaping corporate behavior and performance. This study advances the discussion by analyzing how a firm’s specific competitive situation drives corporate misconduct and how such misconduct affects future market share. Based on a theory-in-use approach, the authors propose the Theory of Market Share–Based Competitive Pressure (TMCP) and introduce four new market share–based constructs that reflect different dimensions of competitive pressure. Using a global sample of 2,145 firms across 254 industries over 11 years, they find that firms that are closer to market leadership and more closely followed by competitors are more prone to misconduct. The results demonstrate that misconduct systematically weakens the very market positions that created the pressure in the first place, with particularly strong penalties for environmental and governance–related misconduct incidents. Importantly, organizational characteristics such as compensation design, board composition, and marketing capabilities condition the extent to which competition translates into corporate misconduct. Together, these findings demonstrate that while misconduct may appear as a shortcut to defend competitive positions, it ultimately undermines them, and there are ways to reduce incentives for misconduct in the first place.

papers.title: “Borrowing intelligence to build a business”: The promise of open‐source AI for entrepreneurship
