Fiscal accountability: Institutional discipline and behavioral frictions
Motherhood and Constraints during Job Search
papers.abstract: Abstract Why do women’s labour earnings drop upon motherhood? We shed new light on this question by analysing the changes in job search behaviour associated with motherhood. We exploit data on the job applications sent on a popular online platform linked with administrative registers for 350,000 involuntarily unemployed workers in France. After losing their job, mothers have a 11.7% lower probability to find a job than similar women without children and send 12.2% fewer job applications. To explore the underlying mechanisms, we analyse the timing of job applications. Unlike other women, mothers’ rate of applications decreases by about 20.5% in the hours when there is no school. Moreover, the French reform that introduced school on Wednesday in 2014 led mothers to send more applications on Wednesdays. Our results highlight that childcare creates constraints on the timing of job search activities for mothers. We finally provide suggestive evidence that these constraints decrease their return-to-search, and thereby contribute to their lower application and job finding rates.

papers.title: Welfare Expenditure Growth and its Impact on Elderly Suicide Rates
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT We investigate the causal effect of increased elderly welfare expenditure in South Korea on the suicide rate among older adults, using predicted expenditure changes induced by the Basic Pension reform as an instrumental variable. Our findings show that higher welfare spending explains 74.5% of the decline in the suicide rate among individuals aged 65+ between 2013 and 2019, with especially large reductions among men aged 80+. Household‐level evidence indicates that while total income remained stable, consumption increased following the reform, particularly in transportation and leisure. We further show that the reform reduced unmet medical needs and stress and increased participation in community and leisure activities, while leaving depressive symptoms unchanged. Overall, the results are consistent with the interpretation that stronger public income transfer programs reduce income uncertainty and expand opportunities for consumption, leisure, and social participation, thereby contributing to lower elderly suicide rates.

papers.title: On Bank Pricing of Single‐Family Residential Home Loans: Are Australian Households Paying Too Much?
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT This paper examines the persistent divergence between observed mortgage rates and a capital‐market‐implied benchmark in the Australian residential housing finance market. Using quarterly data from 1998 to 2025, we construct a synthetic variable‐rate mortgage benchmark based on fixed‐rate mortgage yields, interest rate swaps, and swaptions to isolate fundamental funding costs and embedded interest rate risk. We estimate an autoregressive distributed lag (ARDL) model to decompose the spread between observed and benchmark rates into risk‐based pricing and sluggish pass‐through. The empirical evidence reveals a large and persistent long‐run spread. On average, mortgage rates exceed the synthetic benchmark by approximately 146 basis points, widening to more than 240 basis points during periods of elevated credit risk. This divergence reflects not only risk‐based pricing but also incomplete and delayed pass‐through, consistent with structural market power in Australia's concentrated banking system. As a result, mortgage rates adjust slowly to changes in capital‐market conditions. The persistence of this spread has important economic implications. By raising mortgage rates relative to their capital‐market benchmark, these pricing frictions increase the income required to qualify for homeownership, thereby exacerbating affordability constraints in an already highly leveraged housing market.

papers.title: What Interruptions Say About Your Organizational Culture
papers.abstract: Recent research suggests that interruptions when meeting attendees are speaking are significant moments that affect how employees experience workplace culture and can lead to self-censoring. Taking a different approach to meeting facilitation can help leaders become more aware of when this is occurring so that they can improve participant dynamics, encourage meeting attendees to contribute, and more effectively respond to interruptions.

papers.title: Sustainability Indicators and Product Diversification: An Exploratory Predictive Assessment
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines whether carbon footprint, eco‐friendly manufacturing and recycling programmes help predict recorded product‐line count, used as a limited indicator of product diversification. Using the records from a sustainability dataset, we apply exploratory predictive modelling with linear regression, random forest and gradient boosting. We evaluate sustainability‐only, context‐only and combined models against a training‐mean benchmark using a held‐out sample and fivefold cross‐validation. Adding sustainability information improves some predictions beyond price, country, year and market trend but offers little consistent advantage over simply predicting the average product‐line count. The study contributes by showing the difference between improving a model and providing useful predictions of product‐range size. Uncertain corporate provenance and undocumented product‐line definitions prevent broader conclusions about sustainability's effects on strategic diversification or stakeholder value.

papers.title: Carbon Risk and Syndicated Loans: A Network Analysis Approach
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT As the transition to a low‐carbon economy accelerates, understanding how climate‐related risks propagate through the financial system has become a central concern for regulators and researchers alike. Transition risk—the risk arising from the shift toward lower‐emission business models—is not directly borne by banks but may indirectly affect financial intermediaries through their lending portfolios. As firms face increasing pressure to comply with climate regulations, their credit risk increases, potentially threatening the stability of the broader financial system. This study examines how carbon emissions are financed by financial institutions in the syndicated loan market and whether a bank's structural position in that market is associated with its exposure to transition risk. Using a sample of 6924 syndicated loans from DealScan for 2018, we constructed a directed weighted network of lenders and borrowers and computed three financed emissions metrics calibrated on equivalent data from Eikon and financial data from Orbis. Network centrality measures—including eigenvector, betweenness, and degree centrality—are then correlated with each metric. The results show that more central financial intermediaries are positively and significantly associated with higher shares of financed emissions across all centrality measures, with correlations of the order of 60%. Replicating the analysis on the 2025 vintage of the network yields consistent results, indicating that this association is a stable structural feature of the syndicated loan market rather than an artifact of a single year. Several robustness checks confirm the main findings. The results are relevant for both lenders and borrowers as well as regulators, given the results' systemic implications.

papers.title: Measuring What Matters: Constructing an ESG Controversy Index Using AI and Institutional ESG Frameworks
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) controversies increasingly influence investment decisions, corporate accountability, and sustainability regulation. However, existing commercial controversy measures often rely on proprietary methodologies that limit transparency and make it difficult to understand how controversy assessments are generated. This paper aims to develop an ESG Controversy Index (ESGCI) that combines internationally recognised ESG principles with explainable artificial intelligence to provide a systematic approach to measuring firm‐level ESG controversy exposure. The ESGCI is constructed from more than 5000 annual and sustainability reports issued by S&P 500 firms between 2010 and 2023, together with ESG doctrines published by the United Nations, the Principles for Responsible Investment, the Organisation for Economic Co‐operation and Development and the International Labour Organisation. Natural language processing and supervised machine‐learning techniques are used to identify, classify and aggregate ESG controversies within a structured measurement framework. The proposed index is evaluated through a multi‐layer validation strategy incorporating conceptual assessment, document‐level out‐of‐sample testing, external comparison with Refinitiv ESG controversy measures, inter‐rater reliability, incremental validity and complementary robustness analyses. The findings show that the ESGCI captures controversy‐related information recognised by existing commercial measures while providing additional insights through a fully documented measurement process. The reported relationships remain consistent across alternative weighting schemes, lagged specifications and instrumental‐variable estimations, supporting the robustness of the empirical evidence. Rather than replacing existing ESG controversy ratings, the ESGCI offers a complementary approach that improves methodological transparency and facilitates reproducible ESG controversy measurement. By integrating institutional ESG principles with explainable AI and comprehensive validation procedures, this research seeks to contribute to the advancement of ESG measurement and provide a practical foundation for future research, investment analysis and sustainability reporting.

papers.title: Fair Business Models for Climate‐Smart Agriculture: A Design Science Research Approach
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Organisations in agri‐food value chains face urgent demands to address climate change, environmental degradation and social inequities through climate‐smart agriculture (CSA). However, sustained CSA implementation remains constrained by business models (BMs) that fail to offer fair solutions to stakeholders. Existing business model innovation (BMI) literature lacks conceptualisation of fair BMs and methodology for operationalising fairness in BMs, leading to the research question: How can fair BMs for CSA be defined, designed and developed? Using design science research across five European case studies, the study defines a fair BM as a BM in which the design of the value proposition, creation, delivery and capture enables equitable value distribution, inclusive processes, transparency of information and respectful relationships among stakeholders. The study operationalises fairness across the BMI process with stakeholder engagement and change management, deriving eight design requirements and thirteen stakeholder‐validated prototypes. The study advances BMI literature by offering prescriptive knowledge for operationalising fairness in agri‐food BMI.

Multiheme c -Type Cytochrome-Dependent Arsenate Reduction Enhances Methanogenesis in Methanosarcina acetivorans
papers.abstract: Abstract Microorganism-mediated arsenate (As(V)) reduction plays a critical role in arsenic mobility and microbial adaptation in arsenic-contaminated anoxic environments. Current understanding of microbial As(V) reduction has primarily focused on two pathways: extracellular reduction mediated by membrane-bound As(V) respiratory reductase, and intracellular reduction catalyzed by cytoplasmic As(V) detoxification reductase. Here, we report an extracellular As(V) reduction process that operates independently of both known As(V) reductases and is mediated by methanogenic archaea that are recognized for obligate methanogenesis across diverse anoxic habitats. We demonstrate that a model methanogenic archaeon is capable of concurrently performing intracellular methanogenesis and extracellular As(V) reduction, with the latter process significantly enhancing methanogenic growth. Through a combination of microbial physiological, biochemical, and molecular genetic approaches, we identify multiheme c-type cytochromes (MHCs), which are widely distributed within the order Methanosarcinales and have been previously implicated in extracellular iron reduction, as the key molecular components responsible for extracellular As(V) reduction. Furthermore, employing density functional theory simulations, we propose plausible reduction pathways for As(V) reduction mediated by the heme prosthetic groups of MHCs and confirm their thermodynamic feasibility. This work not only provides new insights into the previously overlooked coupling between arsenic transformation and methanogenesis in anoxic environments on Earth, but also underscores the interconnected nature of iron and As(V) reduction, both of which can be mediated by MHCs.

papers.title: Influence of Urban Form, Weather and Population on Outdoor Airborne Infection Risk: Implications in Greater London for SARS-CoV-2
papers.abstract: Abstract Although airborne infectious disease transmission outdoors is possible, particularly in densely built urban areas with limited ventilation, the role of urban morphology and neighborhood climate heterogeneity in modulating the risk remains poorly quantified. We couple an urban climate model (SUEWS) and a modified Wells-Riley framework to develop a transferable neighborhood-scale approach for mapping outdoor airborne infection risk across morphologically diverse neighborhoods, factoring in urban form, population distribution and meteorologically driven viral infectivity decay. We demonstrate this framework by applying it to SARS-CoV-2 in Greater London. Considering outdoor urban ventilation alone, estimated risk follows a diurnal cycle and peaks at night. Including population distribution, daytime risk in busy commercial centers is up to 7.23 times higher than nighttime. Infectivity decay from ultraviolet B (UVB) exposure reduces risk by 35–45% in less dense areas and up to 99% in high built-density neighborhoods. Despite this mitigation, the highest risks persist in high-rise, high-workplace-density districts (e.g., City of London and Westminster), while lower-rise areas (e.g., Lambeth and Croydon) exhibit reductions exceeding 90%. For SARS-CoV-2, these findings demonstrate strong intraurban heterogeneity in outdoor airborne infection risk in Greater London. More broadly, the transferable framework supports high-resolution mapping to inform targeted, place-based public health interventions.

papers.title: Substantial Emerging Impact of Amine-Based Carbon Capture on Atmospheric Particle Formation under Carbon Neutrality
papers.abstract: Abstract Carbon capture (CC) is indispensable to carbon neutrality, and amine-based absorption using monoethanolamine (MEA) is among the most mature CC technologies. MEA can enhance atmospheric new particle formation (NPF), the primary source of atmospheric particles. However, the atmospheric impacts of MEA escaping from future large-scale CC deployment remain unknown. Here, we develop a three-dimensional model that represents MEA sources, sinks, and H2SO4-MEA nucleation based on quantum chemical and cluster dynamics calculations, to evaluate atmospheric MEA and its impacts from CC deployment at China’s coal-fired power plants under carbon-neutrality scenarios. By 2060, even moderate CC deployment raises atmospheric MEA concentrations to tens of pptv, exceeding dimethylamine (DMA), the canonical urban NPF agent. H2SO4-MEA nucleation consequently overtakes H2SO4-DMA nucleation across extensive CC-deployment regions (∼1 million km2) and is more than 10 times stronger within the CC-intensive core (∼0.2 million km2), raising particle number concentrations by 50–187% and exposing ∼430 million people to levels exceeding the WHO high-exposure benchmark. The associated rise in ultrafine particles is estimated to cause ∼34,800 additional deaths across China in 2060. We reveal that CC deployment may deliver climate benefits while inadvertently worsening particulate pollution and public-health burdens, warranting proactive and early preventive action.

papers.title: Perinatal elimination of genetically aberrant human cortical neurons
papers.abstract: Abstract Human neurons are postmitotic and long-lived, requiring precise genomic regulation. Normal neuronal function is highly dosage-sensitive, with copy number variants (CNVs) and heterozygous point mutations associated with a host of neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric conditions 1–4 . Here we investigated somatic CNVs arising in single neurons to understand the dynamic processes that shape the normal neuronal genetic landscape. Altogether, we sequenced 2,357 single neurons from human postmortem brain from fetal to postnatal life. Two single-cell whole-genome sequencing approaches—Tn5-transposase-based amplification (1,526 neurons, 16 individuals) and primary template amplification 5 (831 neurons, 12 individuals)—showed that an average of 25.9% [12.7–46%] of prenatal cortical neurons have highly aberrant genomes, that is, widespread CNVs involving multiple chromosomes. This proportion reduced by about 4.5-fold after birth across the two single-cell whole-genome sequencing approaches (Fisher meta-analysis P = 3.5 × 10 − 6 ). Neurons with widespread CNVs were mainly eliminated perinatally, timed roughly parallel to periods of programmed cell death 6 , whereas neurons with smaller CNV burdens declined slowly in frequency with postnatal age. CNVs in surviving neurons were depleted for dosage-sensitive genes and genes involved in neurodevelopmental disorders (hypergeometric test P < 0.05), suggesting selective elimination of neurons with these CNVs. Analysis of 44,861 nuclei with single-nucleus assay for transposase-accessible chromatin (snATAC) and single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) showed that neurons with high CNV burdens exhibited abnormal synaptic gene expression, suggesting that abnormal synaptic gene regulation contributes to neuronal elimination. Elimination of defective neuronal genomes might represent an important developmental genome quality-control process that may be vulnerable in neurodevelopmental disease, and suggests purifying selection during human neurodevelopment.

papers.title: Connectome simulations identify a central pattern generator for fly walking
Monolithically and in situ integrated PbS infrared imagers
Tumour assembloids recapitulate tumour–CAF–T cell crosstalk in renal cancer
papers.abstract: Abstract Dynamic interactions between tumours and their microenvironment are crucial for cancer progression and therapeutic outcomes 1,2 . However, our understanding of these relationships remains limited by the constrained capacity of current human model systems to manipulate diverse cellular components and to interrogate complex tumour–stroma crosstalk. Here we generated combinatorial, mix-and-match tumour assembloids by conditionally reconstituting multiple components of human renal cell carcinoma, including cancer cells, cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) and tumour-infiltrating immune cells. Using genetically engineered renal cell carcinoma assembloids with humanized mouse models, we uncovered mechanisms by which CAFs coordinate interactions between tumour cells and CD8 + T cells to maintain non-cell-autonomous CD8 + T cell stemness and drive responsiveness to anti-PD-1 therapy. These interactions operate through a tumour–CAF–T cell signalling axis in which tumour-derived WNT induces CAF expression of activin A, which enhances CD8 + T cell stemness and sensitivity to PD-1 blockade. In non-responders, we also identified a subset of WNT-unresponsive CAFs that do not produce activin A, which leads to impaired CD8 + T cell stemness and resistance to therapy. Together, these findings establish a tumour–CAF–T cell axis as a key determinant of heterogeneous responses to immune checkpoint inhibitors. Moreover, tumour assembloids provide a versatile platform for mechanistic dissection of the tumour microenvironment and evaluation of personalized immunotherapy strategies.

papers.title: Emotion regulation capacity lacks a shared neural signature
papers.abstract: Abstract Cognitive reappraisal refers to changing how one thinks about a situation to alter its emotional impact. It is central to well-being 1 and engages prefrontal regulatory circuits 2 , prompting the assumption that their activity reflects a person’s capacity to regulate emotions 3–5 . Yet evidence for this assumption remains inconclusive and has not been established at scale. Here we analysed 40 task-based functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) datasets in a preregistered consortium with 2,175 participants and show that three widely used indicators of reappraisal capacity—trait questionnaires, task-based affective ratings and amygdala down-regulation—do not converge on a common core. Moreover, none of the three indicators showed the expected association with canonical prefrontal regulatory circuits. Trait questionnaires showed no detectable neural associations across the brain and task-based affective ratings were instead associated with responses in the amygdala and sensorimotor cortices. At the process level, canonical control circuits were engaged during both emotion generation and reappraisal, challenging their presumed specificity for emotion regulation. These findings caution against using activation in putatively regulatory brain regions to infer how well a person regulates emotions, with implications for neural biomarkers, interventions and psychoeducation that link emotion regulation difficulties to specific regional brain deficits.

papers.title: Molecular underpinnings of rheumatic diseases and emerging therapeutic concepts
Rare and common genetic variants shape single-cell immune gene expression
papers.abstract: . Here we describe phase 1 of TenK10K, which leverages single-cell RNA sequencing data from more than 5 million cells across 28 immune cell types, along with matched whole-genome sequencing data from 1,925 individuals. This provides power to detect associations for rare and low-frequency genetic variants that have largely been uncharacterized in their impact on cell-specific gene expression. We map the effects of both common and rare variants in a cell-type-specific manner using a recent method that increases power by modelling single cells directly rather than aggregated 'pseudobulk' counts. We identify putative common regulatory variants for 83% of all 21,404 genes tested and cumulative rare-variant signals for 47% of those genes. We explore how genetic effects vary across cell types and states, develop a framework to determine the degree of single-cell expression quantitative trait loci cell-type specificity and show that about half of the effects are observed only in one or a few cell types. By integrating our results with functional annotations and disease information, we further characterize the likely molecular modes of action for many disease-variant associations. Finally, we explore the effects that genetic variants have on gene expression across continuous cell states, and effects that vary cell-state abundance directly.

papers.title: Delayed electron–hole recombination in a pseudo-direct semiconductor
papers.abstract: Abstract Kirchhoff demonstrated the reciprocity between absorptivity and emissivity for blackbody radiation in 1860 (ref. 1 ), thereby establishing the general principle that a good absorber must also be a good emitter. This principle underpins the generalized Planck’s law 2 and, when applied to semiconductors—in the form of the van Roosbroeck–Shockley equation 3 —results in substantial limitations to solar energy conversion. Here we demonstrate how this reciprocity can be circumvented in semiconductors, such as bismuth sulfide, showing a pseudo-direct bandgap character—that is, featuring a lower-energy indirect transition paired with a direct transition placed a few k B T above. After determining the pseudo-direct bandgap nature of bismuth sulfide, we reveal how this feature substantially retards bimolecular electron–hole recombination in this material with respect to classic direct semiconductors 4 . The resulting combination of a high absorption coefficient and delayed recombination offers the unprecedented possibility of overcoming limitations associated with Planck’s law, with far-reaching potential for solar energy conversion.

papers.title: Stone and water governed early human settlement of the desert
papers.abstract: Abstract Models of early human dispersal rely on climate to predict where populations could settle, with freshwater assumed to govern the timing and geography 1,2 , particularly across the Saharo-Arabian arid belt, where humid windows episodically opened corridors into the desert interior 3 . Yet Pleistocene dispersals into ‘Green Arabia’ were brief and geographically constrained 4,5 , a pattern not explained by water availability alone. Here we show, from an approximately 1,500-km geoarchaeological survey through the Rub’ al Khali of Arabia, the largest sand sea in the world, that the availability of stone for tool manufacture operated as an independent factor on early human settlement. Palaeolake deposits were recorded at 55 of 125 localities investigated, yet no lithic artefacts and no knappable raw materials were found along the transect, with ground-surface visibility exceeding 95%, despite abundant freshwater and contemporary occupation at the desert margins. Spatial modelling of the Peninsula supports the inference that settlement tracked the co-occurrence of water and lithic raw materials rather than water alone. Across the Peninsula, 57% of water-accessible terrain lies on formations that lack knappable stone and adding raw-material availability raises discrimination of known site locations from an area under the curve of 0.695 to 0.768. Convergent patterns from Africa, North America and Asia indicate that the constraint is not peculiar to Arabia. Dispersal models that omit raw-material geology may systematically overestimate the habitable range of stone-tool-dependent populations.

papers.title: Narrow carbon pentaheptite nanoribbon as a covalent metal
A single-molecule spin–photon interface
papers.abstract: Abstract Optical interfaces that connect long-lived spin qubits to photons are a central requirement for quantum networking and distributed quantum information processing. At present, solid-state atomic defects are leading candidates because of their inherent spin and optical coherence 1,2 . Building on these advancements, synthetically tailored molecular systems represent a fundamental change in the field, using precise atomic control and consistent bottom-up assembly 3,4 . However, a molecular platform that concurrently satisfies the demands of a robust spin–photon interface—namely, the combination of bright fluorescence, high spectral stability and long ground-state spin lifetimes—has yet to be realized at the single-molecule level. Here we show that a triplet ground-state carbene molecule, embedded within a structurally matched host crystal, functions as a robust spin–photon interface with single-molecule addressability. The system exhibits narrow ZPLs, spectral stability over more than an hour, spin-selective optical transitions and single-molecule optically detected magnetic resonance. Coherent control yields millisecond-scale dynamical-decoupling coherence and tens-of-milliseconds spin relaxation at a temperature of 4.5 K. These results establish molecular qubits as a viable platform for single-emitter quantum optics 5,6 while preserving the advantages of bottom-up chemical design 7 and processable materials 8–10 .

papers.title: Subcycle videography of Landau–Zener–Majorana transitions in graphene
papers.abstract: Abstract Strong light fields have unlocked entirely new possibilities to tailor coherent electron trajectories, engineer band structures and shape emergent phases of matter all-optically 1–9 . Unravelling the underlying quantum mechanisms requires a visualization of the lightwave-driven electron motion 10,11 directly in the band structure. Although photoelectron momentum microscopy has imaged photoexcited electrons averaged over many cycles of light 12–19 , subcycle band-structure videography has been limited to small electron momenta 8,20 . Yet, lightwave-driven elementary processes in quantum materials often occur throughout momentum space. Here we introduce attosecond-precision, subcycle band-structure videography covering the entire first Brillouin zone and visualize one of the most fundamental but elusive strong-field processes: non-adiabatic Landau–Zener–Majorana tunnelling. The interplay of strong-field-driven acceleration within the Dirac-like band structure of graphene and periodic Landau–Zener–Majorana interband tunnelling manifests in a coherent subcycle displacement and distortion of the carrier distribution at the Brillouin zone edge. The extremely non-thermal electron distributions also allow us to disentangle competing scattering processes and assess their impact on coherent electronic control. Our panoramic view of field-driven electron motion enables a new quality of microscopic understanding of strong-field control of quantum materials.

papers.abstract: T cells. A graph neural network trained on both eQTL and caQTL layers inferred peak-gene links in unpaired multiome data with up to 17.2% higher accuracy than QTL-agnostic data, uncovering 128 additional transcription factor-target pairs (22% increase). Together, these results show that genetic variants shape chromatin accessibility in a cell-type-specific and cell-state-specific manner, influencing immune function and disease risk.

papers.title: SWI/SNF complexes shape 3D chromatin architecture through CTCF and cohesin
papers.abstract: Abstract The BAF (also known as mammalian SWI/SNF) chromatin remodelling complexes are essential regulators of nucleosome positioning and transcription factor binding 1,2 . Loss-of-function (LOF) mutations in genes encoding components of the BAF complexes are among the most frequent across cancer types 3 . However, a unifying mechanism that explains their widespread disruption remains unclear. Here we disrupted BAF function through pharmacological inhibition and ARID1A deletion across various mammalian cell types and tissues and observed a conserved chromatin response: increased accessibility at CTCF-binding sites. ARID1A LOF alone was sufficient to drive these changes, which demonstrates that canonical BAF (cBAF) disruption is the key driver of CTCF gain. Genomic profiling showed increased CTCF and SMC3 occupancy, which reveals an antagonistic relationship between cBAF and CTCF–cohesin complexes. Furthermore, cBAF loss restructured 3D genome organization, which led to a strengthening of topologically associating domain boundaries and subdivision of large domains into smaller insulated structures. Long-range enhancer–promoter loops were replaced by shorter, promoter-proximal loops anchored at CTCF-enriched sites. To determine how CTCF function is enabled following cBAF loss, we profiled CTCF-interacting cofactors and found that CTCF binds directly to fully assembled PBAF. After cBAF depletion, PBAF was recruited to sites of increased CTCF occupancy, which demonstrates that there is an antagonistic switch between SWI/SNF subcomplexes. In vivo, conditional Arid1a deletion in primary mouse cells resulted in the expansion of a highly proliferative population marked by elevated accessibility at CTCF sites. This phenotype was fully reversed by either Ctcf or Pbrm1 deletion, which establishes that cBAF and the activity of CTCF and PBAF have contrasting roles.

papers.title: T and B cells recognize splicing-derived neutrophil neoantigens in lupus
papers.abstract: Abstract Proteome diversity is generated through alternative mRNA splicing 1 . In tumours, mis-spliced transcripts that contain intronic sequences, skipped exons or noncanonical donor/acceptor splice junctions resulting in frameshifts are often translated into neoantigens that drive anti-tumour immunity 2,3 . Here we report that neutrophils from patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), unlike neutrophils from healthy donors or patients with rheumatoid arthritis, contain many aberrantly spliced gene transcripts, the translation of which was predicted to result in novel amino acid sequences that are absent in normal splice variants or any other proteins. Twenty-one peptides derived from these novel amino acid sequences were detected by mass spectrometry on class I major histocompatibility complex molecules in patient samples. Co-culture of T cells from patients with overlapping sets of 15-mer peptides from the novel sequences resulted in the expansion of CD4 + and CD8 + T cells that were rapidly reactivated to secrete interferon-γ. T cell antigen receptor sequencing and re-expression transferred neoantigen reactivity to a reporter T cell. Serum from patients with SLE also contained IgG autoantibodies that recognized epitopes within the novel amino acid sequences. Our findings demonstrate that dysregulated mRNA splicing in SLE neutrophils generates neoantigens that have caused T and B cell activation, clonal expansion, IgG class-switch and autoimmunity.

papers.title: Eukaryotes’ closest relatives are internally simple syntrophic peptidotrophic archaea
papers.abstract: Abstract Eukaryotes are theorized to have an origin associated with the archaeal phylum Promethearchaeota (formerly Asgard archaea) 1–3 . The first cultured representatives revealed valuable insights 4,5 but are still distantly related to eukaryotes, leaving many unknowns regarding eukaryogenesis. Here we report the isolation of two strains, HC1 and SC1, that belong to the archaeal lineage that branches closest to eukaryotes (Heimdallarchaeia); 6–8 these isolates are members of a pure co-culture and a tri-culture with methanogenic partners. Both are obligately anaerobic, syntrophic, peptide-degrading and mesophilic archaea that produce protrusions and vesicles but lack persistent internal membrane structures, like Promethearchaeales 4,5 . All Promethearchaeota isolates demonstrate behaviour focused on cell construction and membrane structures rather than division, in contrast to typical prokaryotes 9 . Strain HC1 possesses genes associated with aerobic lifestyles (such as cytochrome c oxidase (Cox)) but co-cultures cannot grow under (micro)oxic conditions. Meanwhile, the strain demonstrates growth under microoxic conditions when in the presence of aerobes, suggesting that Cox supports oxygen detoxification rather than respiration. Comparative genomics provides evidence that, like HC1, Cox-possessing Heimdallarchaeia studied to date probably do not respire oxygen. The wide conservation of anaerobiosis, cell structure without persistent intracellular membranes and membrane protrusions across Promethearchaeota suggest that the archaeal ancestor of eukaryotes may have had such physiological features. In this cultivation-informed scenario for eukaryogenesis, the archaea–eukaryote transition would involve a steep transition in cell structure and physiological shift from anaerobiosis to (facultative) aerobiosis 10 , with early interactions between the archaeal host and mitochondrial ancestor probably occurring under low-oxygen conditions and at least partially mediated by oxygen detoxification.

papers.title: Tandem repeat variation shapes immune cell type-specific gene expression
Pharmacological inhibition of METTL1 as a therapy against solid and blood cancers
papers.abstract: Abstract The N7-methylguanosine (m 7 G) modification is one of the most prevalent tRNA modifications, mainly catalysed by the METTL1–WDR4 protein complex 1–4 . The m 7 G methyltransferase METTL1 has been linked to oncogenic transformation and the maintenance of several aggressive malignancies; however, the clinical implications of therapeutically targeting a tRNA-modifying enzyme have not been established. Here we present the development and characterization of STM9005, a highly selective and potent first-in-class tRNA methyltransferase inhibitor of METTL1. Treatment of numerous cancer cell models (including leukaemia, melanoma, pancreatic carcinoma, oesophageal cancer and small cell lung carcinoma) with STM9005 blocks cell growth, causes differentiation changes and dysregulates cell cycle progression. These cellular effects were accompanied by a selective decrease in m 7 G on a subset of tRNAs and a reduction in their expression levels, which impacted the translation of oncogenic mRNAs. We show that pharmacological inhibition of METTL1 in vivo impairs tumour growth and significantly prolongs survival in multiple mouse cancer models of different tissue origin. Collectively, our results provide a strong proof of concept that targeting of tRNA methylation is a promising avenue of anti-cancer therapy and illustrate that catalytic inhibition of METTL1 represents a therapeutic strategy against a number of aggressive malignancies.

papers.title: Spatial and sectoral water demand assessment for the African continent
papers.abstract: Abstract Water demand is the volume of water required by a sector to satisfy its needs 1,2 . Across Africa, these demands are frequently unmet 3 , yet their spatial and sectoral distribution remains incompletely characterized, limiting informed water-management decisions 4 . Here, we provide an Africa-wide estimate of water demand for 2020 across six sectors and multiple subsectors at high spatial resolution. Because the analysis integrates heterogeneous datasets and modelling assumptions, the resulting values should be interpreted as harmonized estimates rather than direct observations of realized water use. We estimate total annual water demand at 347 km 3 , comprising 60 km 3 (17%) for municipalities (57–64 km 3 , with ±20% key parameters variations), 225 km 3 (65%) for irrigation (214–233 km 3 , 95% confidence interval, with ±20% variations in irrigation efficiency), 11 km 3 (3%) for livestock, 15 km 3 (4%) for manufacturing, 33 km 3 (10%) for electricity including hydropower and 3 km 3 (1%) for mining (3–4 km 3 , with annual production variations). Estimated demand increased by 26% between 2010 and 2020. The dominant water-demand sector varies across regions and river basins, broadly reflecting established geographical and socioeconomic patterns. In parts of northern and southern Africa, estimated demand exceeds water availability, although results depend on assumptions regarding environmental-flow protection 5 . Elsewhere, water availability exceeds aggregate demand despite limited access to piped drinking water, indicating that physical availability alone does not determine water security. Our analysis therefore provides a spatially and sectorally resolved baseline for identifying water-demand pressures and access constraints rather than establishing a new causal mechanism of water insecurity. Local estimates should be interpreted cautiously given uncertainties in the underlying datasets.

papers.title: Clostridium perfringens Delta toxin targets CD9 to drive NEC and brain injury
papers.abstract: , the microbial factors driving NEC and the following brain pathology remain unclear. Here we identify Clostridium perfringens pathobionts containing Delta toxin in the gut microbiome of individuals with severe and fatal NEC. Clinically, infected infants show worse outcomes, including aberrant systemic inflammation, severe neurological damage and coagulopathy. We establish a mouse model in which Delta-toxin-positive C. perfringens infection, or Delta toxin exposure alone, recapitulates clinical features of NEC, including intestinal necrosis and acute cerebral injury. Mechanistically, Delta toxin preferentially targets macrophages, potently activating inflammasome signalling and pyroptosis, triggering a rapid inflammatory cascade that compromises blood-brain barrier integrity and drives neuroinflammation. Through a genome-wide CRISPR screen, we identify the tetraspanin CD9 as the host receptor for Delta toxin. Using systemic, myeloid-specific and intestinal-epithelial-specific Cd9-knockout mice, we show that systemic and myeloid Cd9 ablation protects mice against toxin-induced lethality, blood-brain barrier dysfunction and multiorgan injury, whereas epithelial Cd9 deletion shows partial protection, implicating macrophage targeting as a primary driver of C. perfringens CD9-dependent pathogenesis. Furthermore, a neutralizing anti-Delta toxin monoclonal antibody confers protection against disease progression. These findings suggest that a subset of NEC is a specific-toxin-mediated disorder and validate the Delta toxin-CD9 axis as a therapeutic target for this subset.

papers.title: Alzheimer’s disease genetics converges on microglial and neuronal dysregulation
papers.abstract: . Here we analysed data from 109,479 cases, 74,141 proxy cases, 2,131,799 controls and 499,708 proxy controls from diverse ancestries, identifying 118 loci in a multi-ancestry analysis and 9 additional loci in ancestry-specific analyses, 48 of which are new. We identified new AD risk genes, prioritized potential drug targets, and found that genes upregulated in microglia and downregulated in neurons in cases compared with controls were enriched for AD-associated genetic risk. Moreover, we improved polygenic prediction and estimated a SNP heritability of 16%, nearly threefold higher than previous estimates. Together, our findings show that the common-variant contribution to AD has been substantially underestimated, and reveal new molecular and cellular mechanisms as well as specific targets for future drug development research.

papers.title: MCT1-dependent mitochondrial lactate import sustains cardiac metabolism
papers.abstract: Abstract The heart possesses a dynamic capacity to oxidize a variety of fuels, including glucose and lactate, to meet its energetic demands under diverse dietary, exertion and injury stressors 1 . Oxidation of carbohydrate substrates is thought to converge on the cytosolic generation of pyruvate, which is transported by the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier (MPC) for entry into the tricarboxylic acid cycle 2 . Here we find that glucose-derived carbon is oxidized in mouse myocardium even when the MPC is genetically ablated. Using genetic and pharmacological tools, we demonstrate that lactate monocarboxylate transporter 1 (MCT1, encoded by Slc16a1 ) is required for the oxidation of glucose carbon by MPC-deficient myocardium. We further observe that MCT1, traditionally localized to the plasma membrane, also resides in the inner mitochondrial membrane of mouse and human cardiomyocytes. Together with matrix-localized LDHB, MCT1 enables mitochondrial lactate conversion to pyruvate and NADH, directly fueling the electron transport chain. Loss of MCT1 impairs lactate oxidation, disrupts metabolic flexibility and accelerates the development of heart failure with increased mortality after hyperactivation of the neurohormonal axis or ischemia–reperfusion injury. Thus, the existence of a parallel lactate-based pathway for carbohydrate oxidation can sustain cardiac energetics and maintain myocardial structure and function under diverse stress conditions.

papers.title: This Arabian desert was once a lush paradise. Why did ancient humans avoid it?
Ribbon made of carbon pentagons and heptagons has metallic properties
papers.abstract: Ribbons that are composed exclusively of five- and seven-carbon rings have metal-like electron transport and conductance. The ribbons can be synthesized by linking previously inaccessible chains of paired five-membered rings, providing a route to making highly conducting carbon nanoribbons. The ‘pentaheptite’ ribbons can be made by joining chains of paired five-membered rings side-by-side.

papers.title: Meta-study sparks questions about what it means to be good at regulating emotions
Genetic variants that alter gene regulation in specific cell types are closely tied to disease
Tethered to stone: how rock and water availability shaped early desert occupation
Lactate takes a shortcut into mitochondria to power the heart
Accounting of Africa’s water reveals a management gap
An unexpected function of a cell-cycle enzyme might explain the toxic effects of its inhibitors
papers.abstract: A previously unknown mechanism required for cells to start proliferating has been identified. A combination of mathematical modelling and cell-based experiments shows that the enzyme WEE1 switches off a protein-degradation complex to allow cell proliferation to start, with implications for WEE1 inhibitors currently in trials for cancer treatments.

papers.title: Clues about complex life come from freshly cultivated archaea
papers.abstract: Two archaeal strains that belong to a lineage closely related to the ancestor of eukaryotic cells (complex cells with membrane-bound organelles) have been brought into culture. Their simple internal organization, elaborate surface structures, microbial partnerships and protein-dependent lifestyle provide clues about how eukaryotic cells arose. Two archaeal strains that share a common ancestor with eukaryotic cells have been examined in culture.

papers.title: Could a giant sunshade in space ‘solve global warming’? Scientists are taking the idea seriously
The shifting sands of research independence: why mid-career scientists crave security
What students think about my teaching doesn’t matter. Am I wrong?
Where have all the saucers flown?
Is research funding now a lottery? Elite funder ERC swamped by applications
How the pandemic changed trust in science — in four charts
These three red flags could unmask dodgy journals
How personalization and psychedelics are revitalizing psychiatry
The grand plan to transform psychiatry — by personalizing mental-health care
Preprint-centric publishing model gets major boost
Correlated Demand Shocks and Asset Pricing
papers.abstract: Abstract I propose a mechanism through which institutional investors’ correlated demand shocks provide a source of market risk in asset pricing. Institutional investors have mandates to beat a similar market index. During periods of strong stock market performance, their incentive to outperform intensifies as more of them fall short of the market index. This incentive induces procyclical risk-taking behavior, generating correlated demand that elevates the market betas and risk premia of exposed stocks. Quasi-experiments using exogenous changes in index membership support a causal interpretation of the mechanism. Elevated betas are associated with a higher perceived cost of capital and reduced firm investment. (JEL G1, G2)

papers.title: Real Activity and Uncertainty Shocks: The Long and the Short of It
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT We propose a nonrecursive VAR identification strategy that separately identifies short‐term and long‐term uncertainty shocks by exploiting sign restrictions implied by a stylized framework and a DSGE model featuring both types of shocks. We find that long‐term uncertainty shocks exert strong and persistent effects on real activity, whereas short‐term shocks have limited real effects. We use the DSGE model to study their differential propagation and show that time‐to‐build is an important ingredient allowing the model to account for the stark empirical asymmetry in investment and, in turn, output—both contract sharply after long‐term shocks but only modestly after short‐term shocks.

papers.title: “Demographic Change and Migration: Facts, Models and Policy Implications” – An Introduction to the Special Issue
papers.abstract: Demographic change, driven by lower fertility rates and declining mortality, is a central long-run phenomenon impacting all major economies around the world.The papers in this special issue study the interactions between demographic change, internal and external migration, technological progress, and economic development, with a particular focus on Asian economies.Scientific collaboration represents one form of cross-border interaction through which knowledge and human capital contribute to economic development.When the international migration of researchers is subject to frictions, international cooperation in the production of scientific output becomes crucial.In Scientific Isolation?The Consequences of Trump's China Initiative on Chinese Research , by Philippe

papers.title: Asset Market Participation, Redistribution, and Asset Pricing
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT We study how redistribution between asset holders and non‐asset holders links macroeconomic fluctuations to expected stock returns. Aggregate and relative consumption growth forecast excess returns with opposite signs and at different horizons. We interpret these patterns using a production‐based asset‐pricing model with limited participation and external habits. Aggregate (relative) consumption captures variation in the price (quantity) of risk. Technology shocks drive macroeconomic fluctuations, whereas redistributive shocks generate large short‐run movements in inequality and are the main source of priced risk. This points to a macro‐finance disconnect between the drivers of business cycles and those governing risk premia.

papers.title: Innovation and Competition on a Rugged Technological Landscape
papers.abstract: We integrate innovation into Hotelling's classic model of spatial competition. Potential entrants arrive sequentially and choose whether and where to innovate. They can innovate beyond the frontier, expanding the boundary of the market, or within a niche between incumbent products. Product quality is learned only after introduction, and uncertainty increases with novelty. Innovation on a rugged technological landscape is irregular, with frequent changes in direction and cycles between frontier and niche innovation. The ruggedness of the technological landscape itself deters innovation, generating fewer entrants, less product differentiation, narrower markets, and more intense competition than under certainty. (JEL D11, D21, D83, L11, L25, O31)

papers.title: Electoral Campaign Attacks: Theory and Evidence
papers.abstract: This paper studies the determinants of electoral campaign attacks. We first propose a model to examine the main factors that influence candidates' decisions to attack. Our theoretical analysis yields a number of predictions that we test using information from “right of reply” lawsuits filed in Brazil. Our empirical analysis exploits a regression discontinuity design based on virtual ties between second- and third-place candidates to show that candidates with an electoral advantage are more likely to receive an attack. We then exploit another discontinuity to show that the patterns of campaign attacks differ significantly under single- and dual-ballot plurality systems. (JEL D72, D74, K16)

papers.title: Monopolistic Data Dumping
papers.abstract: A profit-maximizing monopolist curates a database for users seeking to learn a parameter. There are two user types: “Nowcasters” wish to learn the parameter's current value, while “forecasters” target its long-run value. Data storage involves a constant marginal cost. The monopolist designs a menu of contracts described by fees and data-access levels. The profit-maximizing menu offers full access to historical data, while current data are fully provided to nowcasters but may be withheld from forecasters. Compared to the social optimum, the monopolist keeps too much historical data, keeps too little current data, and may store too much data overall. (JEL C53, C80, D42, L12, L86)

papers.title: Optimal Procurement Design: A Reduced-Form Approach
papers.abstract: Standard procurement models assume that the buyer knows the quality of the good at the time of procurement; however, in many settings, the quality is learned only long after the transaction. We study procurement problems in which the buyer's valuation of the supplied good depends directly on its quality, which is unverifiable and unobservable to the buyer. For a broad class of procurement problems, we identify procurement mechanisms maximizing any weighted average of the buyer's expected payoff and social surplus. The optimal mechanism can be implemented via an auction that restricts sellers to submitting bids within specific intervals. (JEL D44, D82, H57, L15)

papers.title: The Perils of Overreaction
papers.abstract: To study updating rules, we consider the problem of a malevolent principal screening an imperfectly Bayesian agent. We uncover a fundamental dichotomy between underreaction and overreaction to information. If, for some signal realization, the agent's updating rule produces a posterior that lies outside the convex hull of the Bayesian posteriors induced by the signal structure, she can be exploited by the principal without bound: Her ex ante expected loss can be made arbitrarily large. In contrast, an agent who underreacts—whose posterior after each signal realization lies between the prior and the corresponding Bayesian posterior—cannot be exploited at all. (JEL D82, D83)

papers.title: Competitive Bottlenecks and Platform Spillovers
papers.abstract: We provide a general framework to analyze competition between oligopolistic platforms in competitive bottleneck settings, allowing for pricing and nonprice design choices by platforms, and post-participation buyer-seller decisions. We show that equilibrium choices by platforms are distorted against sellers’ interests in a way harmful to welfare (e.g., setting excessive commission fees), and that an increase in the number of competing platforms can exacerbate this distortion. We also characterize how buyer-side heterogeneity in interaction benefits, partial market coverage, platform asymmetry, and cross-platform spillovers further amplify or mitigate welfare distortions. Based on our findings, we discuss policy implications for mobile app platforms. (JEL D43, L13, L25, L96)

papers.title: Targeted Advertising in Elections
papers.abstract: How does targeted advertising influence electoral outcomes? This paper presents a one-dimensional spatial model of voting in which a privately informed challenger persuades voters to support him over the status quo. I show that targeted advertising enables the challenger to persuade voters with opposing preferences and swing elections decided by such voters. Ex ante commitment power is unnecessary—the challenger succeeds by strategically revealing different pieces of verifiable information to different voters. Publicizing all political ads would mitigate the negative effects of targeted advertising and help voters collectively make the right choice. (JEL D72, D82, D83, M37)

papers.title: Cognitive Ability and Perceived Disagreement in Learning
papers.abstract: Do agents believe they agree more with others over time? This paper explores how individuals perceive the belief-updating behavior of others and the resulting disagreement in a sequential experiment with public information. We uncover a persistent gap in the perception of disagreement as a function of cognitive ability. Higher cognitive ability correlates with less perceived disagreement, although the average subject underestimates the extent of actual disagreement. Information about a partner's cognitive ability only impacts perceived disagreement when the partner has a low test score. Our findings highlight the roles of overconfidence and cognitive projection in shaping these perceptions. (JEL C91, D12, D83, D91)

papers.title: Recurring Auctions with Costly Entry: Theory and Evidence
papers.abstract: Recurring auctions are widely used to sell durable assets, with follow-up auctions held for unsold items. We investigate such auctions theoretically and empirically. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that recurring auctions outperform single-round auctions when buyers face entry costs, enhancing efficiency and revenue due to sorted entry of potential buyers. Optimal reserve price sequences are characterized. Empirical findings from home foreclosure auctions in China reveal significant annual gains in efficiency (US$3.40 billion, 16.60 percent) and revenue (US$2.97 billion, 15.92 percent) using recurring auctions compared with single-round auctions. Implementing optimal reserve prices can further improve efficiency (3.35 percent) and revenue (3.06 percent). (JEL D44, D82, R31)

papers.title: Land, Wealth, and Taxation
papers.abstract: This paper examines the role of land in wealth dynamics and its consequences for efficiency and inequality. We focus on the interplay among agents’ bidding for location, mortgage market imperfections, and inheritance in a model in which agents leave to their heirs financial bequests and their housing wealth. The borrowing constraint generates a housing return premium and spatial wealth sorting, which translate into persistent wealth inequality. Since altruism and the borrowing constraint distort land price formation, we show that taxing land rent transmitted between generations is optimal. Land taxation cannot be disconnected from taxation on intergenerational wealth transfers. (JEL D31, D64, H71, Q24, R23, R31, R52)

papers.title: Strategic Limit Orders and Intertemporal Price Dispersion
papers.abstract: We study a two-period commodity market with competitive consumers and Cournot sellers. Without speculation, equilibrium is stationary. A storage-capable, strategically large speculator can profitably create deterministic intertemporal price dispersion using standard order types. A period-1 limit buy order flattens residual demand, induces higher output, and yields a low purchase price. With mandatory liquidation, resale remains below the no-speculation price but above the purchase price, so the speculator profits; consumers gain and sellers lose. With free disposal and a stop-loss, the period-2 price can exceed the benchmark, benefiting sellers but harming consumers. (JEL D43, G12, G14, G41, Q02)

papers.title: Reputation and Competitive Selection
papers.abstract: We demonstrate how selection in competitive markets can impede long-run reputational incentives. In our model, competent firms can exert costly effort to improve expected product quality, but inept firms cannot. With low entry barriers, we show competent firms cannot persistently exert effort, despite bounded memory. Such effort would cause consumers to select firms based on reputations for competence, eventually selecting a monopolist with an arbitrarily high reputation, which has no incentive for effort. More generally, reputation-based selection rules out long-run effort, which undermines the basis for such selection. Intermediate entry barriers provide stronger reputational incentives than low or high barriers. (JEL D21, D40, D82, L15)

papers.title: Learning in the Marriage Market: The Economics of Dating
papers.abstract: This paper develops a search-and-matching model where potential partners can learn about their compatibility as a couple by spending time together (interpreted as dating). We show that a steady-state equilibrium exists and characterize its induced dating patterns. In equilibrium, highly attractive individuals are more selective. We derive conditions under which equilibria induce positive assortative matching and show that even when these conditions hold, the socially optimal outcome can exhibit negative assortative matching. Finally, the framework is applied to study the effect of recent advances in search technologies on dating patterns and the connection between dating and interracial segregation. (JEL C78, D83, J12)

papers.title: Competing Diffusions in a Social Network
papers.abstract: We develop a model of competing diffusions of goods on a social network. There are two types of goods and individuals: mass-market and niche-market. There is a unique stable steady state, and the adoption of a mass-market good is greater than its population share. Greater connectivity and homophily will concurrently increase the prevalence of niche-market goods. If there is a strategic agent who wants to promote a niche good, she will invest more in influencing activities than one promoting mass-market goods. When individuals choose their degree of homophily, niche-market individuals exhibit greater homophily than mass-market ones. (JEL D83, D85, L86, Z13)

papers.title: Degree-Weighted Social Learning
papers.abstract: We study social learning in which agents weight neighbors' opinions differently based on their degrees, capturing situations in which agents place more trust in well-connected individuals or, conversely, discount their influence. We derive asymptotic properties of learning outcomes in large stochastic networks and analyze how the weighting rule affects societal wisdom and convergence speed. We find that assigning greater weight to higher-degree neighbors harms wisdom but has a non-monotonic effect on convergence speed, depending on the diversity of views within high- and low-degree groups, highlighting a potential trade-off between convergence speed and wisdom. (JEL D83, D85, Z13)

papers.title: Symmetric Equilibrium in Pre-auction Investment
papers.abstract: We characterize the symmetric equilibria of a pre-auction game of investment in an internet ad auction environment. For a wide class of auction formats, we show a symmetric equilibrium exists for the pre-auction investment game, is essentially unique, and is the same for all auction formats in the class. We give sufficient conditions for the symmetric equilibrium to be in pure strategies and to achieve the efficient level of investment. Finally, we show comparative statics results with respect to a variety of parameters. (JEL D44, D82)

papers.title: I Want My Country Back! British Euroscepticism after the Eastern European Enlargement
Personality, longevity insurance, and the timing of Social Security claiming
papers.abstract: Abstract Delaying a Social Security claim buys a larger inflation‐indexed annuity, a form of longevity insurance. Because claiming‐age adjustments are uniform within birth cohorts, delay is worth more to those likely to live longer, so traits that predict longer lives should predict later claiming. In the Health and Retirement Study, we relate Big Five traits measured before receipt to the age at first reported Social Security income of any type between 62 and 70. Converting each trait's mortality difference into the claiming age maximizing expected present value gives a benchmark for observed timing. Timing moves toward the benchmark for traits predicting shorter lives, by less than mortality implies, with openness the exception. Conscientiousness, the strongest longevity predictor, implies about 6 months of later claiming per standard deviation, yet we detect no later receipt. Personality makes observable a mortality difference that claiming models treat as latent.

papers.title: Ecological macroeconomics models? Caveat emptor
papers.abstract: Ecological Macroeconomic Integrated Assessment Models (EM-IAMs) have emerged as tools for exploring post-growth narratives and challenging the dominant discourse of continuous economic growth. Their use may be strategically advantageous: by employing modelling approaches that are epistemically legitimate within economics, EM-IAMs can contest the growth paradigm with their own tools. Yet, the framing of socio-ecological processes in EM-IAMs, through quantification and evaluative logics, risks interfering with the other goal of EM-IAMs; to address social inequality and injustices. As such, EM-IAMs risk operating as what ecologist Langdon Winner coined as ‘conceptual Trojan horse’. We question whether EM-IAMs may truly provide “robust modelling tools to explore alternative future scenarios, enabling the ex-ante evaluation of direct and indirect effects of policies on well-being, employment, and the ecosystem” (Ecological Economics, 2025). Our doubts rest upon complexity that does not reduce uncertainty, the politics of model simplification, the limitations of EM-IAM models for aspects that resist quantification, the reinforcement of historical power imbalances, and, ultimately, the performative effects of models themselves. We suggest that, rather than extending EM-IAMs to incorporate well-being analysis, we should adopt a different approach to modelling, learning from ecological values; appreciating diversity, variability in space and time, self-regulation, and entanglements.

papers.title: China’s institution-building amidst (dynamic) network effects: how will the relations between the IMF and newcomer institutions evolve?
papers.abstract: How will the regime complex of balance-of-payments lending evolve amidst ongoing global power shifts? In this paper, we challenge the hitherto static outlook on the viability of external institutional change within the International Monetary Fund’s (IMF) institutional environment. Dominant views in International Political Economy suggest that the IMF’s current focality will persist as China’s reformist approach to balance-of-payments lending and strong network effects favoring the IMF induce (inter-)institutional inertia. In contrast, we argue that the interests of challenger states – particularly China – and their exposure to network effects are dynamic. Depending on challengers’ evolving reformist or revisionist interests and their dynamic exposure to network effects, we derive pathways for external institutional change toward multiple inter-institutional relations between the IMF and newcomer institutions. Based on theoretical extrapolation and empirical trends, we claim that institutional hedging is a probable pathway for China’s institution-building efforts in the near future. For the more distant future, we introduce complementary layering and conflictual counter-institutionalization as highly contingent possibilities and discuss how the (inter-)actions of challengers and defenders during the hedging phase may shape their (non-)materialization. We thereby offer a methodologically innovative and policy-relevant outlook on future institutional change in international finance.

papers.title: The Association Between Physician Organizational Form and Opioid Prescribing
papers.abstract: In theory, there are several reasons why physician organizational form might affect the price, quantity, and quality of physician services. In this paper, we examine the association between three aspects of physician organizational form and opioid prescribing: solo versus group practice; integration with a hospital versus independent practice; and the average age of the other physicians in the physician's group. We present three key findings. First, physicians who switch from solo to group practice, particularly large-group practice, significantly reduce their prescribing relative to those who stay in solo practice. Conversely, physicians who switch from group to solo practice significantly increase their prescribing by approximately the same amount. Second, physicians who switch from independent to hospital-integrated practice (and those who switch from integrated to independent practice) generally do not significantly change their prescribing. Third, among group-practice physicians, there are significant differences in prescribing by the average of age of physicians in the group, holding constant the physician's own age and other characteristics of the group, the physician, and the physician's patients. Physicians in groups with a higher average age (excluding the index physician) prescribe more intensively and are more likely to write inappropriate opioid prescriptions than physicians in younger groups-holding other factors constant.

papers.title: How Has the Health of the United States Population Changed? Evidence From Biomarkers
papers.abstract: Population health is a central input into social welfare, but health itself is complex and multidimensional. Mapping multiple dimensions of health into a single population health index may require strong assumptions about how to aggregate and weight across dimensions. This study adopts a novel nonparametric approach to rank individual health as a function of seven biomarkers associated with major domains of physiological health: body mass index (BMI), glycohemoglobin (HbA1c), total cholesterol, alanine aminotransferase (ALT), estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), systolic blood pressure (SBP), and white blood cell (WBC). This approach avoids arbitrary weighting while requiring only monotonicity and quasi-concavity. Using NHANES data from 1988 to 2018, we document a significant deterioration in the U.S. health distribution, with declines concentrated in the lower tail. Counterfactual decompositions show that one-third of the negative shift can be attributed to an aging, more racially and ethnically diverse population, leaving a remaining portion unexplained by observed factors. The findings highlight the value of distribution-sensitive multidimensional health measures for monitoring health inequality and targeting preventive care.

papers.title: Europe Adrift
papers.abstract: Europe is adrift in the face of great turmoil and transformation. The liberal international order that emerged after the Cold War has disintegrated and the EU lacks a coherent strategic vision for responding to, let alone shaping, the emergent world order. There has been a shift away from market liberalism and toward state interventionism in pursuit of strategic autonomy. While the EU seeks to be more assertive internationally, its efforts are haunted by legacies from the neoliberal era that continue to limit its capacity for effective action. Herein lies the challenge. Europe struggles to overcome internal difficulties while simultaneously facing a security threat from Russia, erratic neo-mercantilism from the US, a competitiveness challenge from China, and declining goodwill in the Global South, all in the context of rapid environmental change. This special issue takes the dynamics of intensifying global inter-state competition as an entry point to survey the erosion of European security, growth and normative power. A Europe Adrift speaks to how the foundations of this erosion were laid on the basis of EU regulatory statehood, the contradictions revealed in the EU’s evolving governance architecture and how European power and prosperity are being reshaped in unexpected ways.

papers.title: Marx and Engels on the Lumpenproletariat and the Poor Laws
papers.abstract: What if the English Poor Laws helped reproduce the social conditions Marx and Engels associated with the lumpenproletariat? This paper argues that their critique of the Poor Laws and their concept of the lumpenproletariat form part of a common analysis of capitalist accumulation and the production of relative surplus population. Marx and Engels understood poor relief as a mechanism embedded in capitalist reproduction, stabilising dependency, exerting downward pressure on wages, and fragmenting the working class. The lumpenproletariat, situated at the lowest strata of pauperism, serves as a conceptual bridge between surplus population and the institutional regulation of poverty. By clarifying this connection, the article repositions Marx and Engels within nineteenth-century debates on poverty and highlights their divergence from classical political economy, particularly regarding the structural limits of reform within capitalism.
