papers.title: Affect-Infused Reflective Process in Responding to Burdensome Role Expectations: An Affect-Cognition Theory Extension of Yagil’s “I Don’t Want To”
Winning at Defense by Playing Offense: Discrediting by Target Firms in Activist Hedge Fund Campaigns
papers.abstract: Prior research highlights the far-reaching strategic and governance consequences for firms targeted in activist hedge fund (AHF) campaigns. Yet, how target firm executives and directors can effectively defend against these campaigns remains underexplored. Drawing on impression management (IM) theory, we reason that executives and directors use discrediting in their public rebuttal letters to negatively influence shareholders’ evaluations of AHFs’ reputation. To nuance this prediction, we develop a taxonomy distinguishing between source-focused discrediting, which directly attacks AHFs’ reputation, and message-focused discrediting, which challenges the validity of AHFs’ claims to indirectly tarnish their reputation. We theorize that both discrediting subtypes enhance target firms’ defense success, particularly when deployed in combination. Adopting a temporal perspective on IM theory, we further argue that the effectiveness of discrediting diminishes as more time elapses between an AHF’s public attack and executives and directors’ rebuttal. A manual content analysis of 841 rebuttal letters issued during U.S. AHF campaigns (2000–2023) provides robust support for these predictions. Beyond contributing to shareholder activism research by offering new insights into the determinants of campaign outcomes, our study advances IM theory by conceptualizing discrediting as a multidimensional influence tactic and exploring its effectiveness and temporal dynamics in adversarial contexts.

papers.title: Analysts’ Perspectives on Climate Change: An Examination of Analyst Reports
Audit Quality and Audit Partner Ownership of Non-Audit Businesses: Evidence from China
Sales-Based CEO Incentives and Their Effect Across the Supply Chain
Robust Auction Design with Support Information
papers.abstract: A seller wants to sell an item to n buyers. Buyer valuations are independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) according to a distribution unknown to the seller; the seller only knows that the support is included in [a, b]. To be robust, the seller chooses a dominant strategy incentive compatible mechanism that optimizes the worst-case performance relative to the ideal expected revenue the seller could have collected with knowledge of buyers’ valuations. Our analysis unifies the regret and the ratio objectives. For these objectives, we derive an optimal mechanism and the corresponding performance in quasi-closed form, as a function of the support information [a, b] and the number of buyers n. Our analysis reveals three regimes of support information and a new class of robust mechanisms. (i) When a/b is below a threshold, the optimal mechanism is a second-price auction (SPA) with random reserve, a focal class in earlier literature. (ii) When a/b is above another threshold, SPAs are strictly suboptimal, and an optimal mechanism belongs to a class of mechanisms we introduce, which we call pooling auctions (POOL); whenever the highest value is above a threshold, the mechanism still allocates to the highest bidder, but otherwise the mechanism allocates to a uniformly random buyer, that is, pools low types. (iii) When a/b is between two thresholds, a randomization between SPA and POOL is optimal. We also characterize optimal mechanisms within nested central subclasses of mechanisms: standard mechanisms that only allocate to the highest bidder, SPA with random reserve, and SPA with no reserve. We show strict separations in terms of performance across classes, implying that deviating from standard mechanisms is necessary for robustness. Lastly, we show that the same results hold under other distribution classes that capture “positive dependence,” namely i.i.d., mixture of i.i.d., and exchangeable and affiliated distributions, as well as i.i.d. regular distributions. This paper was accepted by David Simchi-Levi, revenue management and market analytics. Supplemental Material: The online appendices are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.02703 .

papers.title: From Employer Responsibility to Environmental Irresponsibility: Unintended Impacts of Social Insurance Law on Pollution Emissions
papers.abstract: This study investigates the unintended effect of the introduction of the 2011 Social Insurance Law on corporate pollution emissions. Using a difference-in-differences framework, our analysis reveals that enhanced social insurance contributions lead to higher industrial pollution emissions, as measured by chemical oxygen demand and wastewater emissions. The mechanism analysis indicates that the enforcement of the law increases firms’ labor costs and financial distress, motivating them to reduce efforts on end-of-pipe treatment activities and measures taken during the production process, which results in higher pollution emission intensity. Our study highlights the potential conflict between employee protection and corporate environmental goals. Further analysis suggests that stronger environmental monitoring and environmental, social, and governance disclosure requirements can partially mitigate this tradeoff, providing valuable insights for policymakers. This paper was accepted by Caroline Flammer, sustainability. Funding: Y. Li acknowledges research support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 72403026]. Y. Qin acknowledges research support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 72342031]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.00714 .

papers.title: Estimating the Pricing Kernel: A Simple Regression-Based Dimension-Reduction Approach
papers.abstract: We propose a simple framework for estimating the pricing kernel in factor space by constructing the mean–variance efficient factor portfolio via an ordinary least squares formulation with least absolute shrinkage and selection operator regularization. The method accommodates high-dimensional settings in which the number of candidate factors exceeds the sample size and automatically shrinks redundant factor weights toward zero. We show theoretically that the out-of-sample Sharpe ratio of the estimated portfolio converges to the theoretical maximum at the fastest rate among existing regression-based approaches. Applying the method to 174 characteristic-based factors together with the market factor, we obtain an out-of-sample Sharpe ratio of 3.59, substantially outperforming competing strategies and delivering the smallest aggregate pricing errors. The selected factors vary over time in both composition and number, averaging about 50. We further develop a model comparison test and reject the hypothesis that eight widely used sparse factor models are sufficient to span the pricing kernel. This paper was accepted by Kay Giesecke, finance. Funding: This work was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grants 72671091, 72371079, and 72501192, and Key Program 72432005] and the Science and Technology Planning Project of Guangdong Province [Grant 2023B1515020045]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.03608 .

papers.title: Challenge for some, hindrance for others? How stress appraisals shape employee performance of essential and nonessential work during crises
papers.abstract: Anecdotes during crises frequently highlight essential employees who maintain critical services and perform effectively under adversity. This raises a central question: which types of work are more (vs less) likely to be performed effectively during crises, and why? Drawing on the Transactional Theory of Stress, we propose that performing essential (vs nonessential) work during crises facilitates challenge appraisals and reduces hindrance appraisals of the work performed, which in turn enhances in-role performance and taking charge behaviors. We further propose that organizational adaptive capacity functions as a contextual resource that strengthens these beneficial appraisals. We test our framework in a two-wave multisource survey conducted during the COVID-19 pandemic and two preregistered experiments simulating organizational crises. Results provide broad support for our theorizing. At both occupational and task levels, higher levels of challenge (Studies 1 and 2) and lower levels of hindrance appraisals (Studies 1, 2, and 3) mediate the relationship between essential (vs nonessential) work and performance. The moderating role of organizational adaptive capacity was only supported in our field study. This research advances our understanding of how the socially constructed labels of “essential” versus “nonessential” work shape employee appraisals and performance during crises.

papers.title: From control to co‐construction in identity regulation: A systematic review and an agenda for future research
papers.abstract: Abstract This systematic review synthesises findings from 112 peer‐reviewed articles (1995–2026) to provide a comprehensive and timely understanding of identity regulation, diverse navigation strategies, and multifaceted outcomes. It reveals identity regulation as a multi‐level phenomenon extending to organisations, managers, and teams as distinct targets of regulation beyond the traditional employee focus. It maps the multi‐level mechanisms through which identity is shaped and the diverse strategies individuals (employees and managers) employ to navigate these pressures—from conformity, (dis)‐identification, sensemaking, and balancing to resistance and proactive identity work. The review reveals multifaceted and often paradoxical outcomes affecting individuals physically, emotionally, socially, and ethically, as well as influencing team and organisational dynamics. Notably, findings strongly suggest that a co‐constructive regulatory approach fostering agency yields significantly more positive consequences than a traditional control‐centric approach. This review highlights a conceptual shift from a control‐centric approach towards a co‐constructive approach, proposing a detailed research agenda to significantly advance the field in this dynamic direction.

papers.title: Signaling Climate Transition Capacity: How Environmental Expenditures Attenuate the Carbon Risk Premium
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT This study investigates the pricing of carbon risk among publicly listed firms in Asia. We first develop a theoretical model of the carbon risk premium grounded in information asymmetry, which posits that a firm's environmental expenditures serve as a credible signal of its climate transition capacity. We then test these predictions using a novel panel dataset of 144 green bond issuers from 2005 to 2023. Our empirical analysis confirms the existence of a statistically significant, positive carbon risk premium in the region. Crucially, and consistent with our theoretical framework, we find that this premium is attenuated for firms with higher environmental expenditures. We further uncover that the modest scale of this premium is driven by investor heterogeneity: Long‐term institutional investors penalize high‐emitting firms but reward those with significant environmental spending, while short‐term strategic entities exhibit opposing behavior. Based on these findings, policymakers can mobilize corporate resources to address the carbon risk premium through three complementary levers: implementing stringent climate policy, enhancing climate finance taxonomies, and mandating standardized transition risk disclosure.

papers.title: CEO Tenure and Sustainable Growth: Non‐Linear Effects and Strategic Trade‐Offs Between Sustainability Dimensions
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines how CEO tenure influences firm sustainable growth across economic and social dimensions and whether it is associated with sustainability trade‐offs. Prior research has largely focused on short‐term performance measures and linear CEO tenure effects, providing limited evidence on sustainable growth and potential trade‐offs across sustainability dimensions. Using panel data from 272 publicly listed Vietnamese firms from 2011 to 2022, we employ fixed‐effects models, system GMM, and seemingly unrelated regression. The results show that CEO tenure has non‐linear effects on sustainable growth: a U‐shaped relationship with economic sustainability and an inverted U‐shaped relationship with social sustainability. Evidence of a negative residual correlation between the two dimensions suggests the possibility of sustainability trade‐offs among these two aspects. Furthermore, the relationship between CEO tenure and sustainability trade‐offs is evident only among firms with positive economic sustainability. This study contributes to the CEO tenure and sustainability literature by demonstrating that CEO tenure affects sustainable growth differently across economic and social dimensions and by identifying the non‐linear nature of these relationships. It also extends the sustainability trade‐off literature by showing that CEO tenure is associated with sustainability trade‐offs under specific performance conditions, offering important implications for board succession planning, executive monitoring, and the pursuit of balanced long‐term sustainable growth. These findings highlight the multidimensional and dynamic nature of CEO tenure effects on sustainable growth.

papers.title: The Cost of Being Green: Sustainability‐Linked Eco‐Friction, Trade‐Off Tolerance, and Tourist Satisfaction in Island Reviews
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Sustainability is often assumed to enhance tourism value, yet tourists do not always evaluate green practices positively in lived service encounters. This study examines sustainability‐linked evaluation in island and coastal tourism by distinguishing eco‐delight from eco‐friction, defined as environmentally anchored inconvenience rather than generic dissatisfaction. Using 138,683 Google Maps and TripAdvisor reviews from 10 destinations in Southeast and East Asia, we apply bilingual dictionary‐based text analysis and review‐level econometric modeling. Separate bilingual dictionaries, environmental anchoring rules, manual validation, and broad‐versus‐strict sensitivity analyses are used to reduce construct overlap and make classification uncertainty explicit. In the broad sample, eco‐delight is positively associated with review rating, whereas eco‐friction is negatively associated with it. The negative association of eco‐friction is stronger than the positive association of eco‐delight, indicating sustainability‐specific asymmetric negativity rather than only generic negativity bias. Positive trade‐off tolerance weakens this penalty in the broad specification, but the interaction does not replicate in the much smaller strict eco‐core sample. Accordingly, the text‐derived variables are interpreted as imperfect indicators of sustainability‐linked discourse rather than as latent psychological measures. The study reframes sustainable tourism experience as a trade‐off structure rather than a uniformly positive green premium.

papers.title: Green Innovation Through Artificial Intelligence: Sectoral and Regional Perspectives of China
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT The rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) has transformed manufacturing and promotes firms' green innovation. Concurrently, the significance of green innovation plays an important role in supporting firms' environmental transformation. Against this backdrop, the present study investigates the dynamic relationship between AI and firms' green innovation (FGI), with a specific focus on Chinese manufacturing firms. The results show that manufacturing companies with extensive AI adoption demonstrate heightened levels of green innovation. Furthermore, the study explores the heterogeneous impact of AI on FGI across different types of firms and regions. Notably, AI has a stronger effect on FGI within the eastern region and significantly drives green innovation in non‐SOE, high‐tech, and non‐labor‐intensive firms compared to their counterparts in SOE, labor‐intensive, and non‐tech industries. Additionally, AI contributes to the enhancement of FGI by stimulating investments in green research and development (R&D), reducing operational costs, and facilitating digital transformation initiatives. The study also illuminates the influence of environmental regulations in amplifying AI's promotion of FGI in manufacturing firms. Finally, based on the pragmatic assessments, valuable policy implications are discussed.

papers.title: Linking managerial coaching to engagement in the service-profit chain: Evidence in a quick-service restaurant context
Agentic AI Personalization in Advertising: Realizing the True Potential of N = 1
papers.abstract: With the rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (AI), we have come closer than ever to achieving the holy grail of personalizing advertisements to individual consumers, i.e., the ideal of N = 1. AI-driven ad serving platforms act with unprecedented agency, dynamically creating highly tailored appeals and experiences. Such “agentic AI personalization” has both positive and negative consequences. This article traces the evolution from analog personalization to agentic personalization. It then explicates the latter concept in terms of breadth, depth, and length of personalized messaging. It overviews the processes underlying agentic AI personalization and describes the dualities inherent in both its foundation and operation. Finally, it offers a theoretical framework for studying the effects of agentic AI personalization on consumer responses to advertisements, followed by an illustrative set of propositions for empirical testing.

papers.title: The future workplace: developing the human-machine symbioscape
papers.abstract: Purpose This paper develops the concept of the human-machine symbioscape to explain how work environments shape collaboration between humans and AI-enabled machines. Extending servicescape thinking from customer-employee encounters to hybrid human-machine work systems, the paper positions environmental design as a core antecedent of human–machine adaptive collaboration, with particular relevance for service and frontline settings where visibility, coordination, and role clarity are critical. Design/methodology/approach The paper is conceptual and theory building in nature. It synthesises insights from biological symbiosis, servicescape research, sociotechnical and sociomaterial theory, organisational sensemaking and team adaptation research to develop a deductive typology of the human-machine symbioscape as a three-tiered environmental construct, its cue categories, and its design-critical properties. The framework is further illustrated through a structured coding of relevant human-machine collaboration studies. Findings The paper conceptualises the symbioscape as a three-tier environmental architecture comprising physical–digital, socio-relational, and institutional–ecosystem conditions. Across these tiers, six cue categories shape what human and AI-enabled actors can notice, how they coordinate work, and how collaborative routines are reinforced over time. Drawing on Weick's sensemaking theory, the framework links these tiers to enactment, selection, and retention processes, and explains how they influence adaptation speed, adaptation effectiveness, and adaptation persistence in human–AI collaboration. Research limitations/implications The paper is purely conceptual and does not empirically test the proposed relationships. Its evidence base is limited to published studies and illustrative coding, with a strong emphasis on service and frontline contexts. It identifies an agenda for future research around operationalising symbioscape constructs, testing the proposed relationships empirically, and examining how individual tiers and cross-tier configurations jointly affect human–machine work. Practical implications The symbioscape framework provides managers with a structured lens for designing AI-enabled workplaces. It highlights how deliberate choices in physical–digital visibility and interface design, socio-relational workflow sequencing and interaction load, and institutional governance, training, and role architecture can improve the speed, quality and durability of human–machine adaptation. The framework can be used to diagnose service work environments, where frontline employees must coordinate with intelligent systems under conditions of customer presence, temporal pressure, and operational variability. Originality/value The paper introduces the symbioscape as a novel, three-tier environmental construct for human–machine collaboration, extending the servicescape from customer–employee encounters to hybrid human–AI work systems. It adds a missing environmental layer to human-machine collaboration research by systematically integrating dispersed insights on context into a coherent framework that links environmental cue structures to sensemaking and adaptation outcomes. For scholars, it offers an integrative conceptual architecture; for practitioners, it provides a foundation for designing and structuring future workplaces that foster adaptive human–machine collaboration.

papers.title: Halting Biodiversity Loss Requires a Different Kind of Management Research
papers.abstract: The first business and biodiversity assessment by the Intergovernmental Science‑Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services concludes that voluntary corporate action cannot halt biodiversity loss without broader shifts in the policy, economic, financial, social, and knowledge systems that shape business behavior and environmental outcomes. Yet management research on biodiversity remains largely firm-centric, attending to what individual firms measure, disclose, and do, while often overlooking these wider systems. We propose four interrelated research priorities to reorient the field: the political economy of inaction, the limits of organizational capability, the viability of organizing beyond growth, and reconceptualizing the firm–nature relationship. Pursuing them requires research that is interdisciplinary—drawing on insights beyond management—and transdisciplinary, co‑producing decision‑relevant knowledge with the actors who shape and experience biodiversity outcomes.

papers.title: The critical foundations of truly sustainable environmental auditing
papers.abstract: This essay addresses the urgent need for transformative action in environmental governance and examines how environmental auditing can support diagnostic and transformative agency within social-ecological systems. This requires a radical conceptual reconfiguration of environmental audit. To this end, the essay advances five conceptual foundations for a more impactful and sustainable approach. These include: an overarching commitment to Earth system stability; transcending an organization-centric paradigm; repositioning environmental auditing as a first-order function that drives, rather than follows, accounting; leveraging diverse forms of accounts to generate diagnostic insights into what truly matters within social-ecological systems; and actively coordinating accountability processes. Collectively, these foundations reposition environmental audit as a dynamic practice for nurturing meaningful change in social-ecological systems.

Shared Policy Commitments in the Buyer Ego‐Network and Buyer Financial Performance: A Multiplex Network Perspective
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Public commitments to sustainability policies have become common practice among buyer and supplier companies facing growing sustainability imperatives. Firms often pursue these commitments to address societal expectations and comply with institutional norms rather than to achieve efficiency, frequently endorsing them without a comprehensive assessment of their performance implications. Within the supply chain, when multiple firms commit to similar policies, alignment emerges across network members through shared policy commitments. Such shared commitments differ from traditional buyer–supplier coordinated alignment by introducing an additional layer of complexity beyond contractual dynamics, with potential performance consequences. Adopting an embeddedness perspective, the authors analyze 240 multiplex ego networks that capture both shared policy commitments and structural ties. Results show that shared policy commitments within a buyer ego‐network, between a buyer and its direct suppliers or among those suppliers, are positively associated with the focal buyer's financial performance, with each direction's association conditional on the level of the other. However, the findings also reveal a curvilinear relationship: buyer performance declines as network members' commitments become increasingly centered on the same policies. Network interconnectedness through contractual ties serves as a moderator, unlocking additional benefits of shared commitments. This study provides theoretical and practical insights for managing shared commitments in the buyer ego‐network while avoiding over‐embeddedness.

papers.title: From Experience to Memory: Emotional Pathways in Skip-Gen Travel
papers.abstract: Skip-gen travel, in which grandparents travel with grandchildren without parents, has received increasing attention, yet how such experiences are emotionally interpreted and remembered in later life remains underexplored. This study examines relationships among experiential characteristics, emotions, memory, and post-travel outcomes, drawing on memorable tourism experience research and psychological perspectives on emotion and memory. Using survey data from 790 Chinese grandparents and follow-up interviews with 57 participants, the findings show that rewarding experiential characteristics are associated with positive emotions, whereas stress and fatigue are associated with negative emotions. Positive emotions are positively associated with memory, while negative emotions show a negative association. Memory is associated with well-being, emotional closeness, and behavioral intentions. These relationships are stronger among non-co-residing grandparents, with qualitative findings highlighting variation in relational context within both groups. The findings suggest designing meaningful intergenerational activities, reducing strain for older travelers, and considering family context in skip-gen travel offerings.

papers.title: Archetypal Digital Nomads’ Typology and Implications for Tourism Destinations
papers.abstract: Digital nomadism, characterized by the integration of work and travel, is reshaping how mobile visitors engage with tourism destinations, services, and infrastructure. Drawing on 25 empirically derived work-leisure boundary management practices identified from 224 digital diaries and 32 praxiographic interviews, this study applies archetypal analysis to develop a typology of six digital nomad archetypes. The findings reveal that different configurations of temporal, spatial, material, social, and psycho-emotional practices produce distinct patterns of destination and service engagement. The study advances tourism theory by explaining heterogeneity within digital nomad lifestyle mobility through a practice-based perspective, showing how tourism resources acquire different functions according to work-leisure boundary configurations. The resulting typology explains variations in the use of accommodation, coworking spaces, digital infrastructure, and local services, providing actionable insights for destination planning, hospitality service design, infrastructure development, and tourism policy.

papers.title: Trust or Scrutiny? The Technology Readiness Paradox in Travel Planning With Generative Artificial Intelligence
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence now drafts travel itineraries that travelers cannot easily verify. Integrating privacy calculus theory with a dual-pathway trust model, this study examines how system attributes shape tourist trust and continued usage, and how technology readiness conditions those links. A two-wave panel (433 Chinese and European travelers), a validation wave (372), and 42 interviews were analyzed using structural equation modeling, importance–performance map analysis, fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis, and thematic analysis. Data transparency and content authenticity raised both cognitive and affective trust, and affective trust sustained continued usage most strongly. Technology readiness reversed the expected pattern: readier travelers scrutinized fluent output rather than relying on it, weakening the behavioral effect of trust. Providers should replace generic privacy notices with in-context, verifiable data-use disclosures and checkable citations, and segment interfaces so that ready travelers receive verification tools and less-ready travelers receive reassurance. Regulators can make verifiability, not fluency, the disclosure standard.

papers.title: Sick of change? Sickness absence following ownership conversions in Norwegian kindergartens
papers.abstract: Abstract The expansion of mixed-provider welfare systems has intensified debates about the consequences of public, nonprofit, and for-profit provision. Existing research focuses primarily on efficiency, service quality, and citizens' outcomes, while less is known about ownership conversions’ consequences for employees. We depart from research suggesting that ownership conversions can disrupt employee-organization value congruence as well as change the incentive structures. Leveraging population-wide administrative data from Norwegian childcare services (2015-2019), we examine whether ownership conversions are associated with changes in employee sickness absence. Using a staggered difference-in-differences design, we find that sickness absence increases following nonprofit-to-for-profit conversions. At the same time, public-to-for-profit transitions show little consistent relationship with sickness absence. These findings suggest that employee responses to ownership change are shaped less by the public-private divide than by differences in organizational missions and values. More broadly, the study highlights organizational value congruence as a potential mechanism linking ownership arrangements to employee well-being, and suggests that the nonprofit-for-profit boundary may be more consequential for employees than the conventional public-private divide.

papers.title: Synthetic humanitarianism and algorithmic witnessing: generative AI and the politics of humanitarian representation
papers.abstract: Humanitarian organisations have begun deploying generative AI imagery in their campaigns, a practice this article terms synthetic humanitarianism. The article asks what conceptual framework is required to analyse the ethical and communicative implications of this practice. Drawing on witnessing theory, decolonial critiques of humanitarian visibility, and technocolonialism, I argue that synthetic humanitarianism intensifies extractive and colonial logics that have structured humanitarian communication since its institutional emergence. I develop the concept of algorithmic witnessing to name the communicative condition in which generative AI systems produce the relations of testimony and moral address without any act of witnessing having taken place and, in the typical case, without the participation of those represented. The framework specifies four dimensions, testimonial fabrication, epistemic extraction, delanguaging, and stereoscopic automation, and I apply it to thirteen documented cases of generative AI image use in humanitarian communications between 2022 and 2025. The analysis demonstrates that these dimensions form a mutually reinforcing system in which the elimination of situated meaning-making enables fabricated testimony and the computational encoding of colonial visual archives produces automated stereotype. I argue that the most significant consequence of synthetic humanitarianism is political rather than epistemological. The displacement of situated meaning-making by algorithmic production tends to eliminate the last structural point at which affected communities could intervene in their own representation.

papers.title: From Gender Antagonism to Inclusive Solidarity? Trade Union Membership and Attitudes Toward Women's Employment
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Why and to what extent do union members differ from non‐members in attitudes toward women's employment? This study argues that a masculinized conception of work has historically underpinned gender antagonism in trade unionism, and that the rise of right‐wing populism may have hindered recent progress toward gender equality among union members. Analyzing the European Values Study data, I find that union members hold more egalitarian attitudes toward women's employment than non‐members on average. This relationship further varies across individual and institutional characteristics. After the financial crisis, however, the positive association has weakened particularly in countries where right‐wing populism is influential.

Renewable fuels for hard-to-abate transportation: Exploring the impact of biomass availability and variable renewable potentials
papers.abstract: Decarbonising the hard-to-abate maritime and aviation transport sectors will be challenging. Alternative renewable fuels, such as biofuels and E-fuels, show promising potential for substituting traditional fossil fuels, but carry challenges regarding the expansion of variable renewable energy (VRE) and the availability of sustainable biomass. This study assesses these challenges and regional impacts using a comprehensive sector-coupled energy system modelling framework applied to Europe. Under high biomass availability, a documented substitution effect allows the share of E-kerosene and biokerosene to shift with VRE accessibility, whereas this flexibility declines under biomass scarcity. These differences are reflected in fuel costs: aviation fuel prices are more sensitive to biomass scarcity, while maritime fuel prices are more sensitive to VRE restrictions. Regional resource availability reshapes renewable fuel production and trade. Under the modelling assumptions, accessible VRE resources favour E-fuel supply-chains from Spain, while lower VRE accessibility increases the role of biomass-rich countries, including Germany and Poland, as exporters. Constrained VRE deployment results in increased infrastructure needs, lowers average renewable capacity factors, and raises total system costs by up to 9%. Finally, increasing scarcity increases the importance of carbon management. Biomass is prioritised for fuel production and industrial applications coupled with carbon capture, while direct air capture and carbon reuse become increasingly important for meeting fuel demand. These results highlight the need for coordinated policies on biomass utilisation, VRE deployment, carbon management, and infrastructure planning to achieve cost-efficient decarbonisation of Europe's hard-to-abate transport sectors.

papers.title: Life cycle engineering for battery production within absolute environmental sustainability targets: a climate change case study
papers.abstract: Battery production is growing rapidly, yet whether its environmental impacts remain within planetary boundaries requires investigation. We develop a four-step life cycle engineering framework integrating 1) prospective and probabilistic target derivation, 2) parametric and prospective life cycle assessment, 3) Sobol index-based selection of mitigation measures, and 4) marginal abatement cost curves for cost-effectiveness evaluation. The framework builds on a review of 28 studies and 36 reviews, addressing six of the seven identified research demands. Applied to NMC811 battery production under three SSP-RCP scenarios and two allocation principles (2024–2050), current impacts (138 kg CO₂-eq/kWh) exceed the SSP2-RCP2.6 justice-based and grandfathering targets by factors of 6.2 and 1.9, respectively. Under SSP2-RCP2.6, combined foreground and background improvements reduce impacts by 75% to 34 kg CO₂-eq/kWh by 2050. Sixteen mitigation measures are derived to reach net-zero; 70 kg CO₂-eq/kWh can be abated at negative marginal costs, yielding net savings of €70/kWh (−51%).

papers.title: The sense and sensibility of the circular material use rate: a case study of EU's key circularity indicator
papers.abstract: The Circular Material Use Rate (CMUR) has become a flagship indicator for monitoring progress towards a circular economy in the European Union. Promising in its conceptual simplicity, CMUR is widely employed in policy evaluations, international comparisons, and national target-setting. Yet despite its prominence, the indicator has been subject to limited empirical scrutiny. This paper examines the performance and interpretive validity of CMUR through a case study of Iceland, an economy characterized by high levels of imported materials, large-scale aluminum production, high percentage of renewable energy, significant biomass flows, and substantial domestic extraction of rock, sand and gravel. Based on a calculation of Iceland’s CMUR for 2024 and six policy-relevant scenarios—those being transport-related fossil fuel phase-out, increased recycling of household waste, food-waste reduction, material-efficiency measures in cement use, sufficiency scenarios for electronics and textiles, and all measures combined—the analysis shows that CMUR exhibits limited responsiveness to core circular economy interventions in this particular case. In some scenarios, such as food-waste prevention, CMUR decreases when environmental performance improves. The paper identifies one main structural reason for this behavior: the overwhelming dominance of a few inert and/or structurally non-circular materials in domestic consumption. To address this, the paper explores a contextualization of CMUR by modifying the boundary conditions for those materials. The findings highlight the importance of contextual interpretation when CMUR is used to evaluate circular performance and to inform policy. The analysis further suggests that similar interpretive challenges may arise in other European economies with comparable material-flow structures.

papers.title: Deriving Organism-Relevant Nanoparticle Safety Exposure Limits from In Vitro Toxicity Data
papers.abstract: Abstract Establishing human safety limits of engineered nanoparticles remains a challenge. In vitro assays have become a major toxicity data resource, driven by the demand for new approach methodologies (NAMs) that reduce animal testing. However, robust tools that bridge in vitro data with in vivo outcomes are still lacking. Here, we present an integrated computational framework using physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) modeling to derive organism-level BMD10-based dose estimates directly from in vitro liver toxicity data. For 4 nondissolvable nanoparticles (TiO2, SiO2, Au, and graphene oxide), we curated in vitro toxicity data sets spanning 7 liver-relevant cell systems (5 human and 2 mouse) across 24 assays and estimated in vitro effect thresholds using the benchmark dose for a 10% response (BMD10). Mouse in vitro BMD10 values were then reverse-translated into predicted BMD10IVIVE values using a validated mouse PBPK model and benchmarked against available mouse-derived in vivo effect threshold (BMD10eq) data to ensure consistency. The resulting nanoparticle-specific BMD10IVIVE ranges showed qualitative concordance with animal-derived reference doses, supporting the biological plausibility of these screening-level dose estimates. We further applied the same workflow to human liver cell systems to derive human-relevant BMD10-based points of departure. This approach establishes a scalable and prospective animal-free workflow for human nanoparticle risk assessments, overcoming a critical translational gap.

papers.title: Nanoconfinement Decouples Calcium-Enhanced Phosphate Capture from Calcium Phosphate Crystal Maturation
papers.abstract: Abstract Calcium phosphate (Ca–P) scaling, which is ubiquitous in nature and in water systems, has been shown to interfere with the capture of phosphate by ferric oxide-based sorbents, thereby deteriorating their decontamination performance in repeated cycles. Here, we show that a specifically designed gel-type nanocomposite, namely HFO@N201, enables Ca-enhanced phosphate sequestration while restricting Ca–P scaling via nanoconfinement. Increasing the initial Ca2+ concentration from 0 to 160 mg/L improved phosphate uptake from ∼4.5 to ∼6.2 mg/g in the first cycle. After 20 adsorption-regeneration cycles, phosphate uptake remained at ∼6.4 mg/g in the Ca-containing system, twice that of ∼3.2 mg/g in the Ca-free system. In fixed-bed tests, the presence of Ca2+ enhanced the working capacity from ∼1350 to ∼1800 bed volumes, which could be observed again in the subsequent cycle. Asynchronous release of Fe, P, and Ca during acidic elution of P-loaded HFO@N201 indicates heterogeneous and nonstoichiometric Ca-associated phosphate retention rather than formation of a mature bulk Ca–P phase. XRD, TEM, EXAFS, and Mössbauer spectroscopy further show that the retained Ca–P species remained weakly ordered and that the nanosized ferrihydrite-like Fe phase persisted during cyclic operation. Thermodynamic analysis, classical nucleation theory, and molecular dynamics simulations further support that the nanoconfinement structure of HFO@N201 (∼2 nm) creates a low-mobility hydration environment that restricts solvent exchange, ion rearrangement, and long-range ordering, thereby stabilizing Ca–P species in a weakly ordered interfacial state. Our work demonstrates nanoconfinement as a strategy to exploit Ca-enhanced phosphate capture while reducing Ca–P scaling in regenerable sorbents.

papers.title: Influence of COVID-19 Lockdown on Atmospheric Nitrate Sources and Chemistry in the Northeastern US
papers.abstract: Abstract The outbreak of COVID-19 and subsequent lockdowns caused widespread restrictions on human activities. This presented a unique opportunity to track atmospheric chemistry changes under rapid emission reductions. Using stable nitrogen (δ15N) and triple oxygen isotopes (δ18O and Δ17O) of particulate nitrate (pNO3) collected from 2019 to 2020 in the northeastern US, combined with 0-D box-model simulations, we investigate the response of atmospheric nitrate chemistry during the COVID-19 lockdown period (March 2020) in the northeastern US. Triple oxygen isotope measurements indicate that emission reductions altered the relative contributions of NOx oxidation pathways, with a shift toward the NO2 + OH pathway and a reduced contribution from N2O5 hydrolysis. This shift was consistent with the modeled increase in OH concentrations and the observed and modeled decrease in O3 during the COVID-19 lockdown, which limited N2O5 formation and subsequent heterogeneous nitrate formation. Moreover, nitrogen isotope-constrained sensitivity analysis suggests that a reduction of approximately 40(±10)% in transportation NOx emissions relative to the annual emission inventory estimates may be required to reproduce the observed decrease in δ15N(pNO3) during the COVID-19 period. These findings highlight the utility of isotopes to detail the complex interactions between emission reductions, atmospheric oxidation chemistry, and secondary aerosol formation. Understanding these interactions is critical for effectively determining air pollution mitigation strategies and testing air-quality models, particularly under rapidly evolving emission conditions associated with energy transitions and policy interventions.

papers.title: Unveiling Seven-Decade Disparities of Methane Emissions across China
papers.abstract: Abstract China’s century-long economic transition generated substantial methane emissions, yet the trajectory and factors of this evolution remain poorly quantified. A systematic understanding is essential for reconciling China’s economic growth with emission mitigation targets and for informing Global South nations. Using a bottom-up estimate of subnational methane emissions (1949–2022), we uncover a fundamental shift from agriculture-dominated to industry-dominated methane emissions in China. Nationwide emissions peaked in 2012, declining 3.8% by 2022, yet provincial disparities widened by 48%. While superficially reflecting heterogeneous fossil fuel use, these disparities are attributable to a shift in explanatory dominance from purely economic to dual economic-policy factors, particularly carbon policies. The long-term stability in agricultural sectors reflects nationwide efforts to food security, which maintains a baseline level of production across provinces. Recent regional decoupling masks the disproportion between emissions and economic gains. Western provinces (e.g., Shanxi, Ningxia, Guizhou) continue to exhibit high-emission but low-return economic profiles. The average of their methane emissions per GDP was 4.8 times that of eastern regions in 2022, with extremes reaching 150-fold differences. For equitable mitigation, future focus should shift from “who emits” to “why emits”, establishing a scientific basis for fair compensation between resource-dependent and resource-consuming regions.

papers.title: Subsoil versus Topsoil Straw Addition Shifts Microbial Carbon Allocation for Enhanced Carbon Sequestration and Emission Mitigation
papers.abstract: Abstract Subsoils (>20 cm) represent an underutilized sink for soil organic carbon (SOC) sequestration because C inputs in subsoil are typically limited. To clarify how organic inputs regulate subsoil SOC accrual and C emissions in rice paddies, we combined a 2-year field experiment with 13C-labeled straw incubation and validated the results with a global meta-analysis. Results showed that compared with no addition and topsoil straw addition, subsoil straw addition increased SOC stocks by 10.5% and 2.2%, respectively, primarily via enhanced mineral-associated organic C (MAOC) formation at 0–30 cm. The 270-day incubation revealed that subsoil addition accelerated microbial conversion of straw C into amino sugars, evidenced by 13C-phospholipid fatty acids, promoting MAOC formation. Relative to topsoil addition, subsoil addition reduced CH4 emissions by 15.3%, driven by improved root growth and enhanced CH4 oxidation, and decreased CO2 emissions by lowering topsoil C availability and peroxidase activity. Meta-analysis confirmed that C emissions decrease progressively with increasing incorporation depth, and machine-learning models indicate that deeper incorporation (>20 cm) mitigates global C emissions by half under future climate change. Overall, compared with topsoil addition, subsoil addition represents a win–win strategy that simultaneously enhances SOC sequestration and reduces C emissions, with potential applicability beyond paddy systems.

papers.title: The Subclinical Cardiovascular Effects of Nonoptimum Ambient Temperature: A Longitudinal Study in 15 Chinese Cities
papers.abstract: Abstract Short-term ambient temperature is linked to cardiovascular morbidity and mortality, but subclinical responses remain unclear. Using repeated health examinations from 247,641 adults in 15 Chinese cities (2013–2020), we assessed 20 cardiovascular indicators with linear mixed-effects and distributed lag nonlinear models. The indicator-specific sample sizes ranged from 1119 to 219,090 participants. Exposure–response relationships were near-linear or inversely J-shaped for ten indicators, U-shaped or inverted U-shaped for seven, and atypical or unclear for three. Low temperature was associated with 18 indicators, peaking at lags 0–5 days, whereas high temperature was associated with seven, peaking at lags 0–6 days. Relative to the reference temperatures, extremely low-temperature exposure (P1, −9 °C) was associated with cumulative increases over lag days 0–10 of 6.52%–13.99% in blood pressure, 4.63%–46.23% in inflammatory markers, 5.11%–10.48% in cardiac-associated enzymes, and 6.29% in homocysteine, as well as cumulative changes ranging from −2.68% to 5.36% in hemorheological parameters and from −4.96% to 12.05% in lipid-related indicators. Extremely high-temperature exposure (P99, 32 °C) was associated with cumulative changes ranging from −1.47% to 4.84% in hemorheological parameters and increases of 1.62%–1.91% in lipid indicators and 1.32%–15.13% in cardiac-associated enzymes. These findings provide multicenter evidence that nonoptimum temperature is associated with early cardiovascular alterations.

papers.title: Correction to “Exposure to Intermittent Environmental Hypoxia Promotes Vascular Remodeling through Angiogenesis in the Liver of Largemouth Bass ( Micropterus salmoides )”
Nontargeted Identification and Prioritization of Organic Contaminants in Biosolid-Amended Soils across the United States
papers.abstract: Abstract The widespread use of biosolids as an agricultural soil amendment has raised concerns about the release of organic contaminants into the environment. This study identifies biosolids-associated organic contaminants (BOCs) in soils from municipal biosolid-amended plots across the United States. Soil samples were collected from 18 sites in 15 states, representing biosolids applications from the 1980s to the present. Samples were taken at three depths (30, 90, and 180 cm) from plots with no, low, and high application histories. Samples were extracted using QuEChERS and analyzed by liquid chromatography–high-resolution mass spectrometry (LC-HRMS) using a nontargeted analysis (NTA) approach. A total of 111 BOCs were detected across biosolid-amended plots. BOCs were detected most frequently in surface soils (30 cm), with significantly fewer detections at subsurface depths (p < 0.001). Cumulative loading rate and application frequency were significant predictors of the number of BOCs detected (p = 0.003 and p = 0.017, respectively). Quality-adjusted hazard scores for human health, ecological impact, and environmental fate identified 4-nitrophenol (44%), PFBS (41%), and miconazole (38%), among others as the highest-priority BOCs. This NTA-hazard prioritization workflow provides a strategy for identifying compounds warranting further evaluation for potential environmental and human health risks.

papers.title: Unraveling the Bound-Water Removal Mystery: Preoxidation Enhances Sludge Dewatering via Cell Permeabilization and Transformation of Intracellular Polymeric Substances to Extracellular Polymeric Substances
papers.abstract: Abstract The effect of oxidation degree on sludge dewaterability during oxone-induced preoxidation was investigated. The optimal oxone concentration increased free cells and membrane permeabilization while limiting cell lysis, releasing bound water, and producing a drier sludge cake without reducing the filtrate volume. Dewaterability enhancement was mainly driven by the shift of low-molecular-weight proteins and polysaccharides (<20 kDa) from intracellular polymeric substances (IPS) to extracellular polymeric substances (EPS), along with selective degradation of hydrophilic glucose and peptidoglycan in EPS. Organic matter transferred to the outer EPS layer was mainly derived from the cellular constituents of Gram-negative bacteria in sludge. Importantly, IPS was found to exert a distinct and non-negligible influence on sludge dewatering with its oxidative response fundamentally differing from that of EPS. As the oxidation intensity increased, the ratio of protein to polysaccharide rose in loosely bound EPS but declined in IPS, whereas carboxyl and lactone groups decreased in both soluble and loosely bound EPS fractions, while carboxyl groups concurrently increased within IPS. IPS contained more hydrophobic components than did EPS at all oxone concentrations. Excessive oxidation induced cell disruption and hydrophilic debris, impairing sludge dewaterability. Cell membrane permeabilization, rather than cell lysis, was the key factor affecting sludge dewaterability.

papers.title: Electron Transfer at Microbe–Mineral Interfaces: From Molecular Mechanisms to Ecosystem-Scale Biogeochemical Cycling and Remediation
papers.abstract: Abstract Microbe–mineral electron transfer (MMET) drives key microbial processes and biogeochemical cycling, but linking these microscopic interactions to ecosystem-scale dynamics remains a major challenge. MMET couples intracellular metabolism to extracellular mineral transformations. The resulting changes in mineral redox state and reactivity can, in turn, influence microbial energy conservation and metabolism. MMET flux could therefore provide a quantitative link between nanometer-scale electron exchange and larger-scale biogeochemical processes. In energy-limited and contaminated environments, electroactive microorganisms may transfer electrons to or acquire electrons from redox-active minerals, depending on their metabolic capabilities and local redox conditions. These interactions can support energy conservation, mitigate toxic stress, and generate localized zones of high biogeochemical activity. As their effects accumulate across space and time, microscale electron transfer may influence ecosystem-scale elemental cycling, microbial community succession, organic carbon stabilization, and contaminant fate. Building on established modeling approaches, we suggest that integrating individual-based models (IBMs) with genome-scale metabolic models (GSMMs) could translate spatially heterogeneous, genome-informed microbial responses into collective MMET fluxes across scales while accounting for key thermodynamic and kinetic constraints. More broadly, progress requires characterizing electroactive microbial diversity and mechanisms, engineering microbe–mineral interfaces through computational design and synthetic biology, and translating MMET principles into scalable environmental applications.

papers.title: Longitudinal Multiomics Reveals Core Microbiome Disruption and Potential Keystone-Associated Recovery Following Pesticide Exposure
papers.abstract: Abstract Pesticides have become indispensable in modern agriculture, serving as a primary tool to minimize crop loss amid increasing human population pressures. While the negative effects of pesticides on the soil microbiome have been reported, the temporal dynamics of soil microorganisms under pesticide use remain underexplored. Specifically, limited knowledge exists regarding how the soil microbiome responds to pesticides before and after the manufacturer-labeled ‘safe period’ of 21 days after application. We conducted a longitudinal microcosm study to investigate the temporal impacts of herbicide, fungicide, and insecticide on soil microbial diversity, composition, network complexity, and functional pathways across five time points. Our results show that soil microbial communities are negatively impacted by pesticide applications, but there is a trend of recovery after 21 days. We found a significant impact of the temporal persistence of pesticides on both bacterial and fungal community composition, with a stronger effect on fungi. Network analysis revealed that core microbiome networks were negatively impacted by pesticide applications, with the core microbial nodes, raw associations, and modularity declining in pesticide-treated soils, and this negative effect was particularly strong for pyrethroid insecticides. We identified several differentially abundant taxa, including Xanthobacteraceae and Vicinamibacteriales among bacteria, and Mortierella, Mytilinidales among fungi, which could serve as useful biomarkers for pesticide-affected soils. Results from microbial co-occurrence network analysis revealed that one ASV assigned to the Methyloligellaceae family consistently emerged as a keystone taxon in pesticide-treated soils. Using genome-resolved metagenomics, we assembled the genomes (MAGs) of Methyloligellaceae members and found these taxa harbor putative genes associated with pesticide degradation and antimicrobial resistance, suggesting their possible role in community recovery. Given the remarkably dynamic nature of soil microbial communities, our findings bridge an important knowledge gap regarding the short-term dynamics of microbial structures and functional pathways in response to major pesticides.

papers.title: Mapping the Carbon Footprint of Organic Chemicals in Commerce
Novel NIR-II Imaging Reveals Gut-First, Brain-Later Inorganic Mercury Signals with Structural Injury in Zebrafish
papers.abstract: Abstract Mercury (Hg) neurotoxicity has generally been assessed by organic methylmercury, whereas inorganic mercury [Hg(II)] is often considered less likely to cause direct brain exposure. Conventional approaches cannot resolve the in vivo spatiotemporal distribution of Hg(II) across tissues. In this study, we first developed an Hg(II)-responsive aggregation-induced emission sensor for second near-infrared (NIR-II) fluorescence imaging, which was then employed to track Hg(II) signals in live zebrafish. The sensor produced enhanced NIR-II signals in the presence of Hg(II), allowing low-background, noninvasive, and real-time imaging. We observed that Hg(II)-responsive sensor signals first appeared in the intestinal region and later increased in the brain region, revealing an intestine-first and brain-later temporal pattern in living zebrafish. During a 48-h continuous exposure followed by depuration, brain-region Hg(II)-responsive sensor fluorescence increased with exposure concentration and time and remained detectable during the depuration phase. Expansion microscopy further showed that low-dose Hg(II) exposure reduced the brain cell density and average cell size, and disrupted the local tissue organization. These results provided in vivo evidence of Hg(II)-responsive sensor in the brain region and its association with structural brain injury during development. Thus, inorganic Hg should also be considered in the assessments of developmental brain exposure and neural structural injury.

papers.title: Solar Activation of Peroxymonosulfate by Chromophoric Dissolved Organic Matter Enables Predictable Micropollutant Attenuation in Real Waters
papers.abstract: Solar-driven activation of peroxymonosulfate (PMS) is a promising advanced oxidation process for water and wastewater treatment; however, the kinetics of emerging contaminant removal in real water matrices remain poorly understood. In this study, we investigated PMS photosensitization in three environmentally relevant water matrices and evaluated its role in the abatement of 42 pharmaceuticals and personal care products (PPCPs). Under simulated solar irradiation, CDOM promoted PMS transformation and generated multiple photochemically produced reactive intermediates (PPRIs). A multiple-probe chemical method was employed to quantify the cumulative exposure doses of HO•, SO4•-, Cl2•-, CO3•-, and 1O2. Across the tested matrices, PPRI exposure doses followed the order CO3•- > 1O2 > Cl2•- ∼ SO4•- > HO•. The measured PPRI exposure doses, together with second-order rate constants, reasonably predicted PPCP removal in the solar/PMS/CDOM system. For several phenolic and aniline-containing PPCPs, DOM-mediated inhibition was observed and was attributed to reductive back-reaction of one-electron oxidation intermediates; incorporating inhibition factors improved the agreement between calculated and experimental removal efficiencies. Furthermore, four commonly detected PPCPs, sucralose, metformin, caffeine, and carbamazepine, were first identified as practical indicator compounds for estimating PPRI exposure without adding external probe chemicals. These findings provide a mechanistic framework for predicting PPCP attenuation during solar/PMS treatment in CDOM-rich waters and highlight the importance of secondary radicals in real aquatic matrices.

papers.title: Upcycling agricultural biomass waste into sustainable carbon dots with dual-color emission for optical security applications
Quantitative evolution of unfixed dyes, clearing mechanism, and universality of low-pollution sulfonated polymer-assisted reduction-free clearing of disperse-dyed polyester fabrics
Life cycle assessment for disposal of polypropylene food packaging plastic waste
Bio-based gelatin supramolecular microcup arrays via molecular engineering towards sustainable electrophoretic displays
Power-reduction detection and classification in photovoltaic modules using clustering of parametric deviations
papers.abstract: Power reduction in photovoltaic modules may be caused by environmental conditions, faults, and degradation mechanisms, whose correct identification is essential to improve the reliability, safety, and energy yield of photovoltaic systems. This article proposes a classification approach for power-reduction scenarios based on parametric deviations extracted from a Global Nonlinear Model (GNLM) derived from the Single-Diode Model (SDM). The methodology starts with the construction of a GNLM representative of a healthy reference photovoltaic module, capable of describing its electrical behavior under different irradiance and temperature conditions. For each evaluated experimental current–voltage ( I–V ) curve, selected SDM parameters associated with this healthy reference model are adjusted to approximate the electrical behavior of the analyzed module. The deviations required for this adjustment, calculated with respect to the healthy reference condition, are used as diagnostic markers for clustering-based classification. Different power-reduction conditions were evaluated, including soiling, short-circuited bypass diodes, open-diode conditions under different shading levels, front-glass breakage, and partial shading (PS). To reduce the overlap between scenarios with distinct electrical behaviors, the samples were initially separated according to the number of maxima in the power–voltage ( P–V ) curve, denoted by N peak , distinguishing cases with N peak = 1 from those with N peak > 1 . Based on these diagnostic markers, two strategies are investigated according to the set of SDM parameters used in the classification process. Strategy 1 uses deviations in the diode ideality factor ( n ) and photogenerated current ( I p h ), achieving the best performance, with an overall accuracy of 99.6%. Strategy 2 uses deviations in the n , series resistance ( R s ), and shunt resistance ( R s h ), achieving an overall accuracy of 98.3%.

papers.title: A decoupled dual–stream CNN–LSTM with adaptive attention mechanism for joint multivariate forecasting of solar irradiance and wind speed
Investigation and parametric optimization of external spray cooling for gas turbine inlet air via computational fluid dynamics simulation and response surface methodology
Microplastics as vectors and reservoirs of pharmaceuticals and drugs of abuse: experimental evidence, mechanistic predictions and analytical challenges
Strategic phosphorus recovery clusters in Europe: Linking geospatial resource availability with thermochemical recovery potential
papers.abstract: Phosphorus (P) is an essential, non-substitutional resource, yet Europe's supply of elemental P (P 4 ) - classified as critical raw material – remains highly vulnerable. This study assesses whether Europe's secondary organic P resources can support centralized P 4 recovery by linking demand, resource availability, spatial distribution and thermochemical recovery potential. European P 4 demand was estimated at 34.7 kt(P 4 )/a from foreign trade statistics for 2017–2022. Sewage sludge alone contains an estimated 190.9–220 kt(P)/a across the EU-27 and the United Kingdom, demonstrating that resource availability exceeds current demand but is spatially distributed. Geospatial clustering identified nine phosphorus resource centers (PRCs) containing 19.5% of the European sewage-sludge-derived P 4 potential, while 80.5% remains distributed outside these hotspots. The PRCs differed substantially in plant size and feedstock distribution, highlighting spatial aggregation, not P availability, as a key constraint for centralized recovery. Highest P-flux Ruhr-area PRC was subsequently evaluated using a METSIM-based FlashPhos digital twin. Co-processing sewage sludge with Category 1 meat-and-bone meal (MBM) reduced the Fe:P ratio and increased the modeled P 4 recovery from 73.42% to 78.09%, corresponding to a potential output of up to 5350 t(P 4 )/a, or 16.5% of European demand. MBM co-processing provided an additional gross economic contribution of 4.02–5.25 million€/a through increased P 4 production and avoided CaO expenditure. The results demonstrate that Europe possesses sufficient secondary P resources to substantially exceed current P 4 demand, but their decentralized distribution makes spatial aggregation a principal constraint. High-density PRCs combined with complementary feedstocks therefore represent promising targets for future site-specific logistical, techno-economic and experimental assessment of centralized P 4 recovery.

papers.title: Pesticide-driven bacterial adaptation: biodegradation pathways and co-selection of antibiotic resistance
papers.abstract: The intensive use and misuse of pesticides has increased the chemical pressure exerted on soil microbiomes. According to the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), the global pesticide used in agriculture in 2023 reached 3.73 million tonnes of active ingredients, highlighting the magnitude of environmental exposure. Soil bacteria can adapt to pesticide contamination through catabolic pathways encoded by chromosomal genes and/or mobile genetic elements (MGEs), enabling pesticide transformation and sometimes supporting bioremediation. In parallel, a growing body of evidence indicates that non-antibiotic chemicals including herbicides and insecticides can contribute to the emergence and persistence of antibiotic resistance through co-selection. Mechanisms include cross-resistance mediated by multidrug efflux pumps and permeability changes, stress-induced responses and enhanced horizontal gene transfer (HGT) that facilitates the dissemination of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) and MGEs in environmental ecosystems including soil, water and others. In this review, we summarise current knowledge on biodegradation pathways, genetic determinants and documented evidence linked to antibiotic resistance for five selected pesticide case studies: glyphosate, atrazine, cypermethrin, chlorpyrifos and paraquat. We identify where evidence is strongest (e.g., herbicide-associated AMR outcomes) and where major gaps remain, particularly regarding causal attribution under environmentally realistic concentrations and the frequency of ARG co-localisation with catabolic loci. We further propose an explicit mechanistic framework in which biodegradation and antibiotic resistance are examined as potentially interconnected components of bacterial adaptation, connected by a shared mobilome, a shared efflux and stress-response, the reactive intermediates of incomplete catabolism, and nutrient-driven community restructuring.

papers.title: Relevant disruptions in critical mineral supply chain sustainability: A systematic literature review
papers.abstract: Critical mineral supply chains are central to the energy transition but are increasingly exposed to disruptions that affect their economic, environmental, and social performance. Existing research has quantified the sustainability outcome, examined tier-specific research, and identified the wide range of disruption risks. However, these concepts remain fragmented and rarely integrate into a single analytical framework. Furthermore, few studies systematically prioritise the disruptions' relevance based on their tier's prevalence and the strength of their sustainability evidence within the supply chain. This paper addresses this gap through a systematic literature review of 103 Scopus- and Web of Science-indexed articles on critical mineral supply chain disruption and sustainability. The review descriptively classifies the literature by mineral type, geographical focus, research method, disruption category, supply chain tier, and sustainability dimension, using a full-text-coded article. It then develops a two-parameter, structured content analysis to assess which disruptions are most relevant in the literature, based on tier-based prevalence and sustainability-impact evidence. The finding indicates that price volatility and supply-demand imbalance are among the most prominent disruptions affecting supply chain sustainability performance, while logistics and transportation-related have received comparatively limited attention. The finding also reveals further research avenue to address county- and mineral-specific studies, a dynamic approach that integrates social performance and robust disruption assessment.

Performance analysis of waste heat utilization system for magnesium smelting flue gas
Co-pollutant mortality effects of short-term exposure to fine particles and ozone: A global systematic review and meta-analysis with omitted variable bias correction
Sustainability assessment of low-carbon soil stabilization strategies for cold region transportation infrastructure: an integrated life cycle and multi-criteria decision-making framework
Integrated Prediction and Analysis of Soil Erosion and Soil Organic Carbon Loss in the Dayekou Watershed, Qilian Mountains
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Soil erosion poses a critical threat to ecological security in mountain watersheds worldwide. Predicting its dynamics and associated soil organic carbon (SOC) loss remains an ongoing challenge during the 21st century due to complex interactions among climate, land use, and topography. This study developed an integrated modeling framework by combining Long Short‐Term Memory (LSTM) neural networks, Cellular Automata‐Markov (CA‐Markov), and the InVEST Sediment Delivery Ratio module to predict soil erosion and SOC loss in the Dayekou Watershed in northwest China's Qilian Mountains. LSTM accurately forecasted 48 months of rainfall (RMSE: 177.9–211.7) using 300 months of historical data (2000–2024), while CA‐Markov simulated land use patterns (2024–2028) with high precision (Kappa = 0.85). Results revealed that severe erosion areas (< 9% of watershed) contribute > 97% of total soil loss, concentrated above 3750 m elevation of the watershed. Land use type dominated erosion spatial distribution ( q = 78.8%), with glacier/snow and bare land exhibiting the highest erosion modulus. Average SOC loss increased from 9.877 to 21.524 t/(km 2 ·a) (2000–2023), with forested areas experiencing disproportionate carbon depletion despite lower erosion rates. The coupled framework demonstrates its robustness in predicting dynamic erosion in complex mountain systems, providing strong evidence‐based conservation support for protected areas in northwest China.

papers.title: Trade‐Offs Between Maize Productivity Improvement and Topsoil Salinization Risk Under Shallow Burial Drip Irrigation in Semi‐Arid Regions
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Drip irrigation is widely used to conserve water and maintain crop production in water‐limited regions. However, how contrasting drip irrigation systems shape soil water‐salt movement, water and nitrogen (N) use, and maize productivity in semi‐arid environments remains poorly understood. Here, we conducted a two‐year field experiment (2019–2020) with a randomized complete block design to compare shallow buried drip irrigation (SBDI) and mulched drip irrigation (MDI). Relative to MDI, SBDI increased grain yield, dry matter accumulation, and N uptake by 5.86%, 3.11%, and 9.58%, respectively, contributin to greater water and N use efficiency. Soil salinity dynamics were closely coupled with soil water movement, representing a remarkable accumulation in the 0–20 cm soil layer under SBDI compared to MDI, owing to higher evapotranspiration. Although both irrigation systems resulted in soil salt accumulation, SBDI was more conducive for chloride ion elution. Partial least squares path modeling, Random forest, and Mantel tests suggested that water N utilization and salt dynamics were highly related to maize productivity. Our findings enrich the theoretical framework for preventing secondary soil salinization by inhibiting soil resalinization via water regulation or interlayer installation. In the future, the integration of SBDI with desalination measures may be a crucial strategy for enabling sustainable high‐yield maize production in semi‐arid regions.

papers.title: Producing spatial justice: Scalar governance and territorial differentiation in coastal China’s nuclear development
papers.abstract: Nuclear infrastructure development highlights an important empirical case in environmental governance: nuclear facilities concentrate environmental and social burdens locally, yet many projects proceed without sustained opposition. In the context of China, this paper argues that such outcomes are produced through county-level scalar governance strategies. Focusing on the Zhangzhou Nuclear Power Project, the study reconstructs how local authorities designed four concentric governance zones (20 km, 10 km, 2 km, 200 m) and calibrated distance-based interventions—compensation and relocation, tiered emergency planning and monitoring, graded communication and participation, and differentiated infrastructure and welfare investments—so that governance intensity corresponded to spatial exposure. Drawing on archival materials, policy documents, and semi-structured interviews with officials and project actors, corroborated by administrative records and implementation milestones, the analysis shows that scalar governance pursued distributive, procedural, and recognition objectives across zones. Importantly, the absence of organized resistance is interpreted not as conflict resolution but as the managed incorporation of grievances into institutional channels within a constrained political environment. By reframing nuclear legitimacy as the outcome of territorially differentiated state action, the paper contributes to debates on territory, scale, and environmental governance and positioning spatial justice as a conditional mechanism for managing uneven infrastructural risk.
papers.journal_name: Environment and Planning C: Politics and Space

papers.title: Matching on Gender and Sexual Orientation,
papers.abstract: Abstract We study the mating patterns of non-heterosexual individuals, who represent a significant and increasing portion of the population, particularly among the youth. We estimate a multidimensional matching model of the marriage market where partner’s gender is endogenously chosen conditional on the agent’s sexual orientation, and is subject to trade-offs that depend on both the agents’ preferences and the pool of potential partners. We show that same-sex couples experience lower gains from live-in relationships, a “same-sex penalty”. Absent this penalty, the share of same-sex couples in the U.S. would increase by about 50% (from 1.36% to 2.04% of all couples).
papers.journal_name: Journal of the European Economic Association

papers.title: Union Membership and Native-Immigrant Labour Market Gaps
papers.abstract: Abstract We estimate the causal effects of union membership on labour market outcomes for natives and immigrants, exploiting quasi-experimental variation from large increases in Norway’s tax deduction for union dues. Union membership raises earnings and improves employment protection for native workers, while the private returns for non-Western immigrants are substantially smaller and often close to zero. Complementary survey evidence suggests that this gap is not explained by differences in information, preferences, or engagement with unions: immigrants receive similar information when joining, report similar preferences over job amenities, and are more likely than natives to seek union assistance. Instead, the combined administrative and survey evidence is consistent with differences in union-side behaviour. Immigrants report lower satisfaction after contacting unions for support and are more likely to believe that native workers and those with strong local networks receive greater benefits from membership. The impact is most pronounced in concentrated labour markets, indicating that relying on unions to address monopsony-based market failures may unintentionally amplify group inequalities.

papers.title: Production-Based Option Pricing
papers.abstract: We show that a structural model incorporating firms’ real options and financial leverage decisions can generate forward-looking equity distributions of various shapes, resulting in highly flexible implied volatility surfaces. In contrast, exogenously specified models with stochastic volatility and jumps can only generate smiles and downward-sloping curves. We explain the observed negative relationship between downward sloping implied volatility surfaces and the value of real options: real options contribute positively to equity skewness, and more so the more convex their payoff, which is the case when the real option is “at-the-money” and has the lowest value.

authors: Duro, Juan Antonio; Galiana, Pau; Soldevila, M. Victòria; Piñol, Josep M.; Martín, Mónica; Sardà, Jordi; Ponce-Alifonso, Xavier; Farré Albendea, Fco Javier
