Influence of Geopolitical Risk on Energy Transition and Climate Change
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Geopolitical tensions can influence energy transition, which, in turn, can impact climate change. Thus, we construct a framework that integrates these processes, analyzing 17 economies from 1990 to 2020 using a GVAR model. We hypothesize that geopolitical risk shocks affect economies through domestic financial markets. The results demonstrate that geopolitical risk shocks (i) hinder national energy transitions and contribute to increased carbon emissions; (ii) induce fluctuations in financial markets; (iii) have a minor direct impact on energy transition, except in Scandinavia and the United States; (iv) indirectly influence economies through financial markets (particularly stock markets); and (v) generate spillover effects and heterogeneities. We corroborate our findings through shock identification, treating financial markets as conduits for the geopolitical risk shock. Additionally, we conduct a battery of robustness checks addressing structural breaks, time‐varying bilateral trade, and bilateral financial flows (instead of bilateral trade), all of which confirm the consistency of our results. We conclude by discussing fiscal policies aimed at counterbalancing the negative effects of geopolitical risk on energy transition and climate change, emphasizing the importance of international cooperation for the effectiveness of these policies.

papers.title: Navigating Climate Risk for Resilience: A Roadmap of Research Patterns and Emerging Trends
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Climate risk has become a defining challenge for business strategy, yet its research landscape remains fragmented across disciplines. This study maps the intellectual structure of climate risk research through a bibliometric analysis enriched with latent Dirichlet allocation (LDA) topic modeling of 2715 peer‐reviewed articles. Our analysis first identifies the following six consolidated research patterns: (1) climate adaptation and community resilience, (2) climate risk and insurance mechanisms, (3) climate finance and green investment, (4) climate extremes and scenario modeling, (5) climate impacts and agricultural resilience, and (6) climate mitigation and energy transition. Analysis of the 2020–2024 literature reveals four emerging trends: urban climate adaptation, climate risk and financial stability, extreme climate events and climate modeling, agriculture, food security and household security. The findings indicate a shift toward integrated approaches connecting the physical, social, and financial dimensions of climate risk. The resulting roadmap identifies converging risks and strategic priorities for organizational resilience while providing policymakers with an evolving evidence base to support climate governance and informed decision‐making under deepening uncertainty.

papers.title: Structural Dynamics of the European Circular Economy Through a Consumption–Circularity–Efficiency Framework
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT The transition toward a circular economy requires analytical approaches capable of capturing the interdependence between resource consumption, material circularity, and economic efficiency rather than assessing these processes through isolated indicators. This study develops and empirically evaluates the Consumption–Circularity–Efficiency (CCE) framework as an integrated representation of circular‐economy performance across the EU‐27. A balanced panel of 378 country–year observations covering 27 Member States over 2010–2023 was constructed from 10 harmonized Eurostat indicators. Principal component analysis (PCA) was used to identify the dominant multivariate structure, followed by robustness and alternative‐retention analyses, construction of dimension scores and a composite CCE index, country‐level and temporal assessment, and complementary observed‐variable structural equation modelling (SEM) with country‐clustered robust inference. Three retained PCA components explain 71.44% of total variance and correspond to Consumption, Circularity, and Efficiency, although substantive cross‐loadings show that these dimensions are interconnected rather than empirically isolated. The variance‐weighted CCE index proved highly robust to equal weighting ( r = 0.983, p < 0.001), indicating that comparative positioning is not driven by the aggregation rule. Country‐level results reveal pronounced structural heterogeneity: Similar composite CCE scores arise from markedly different combinations of consumption intensity, circular‐resource performance, and efficiency. Temporal analysis indicates an overall improvement in relative EU‐27 CCE performance between 2010 and 2023, accompanied by non‐linear evolution and persistent divergence in national transition pathways. SEM provides complementary structural corroboration by identifying RMC, resource productivity, and GDP per capita as interconnected interfaces between material throughput, circularity, and economic performance; several relationships operate through significant indirect pathways rather than direct associations alone. Global SEM fit is mixed, supporting structural compatibility rather than complete confirmatory fit or causal interpretation. The study contributes to circular‐economy research by integrating dimensional identification, composite measurement, structural configurations, temporal dynamics, and pathway analysis within a single empirical architecture. The CCE framework therefore provides a configuration‐based diagnostic approach that can support differentiated circular‐economy strategies while preserving the structural information concealed by conventional aggregate rankings.

papers.title: Transitioning to Circular Beauty: the Sense–Trust–Adopt (STA) Framework for Scaling Upcycled Ingredient Integration in Sustainable Cosmetics
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT The cosmetics industry faces increasing pressure to integrate upcycled agro‐food by‐products, yet consumer adoption remains constrained by contamination concerns that are strongest for products applied directly to the body. Linear attitudinal models offer limited insight into how meaning is constructed around novel “waste‐derived” claims. This study therefore examines how consumers interpret, evaluate, and negotiate trust in cosmetic formulations containing upcycled ingredients. Thirty‐one in‐depth interviews with UK consumers were analyzed through reflexive thematic analysis, combined with close attention to the language participants used, and structured by the FRASE elicitation framework (familiarity, reflection, articulation, sentiment, engagement). The findings show that evaluation unfolds in stages rather than as a single attitudinal judgment: Most participants initially misunderstood the category, typically assuming that upcycled cosmetics are made from recovered used products, and this misreading—rather than weak environmental motivation—constituted the first barrier to acceptance. Trust was then negotiated on two fronts: whether the product is safe and effective, and whether the claim itself is credible and independently verifiable. Acceptance thresholds varied by application zone: A majority of participants demanded stronger evidence for facial products than for body products—a pattern termed contextual gatekeeping—although a substantial minority applied uniform standards across zones. These insights are integrated into the sense–trust–adopt (STA) framework, advanced as a provisional interpretive framework rather than a tested model of behavior. Implications are developed for communication strategy, certification design, market‐entry sequencing, and policy support for circular business models aligned with SDG 12. The contribution lies in locating the barrier to circular adoption in comprehension and trust negotiation rather than in environmental attitudes alone.

papers.title: Examining the Relationships Between Sustainability Orientation, Entrepreneurial Orientation, and SME Financial Performance in the Italian Agri‐Food Sector
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT This study investigates the relationship between sustainability orientation, entrepreneurial orientation (EO), and financial performance of Italian agri‐food SMEs, using panel data (2017–2022) and random‐effects models. The analysis identifies three sustainability dimensions—social, environmental, and external stakeholder‐oriented—examined alongside EO dimensions through a multidimensional approach. Results show that environmental sustainability is not significantly associated with financial performance. Social sustainability is negatively associated with operating and net income, while external stakeholder‐oriented sustainability is negatively associated with operating and net income, ROI, and ROA. EO dimensions show heterogeneous associations: innovativeness is positively associated with ROA, proactiveness with operating and net income, and risk‐taking is negatively associated with ROE. Competitiveness and autonomy show no significant associations with financial performance. Overall, the findings highlight heterogeneous relationships between sustainability and EO dimensions and different measures of financial performance, underscoring the value of examining both strategic orientations at the dimensional level over time.

papers.title: Modeling ESG Performance Drivers in the Shipping Industry: An LLM‐Assisted q‐ ROFRS‐Delphi‐WINGS‐FCM Framework for Causal Analysis and Simulation
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT The shipping industry plays a vital role in global trade and also exerts significant environmental and social pressures due to high fuel consumption, greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, and intensive port activities. Implementing environmental, social, and governance (ESG) practices offers a strategic pathway to enhance sustainability performance in this sector; however, it remains difficult to determine which managerial and operational actions can most effectively drive improvements in ESG performance. To address this challenge, this study proposes a novel framework that integrates a large language model (LLM), an extended q‐ rung orthopair fuzzy rough set ( q‐ ROFRS)‐based Delphi‐weighted influence nonlinear gauge system (WINGS) model, and a fuzzy cognitive mapping (FCM) simulation. This approach systematically identifies critical success factors (CSFs), analyzes their cause–effect relationships, and simulates their dynamic influence on ESG performance in the shipping industry. The findings reveal that six CSFs, including structured board oversight, global policy engagement, comprehensive legal compliance framework, employee‐centric culture, effective communication strategy, and integrated water resource management, serve as key causal drivers within the ESG system. FCM‐based scenario simulations suggest that full activation of these modeled drivers could substantially improve projected ESG performance under the assumed scenario conditions. This research offers a dual contribution: Theoretically, it extends fuzzy decision‐making and AI‐driven causal modeling to complex sustainability systems; practically, it provides actionable guidance for shipping companies and policymakers to strengthen ESG integration, meet the International Maritime Organization's net‐zero targets, and advance the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

papers.title: From Friends to Filings? Social Connectedness and the Demand for Public Information
papers.abstract: Exploiting social network data from Facebook, we show that investors acquire more publicly disclosed information about firms located in counties that are more socially connected to their home counties. Using significant information events as shocks to private communication within social networks, we find that this relation is stronger in the weeks leading up to these events, consistent with private communication via social networks stimulating investors’ demand for public information. The relation is also stronger when there is greater scope for complementarity between private communication and public information. Furthermore, we provide evidence that stock prices respond to earnings announcements more rapidly for firms headquartered in more socially connected counties, suggesting social networks improve price discovery. Overall, our study provides new insights into how social communication shapes investors’ acquisition of public information.

papers.title: The great slowdown? Trajectories of sustainability reporting boundary change from a value chain perspective 1990–2020
papers.abstract: Purpose As sustainability has become an increasingly urgent and critical challenge, firms have faced growing expectations to broaden the scope of accountability by extending their sustainability reporting boundaries. This article analyses sustainability boundary change from a value chain perspective across different phases of sustainability reporting. Design/methodology/approach We analysed sustainability boundaries, i.e. the extent to which a firm accounts for impacts across its own operations and wider value chain, in a single value chain of steel-adjacent firms in Sweden, using a firm- and value chain-level assessment framework developed in the article. Reports from 1990, 2000, 2010 and 2020 were analysed qualitatively and quantitatively to identify boundary trajectories based on an institutional theory framing. Findings Boundaries expanded significantly between 1990 and 2020; however, this trajectory slowed between 2010 and 2020 as sustainability reporting became stabilised as a practice, with extensions primarily occurring upstream rather than downstream or societally. No firms were found to use holistic reporting by including a full value chain perspective. Research limitations/implications Firm-centric reporting is shown to be the dominant approach over time; this sits in tension with mounting expectations to report on sustainability topics more broadly. It is suggested that future studies explore other institutional contexts, countries and value chain configurations to support and expand on the findings. Studies on a more granular level than the 10-year increments used in this study could also reveal nuances of boundary extension over time. Originality/value We distinguish between scope and depth, two dimensions of sustainability boundaries, to develop a framework of boundary approaches: firm-limited reporting, insular reporting, value chain aware reporting and holistic reporting. Based on these, we identify opportunities and challenges for adopting a value chain perspective in sustainability reporting, noting that, while the number of topics (i.e. depth) can be increased by using reporting frameworks like Global Reporting Initiative, incorporating topics at the value chain level (i.e. scope) remains a key challenge for firms due to the firm-centric logic used in both financial and sustainability reporting.

papers.title: Accounting for the working conditions of social compliance auditors investigating modern slavery in supply chains
papers.abstract: Purpose This study explores the working conditions of social compliance auditors who investigate modern slavery in global supply chains. This issue is important for understanding how auditors' working environment shapes audits as a key mechanism for detecting modern slavery. Design/methodology/approach We conducted 32 interviews with actors involved in social compliance auditing, including auditors, certification bodies, NGOs and accreditation agencies. Drawing on labour process theory and the complex role of multi-principal employment networks, we analyse how the work of auditing, the objects of that work and the instruments that structure it organises control, dependency and risk across external modern slavery audits. Findings Our findings show that social compliance auditing can be intensive, under-resourced work in remote, often hostile settings, producing heightened vulnerability for auditors. We also find that auditors periodically face physical harm and managerial coercion, including intimidation, violence and efforts to manipulate or suppress critical findings precisely because those findings pose a threat to business interests when non-compliant labour practices are found. Nonetheless, we show how auditors draw on “buffers of culpability” which include micro-resistance, safety-driven adaptation and agentic use of informal tools, relationships and planning, to preserve some investigative integrity despite these adverse conditions. Originality/value Businesses are increasingly held accountable for labour conditions in their supply chains and rely on social compliance auditors to independently assess operating facilities, yet auditors' own working conditions and structural vulnerabilities remain poorly understood. We specify implications at both agentic (micro) and structural (macro) levels for the governance and reform of social compliance auditing in the context of fragmented and multi-principal employment networks.

papers.title: The Role of Institutions in the Relationship Between Informal Competition and New Product Development in Emerging Economies
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Academic Summary Research has argued that informal competition (IC)—the competitive pressure from firms that are unregistered but derive income from the production of legal goods and services—increases formal (i.e., legally registered) firms' engagement in new product development (NPD) in emerging economies. However, other studies have suggested that IC may decrease such engagement. Drawing on an institutional perspective, we argue that the relationship between IC and NPD is contingent on the level of IC and the influence of formal and informal institutions. A multilevel analysis of 29,520 formal firms across 21 emerging economies indicates an inverted U‐shaped relationship between IC and NPD probability. Low to moderate levels of IC increase NPD probability, whereas higher levels reduce it. The findings also reveal that this relationship varies across emerging economies, with significant cross‐level interactions between IC and elements of formal (e.g., regulatory control, availability of finance) and informal institutions (e.g., survival vs. self‐expression and traditional vs. secular‐rational values) shaping NPD probability. Managerial Summary Informal competition can stimulate formal firms' new product development at low to moderate levels, but high levels of IC can discourage it. Because informal firms spur innovation among their formal counterparts, policymakers should not automatically seek to eliminate IC. Instead, they should consider IC as a changing condition and adapt enforcement to its intensity. At low to moderate levels of IC, minimal enforcement may be appropriate as the innovation and consumer benefits associated with IC may outweigh its costs. As IC becomes more intense and begins to undermine formal firms' NPD, policymakers can tighten enforcement while offering informal firms incentives to formalize. For managers, the findings suggest that the strategic response to IC should also depend on its intensity. When IC is low, formal firms may continue to innovate despite financial constraints; managers can therefore pursue low‐risk, affordable products using frugal innovation methods, while policymakers can support these efforts through improved access to finance. Managers are also well‐advised to consider the institutional context. Unlike their counterparts in countries leaning toward survival values (e.g., India), formal firms operating in societies that lean toward self‐expression values (e.g., Uruguay) are more likely to engage in NPD when IC is low; the probability decreases as IC becomes higher.

papers.title: Pathways Out of Cybercrime: Perceived Desistance From Criminal Hacking
papers.abstract: The present study seeks to understand how criminal hackers self-report to desist from the world of cybercrime. In doing so, we address significant gaps in criminological literature, as little is known about pathways out of cybercrime offending. Interviews were conducted with 22 individuals involved in cyber-dependent crime, primarily from the Netherlands. Of these, 15 respondents were justice-involved youth and 7 respondents self-identified as criminal hackers. The interviews offer unique insights into the stages offenders navigate following their involvement in cybercrime. Findings reveal that young hackers may be susceptible to behavioral change through various mechanisms. Desistance from cybercrime is a process that warrants a multidisciplinary perspective, influenced particularly by social bonds, prosocial daily routines, and deterrent experiences. A combination of police intervention and alternative approaches that emphasize ethical application of skills may be a promising route for young hackers in particular, although actual intervention effects remain unverified. We encourage evaluations of current programs for hackers as well as additional quantitative assessments of protective factors among cybercrime offenders.

papers.title: The Cost of Capturing: How Smartphone Photo-Taking Alters Memory Performance and Cognitive Self-Esteem: The Role of Smartphone Self-Expansion
papers.abstract: Taking photos to manage memories with smartphones is a routine strategy in the digital era. However, it remains unclear how smartphone photo-taking affects memory performance and self-evaluation. This research examined whether smartphone photo-taking is associated with a pattern consistent with the “Google effect,” and whether these associations vary with self-expansion via smartphone use. Across three experiments ( N = 363), participants photographed or observed materials before completing memory tests and measures of cognitive self-esteem. Study 1 tested the basic photo-taking effect; Study 2a examined device ownership as a contextual proxy for smartphone self-expansion; and Study 2b examined trait self-expansion as a continuous moderator. Results showed a photo-taking-impairment effect on memory, alongside higher cognitive self-esteem following photo-taking. Moreover, higher smartphone self-expansion was associated with stronger increases in cognitive self-esteem and greater memory overestimation, whereas its role in objective memory impairment remained inconclusive. Altogether, the findings suggest that smartphone photo-taking can reduce memory performance while increasing cognitive self-esteem.

Pesky Metals: Historical Perspective, Advances, and Challenges for Remediation of Problematic Metal Contaminants
papers.abstract: Abstract Persistent and problematic toxic metal and metalloid pollutants (in particular, As, Hg, Pb, Cd, and Cr) have long been challenging and expensive remediation targets in contaminated surface and subsurface environments. Since the advent of environmental regulations and cleanup in the late 20th century, much progress has been made to address sites of legacy metal pollution and limit new contamination. Despite this, metal pollution remains a global problem, particularly in soils and sediments, with many large legacy sites inadequately remediated, metal contamination widespread in developed and developing nations, and new pollution occurring from informal and often illegal extraction and recycling processes. In this perspective, we highlight advances and challenges in science and technology, and key economic and social factors, that have influenced remediation of these “pesky” metals over the last ∼50 years. Through this lens, we consider emerging challenges and opportunities associated with legacy and critical metals, climate resilience, and sustainability.

papers.title: A Framework for Time-Explicit Life Cycle Optimization
papers.abstract: Abstract Life cycle optimization (LCO) selects optimal processes and supply chains from a set of alternatives given environmental constraints and objectives, supporting the design of sustainable systems and their transitions. However, current approaches rely on static assumptions, overlooking two interacting temporal dimensions: temporal distribution (flows are spread over time) and temporal evolution (processes and supply chains change over time). Because distribution and evolution jointly dictate the magnitude of a flow at a given time, both must be considered simultaneously to accurately optimize against cumulative environmental impacts and time-specific environmental constraints. We present a framework for time-explicit LCO that captures these interdependencies to determine optimal transition pathways. The framework tracks flow timing relative to process installation and dynamically determines flow magnitudes from time-specific process parameters and background supply chains. A case study on integrated methanol and pig iron production demonstrates how time-explicit LCO enables optimization against time-resolved environmental impacts and constraints, revealing mitigation strategies inaccessible to static approaches: prioritizing early high-efficiency technology installation to idle older processes as operational savings outweigh embodied impacts of stranded assets, and avoiding transient resource bottlenecks through diversification. To facilitate widespread application, we provide the open-source Python package optimex, enabling practitioners to design transition pathways that rigorously respect environmental limits.

Tree Species Configuration Shapes Soil Phosphorus Fractions and Microbial Communities in Uneven‐Aged Multilayered Chinese Fir–Broadleaved Mixed Forests
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Chinese fir ( Cunninghamia lanceolata ) plantations in southern China are often limited by phosphorus (P) availability, constraining productivity and sustainable management. We hypothesized that multi‐species, multilayered, uneven‐aged configurations would enhance soil P availability by regulating P fractions and microbial P transformation. This study aimed to identify the optimal tree species configuration for alleviating P limitation and improving soil quality. Four configurations were compared: pure Chinese fir (M0), Chinese fir + Phoebe bournei (M1), Chinese fir + P. bournei + Taxus wallichiana var. chinensis (M2), and Chinese fir + P. bournei + T. wallichiana var. chinensis + Schima superba (M3). Soil samples were collected from the 0–20, 20–40 and 40–60 cm layers and analysed for P fractions, acid phosphatase (ACP) activity, soil properties, and bacterial and fungal communities. Multivariate analysis, network analysis, structural equation modelling (SEM), and soil quality index (SQI) analysis were used to identify regulatory pathways. Different tree species configurations significantly altered soil P pool composition and its vertical distribution. Mixed configurations increased organic phosphorus (Po) and available phosphorus (AP), mainly enhanced surface soil organic matter (SOM) and total nitrogen (TN), and reshaped bacterial and fungal communities. M1 was enriched in P‐activating fungi such as Penicillium and Trichoderma , whereas M2 exhibited the highest fungal network complexity and SQI value, as well as higher AP content than the pure plantation. SEM indicated that available Fe (AFe) was an important driver of AP formation, while Al‐bound P (AlP) and occluded P (OP) negatively affected AP. Overall, M2 was the most favorable configuration for improving soil P availability and soil quality.

papers.title: The global geography of threats to freshwater biodiversity
papers.abstract: Human activities are eroding biodiversity, especially in freshwater systems. Despite major advances in quantifying species vulnerability and threats, we still lack a crucial understanding of where threats are affecting freshwater species globally. Here, we produced a species-centered spatial assessment of threats, mapping the impact of 45 threats across 21,490 freshwater species of amphibians, fish, mammals, odonates, and reptiles. We found that species in highly developed and water-managed regions are strongly affected by multiple overlapping threats. Although threats vary across taxa and regions, increasing threat probabilities elevate extinction risk and population declines, with freshwater species experiencing greater threat intensity and distinct spatial patterns than terrestrial species. Our findings establish a spatially explicit baseline for targeting the most urgently needed freshwater conservation and management interventions.

papers.title: Data-driven discovery and rapid, direct synthesis of MXenes
papers.abstract: MXenes are a rapidly expanding family of two-dimensional transition metal carbides and nitrides, yet scalable synthesis routes remain limited and historical reports suggest a broader, largely unexplored chemical space. We used machine learning–assisted database mining to uncover hidden multilayer MXenes. Screening reveals 33 previously synthesized but unrecognized MXene candidates. Guided by these findings, we synthesized seven multilayer MXenes using a rapid, scalable self-propagating high-temperature method that requires no sustained external heating and completes within minutes. We further realized 11 previously unexplored rare earth–based MXenes (M = praseodymium, neodymium, samarium, gadolinium, terbium, holmium, and thulium). Experiments and modeling suggest semiconducting behavior and diverse magnetic states across this family. Together, these results expand the MXene family and demonstrate a data-driven strategy for accelerating materials discovery through sustainable methods.

papers.title: The delocalized nature of chemical bonding at a catalytic metal surface
papers.abstract: Adsorbate bonding at metal surfaces requires hybridization of localized molecular orbitals with delocalized electronic bands of the metal; hence, the electronic wave function involved in bonding may extend far beyond the adsorption site. We revealed the consequence of this delocalization by determining the distance over which structural variations of the metal surface influence the molecule-metal bond strength. Velocity-resolved kinetics provided adsorption energies for three molecules bound at atomic steps of platinum (Pt), each exhibiting bond-strength changes of up to 0.2 electron volts as the step-step distance varied over 100 angstroms. We observed molecule-specific behavior reflecting the hybridization of molecule-specific orbitals with symmetry-selected orbital bands of the metal that respond differently to structural modifications of the solid. We discuss implications of these observations for adsorption on Pt nanoparticles.

papers.title: Intrinsic gestational timing governs human cerebellar development after preterm birth
papers.abstract: Intrinsic programs shape brain maturation; however, which of these programs are perturbed by prematurity as well as the molecular pathways involved remain unknown. The human cerebellum serves as a paradigm of extrauterine development—its accelerated growth and circuit formation align with the third trimester, a period disrupted by preterm delivery. Using multimodal datasets encompassing in vivo neuroimaging and neurodevelopmental outcomes with postmortem spatial-transcriptomic and histopathological profiling, we show that prematurity diverts the cerebellar developmental trajectory. Cerebellar growth and functional outcomes scaled with gestational age, despite modifying perinatal exposures. Spatially resolved developmental programs underlying macroscopic trajectories were marked by incomplete granule cell maturation and impaired Purkinje cell structural refinement, which indicate lineage-specific developmental asynchrony. Thus, prematurity constitutes biologically displaced maturation, in which infants of equivalent postmenstrual age occupy divergent developmental states.

papers.title: A commensally regulated immune rheostat fine-tunes skin barrier fitness
papers.abstract: At the skin’s surface, the epidermis must balance stem cell renewal with barrier maintenance to withstand environmental stress and shield against pathogens. In this study, we identify a microbial-immune-epithelial feedback mechanism that integrates environmental information into stem cell regulation in mice. Specifically, we show that Langerhans cells (LCs), an intraepithelial macrophage population, orchestrate this circuit by producing prostaglandin E 2 , which restrains stem cell proliferation, promotes epidermal differentiation, and maintains barrier integrity during homeostasis. Upon pathway disruption, stem cells become overactivated, hindering terminal differentiation and weakening barrier function. Upstream, LC activity is tuned by the local microbial environment in a rheostat-like fashion, coupling commensal sensing to stem cell dynamics. Our findings provide a general framework for how barrier tissues achieve adaptive homeostasis amid continual external fluctuations.

papers.title: Stimulated protein degradation to promote mitochondrial function and neuronal survival
papers.abstract: Targeted protein degradation is a promising modality to treat cancer or inflammation, but whether it can provide a similar benefit for disorders caused by pervasive protein dysregulation is unclear. We describe stimulated protein degradation (SPD) as a strategy that leverages agonists of stress-responsive E3 ubiquitin ligases to simultaneously eliminate multiple pathogenic factors. Specifically, we show that activators of the reductive stress response E3 CUL2 FEM1B boost degradation of multiple physiological substrates to improve mitochondrial import and electron transport chain assembly. In this manner, CUL2 FEM1B agonists preserve mitochondrial function and neuronal survival in models of neurodegenerative COX deficiency syndrome and Friedreich’s ataxia. By activating E3 ligases that evolved to safeguard cellular integrity, SPD expands the use of compound-induced protein degradation to complex pathologies of high unmet need.

papers.title: Altermagnetism revealed by polarized neutrons in MnF 2
papers.abstract: Altermagnets are compensated magnets with symmetry-enforced spin split bands. Direct spectroscopic evidence for their existence has been reported in several materials. For example, inelastic neutron scattering (INS) has recently been used to witness a splitting of magnon bands in MnTe that is compatible with altermagnetism. Here, we present polarized INS results on MnF 2 showing that it is altermagnetic. Our data reveal a splitting coming from the long-range dipolar coupling. Furthermore, using a domain-biased sample, the data reveal a nonzero chirality in the neutron scattering cross section that reverses the sign between the two magnon modes. It is this feature that clearly demonstrates altermagnetism in MnF 2 . This finding highlights the potential for polarized INS to characterize altermagnets through its sensitivity to fine structure in magnon spectra.

papers.title: Rapid longitudinal flights cause time shifts and Sun compass error
papers.abstract: Many animals use the Sun compass to guide their movement, sometimes over thousands of kilometers. Consistent use of the Sun compass relies on the endogenous clock to track the Sun’s arc, yet animals traveling east-west experience time shifts, potentially causing mismatches between their internal clock and local time. Using GPS, we reveal that Manx shearwaters ( Puffinus puffinus ) experience such shifts during homing flights, generating predictable errors in Sun compass orientation. Use of the Sun compass persists even when shearwaters have access to compass-independent cues during coast following. Our findings provide a new avenue for chronobiology research in the wild, suggesting that rapid longitudinal movements may affect other processes governed by the endogenous clock and that conserved chronobiological mechanisms impose substantial constraints on navigation.

papers.title: Pervasive patterns in bird songs resemble those in human speech and song and are independent of vocal learning
papers.abstract: Bird songs are often described as analogs to human speech and songs, but expansive comparisons are necessary to determine analogy and mechanistic substrates. By analyzing global corpora consisting of 367 bird species (>74,500 vocal elements from ~5900 songs) within two clades of vocal learners (oscines and hummingbirds) and related nonlearners (suboscines and nightjars) and 52 human languages (>15,000 elements in >800 speech or song phrases), we revealed common patterns in bird songs that resemble prevalent patterns in human speech and song with variation in resemblance to speech or song. Vocal learning did not systematically affect acoustic patterning or similarity to human vocalizations. These data underscore the deep analogies between bird and human vocalizations and convergent motor mechanisms shaping communication.

papers.title: Whole-body single-cell atlas of an adult vertebrate, Danionella cerebrum
papers.abstract: A complete cell type transcriptome atlas of a vertebrate could promote understanding of animal cell type composition, organization, and evolution. The miniaturized, transparent, and regenerative teleost Danionella cerebrum brings whole-vertebrate single-cell profiling experiments within reach. We performed region-stratified single-cell RNA sequencing across the adult Danionella body and mapped cell types and gene expression at single-cell resolution using spatial transcriptomics. We delineated spatially distinct neural cell types on the basis of their regional gene expression signatures. The body-wide atlas elucidated cell types harboring adult molecular positional memory, uncovered paedomorphic features, and revealed conserved body-region and appendage-specification programs in adult connective tissue. Comparative analyses revealed conserved neural cell types, and regeneration datasets uncovered expression dynamics during telencephalon regeneration. This whole-vertebrate transcriptome atlas yields a comprehensive resource for myriad questions in biology and neuroscience.

papers.title: Genomic erosion across avifauna in a biodiversity hotspot sounds a conservation alarm
papers.abstract: Loss of biodiversity can have a hidden dimension—the cryptic erosion of genetic diversity even in the face of apparent species resilience. We quantified changes in genetic diversity by comparing historical and modern genomes of 62 songbird species from the Gaoligong Mountains, a biodiversity hotspot in southwestern China. We identified genomic loss averaging between 43 and 49%; and, unexpectedly, common species were disproportionately affected. We argue that this loss was driven primarily by habitat fragmentation (and mitigated by dispersal ability) and show that it exceeds prior estimates and conservation policy thresholds. Species identified as having lost diversity continue to be listed as “Least Concern” on the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s Red List of Threatened Species, exposing a blind spot in extinction risk monitoring. We call for genomic metrics to be rapidly integrated into global conservation frameworks.

papers.title: Western Pacific double subduction drives Gulf of California rifting
papers.abstract: Continental rifting reflects the balance between tectonic forces and lithospheric strength, yet the mechanisms of breakup remain debated. Rapid rifting of the Gulf of California oblique rift (GOCOR) ~6 million to 8 million years ago is a key example; it may have resulted from the lithosphere responding to external kinematics or acceleration of long-lived extension. The dynamics of either scenario remain incompletely understood. In this study, we highlight that the rapid rifting of the GOCOR coincides with the initiation of Western Pacific double subduction. Using three-dimensional geodynamic models, we show that such subduction reorganization can transmit extensional stresses of ~5 to 15 megapascals across the Pacific plate, loading the GOCOR and the southern San Andreas fault. Subduction reorganization may represent the missing driver for the initiation of rapid GOCOR rifting within a preconditioned lithosphere and may be an overlooked tectonic force behind other rifting events.

Papaver self-incompatibility is controlled by two multiallelic idiomorphs
papers.abstract: Self-incompatibility (SI) prevents self-fertilization through highly polymorphic genetic recognition at the S locus with multiple alleles. In Papaver rhoeas , the S determinants were previously identified as PrpS and PrsS . However, we found that PrpS-PrsS was absent in many S haplotypes. In this work, we report the identification of an alternative pair of polymorphic S genes, S locus oligopeptide transporter ( SOPT ) and S locus glycine-rich protein ( SGRP ), segregating at the S locus when PrpS-PrsS is absent. SOPT and SGRP display hallmark S determinant features and confer SI when heterologously expressed in Arabidopsis thaliana . Therefore, instead of having allelomorphs with homologous variants, the Papaver SI system is determined by two multiallelic idiomorphs sharing no obvious common ancestry. This discovery of a dual-idiomorph system reveals a distinct genetic basis for polymorphism, with implications for the evolution of allorecognition mechanisms.

papers.title: It’s not perfect—but it’s me
Chiral altermagnon in MnTe
papers.abstract: Altermagnetism has been recognized as a magnetic phase that bridges the properties of ferro- and antiferromagnetism. The momentum-dependent spin splitting observed in these materials reflects their distinctive symmetry characteristics, which also establish the conditions for chiral magnons to emerge. Here we provide direct experimental evidence for a chiral magnon in the altermagnetic candidate manganese telluride (MnTe) revealed by circular-dichroism resonant inelastic x-ray scattering. This mode, which we term chiral altermagnon, exhibits a distinct momentum dependence of its spin polarization consistent with the altermagnetic g -wave symmetry of MnTe. Our polarization-resolved data corroborate the existence of a discrete class of magnetic excitations, demonstrating how altermagnetic order shapes spin dynamics and paving the way for advances in spintronic and quantum technologies.

papers.title: Spatial coordination in the codevelopment of the human urogenital system during organogenesis
papers.abstract: The human urogenital system originates from a common embryonic domain, yet the mechanisms guiding its spatiotemporal coordination remain understudied. Here, we combined high-resolution spatial transcriptomics with single-cell multiomics to profile human embryos from Carnegie stages 15 to 23, capturing the codevelopmental dynamics of the urogenital system. We revealed mesonephros- and adrenal primordium–derived signals that promote gonadal specification and enable efficient in vitro generation of cells resembling early gonadal lineages. We also uncovered a possible mesonephric origin of gonadal supporting cells through rete testis or ovarii linking the mesonephros. Finally, we delineate three transcriptionally distinct steroidogenic lineages differing in cholesterol sourcing, cortisol synthesis, and sex hormone production that together orchestrate sex differentiation. These findings deepen our understanding of urogenital system assembly and guide the exploration of coordinated multiorgan development.

papers.title: When AI takes away the thrill of discovery
papers.abstract: “Pure math is being devastated or revolutionized, depending on your point of view.” So said Cornell professor Steven Strogatz after the artificial intelligence (AI) company OpenAI announced in early September a potential solution to the Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness problem, one of the seven Millennium Prize problems that represent the highest goals for mathematical proofs. OpenAI’s solution involved unleashing an army of AI agents at a cost of millions of dollars in computing power, and it also certainly drew on decades of human effort in mathematics before it. Then a few weeks later, OpenAI posted 722 manuscripts describing progress on 372 mathematical problem families, and Google DeepMind published (in Science ) solutions from their own AI math system. These events are potentially exciting for those who long to know the answers to these problems as soon as possible, but they have also sent the world of mathematics reeling, and pose an even bigger question for all fields: Can the satisfaction of understanding ever replace the thrill of discovery?

papers.title: Emergence of Chern metal in a moiré Kondo lattice
papers.abstract: A Chern metal is a two-dimensional metallic state of matter carrying chiral edge states. We report the observation of a Chern metal at the onset of the magnetic Kondo breakdown in a frustrated moiré Kondo lattice--angle-aligned MoTe 2 /WSe 2 bilayers. The state is compressible and is manifested by a nearly quantized Hall resistance and a finite longitudinal resistance arising from a bad metallic bulk. We demonstrate the presence of a chiral edge state by nonlocal transport measurements and current-induced quantum anomalous Hall breakdown. Magnetic circular dichroism measurements further reveal a magnetization plateau for the Chern metal before a metamagnetic transition at the Kondo breakdown. Our results open an opportunity for moiré engineering of exotic quantum phases through the interplay between band topology and Kondo interactions.

papers.title: A Martian meteorite that formed ≳4.1 billion years ago samples Mars’ early crust and mantle
papers.abstract: Martian meteorites provide a record of the planet’s geological history. However, most are geologically young samples that are not representative of Mars’ surface, which is dominated by ancient rocks. We describe the Martian meteorite Teghaza 001 (Teg 001), a slowly cooled igneous rock that formed at least 4.1 billion years ago. Its composition, mineralogy, and texture are distinct from other Martian meteorites. We determine that Teg 001 is a sample of ancient crust, which formed from a geochemically distinct mantle source with primordial composition. The presence of aqueously altered minerals, combined with bulk and mineral-specific oxygen isotope measurements, indicate that Teg 001 experienced reactions with fluids enriched in 18 O, before ejection into space by an impact.

papers.title: How the US mid-term elections could shake up science
Even stupendous black holes can’t explain dark matter

Daily briefing: The future of psychedelics
Diet at disease onset determines tissue inflammatory memory
papers.abstract: Abstract Obesity, which is often associated with prolonged exposure to an obesogenic diet, substantially alters immunity 1–7 , but whether brief dietary changes shape acute inflammatory responses and long-term tissue memory remains unclear. Here we show that transient high-fat diet (HFD) exposure at the onset of acute type 17 skin inflammation exacerbates disease in lean mice to levels comparable to those associated with chronic obesity. This effect is restricted to a discrete 4-day peri-initiation window; HFD outside this window has no impact, whereas switching obese mice to a low-fat diet (LFD) during a similar window fully blunts disease amplification. Mechanistically, HFD rapidly recruits neutrophils into the skin, and neutrophils in challenged skin express high levels of Nlrp3 (ref. 8 ) and Il1b . Neutrophil depletion, genetic Nlrp3 deficiency and pharmacological NLRP3 inhibition each blunt the HFD-induced inflammatory amplification. These findings nominate a neutrophil–NLRP3–IL-1β axis that licences pathogenic IL-1R1 + CD4 + T helper type 17 (T H 17) cells 9,10 . After recovery, a chromatin-poised tissue-resident memory T cell population persists. Consequently, mice exposed to HFD at disease onset develop exaggerated inflammation upon recurrence, despite recovery and maintenance on LFD. Transient HFD similarly amplifies lung T H 17 inflammation through neutrophil- and IL-1R1-dependent mechanisms. Together, these findings show that dietary state during a narrow temporal window can durably reprogram disease trajectory, suggesting that short-lived physiological states may become embedded in local immune memory 11 when they coincide with tissue inflammation.

papers.title: Political Parties as Drivers of US Polarization: 1927–2018
Do Experimental Asset Market Results Replicate? High‐Powered Preregistered Replications of 17 Key Results
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Experimental asset markets provide a controlled approach to studying financial markets. We attempt to replicate 17 key results from four prominent studies, collecting new data from 166 markets with 1,544 participants. Only three of the 14 original results reported as statistically significant were successfully replicated. We fail to replicate findings on emotions, self‐control, and gender differences in bubble formation but confirm that experience reduces bubbles and cognitive skills explain trading success. Our study demonstrates the importance of replications in enhancing the credibility of scientific results in this field.

papers.title: Decoupling voting and cash flow rights
State capacity and wildfire mitigation: Evidence from state-led forest conservation in China
People, places, and firms: improving our understanding of wage and productivity disparities
papers.abstract: Abstract In many countries spatial disparities in wages and productivity are large and persistent. This raises questions about the causes and consequences of such disparities. Two inter-related issues—the sorting of high skilled workers and the productivity benefits of urban density—are central to the way in which urban economists have approached these questions. In this commentary, we argue that despite the emerging consensus that sorting matters for wage disparities, the literature has made less progress on other dimensions of these disparities and a number of methodological issues remain unresolved.

papers.title: Impacts of Corporate Tax Cuts on Firms and Workers: Evidence from Small Businesses
papers.abstract: This paper assesses the effects of corporate tax cuts on small firms and their workers. Following a reform in Quebec, Canada, firms receiving tax cuts expand and their workers’ earnings increase compared to workers and firms without tax cuts. We estimate that overall workers bear 35 percent of the tax burden, with larger incidence falling on those with ownership in the companies they work at, through increased profits. Additionally, workers across each tercile of the within-firm earnings distribution benefit from tax cuts, possibly because fair-wage concerns matter when after-tax profits rise due to close interactions among workers in small corporate environments. (JEL D22, H22, H25, J31, L25)

papers.title: The Pass-Through of Retail Crime
papers.abstract: This paper shows retailers increase prices in response to organized retail crime. We match store-level crime data to scanner data from the universe of transactions for cannabis retailers in Washington state. Using quasi-experimental variation from robberies and burglaries, we find a 1.7–1.8 percent price increase at victimized stores and nearby competitors. This rise is not driven by short-to-medium-term demand changes but is consistent with crime-related cost shocks. Effects are larger for independent stores and less concentrated markets. We estimate crime imposes a 1 percent “hidden” unit tax on affected stores, implying $30.7 million in additional social costs, primarily borne by consumers. (JEL D22, H22, H76, K42, L81)

papers.title: On-Demand Assistance: Experimental Evidence from Indonesia
papers.abstract: Given labor informality in developing countries, addressing employment shocks is challenging. We study Indonesia’s new approach for on-demand online applications for temporary cash assistance and online job training. Through 20 lotteries over two years, 11 million beneficiaries were selected. In nationwide representative surveys matched with administrative data, most beneficiaries report not receiving the assistance, with no detectable impact on employment or consumption. In contrast, survey data from applicants with working phones reveal high reported take-up and higher incomes. The results suggest that, while flexible, on-demand assistance has potential, design features that allow for flexibility could hinder receipt and, thus, impact. (JEL E21, E24, I38, J24, J46, O15)

papers.title: Trade Protection along Supply Chains
papers.abstract: We study the effects of trade protection along supply chains. We focus on temporary trade barriers against China, which has been the main target of US trade protection during the last decades. To deal with endogeneity concerns, we use an instrumental variable strategy, exploiting changes in the identity of swing states across presidential terms and heterogeneous exposure to these political shocks across industries. We find that politically motivated trade protection generates winners and losers: It fosters employment growth in protected industries but hampers employment growth in downstream industries. Our estimates imply a negative overall impact on US jobs. (JEL D72, F13, F14, L14, O19, P33)

papers.title: Childhood Health Shocks and the Intergenerational Transmission of Inequality
papers.abstract: This paper documents a socioeconomic gradient in adult labor market penalties stemming from a single chronic and treatable childhood health shock in a country with universal access to health care. Using childhood onset type 1 diabetes, Danish administrative registry data, and causal forests, we estimate substantial variation in the employment and earnings penalties at age 30. These penalties vary systematically with parental income and maternal educational attainment. Our findings help explain the income-health gradient and have important implications for policy discussions related to the design of health care systems. (JEL H51, I12, I13, I18, J16, J23, J31)

papers.title: Polluted IPOs
papers.abstract: Chinese companies must undergo a review by a regulator-appointed committee before proceeding with initial public offerings (IPOs). We find that firms—particularly, politically unconnected ones—are more likely to pass this review on polluted days (i.e., with a high level of PM2.5). The effect appears driven by reduced cognitive capacity among reviewers, reflected in fewer and simpler questions raised during review sessions. Notably, firms approved on polluted days show no significant performance difference from other firms within three years after the IPO. The findings suggest that pollution-induced cognitive fatigue may paradoxically reduce distortions in a politically influenced approval process. (JEL D22, G24, G32, K22, P28, P31, Q52)

papers.title: The Role of Race in the Legal Representation of Low-Income Defendants
papers.abstract: Little is known about the role of race in the defense of low-income defendants by court-appointed attorneys. Exploiting the quasirandom assignment of court-appointed attorneys to cases, we test whether attorneys secure better deals for same-race defendants. Results indicate that while Black and White attorneys are similarly effective at representing White defendants, Black defendants who are represented by White rather than Black attorneys are 14–16 percent more likely to have their charges dismissed and 15–26 percent less likely to be incarcerated. Moreover, we find no evidence that having a different-race attorney increases the likelihood of reoffending in the future. (JEL H76, J15, K14, K42)

papers.title: How Effective Are R&D Tax Incentives? Reconciling the Micro and Macro Evidence
papers.abstract: Recent firm-level studies find R&D tax incentives to be much more effective at stimulating firms’ R&D investment than aggregate analyses suggest. Based on a distributed analysis of official R&D survey and administrative tax relief microdata for 19 OECD countries, we show that two factors can reconcile these contrasting results. First, the limited uptake of R&D tax incentives in most countries makes aggregate studies underestimate the effectiveness of R&D tax incentives. Secondly, R&D tax incentives are (much) less effective for large and R&D-intensive firms, which account for a small share of R&D-performing firms but most aggregate R&D tax relief. (JEL D22, H25, H32, L25, O31)

papers.title: Can You Erase the Mark of a Criminal Record? Labor Market Impacts of Criminal Record Remediation
papers.abstract: We investigate whether removing a previously obtained criminal record improves employment outcomes. We estimate the causal impact of criminal record remediation laws that have been widely enacted with the goal of improving employment opportunities for millions of individuals with records. We find consistent evidence that removing an existing record does not improve labor market outcomes, on average. A notable exception is participation in gig work through online platforms, which often screen workers based on their records but not their employment histories. The evidence is consistent with records initially scarring labor market trajectories in a way that is difficult to undo later. (JEL H76, J22, J23, K14, K42, M51)

papers.title: The Unintended Consequences of Academic Leniency
Prioritizing Benefit? How Low-Income Patients Respond to Prescription Cost Sharing
papers.abstract: This paper measures how cost sharing impacts older low-income patients, exploiting a discontinuity in eligibility for a prescription drug subsidy for those who lose access to the Medicaid-linked program. Higher drug prices resulting from subsidy loss lead to a 40 percent reduction in prescription expenditures, driven by a 16 percent quantity reduction of prescriptions filled. Patients economize on purchases of higher-priced drugs, irrespective of their health benefits. For example, patients reduce insulin purchases by 35 percent. There is no evidence that cost sharing prompts switching from branded drugs to generics. This behavior suggests that cost sharing reduces prescription accessibility without enhancing cost-effectiveness. (JEL D24, I11, I18, I32, I38, L65)

papers.title: Inclusive Teaching: Spotting Social Isolation in the Classroom
papers.abstract: We evaluate an intervention aimed at addressing social isolation in classrooms. The treatment provides teachers with their students’ social networks and information on developmental risks associated with social exclusion. Using friendship data and incentive-compatible measures, we find that the intervention reduces social isolation and antisocial behavior but does not increase prosocial behavior. Lower antisocial behavior enhances economic efficiency, reflected in higher average student payoffs and reduced inequality. Our findings highlight the personal and communal benefits of addressing social exclusion and antisocial peer dynamics in schools. (JEL D91, I21, I24, I28, J13, Z13)

papers.title: A Matter of Time? Measuring Effects of Public Schooling Expansions on Families
papers.abstract: We leverage pronounced changes in the availability of public schooling for young children—through duration expansions to the kindergarten day—to better understand how an implicit childcare subsidy affects mothers and families. Exploiting full-day kindergarten variation across place and time from 1992 through 2022 and novel data on state-level policy changes, combined with a comparison of children of typical kindergarten-age to older children, we measure effects on parental labor supply and family childcare expenses. Full-day kindergarten expansions were responsible for as much as 24 percent of the growth in employment of mothers with kindergarten-age children in this time frame. (JEL H75, I21, J12, J13, J16, J22)

papers.title: China’s Nationwide CO 2 Emissions Trading System: A General Equilibrium Assessment
papers.abstract: China’s CO 2 emissions trading system, the world’s largest, aims to significantly reduce CO 2 emissions. The system is a tradable performance standard (TPS), differing from cap and trade (C&T). We provide a dynamic general equilibrium assessment that uniquely considers institutional and fiscal features of China that affect policy costs and distributional impacts. Key findings: The TPS’s environmental benefits exceed its costs by a factor of five or more. Interactions with the fiscal system reduce or eliminate the TPS’s cost disadvantage relative to C&T. Introducing auctioning as a complementary source of allowance supply can reduce costs by 30 percent. (JEL D58, O13, P28, Q54, Q58)

papers.title: The Effect of Deactivating Facebook and Instagram on Users’ Emotional State
papers.abstract: We estimate the effect of social media deactivation on users’ emotional state in two large randomized experiments before the 2020 US election. People who deactivated Facebook for the six weeks before the election reported a 0.060 standard deviation improvement in an index of happiness, depression, and anxiety, relative to controls who deactivated for just the first of those six weeks. People who deactivated Instagram for those six weeks reported a 0.041 standard deviation improvement relative to controls. Exploratory analysis suggests that the Facebook effect is driven by people over 35, while the Instagram effect is driven by women under 25. (JEL D12, D91, I31, J16, L82)

papers.title: Identifying Tax Compliance from Variation in Tax Policy: Theory and Empirics
papers.abstract: Governments increasingly use changes in tax rules to combat evasion. We develop a general approach to point-identify tax compliance along with supply and demand elasticities. Identification requires data on prices and quantities, variation in tax policy, and a demand or supply shifter. We illustrate our approach using data on Airbnb collection agreements, where taxes are enforced by shifting the statutory burden away from hosts and onto renters via the platform. We find that taxes are paid on roughly 0 to 1.6 percent of Airbnb transactions prior to enforcement. (JEL H25, H26, H71, K34, L83)

papers.title: Host-country media discourse and China’s economic presence in Africa
papers.abstract: China’s economic engagement in Africa takes place in changing host-country discourse environments, yet the consequences of adverse media reporting for China’s overseas presence remain unclear. We argue that worsening media tone can signal rising operating risk and may therefore trigger adjustment across different margins of presence. Using an annual panel of 54 African countries for 2010–2023, we construct lagged media-tone shocks from the Global Database of Events, Language, and Tone and estimate their dynamic association with Chinese project personnel and FDI stocks. We combine Double Machine Learning with two-way fixed effects, conventional fixed-effects benchmarks, balanced-sample checks and an Afrobarometer exercise. The evidence is consistent with a selective-adjustment pattern. Negative media-tone shocks are associated with a delayed reduction in Chinese project personnel, with effects that emerge at the three- and four-year horizons. Positive shocks show no comparable expansion effect. Chinese overseas presence adjusts primarily to negative shifts in discourse through the more flexible personnel margin, while FDI stocks respond slowly and less consistently. The host country’s institutional context also influences the staffing response. The findings suggest that hostile discourse becomes especially materially consequential when it is likely to translate into operating risk.

papers.title: Environmental Policy and Automation
Medicated Optimism
papers.abstract: Do people experiencing depression form accurate expectations about losing their jobs? Linking Estonian panel survey data to administrative employment, diagnosis, and prescription records, I track within-person changes in expected job loss and subsequent realized job loss as individuals move into and out of depression and depression medication. Using individual fixed effects and controls for depression severity and physical health, I find that as the same worker enters the medicated depression state from no depression, expected job loss falls by 3.6 percentage points while realized job loss rises by 5.1 percentage points. The resulting 8.7 percentage-point fall in the forecast error is split almost evenly between less over-prediction among workers who keep their jobs and more under-prediction among workers who lose them. This shift toward optimism is larger for medication classes more closely linked to reward-related pathways and is absent when prescribed medication is not purchased. The welfare implications are two-sided: more optimistic beliefs may reduce worry about job loss, but workers who understate rising risk may prepare less for a separation.

papers.title: Passive market impact: a point process approach
Intra-Horizon Risk Measures and Continuation Liquidity Requirements in Commodity Futures Markets
papers.abstract: Traditional Value at Risk (VaR) and expected shortfall (ES) measures that are based on terminal loss may underestimate the risk induced by interim price movements. In this article, we evaluate the intra-horizon risk measures MaxVaR and MaxES as measures of the continuation liquidity buffer required to sustain futures positions. We propose models with asymmetric jumps and/or seasonal volatility and generate out-of-sample MaxVaR and MaxES forecasts over 10-, 22-, and 66-day horizons. Using data for heating oil, natural gas, corn, and soybeans from 2000 to 2021, we find that considering both asymmetric jumps and seasonal volatility generates the most accurate MaxVaR and MaxES forecasts. Liquidity buffers that are based on these measures also exhibit substantial seasonal variation and significant asymmetry between long and short positions. Furthermore, comparisons with initial margins indicate that continuation liquidity buffers represent a substantial component of the total liquidity capacity required to initiate and maintain futures positions.

papers.title: Pursuing fiscal credibility, performing fiscal discipline: epistemic politics and status seeking in Italy and Spain’s Eurozone accession
papers.abstract: There is a prolific literature on the politics of austerity, highlighting how its confidence effects arise from fiscal retrenchment embodying and signalling a credible commitment to markets’ interests. However, I argue that this implicitly performative account of fiscal credibility is too functionalist, underplaying how states continually negotiate it with different audiences. To overcome these issues, this article develops an alternative theorisation of (fiscal) credibility as a perlocutionary performative, meaning it is dependent on felicitous conditions to be brought about. Channelling a ‘practice-based constructivist’ framework through an ‘epistemic politics’ and ‘status seeking’ lens, I use archival and biographical research to study Italy and Spain’s Eurozone accession during the 1990s. My argument is that the success of their austerity programmes, and therefore of their accession strategies, depended on a series of cognitive and strategic dynamics beyond fiscal retrenchment – mainly, based on the epistemic politics of multilateral surveillance, national status claims to fiscal credibility, and the social construction of ‘credibility’ under a broad set of fiscal and non-fiscal parameters. As such, this article contributes to recent constructivist research on the practical life of ideas and on epistemic politics, showing the dynamics of construction, performance, and contestation surrounding austerity and fiscal credibility.

papers.title: The semi-periphery's ‘defence dividend’: redistribution of labour in Europe's defence industry
papers.abstract: The ramp up of European defence industrial production raises a critical question for the future shape and competitiveness of the European Defence Technological and Industrial Base (EDTIB): will it continue to be dominated and limited by core European Union (EU) producers or is there an ongoing redistribution of defence production? We argue a significant redistribution is underway, although not caused by recent geopolitical shocks, but by the long-term agency of the semi-periphery itself. Our analysis identifies a distinct long-term pathway of defence-industrial upgrading in Eastern and Central Europe (ECE), which unfolds within the broader context of Dependent Market Economies (DMEs) and which we term the Militarised DME (M-DME). The EU’s recent geoeconomic turn did not create this trajectory but validated and accelerated it. Using time-series cluster analysis of EU arms export data, we identify a sustained rise in high-value-added (HVA) exports associated primarily with indigenously controlled actors. Ultimately, our findings point to a contested re-division of labour that predates the current security crisis and has important implications for European strategic autonomy, industrial integration, and the future shape of the EDTIB.

papers.title: The Future of Entrepreneurship Research Includes Online Panel Data—If Used Correctly
papers.abstract: As online panel data (OPD) become more widely used across the behavioral sciences, editors, reviewers, and researchers in entrepreneurship are asking whether it has a legitimate place in our field. We believe the answer is yes—provided three conditions are met. First, the online panel’s participants and definition of entrepreneur must match the research question. Second, studies must incorporate best practices for sample verification. Third, generalizability must be explicitly addressed as part of the study (or set of studies). If researchers do these things, OPD can meaningfully advance both theory and practice in entrepreneurship research. That said, real questions remain. What kinds of studies are suitable for OPD? Who are these respondents, and are they who they say they are? Are they human, and are they entrepreneurs as commonly defined in the literature? Our recommendations and checklist aim to enable entrepreneurship researchers to answer these questions and make informed choices when collecting data and publishing results using OPD.

papers.title: Inflexibility and Leverage
papers.abstract: Firms’ inflexibility to adjust their scale persistently explains capital structure variations in a comprehensive sample and randomly selected subsamples. Higher inflexibility leads to lower financial leverage, potentially due to higher default risk and lower value of tax shields. Contraction inflexibility determines leverage more than expansion inflexibility. Moreover, our inflexibility measure explains financial leverage significantly better than other variables that potentially capture certain aspects of adjustment costs for capital or labor. In addition, inflexible firms increase leverage more following a positive credit supply shock. Analyses employing instrumental variables estimation confirm our main finding. Our results suggest inflexibility shapes corporate financial policies. This paper was accepted by Bo Becker, finance. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.08672 .

papers.title: Multitype Information Acquisition in a Strategic Trading Model
papers.abstract: We analyze information acquisition in a strategic trading model with multidimensional uncertainties. Our main result is that the equilibrium can exhibit multiplicity because of the integer nature of the number of informed traders and the strategic interactions across different types of informed traders. We show that the number of equilibria can be arbitrarily large. Moreover, asymmetric equilibria can arise even in symmetric settings. As information costs rise, fewer traders acquire information, yet prices can become more informative. These results shed light on the instability of financial markets and yield testable empirical predictions. This paper was accepted by Lukas Schmid, finance. Funding: This work was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grants 72472171 and 72372011]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.08463 .

papers.title: Contest or Contract: Assessing the Effectiveness of Contests in Online Labor Markets
papers.abstract: Online labor markets have become increasingly popular among companies seeking global access to workers. Some platforms have adopted a contest-based scheme, allowing employers to review multiple submissions before selecting the best one. This practice raises a crucial question: Given a predefined budget, should employers choose a contest or contract scheme for tasks? This study examines the comparative effectiveness of contests versus contracts in achieving better job outcomes, focusing on design tasks characterized by high uncertainty. Using a comprehensive data set from a leading online labor market, we employ multiple empirical strategies, combined with machine learning and text mining techniques, to examine the impact of compensation schemes on job quality. Our results suggest that contract-based jobs yield better performance than contests in the context of ideation tasks. Further analysis, such as examining image similarity among pairwise solutions within a task, identifies “copying” behaviors as a key mechanism undermining the effectiveness of contests. In the public setting of contests, workers can observe others’ submissions and revise their own, leading to imitation rather than innovation. As competition intensity increases, workers have weaker incentives to exert effort, reducing solution quality. Consequently, the negative incentive effects in contests outweigh both the potential positive incentive and parallel effects. Moreover, although information availability can enhance work quality, contests inherently offer limited informational advantages compared with contracts. Taken together, our findings suggest that contract-based schemes are more effective than contests for design tasks, offering important implications for both employers and platform designers in online labor markets. This paper was accepted by Karan Girotra, operations management. Funding: N. Zhang acknowledges the support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 72302053]. Supplemental Material: The online appendices and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.07082 .

papers.title: Willingness to Compete in Dirty Competitions
papers.abstract: Competitive environments often leave room for “dirty” practices such as sabotage, retaliation, or dishonesty. We use an online experiment to document aggregate levels and individual differences in the willingness to engage in dirty competition and in the willingness to enter competitions where the opponent may play dirty. We then use the experimental data to validate a set of survey questions that capture willingness to engage in dirty competition above general willingness to compete. We elicit these questions in a representative survey panel and show that willingness to engage in dirty competition is a strong predictor of holding a management or supervisory position and of working in the private—versus the public—sector, but also of worse self-esteem, worse social relationships, and increased feelings of guilt and shame. Men, younger people, and lower-educated people are on average more willing to engage in dirty competition. This paper was accepted by Dorothea Kübler, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.01218 .

papers.title: When People Management Backfires: A Qualitative Study of Unintended Consequences of Line Managers' Support for Employees
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT This article examines how and why well‐intended people management can backfire, resulting in unintended consequences such as reduced well‐being and performance. Although people management—the combination of line managers' implementation of HR practices and their leadership behavior in supporting employees—is generally assumed to result in positive outcomes, emerging evidence suggests that benevolent line manager behavior may have adverse effects. However, insight into the underlying mechanisms through which such backfire occurs remains limited. To address this gap, we utilized a multi‐actor qualitative approach by conducting 55 interviews among line managers and employees in the Dutch hospital sector using the Critical Incident Technique. We identify three mechanisms through which backfire unfolds: (1) constrained communication in the context of policies and regulations, (2) overcompensation in the context of performance pressure, and (3) accountability in the context of conflicting fairness perceptions. Across these mechanisms, we show that backfire emerges not from poor managerial intent but from the interaction between line managers' intentions and behaviors, employees' interpretations, and structural constraints. By conceptualizing backfire as a structurally constrained and interactional process, this study advances people management research beyond dominant explanations focused on implementation quality or outcome trade‐offs, and highlights the importance of context in shaping employee responses.

papers.title: The Problem of Ignoring the Ignorability Assumption in Advertising Measurement: A Matrix Completion Solution
papers.abstract: This paper frames the overlap violation problem in online advertising auctions as a missing-data problem and proposes a matrix completion approach to correct the resulting bias in observational studies with algorithmic ad allocation.

papers.title: Unmanagement Education for the Age of Climate Crisis
papers.abstract: Abstract This paper examines how embodied, situated and relational experiences outside‐the‐classroom can open space for epistemic dislocations in Management Education under conditions of ecological crisis. Drawing on a qualitative pedagogical experience in a sustainability course in Brazil, informed by Design‐Based Research—whose assumptions of control, design and predictability we critically question–we explore conditions under which radical imaginaries may emerge through such experiences. Students engaged in encounters with human and non‐human others that generated discomfort and tension with habitual ways of knowing, opening possibilities for the emergence of (dis)enchanted imaginaries of Nature and (de)colonial imaginaries. These dynamics were intensified through situated and embodiment engagements, which at times gave rise to epistemic dislocations, or moments in which established ways of knowing lose their capacity to organize experience as alternative imaginaries become available. Those dislocations created temporary openings for participants to re‐examine their understandings of Nature, coloniality and socio‐ecological relations, remaining susceptible to reabsorption into dominant managerial frames. We contribute to climate‐oriented pedagogy by introducing Unmanagement Education, a reflexive pedagogical approach grounded in non‐mastery, embodiment and situated relationality, that may unsettle instituted imaginaries, opening space for epistemic dislocations to emerge under conditions of ecological crisis.

papers.title: Digitalization and Cybersecurity: Firm‐level Evidence
papers.abstract: Abstract Digitalization has opposing effects on cybersecurity: While new digital technologies can strengthen security capabilities, they simultaneously expand potential attack surfaces.
