The standard deviation and coefficient of variation ranged from 27 rpm to 869 rpm and 0.06% to 2.01% for engine speed, from 0.11 N to 0.78 N and 0.59% to 7.89% for thrust force, and from 0.07 L/h to 0.20 L/h and 0.38% to 2.91% for volumetric fuel flow rate, respectively. Overall, the diesel fuel formulation containing lubricating oil exhibited performance and vibration characteristics closest to those of Jet A formulation containing lubricating oil under the investigated conditions, while the biodiesel formulation containing lubricating oil resulted in higher fuel consumption and slightly increased vibration amplitudes at high operating regimes. These findings are limited to the short-duration operating conditions investigated in the present study.

papers.title: Pragmatic muddling as an enabler for coastal adaptation? Implementation of seawalls as protection against sea-level rise in Aceh, Indonesia
papers.abstract: There is growing scholarly interest in pragmatic approaches to local-level implementation of climate change adaptation. However, hard coastal protection arguably requires a coordinated approach across time and space, and a high level of technical knowledge. Our objective is therefore to assess the extent to which pragmatic approaches can enable effective local adaptation to sea-level rise through hard coastal protection, with a specific focus on seawalls. We use the analytical framework of pragmatic muddling to evaluate how local government officials in Aceh, Indonesia realise the construction of seawalls within a complex governance landscape, drawing on data collected from interview and site visit methods. Our principal findings are that local officials in Aceh do indeed draw on aspects of pragmatic muddling to support seawall implementation, especially by framing projects differently to draw down multiple funding sources; but that the scale and complexity of coastal change can exceed the level of protection that can be realised through local-level pragmatic approaches. The key implications of our findings are: reduce complexity in adaptation governance through better coordination mechanisms, so that local officials can use their context-specific knowledge within a wider programme of interventions; support the development, resourcing and retention of capable personnel at local levels of government who know what the challenges are and what needs to be done; and strengthen mechanisms for systematic evaluation of interventions, including those undertaken on a piecemeal or pragmatic basis, to create a pathway from pragmatic muddling to more transformative adaptation outcomes.

papers.title: Free to Fail? Paternalistic Preferences in the United States
papers.abstract: Abstract This paper examines paternalistic preferences in two large-scale experiments with participants from the US general population. Participants decide whether to intervene when a stakeholder is about to make a choice misaligned with the stakeholder’s own preferences. Willingness to intervene depends on which intervention is available: only a minority implements a hard intervention, which restricts the stakeholder’s choice set, while a majority implements a soft intervention that provides information without restricting choice. A substantial share of participants does not defer to the stakeholder’s stated preferences when evaluating welfare. Our framework estimates that about half are welfarists and a third libertarian paternalists.

papers.title: Who pays for decarbonizing homes?
papers.abstract: The decarbonization of the residential building sector requires large upfront investments in heating system replacement and thermal renovation that fall disproportionately on lower-income households. Faced with political constraints on carbon pricing and technology mandates, investment subsidies have become the main policy instrument.This paper analyzes the distributional effects and fiscal costs of this policy approach for Austria. We develop a microsimulation model that links household-level investment needs to landlord wealth distributions,allowing us to assign the incidence of subsidies and financial burden across homeowners and landlords within a unified empirical setting.We find total investment needs amount to 78–92 billion euros over the transition period to 2040 (approximately 1% of GDP annually), implying fiscal costs of 33–40 billion euros under the 2023 subsidy scheme. Despite a targeted low-income component, approximately 45% of subsidy outlays accrue to the top three income deciles. Net investment burdens remain strongly regressive when thermal renovation is required, exceeding three annual incomes for low-income single-family homeowners. We further document substantial horizontal disparities within income groups and show that Austria's fragmented housing law is a first-order determinant of investment feasibility in the multi-apartment (rental) sector.Addressing distributional and feasibility concerns under fiscal constraints may require a policy mix combining mandates, income-contingent transfers, liquidity-support instruments and housing law reform.

papers.title: Do the trophic impacts which jaguars have on wildlife communities matter to farmers? Diverging farmer preferences for jaguar-associated benefits and costs
Actualizing entrepreneurial futures: Imaginaries, Visions, and the Olivetti Corporation
In Value Creation: The Mediating Roles of Lean Sustainability and Sustainable Quality Culture in Linking Values‐Based Leadership to Organizational Outcomes
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT This research investigates the mechanisms by which value‐based leadership (VBL) impacts critical organizational outcomes, namely, operational performance (OPP), business performance (BSP), and business survival (BSV). Specifically, it examines the mediating roles of lean sustainability (LES) and sustainable quality culture (SQC) in translating leadership into tangible results. The research employs a quantitative research design using survey data collected from 402 middle and senior‐level managers. The proposed research model and hypotheses were tested using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS‐SEM) with SmartPLS 4. A two‐stage analytical approach was followed, involving the evaluation of the measurement model (reliability and validity) and the structural model (path coefficients and mediating effects). The direct effect of values‐based leadership on sustainable quality culture (β = 0.759; t = 26.912; p < 0.001) was identified as the strongest relationship in the model. In the mediation analysis, the indirect effect of values‐based leadership on lean sustainability through sustainable quality culture (β = 0.395; t = 12.494; p < 0.001) emerged as the most prominent mediation mechanism. All seven proposed hypotheses (between H1 and H7) were statistically supported, with coefficients excluding zero within the 95% confidence interval and significance levels of p < 0.001. While the research uses a robust sample of 402 managers, the use of non‐probability purposive sampling may limit generalizability. Future research could adopt longitudinal designs to further validate causal links over time or examine these dynamics across different sectors to determine whether sectoral nuances affect the mediating effect.

papers.title: Who Governs Carbon? Board Diversity and Incentive‐Linked Pay as Key Drivers of Disclosure in FTSE 100 Firms
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Corporate boards are increasingly expected to drive climate accountability, yet evidence on which governance mechanisms shape carbon transparency remains contradictory. Using an unbalanced panel of 618 firm‐year observations from 62 FTSE 100 nonfinancial firms (2015–2025), this study examines how board structure, composition and incentive design shape both the decision to disclose carbon emissions via the Carbon Disclosure Project (CDP) and the depth of that disclosure (a 0–8 quality scale). Combining pooled OLS, fixed‐effects, random‐effects and logit regressions with structural equation modelling, we find that gender diversity and sustainability‐linked executive compensation are the only governance mechanisms consistently and robustly associated with both disclosure outcomes; board size is positively associated with disclosure depth but not with the disclosure decision itself. Board independence, meeting frequency, attendance and sustainability committees show no material effect once firm‐specific heterogeneity is controlled for. Structural equation modelling further reveals a negative covariance between governance and financial‐capacity constructs, suggesting a long‐term sustainability trade‐off. These findings extend recent cross‐country meta‐analytic evidence by showing that, once structural governance adoption is near‐universal, incremental gains in carbon transparency come from incentive alignment and compositional diversity rather than additional structural apparatus. For policymakers, investors and boards, the implication is that diversity targets and ESG‐linked pay are more reliable levers of carbon transparency than procedural governance metrics.

papers.title: Business Model Innovation Under Institutionalized ESG Regulation: An Ontological Account of Paradox Closure
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Institutionalized environmental, social, and governance (ESG) regulation is reshaping how firms justify value, responsibility, and viability across industrial value chains. This paper examines how Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive requirements enter business model innovation in SMEs embedded in five industrial value chains. Drawing on a 3‐year longitudinal qualitative study of 25 SMEs, the findings show that ESG was initially treated as an external layer associated with documentation, compliance, and customer demands. When translated into business model reasoning, ESG surfaced persistent tensions among economic, environmental, social, and governance logics. These tensions were frequently closed through sequencing, commensuration, deferral, and compliance‐oriented reasoning. Artifact‐mediated workshops were associated with moments of provisional copresence, while the wider analysis identified governance constraints arising from the separation of ESG responsibility and decision authority. Building on these patterns, the paper advances the abductively grounded proposition that assumptions embedded in dominant BMI frameworks may reinforce ontological closure under institutionalized ESG conditions. It introduces the E 2 SG Flower as an analytically grounded paradox‐navigation proposition whose effects and transferability beyond the studied industrial value chains require further empirical validation.

papers.title: AI‐Enabled Capabilities for Open Circular Innovation and Industrial Symbiosis: Towards Agentic AI Orchestration
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Industrial symbiosis supports circular economies through resource exchanges. Yet, this collaborative approach faces information asymmetries, fragmented networks and coordination challenges. This study synthesises the extant literature and examines five industrial symbiosis initiatives with varying levels of digital maturity. Cross‐case analyses identify five interconnected capabilities, including knowledge discovery, ecosystem orchestration, resource matching, resource‐exchange facilitation and value‐chain integration. The findings indicate that, for the time being, existing platforms remain AI assisted rather than fully autonomous. Building on these empirical insights, the study proposes an agentic industrial symbiosis (AIS) framework that conceptualises how these capabilities could support future agentic AI orchestration. The framework extends existing research on industrial symbiosis by clearly explaining the potential transition from AI‐enabled capabilities towards autonomous ecosystem coordination. It offers novel theoretical and practical implications for circular innovation. Moreover, it provides a foundation for future empirical research.

papers.title: Human resources governance and human capital management disclosure following the SEC mandate
papers.abstract: When do board-level governance mechanisms enhance human capital management (HCM) disclosure? Drawing on the concept of governance complementarity, we argue that individual human resources (HR) governance mechanisms, i.e., committee with HR oversight mandate and board-level HR expertise, lack sufficient organizational capacity to improve HCM disclosure on their own; rather, they become effective when configured together. Using a measure of HCM disclosure transparency that integrates readability, numerical intensity, and specificity for S&P 500 firms following the SEC's, 2020 mandate, we find that neither mechanism individually is associated with greater transparency, but their joint presence relates positively with HCM transparency. Partitioning the sample indicates that this relation reflects internal capabilities rather than external incentives to disclose transparently. A falsification test confirms this relationship is specific to HCM disclosure and does not extend to non-HCM portions of Item 1 in 10-K filings. More transparent HCM disclosure is related to better labor market outcomes. This study contributes to the governance literature by highlighting the importance of calibrating governance mechanism bundles for effective governance. From a regulatory perspective, this study informs policy discussions about the board's role in overseeing HCM.
papers.journal_name: Journal of Accounting and Public Policy

papers.title: Constructing sustainability expertise: capital conversion and the making of a sustainability CFO
papers.abstract: Purpose This paper examines how a Chief Financial Officer (CFO) in a Sri Lankan state-owned bank constructed sustainability accounting as a new domain of professional expertise. Extending Baxter and Chua's (2008) conception of accounting expertise as an organisational accomplishment, the paper asks how entirely new forms of accounting expertise are constructed before organisational legitimacy, evaluative criteria and professional jurisdiction have been established, drawing on Bourdieu's theory of field, habitus and capital to explain this process. Design/methodology/approach The study uses a longitudinal qualitative case study of a CFO in a Sri Lankan state-owned housing bank, whose sustainability agenda developed during the country's post-tsunami reconstruction. Data were collected across two phases (2013–2014) using 44 semi-structured interviews with 25 participants, supplemented by field notes and documentary analysis of sustainability reports, policy documents and media coverage. Data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis, proceeding from inductive coding through temporal coding to theoretical interpretation via Baxter and Chua (2008) and Bourdieu, tracing the sequential conversion of cultural, symbolic, social and positional capital. Findings Sustainability accounting expertise was constructed through a cumulative process of capital conversion. An entrepreneurial habitus generated the disposition to recognise emerging opportunities, enabling the accumulation of cultural capital through learning, authorship and reporting innovation. This cultural capital was converted into symbolic capital through managerial endorsement and award recognition, which expanded social capital through strategic alliances, and was ultimately converted into positional authority, redefining the finance function's organisational jurisdiction. However, this expertise construction did not automatically translate into institutionalisation: sustainability expertise remained concentrated in a single individual rather than becoming embedded in organisational systems and routines. Research limitations/implications The single-case design prioritises theoretical development over statistical generalisation; future research should examine whether similar processes of expertise construction occur across different organisational, professional and national settings. The case also centres on an unusually entrepreneurial CFO, and alternative trajectories may emerge where sustainability initiatives are collectively led or externally mandated. The longitudinal design captured the construction of expertise but not its longer-term reproduction following leadership succession, pointing to a need for future research on how such expertise diffuses, evolves or declines once its original architect departs the organisation. Practical implications Organisations should not equate the success of a prominent sustainability champion with the institutionalisation of sustainability capability. Individual actors can mobilise resources, secure legitimacy and accelerate organisational innovation, but sustained transformation depends on converting individually held expertise into collective organisational capability. Building durable sustainability capacity therefore requires deliberate investment in knowledge sharing, succession planning and cross-functional learning, alongside organisational systems that embed expertise beyond the individual who originally constructed it, reducing organisations' dependence on any single actor for the continuity of their sustainability agenda. Originality/value The paper offers a distinctive contribution by reconceptualising accounting expertise as something that must first be constructed, rather than simply organisationally accomplished, in emerging domains such as sustainability accounting. By integrating Bourdieu's theory of field, habitus and capital with Baxter and Chua's (2008) framework, it identifies cumulative capital conversion as the specific social mechanism underlying this process – a mechanism not previously articulated in the sustainability accounting literature. It further offers the original insight that expertise construction and organisational institutionalisation are analytically distinct, showing that individually constructed expertise can achieve legitimacy while remaining fragile and undiffused across the organisation.

papers.title: Cisnormative accounting organizations: recording the experiences of transgender people in Brazil
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aimed to record, understand and problematize, in the light of transfeminism, the experiences of transgender people who have transited and/or are transiting through accounting organizations in Brazil. Design/methodology/approach This article provides detailed information on the oppression present in accounting offices in Brazil and how oppressive actions impact the experiences of trans workers in the workplace. Six semi-structured interviews were conducted with: a) two transgender women, b) two transgender men and c) two non-binary people, with various identity markers in relation to gender, race, sexuality, age, disability and socio-economic class. The stories were categorized and analyzed using Dialogic Thematic Analysis. After the analysis, we present a map of resistance strategies in the Brazilian accounting environment. Findings The participants reported negative experiences in organizational accounting environments in Brazil, marked by prejudice, discrimination, disrespect for gender identity, erroneous pronoun treatment and physical and psychological violence committed by cisgender managers and co-workers, mainly cisgender men. We identified the use of resistance strategies in these environments in the participants' narratives, including the development of technical skills, professional experience, remote training and the use of cisgender passability as a coping mechanism. Originality/value This study makes significant contributions to understanding the experiences of transgender workers in accounting organizations in Brazil, the most oppressive country for this population in the world. Our findings fill gaps in the literature on the experiences of non-cisgender gender identities in accounting and can help improve corporate actions for the inclusion, permanence and belonging of diverse people in accounting organizations. This study also contributes to the gap in the literature, encouraging the development of new studies so that the voices of trans workers can be heard, stories can be told and recorded and oppression denounced.

Small Modular Electrochemical Containers for Decarbonization of AI Data Centers
papers.abstract: Abstract The rapid growth of artificial intelligence (AI) is increasing data-center electricity demand and reinforcing the near-term role of fossil-fuel power generation. Decarbonizing this infrastructure requires carbon capture systems that are efficient, compact, modular, and compatible with space-constrained data centers. Here, we evaluate Small Modular Electrochemical Containers (SMECs) as a deployment-oriented application of a two-stage, membraneless electrochemically mediated amine regeneration (EMAR) process. The design integrates CO2 absorption and electrochemical desorption within one gas-diffusion-electrode cell, eliminating absorber columns and ion-exchange membranes. Single-cell experiments were conducted under simulated natural-gas and coal-derived flue gas. Polarization mapping identified optimized operating conditions, which were then used in a 300-cycle, 50-h accelerated stability test with periodic polarity switching. The cell maintained repeatable voltage and CO2 absorption/desorption profiles, with absorption and desorption efficiencies of ∼90% under optimized conditions. The energetics ranged from 50–85 kJe/molCO2, and GC/IC analyses showed no detectable gaseous or liquid side products. The paper further includes theoretical modeling of SOx and NOx effects on the absorbent. In a case study for a 360 MW data-center power plant, the TEA showed that fewer than 20 SMEC units could achieve near-complete decarbonization, increasing the levelized electricity cost from about \$58/MWh to \$74/MWh.

How to manage meadows effectively? Flagship, keystone & diagnostic species perspective
papers.abstract: We investigated the long-term effects of meadow management regimes (abandonment vs. mowing, and its frequency), plant invasion, and habitat availability on three different meadow ecosystem components. The system consists of (1) native plant Sanguisorba officinalis , (2) ant assemblages, and (3) butterfly species of the genus Phengaris , known as flagships for biodiversity conservation. The investigated wet meadow communities responded quite similarly to management regimes. In general, declining biodiversity was related to either complete abandonment or more intensive management (with mowing more than once per year). The focal native plant cover was affected by management and invasive plants. Mowing frequency did not affect ant diversity or population fluctuations of Phengaris butterflies over a five-year period. Low frequency mowing (one cut per year) is crucial to long-term persistence of the studied species, and S. officinalis cover is a good indicator for assessing habitat condition of studied meadows. The establishment of non-intensive management and occasionally more intensive mowing for active control of invasive plants is needed to preserve the investigated wet meadows of high conservation value and complex system of organisms inhabiting them.

Dairy farm system configurations and predictors of multidimensional climate-smart practice adoption in the U.S.
Reevaluating the energy performance after considering thermal pollution treatment in humidification-dehumidification desalination
Assessing the association between street view–derived perceived liveliness and street thefts
papers.abstract: Crime geographers are attentive to how the spatial characteristics of the environment affect criminal behaviors. Recently, scholars have found that aside from physical and social attributes, the perception of the environment, such as safety perception, is also associated with crime occurrence. However, perceived liveliness, a visual perceptual proxy for potential routine activity settings that are closely linked to routine activity theory and crime pattern theory, is rarely explored in prior research. This study examines the association between perceived liveliness and street thefts in the City of Cincinnati, the United States. The liveliness perception scores are derived from street view imagery using a support vector machine model trained on the MIT Place Pulse V2 crowdsourcing image survey. Negative binomial regression models are used to test the relationships between perceived liveliness and street theft, with social and physical environmental attributes controlled. Results show that perceived liveliness significantly improves model performance and is positively associated with street theft. This study provides the first evidence that perceived liveliness helps explain crimes. The positive relationship between perceived liveliness of the built environment and crime adds a new dimension to the routine activity theory and the crime pattern theory. It also offers a scalable and cost-effective measure that can assist urban planners and law enforcement in identifying potential theft hotspots using readily available street view imagery.

Somewhere over the transcontinental burrito tunnel
Residential Segregation and Unequal Access to Local Public Services in India: Evidence from 1.5 Million Neighborhoods
papers.abstract: We study residential segregation and access to public services across 1.5 million urban and rural neighborhoods in India. Muslim and Scheduled Caste segregation in India is high by global standards and only slightly lower than Black-White segregation in the United States. Within cities, public facilities and infrastructure are systematically less available in Muslim and Scheduled Caste neighborhoods. Nearly all regressive allocation is across neighborhoods within cities—at the most informal and least studied form of government. These inequalities are not visible in the aggregate data typically used for research and policy. (JEL H76, J15, O15, O17, O18, R23)

papers.title: Inequality and Racial Backlash: Evidence from the Reconstruction Era and the Freedmen's Bureau
papers.abstract: How do majority groups respond to narrowing inequality in racially polarized environments? We study this by examining the Freedmen's Bureau, an agency created after the US Civil War to aid former slaves and launch institutional reform in the South. Using new historical records and an event-study approach, we estimate the bureau's impact on political, social, and economic outcomes. Vote shares for Democrats, the party that previously championed slavery and opposed Black civil rights, initially eroded in bureau counties, but these impacts faded as federal oversight weakened. Racial backlash emerged rapidly and persisted, suggesting White majorities sought to offset Black progress. (JEL D63, D72, J15, N31, N41)

papers.title: Union Bargaining Power and the Amenity-Wage Trade-Off
papers.abstract: This paper studies how collective bargaining affects wages and amenities. By merging collective bargaining agreements (CBAs) to linked employer-employee data in Brazil, I combine rich contracted amenities with wage information. I implement a difference-in-differences strategy that exploits a court ruling enforcing CBA continuation (i.e., ultra-activity) to estimate the effects of union bargaining power. Strengthening unions raises wages and amenities without reducing employment—increasing retention despite some labor-labor substitution. A revealed-preference approach shows that amenities account for 45 percent of total compensation gains. These findings suggest that collective bargaining can offset monopsony power, but employers retain the right-to-manage workforce composition. (JEL J31, J32, J42, J51, J52, O15)

papers.title: The Returns to Government R&D: Evidence from US Appropriations Shocks
papers.abstract: Based on a narrative classification of all significant postwar changes in R&D appropriations for five major federal agencies, we find that an increase in nondefense R&D appropriations leads to increases in various measures of innovative activity and higher business-sector productivity in the long run. We structurally estimate the production function elasticity of nondefense government R&D capital using the SP-IV methodology of Lewis and Mertens (2024) and obtain implied returns of 140 to 210 percent over the postwar period. The estimates indicate that government-funded R&D accounts for one-fifth of business-sector TFP growth since WWII and imply substantial underfunding of nondefense R&D. (JEL D24, E23, H50, O31, O33, O38)

papers.title: The Causal Effects of Global Supply Chain Disruptions on Macroeconomic Outcomes: Evidence and Theory
papers.abstract: We study the causal effects of global supply chain disruptions by constructing a new index of real-time port congestion using Automatic Identification System data from container ships and a spatial clustering algorithm. We develop a model with search frictions between producers and retailers that links upstream production slack to downstream supply shortages and captures output and price responses to supply chain shocks. The co-movements of output, prices, spare capacity, and market tightness provide novel identification restrictions. We find that demand and supply shocks drove US disinflation in 2020, while the inflation surge in 2021 was driven mainly by supply chain shocks. (JEL C43, E31, F14, F23, L14, L92)

papers.title: Durables and the Marginal Propensity to Spend
papers.abstract: Durables represent a large share of households' marginal propensity to spend (MPX). We develop a quantitative model of spending that takes durables into account and matches a rich set of empirical regularities simultaneously. Scaling the response of nondurables provides a poor approximation of the MPX on durables when it comes to its distribution in the population, its persistence over time, and its cyclicality. As an application, we study how the MPX varies with the size of stimulus checks and find that it declines more slowly compared to a model of purely nondurable spending. (JEL D11, E21, E32, E62, G51)

papers.title: Firm Adaptation in Production Networks: Evidence from Extreme Weather Events in Pakistan
papers.abstract: This paper considers how far private adaptation may reduce future vulnerability to climate risks. Using data on monthly firm-to-firm transactions from Pakistan, we find that flood-affected firms are more likely to relocate to safer ground and shift purchases toward suppliers in less flood-prone regions and reached via less flood-prone roads. The results indicate that firms are imperfectly informed about flood risk and update their beliefs following floods. We quantify aggregate impacts using a spatial model of endogenous production network formation. The findings suggest that firms' learning will shape the economic impact of increasingly frequent climate-related disasters. (JEL D22, L14, O13, O14, Q54, R32)

papers.title: Reproducible Aggregation of Sample-Split Statistics
The Unequal Economic Consequences of Carbon Pricing
papers.abstract: This paper studies the economic impacts of carbon pricing. Exploiting institutional features of the European carbon market and high-frequency data, I identify carbon policy shocks and trace their dynamic effects. A restrictive carbon policy shock raises energy prices, reduces emissions, spurs green innovation, but decreases economic activity—disproportionately burdening poorer households. Not only are the poor more affected because of their higher energy spending, but they also experience larger income losses. These indirect, general equilibrium effects via income and employment play an important role in the transmission of carbon pricing policies, accounting for about two-thirds of the aggregate consumption response. (JEL E23, E24, O44, Q41, Q54, Q55, Q58)

papers.title: The Inflation Attention Threshold and Inflation Surges
papers.abstract: The recent inflation surge brought inflation back on people's minds. I quantify when and how much attention to inflation changes and derive the macroeconomic implications of these attention changes. I estimate an attention threshold at an inflation rate of 4 percent, that attention doubles when inflation exceeds this threshold, and that supply shocks have stronger and more persistent effects on inflation in times of high attention. Developing a model featuring the attention threshold, I show that attention changes offer a joint explanation for inflation surges, inflation's co-movement with inflation expectations, and a long last mile of disinflation. (JEL D84, E12, E31, E43, E52)

papers.title: A Model of Enclosures: Coordination, Conflict, and Efficiency in the Transformation of Land Property Rights
A Theory of Redistribution and Public Good Provision under Nondemocracy
The Evolution of the Market for Corporate Control
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT We consider an informed large shareholder who can choose between making a takeover bid herself and initiating a sale to another acquirer. Such takeover activism complements direct takeovers because the very choice mitigates the asymmetric information problem, thereby improving efficiency. As more investors enter the market for corporate control, takeover activism increasingly replaces direct takeovers as the prevailing mode of disciplinary control change, matching the evolution in practice. Our model shows how this evolution, characterized by a symbiotic relationship between investor activism and private equity, arises to overcome asymmetric information and collective action problems through intermediated transactions.

Information Aggregation With Delegation of Votes
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Liquid democracy (LD) combines elements of direct and representative democracy: voters can either vote directly or delegate their votes to others. We study its information aggregation properties in a setting with heterogeneously and privately informed independent and partisan voters. We establish that LD always has equilibria that improve welfare and information aggregation relative to direct democracy, identify economically interpretable conditions under which these gains are strict, and characterise optimal delegation for salient classes of committees. However, while delegation improves the best‐equilibrium, it can also introduce robust inefficient equilibria that perform worse than direct democracy.

papers.title: Launching for the “Greater Good”: Spillover Effect of ESG Funds
papers.abstract: We examine the incentives for mutual fund families to launch ESG funds. Our analyses reveal that introducing a new ESG fund leads to a significant increase in capital inflows to sibling non-ESG funds in the family. This flow spillover accounts for a significant portion of the monetary awards for families to offer ESG funds. We also find that spillover is stronger among retail funds and cannot be attributed to changes in the ESG profiles or abnormal returns of the sibling funds. Further evidence suggests that affect-based judgments, particularly the halo effect, are the key drivers of this spillover effect.
