papers.title: Pilot study testing varenicline combined with a behavioral intervention for promoting smoking cessation and pain management among patients with cancer
papers.abstract: Abstract Purpose Many patients with cancer smoke and also experience pain. Smoking offers short-term pain relief but exacerbates pain long-term. We pilot tested the feasibility, acceptability, and preliminary efficacy of adding varenicline to a combined behavioral treatment that addresses smoking cessation and pain management. Methods We conducted a single arm pilot study in which we provided varenicline paired with a 4-session behavioral treatment that uses the same techniques to help people quit smoking and manage their pain. Our primary outcome was 7-day point prevalence abstinence at 6-months post-randomization. Results We recruited 19 patients with cancer. 80% of the patients who received the intervention rated it as extremely useful (4 or 5 out of 5) in helping them quit smoking; 60% rated it as helpful in managing their pain. Further, 81% would recommend the program to other patients with cancer. Over one-third (35%) reported biochemically validated abstinence at 6 months post-randomization. We did not see improvements in reported pain but did see improvements in pain self-efficacy. Conclusions Our pilot data suggest the feasibility, acceptability, and preliminary efficacy of this approach for promoting cessation. We need to refine aspects to help address pain, yet addressing pain in addition to smoking cessation might motivate more patients with cancer to join the program. The next step is to conduct a large randomized controlled trial to fully test the efficacy of the combined behavioral program with varenicline. Implications for Cancer Survivors: A combined smoking cessation and pain program paired with varenicline might help patients with cancer quit smoking.

Environmental, circularity, and criticality assessment of end-of-life lithium-ion batteries: Implications for management strategies in Mexico
papers.abstract: Mexico's rapid growth in battery electric vehicle (BEV) adoption has not been accompanied by a regulatory framework for the end-of-life management of lithium-ion batteries (LIBs), creating environmental risks and limiting the recovery of strategic materials. This study evaluates four end-of-life management strategies for BEV LIBs in Mexico (controlled disposal, hydrometallurgical recycling, pyrometallurgical recycling, and repurposing) using an integrated framework that combines Life Cycle Assessment (LCA), the Material Circularity Indicator (MCI), and a criticality-weighted extension (MCI-c). The proposed MCI-c incorporates material criticality into the circularity assessment, allowing resource recovery to be evaluated not only in terms of material recirculation but also considering the strategic importance of recovered materials. Repurposing achieved the best overall environmental and circularity performance, while hydrometallurgical recycling consistently outperformed pyrometallurgical recycling among recycling alternatives. Incorporating criticality into the assessment altered the prioritization of management strategies under increasing lithium criticality, demonstrating that criticality can influence end-of-life management priorities. These findings highlight the importance of integrating environmental performance, material circularity, and criticality into the evaluation of end-of-life LIBs management strategies. For Mexico, they support the development of a dedicated regulatory framework that prioritizes higher-value recovery strategies and incorporates criticality into end-of-life decision-making. More broadly, the proposed framework provides a practical approach for evaluating end-of-life LIBs management in countries facing similar challenges in battery circularity and critical material supply.

papers.title: A comparative TEA–LCA study of biomethane production through anaerobic digestion and five upgrading technologies: Amine scrubbing, water scrubbing, membrane separation, PSA, and cryogenic separation
papers.abstract: Producing grid-quality biomethane from sewage-sludge biogas is promising, yet selecting an upgrading route remains uncertain because mature technologies differ in energy use, cost, methane losses in off-gas or vent streams, and the fate of biogenic CO 2 . This study evaluates anaerobic digestion integrated with five commercial upgrading technologies: amine scrubbing, water scrubbing (WS), membrane separation (MEM), pressure swing adsorption (PSA), and cryogenic separation (CRYO), modelled for a municipal wastewater treatment plant. All configurations deliver grid-quality biomethane, while separated CO 2 is compressed and liquefied where feasible; venting is assumed for the dilute CO 2 stream from WS. Aspen Plus simulations were coupled with techno-economic analysis (TEA) and consequential life cycle assessment (LCA). The results show clear trade-offs. Amine scrubbing has the highest thermal demand (1207 kW), whereas CRYO and MEM have the highest upgrading-unit electricity demands (257 and 201 kW, respectively). Economically, without an additional emission charge, WS is the most attractive option, with the lowest levelized cost of biomethane (LCOM) of 436 €/t, while amine scrubbing is the most expensive (652 €/t). Hypothetical charges on vented biogenic CO 2 and CH 4 progressively increase the LCOM of WS above those of MEM, CRYO, PSA, and amine scrubbing at approximately 36.5, 37.7, 43.2, and 120.4 €/t CO 2 -eq, respectively. From an environmental perspective, consequential LCA shows that PSA, MEM, and CRYO outperform solvent-based routes in human health, ecosystem, and climate performance due to efficient CO 2 liquefaction and avoidance of upgrading-stage venting. In the deterministic base case, PSA delivers the highest net human-health savings and the largest net GHG reduction, whereas WS shows the weakest climate performance. The economic preference for WS depends on emission-pricing assumptions, while PSA, MEM, and CRYO are more suitable for carbon-circular biorefineries.

Greenwashing or Sustainability Misalignment? Analysing Organisational, Workplace and Real Estate Strategies Through an Iceberg Lens
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Environmental sustainability and the broader Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) agenda have become prominently proclaimed organisational priorities, yet their integration into core decision‐making remains uneven. While greenwashing research has largely focused on communication and disclosure, it has paid less attention to the internal strategic dynamics that underpin sustainability outcomes. This paper examines how environmental sustainability and ESG shape organisational decision‐making in workplace and corporate real estate (CRE) strategies. Drawing on organisational culture and institutional theory, the study adopts an iceberg perspective, conceptualising sustainability as a visible commitment underpinned by less visible strategic, cultural and institutional dynamics. Using a mixed‐methods design, the study combines quantitative analysis of two waves of large‐scale survey data from senior CRE professionals with qualitative insights from semistructured interviews with employees, senior executives and CRE managers. The findings show that sustainability and ESG considerations may be unevenly associated with workplace and CRE strategies. It revealed that sustainability may be largely peripheral to future strategic decision‐making, with stronger links to workplace adjustments than to fundamental CRE portfolio decisions. Qualitative evidence further shows that economic, operational and social priorities dominate stakeholder workplace considerations, while organisations weakly prioritise environmental sustainability in routines. The study shows that sustainability may be rhetorically prominent yet strategically peripheral, reframing sustainability misalignment as an underlying strategic integration challenge that spans business, organisational strategy and sustainability research, and offering insights for organisations seeking to align ESG commitments more effectively with asset‐intensive strategies.

papers.title: Global Manufacturers' Approaches to Managing Waste in Their Production Networks
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT This research investigates how global manufacturers organize local waste management within their global production networks to aid the implementation of circularity. This study aims to identify the approach to managing waste in the global production network and the extent of engaging in waste‐to‐resource activities. We methodologically study this through six industrial case studies in the household electronics industry, which we explore through qualitative analysis of archival data, such as sustainability and annual reports. Our findings reveal how bottom‐up and top‐down approaches to managing waste in the global production network are characterized. We further identify relationship management with external actors in the waste‐based supply chain. We identify and discuss how these two factors affect the global manufacturer's extent of engaging in waste‐to‐resource activities. This research contributes to academic understanding on global operations by identifying the factors that are required to enable circularity implementation for global manufacturers.

papers.title: Generative AI in ESG Reporting: A Case Study and Process Framework
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT The emergence of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is found to have a remarkable impact on environmental, social, and governance (ESG) reporting. Although there is abundant literature on ESG reporting, very few studies have examined the adoption of GenAI in ESG reporting. As a result, this study examines how companies can use GenAI to generate value in ESG reporting. We obtain the following three findings that we articulate in this paper: (i) GenAI drives digital innovation in ESG reporting via automated data extraction, accelerated analytics, and dynamic reporting; (ii) GenAI‐powered platforms enhance stakeholder engagement by integrating diverse data sources and improving information accessibility; and (iii) organizations encounter significant challenges in data governance and human‐AI collaboration. We also propose a framework for adopting GenAI in digital ESG platforms.

papers.title: The Immortality Paradox: One‐Party Dominance, Political Tenure, and Organizational Continuity in Japanese Agencies
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT In his classic 1976 study on organizational survival, Kaufman argued that public organizations are “immortal”. More recent research, however, has come to the opposite conclusion, finding that public organizations are frequently terminated. These findings largely relate to contexts where changes to the ruling party occur regularly. In contrast, this study examines the survival of government agencies in Japan, where the postwar political system has been characterized by one‐party dominance and short‐lived political leadership. The findings suggest that Japanese agencies remain largely “immortal,” and that when they do undergo transitions this tends to be linked to prime ministers with longer tenures who are able to implement minor, cosmetic changes; hence agencies typically persist even after such events. This study thus sheds new light on how political–administrative relations shape patterns of agency transition and highlights the importance of leadership tenure in sustaining commitments to organizational change.

A New Approach to Household Flood Resilience Assessment using the Recovery-Damage Ratio (RDR) Index
papers.abstract: Flood resilience is the ability of a system to withstand and efficiently recover from flood damage. Although resilience has become central to disaster research, most household-level flood assessments remain focused on estimating immediate damage, offering limited understanding of post-flood recovery dynamics. To address this gap, this study develops a new approach that extends conventional flood damage assessment toward resilience, capturing variations in household recovery trajectories across different resilience properties. The novelty of this research lies in the formulation of a new index that quantifies the dynamic nature of post-flood recovery relative to the damage incurred. We achieve this by coupling empirical flood damage curves with a time-dependent Recovery–Damage Ratio (RDR) index, creating the flood resilience curve. As a proof of concept, we utilized survey data from Marikina City, Philippines, and set the longitudinal information of income, post-flood financial aid, and house type as surrogate indicators of the four properties of resilience, namely robustness, redundancy, rapidity, and resources. This analysis reveals disparities in recovery speed associated with income class and external assistance. This also uncovers a paradox that while structural robustness dictates initial damage, low-flood depth households may delay repairs, whereas highly inundated households rapidly mobilize reconstruction. Furthermore, the comparison of paired flood events shows a shift in household resilience after experiencing severe flooding, consistent with localized flood adaptation and preemptive actions. Ultimately, this approach offers a reproducible framework to quantify post-flood recovery through the lens of interdependent resilience properties.

Smart-city pilot vs. non-pilot cities: Long-term trends in urban resilience in China
papers.abstract: Urban resilience has become a critical component of sustainable urban development under increasing climate risks and disaster uncertainty. Smart city initiatives have been widely promoted as a strategy to enhance urban governance and resilience. However, their long-term relationship with urban resilience remains insufficiently understood. This study investigates the resilience evolution of 300 Chinese cities, including 155 smart city pilot cities and 145 non-smart cities, from 2004 to 2023. A multidimensional resilience evaluation framework consisting of four dimensions and 48 indicators was constructed, and social network analysis was used to calculate resilience index for each city group and year. The results indicate that pilot cities had a mean resilience index of 0.795, compared with 0.478 for non-pilot cities, and permutation tests showed that this difference was significant in every year. However, the difference was largest in 2004, before the pilot program began, and narrowed mainly before 2013, as the resilience of non-pilot cities increased, and did not widen after the pilot program began. Given the non-random selection of pilot cities, these differences should be interpreted as an association that mainly reflects pilot selection rather than a direct causal effect of smart city policies. Early smart city pilots showed higher and comparatively stable resilience (mean 0.935) than the second (0.621) and third (0.180) batches. Institutional and infrastructure resilience increased in both groups, agent resilience changed little, and environmental resilience declined in both pilot and non-pilot cities, suggesting persistent challenges in ecological sustainability. The findings suggest that smart-city policy evaluation should account for baseline differences, and that future resilience-oriented policies strengthen environmental integration and support for less developed cities alongside technological advancement.

papers.abstract: In Surviving Rome, Bowes sounds a clarion call for researchers to focus on the understudied economic lives of the majority 'ninety percent' inhabitants of the early Roman Empire.The dramatis personae of her book are the potters, hustlers, weavers, small holders (emphatically not peasants!),sex workers, children, and drovers.Here, we have the masses, the rustics and urban mob, decried and denigrated by Roman elite writers.It was these masses -the agricultural producers, craftspeople, and purveyor of services -who literally built the Roman Empire and its material world.In many ways, the volume is an antidote to our imaginary Romes and the preconceptions, drawn from textual sources, hazy economic theory, and the odd ethnohistoric analogy, that have sketched their outlines.Sacred cows are slaughtered, and strawmen are burnt along the way.The consumer city, autarkic peasants, 'Cicero & Co', and calculating ancient GDP are definitely out.In their place is a series of micro-narratives: pieces of lives glimpsed through the waste paper bin of Egyptian papyri and the boxes of pottery sherds, animal bones, and burnt seeds recovered by archaeologists.We learn that the 'ninety percent' were exploited -by the state, landlords, and others.They led hard, gruelling lives and made choices in a struggle to surf the wave of precarity.These individuals and families were faced with choices that are unenviable to modern eyes -prostituting a close relative or sending their small children out to work -but these strategies, along with others, enabled those individuals to survive and more at a level greater than that of modern economists' idea of 'subsistence'.The seven chapters are a joy to read.Bowes' prose is compelling, written with a simple clarity that is both elegant and seductive.It is easy to be carried along, and the reliance on the Egyptian textual evidence is a case in point.The papyri and ostraca provide vignettes of past lives that are fascinating and have an immediacy that is hard to ignore.Yet, they stand as a proxy for All rights reserved, including rights for text and data mining and training of artificial intelligence technologies or similar technologies.

papers.title: Peripheral participation, metropolitan ownership: core and periphery configurations in Japan’s Green Transformation technological paths
papers.abstract: Abstract Research on innovation beyond metropolitan cores has paid less attention to whether peripheral participation is matched by formal ownership of patents on key technological paths. We distinguish spatial and network participation from the headquarters geography of patent applicants, and apply kernel density, core–periphery network, and main-path analyses to sixty-two Japanese Green Transformation technologies. Four technology participation configurations emerge. Yet most main-path patent–firm links involve firms headquartered in Japan’s three major metropolitan areas. The study highlights that participation in main technological paths differs from ownership, which marks the tensions between core and peripheral configurations of inventive activity.

Forecasting seasonal changepoint models utilizing changepoint uncertainties
papers.abstract: Forecasting in the presence of changepoints is a challenging task. However, if changepoints occur regularly across seasons, we want to utilize that information in our predictions for the next season. In this paper, we develop a framework for forecasting seasonal data that contain within-season changepoints. In our forecasts, we account for uncertainty in the changepoint locations both within and across seasons via a weighting approach across changepoint uncertainties. The framework is very flexible across different changepoint model assumptions and approaches to identifying changepoint confidence sets. We demonstrate the improvement in forecasting performance of our framework for atmospheric pressure with a multivariate changepoint approach, and for air pollution ( PM 2.5 ) with a univariate changepoint approach.

Military experience and ethical restraint: Evidence from CEO insider trading
papers.abstract: Abstract We examine the relation between CEO military experience and insider trading in U.S. public firms. Military CEOs earn significantly lower insider trading profits than non‐military CEOs, particularly those who attained commissioned ranks or served in the Air Force, Army, or Marine Corps. The negative relation holds for both purchase and sale transactions. Military CEOs also exhibit longer investment horizons and are less likely to trade in the month preceding earnings announcements. Overall, the findings are consistent with military socialization promoting discipline, rule adherence, and ethical restraint in exploiting informational advantages for personal gain.

Water Markets for Climate Change Adaptation: Trade, Storage, and Investment Under Stochastic Water Supply
papers.abstract: Abstract It is widely accepted that water markets can support adaptation to climate change. However, quantifying this adaptive capacity is difficult as it requires models that represent both stochastic water supplies and forward-looking behaviour by market participants. We develop a stochastic dynamic model of the Murray-Darling Basin water market in which irrigators form rational expectations over future water prices, and make monthly water use, annual crop planting, and long-run investment decisions. The model is solved using reinforcement learning methods to approximate expectations, combined with mathematical programming to estimate market equilibrium. We validate the model against observed prices and irrigation activity from 2008 to 09 to 2021–22 and apply it to an ensemble of 37 CMIP6 climate projections for the southern Basin. Under drier future climates, water markets support adaptation through increased inter-regional trade flows into the downstream Murray, and larger storage reserves through more conservative crop planting. However, under the driest projections, inter-regional trade constraints bind, price differences widen across zones, and long-run irrigation development contracts by up to 16 per cent. The results highlight both the value and the limits of market-based adaptation, with implications for the design of water market institutions under a non-stationary climate.

papers.title: Do Protected Areas Affect the Income Levels in Remote Regions? Evidence from Italian Inner Areas
papers.abstract: Abstract The economic impact of protected areas (PAs) on local development remains a debated topic in regional economics, particularly in peripheral regions facing demographic and economic decline. While protected areas provide essential ecological benefits, their effects on local economies remain debated, with concerns about land-use restrictions potentially limiting economic opportunities alongside potential gains from tourism and ecosystem services. This study investigates the causal effect of PAs on per capita income in Italian municipalities classified as inner areas under the National Strategy for Inner Areas. We exploit variation in the share of municipal land covered by protected areas using a Difference-in-differences approach with continuous treatment in a dose-response framework. The results show a robust, positive, and statistically significant relationship between PAs and local economic growth. The expansion of protected areas is associated with increased per capita income, suggesting that environmental protection contributes to development in Italy’s marginalized inner regions.

papers.title: Policy uncertainty shocks and farm investments in Europe: Evidence from a newspaper‐based index
papers.abstract: Abstract In order to quantify the impact of agricultural policy uncertainty on European farmers' investment behavior, we construct a newspaper‐based monthly index of European agricultural policy uncertainty from 2013 to 2023. We use 327,224 newspaper articles to assess and compare the trends in policy uncertainty across five top agricultural producers in Europe, that is, Germany, the United Kingdom, France, Spain and Italy. We connect this index of policy uncertainty to bookkeeping data from 13,706 farms in these five countries over the period 2014–2018 ( N = 68,530) to estimate the relationship between policy uncertainty and investment decisions. We find an increasing trend in agricultural policy uncertainty, with significant peaks around key events such as the COVID‐19 pandemic, the introduction of the European Green Deal and Brexit. Despite the presence of a common policy environment, agricultural policy uncertainty is heterogeneous across countries and captures country‐specific uncertainties such as elections and weather shocks. Anticipated policy uncertainties, such as those arising from Brexit and the European Green Deal, allow farmers to analyze optimal responses and make investment plans, and therefore, if they affect farm investment, they do so smoothly over time (e.g., bringing investment forward). In contrast, unanticipated uncertainties, or policy uncertainty shocks, like those caused by the Russian food import ban of 2014 or the US‐China trade war are negatively correlated to farm investment.

papers.title: Navigating the Family Support Dilemma in Female Entrepreneurship: An Embeddedness Perspective
papers.abstract: Drawing on family embeddedness and gender performativity, we examine how family support is enacted and governed through gendered norms, and how female entrepreneurs navigate these dynamics. Based on indepth interviews with female entrepreneurs and family members in Ethiopia, we introduce the family support dilemma: a process in which support enabling female entrepreneurship simultaneously generates explicit or internalized obligations that constrain sustained engagement and growth over time. Our findings show that family support is embedded in gendered social structures, functioning as a site of norm enforcement where support is granted or withdrawn based on women’s enactment of gender role expectations.

papers.title: From Contested Endogenization to Regulatory Unravelling of Mandatory Human Rights Due Diligence: Extending the Endogeneity of Law Framework
papers.abstract: Abstract Drawing on the endogeneity of law framework, this study examines how business, legal, public, and civil society actors constructed the meaning and practice of mandatory human rights due diligence in the context of the German garment industry and the German Supply Chain Act. Using interview, document, and observation data spanning the period 2019 to 2026, our findings reveal a two‐stage process: an initial phase of contested endogenization in which actors experienced with private regulation prevented convergence on a managerialized interpretation of the law, followed by regulatory unravelling in which changes in the political‐economic climate provided avenues for substantively weakening the law and preventing its implementation. We discuss how the dual processes of managerializing a law and legalizing of organizations is complicated by three boundary conditions: the complexity of the regulatory issue, the field's regulatory maturity, and the degree of regulatory uncertainty. Connecting the endogeneity of law framework with research on the public and private governance of global supply chains allows us to theorize refinements to this framework when applied to contested, complex governance fields, and to derive a set of theoretical and practical implications for public supply chain regulation.

papers.title: The coevolution of trust and behavioral uncertainty: Toward a theory of vulnerability acceptance in entrepreneurial ventures
papers.abstract: Abstract Research Summary This conceptual study develops a process theory of vulnerability acceptance explaining how trust and behavioral uncertainty coevolve as entrepreneurial actors form, interpret, and realize opportunities. Trust is frequently invoked to explain creativity, exploration, and opportunity formation, yet remains theorized through predictability and evaluability, which entrepreneurial opportunities often lack ex ante. We distinguish three forms of vulnerability acceptance: uncertainty creating, releasing, and decreasing trust. Each transforms the uncertainty it engages, which in turn reinforces or unsettles that form, so no form is terminal. Their salience shifts across opportunity formation, interpretive recombination, and realization, and misalignment between a form and the conditions it confronts impairs entrepreneurial progress. Trust thereby becomes a means through which epistemic conditions are produced, not only a response to them. Managerial Summary Entrepreneurship exposes forms of vulnerability that cannot be explained by risk‐based models of trust alone. Entrepreneurs often face the practical question: “Trust them to do what?” The answer depends on the kind of agency they are willing to be vulnerable to, and it changes as an opportunity takes shape. That may mean backing people to take the work somewhere no one can yet specify, relying on others' expertise to make sense of what is emerging, or counting on them to deliver what was agreed. Trust is therefore not only a way of reducing uncertainty but a means of transforming it, and progress depends on recognizing when the prevailing form fits the conditions and when it does not.

papers.title: Swap and Save: How a Button Shapes Lasting Online Grocery Shopping Behavior
papers.abstract: A well-documented phenomenon in the literature is that consumers exhibit persistence in their choices. Using data from the mineral water category on a price comparison platform that delivers real-time prompts of cheaper alternatives through "swap and save" buttons, this study examines whether and how these prompts influence persistent product choices in online grocery shopping. The findings reveal that shoppers who switched to an alternative product after receiving a prompt were 23.7 percentage points more likely to select that alternative product in subsequent visits, with this effect lasting for up to 10 shopping trips. Our analysis suggests that this sustained impact is driven not by long-term cost savings but by product discovery enabled through these real-time prompts.

papers.title: The psychodynamics of contemporary careers: Anxieties and defenses in deconstructed work
papers.abstract: To gain flexibility, organizations increasingly deconstruct jobs, shifting from relatively stable bundles of tasks and titles to dynamic task–project constellations matched to employees’ skills. Yet this redesign also weakens the psychological containment through which jobs have historically stabilized workers’ lived experience of work inside organizations. Drawing on systems psychodynamics, we theorize that as the job’s psychological containment function weakens, workers experience three shared anxieties—about finding their place in shifting configurations of work, having their competence recognized, and forming and maintaining secure work relationships. Workers respond, collectively and often unconsciously, with social defenses: projecting familiar roles and rules onto deconstructed work, splitting off the generalist competence such work demands, and falling back on safe relationships. These defenses provisionally contain anxiety, but they also reorient workers toward familiar ways of organizing, evaluating, and relating that job deconstruction is meant to transform, keeping the redesigned work system in defensive stasis. By reconceptualizing job deconstruction as both a design property of work and a lived condition of shared anxiety, we explain why flexible work redesigns, though fluid in theory, are often frozen in practice, and how organizations can intervene to contain anxiety in new ways as they transition to the new world of work.

papers.title: Do Geopolitical Risk, Economic Policy Uncertainty, and Trade Policy Uncertainty Drive Corporate Carbon Transition Risk in China?
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines the effects of geopolitical risk (GPR), economic policy uncertainty (EPU), and trade policy uncertainty (TPU) on corporate CTR in China from January 2010 to December 2022. Using a combination of complementary quantile‐based approaches, including quantile‐on‐quantile regression (QoQR), quantile‐on‐quantile Granger causality (QoQGC), and wavelet quantile correlation (WQC), this study reveals substantial nonlinear, asymmetric, and time–frequency‐dependent relationships between external uncertainty and corporate CTR. The QoQR results show that GPR, EPU, and TPU generally increase corporate CTR as uncertainty rises from low to moderate levels; however, their marginal effects weaken and, in some regimes, become negative at extreme uncertainty levels. The QoQGC results reveal that predictive causality varies across uncertainty regimes: GPR and EPU exhibit strong predictive relevance at extreme uncertainty levels, whereas TPU shows predictive relevance across a broader range of low‐to‐moderate uncertainty regimes. The WQC results demonstrate that the uncertainty–CTR relationship also varies across both the CTR distribution and time‐frequency dimensions, with stronger positive co‐movement generally observed at middle‐to‐upper CTR quantiles and over medium‐ to long‐run horizons. Overall, the findings demonstrate that external uncertainty does not affect corporate CTR uniformly; rather, its transmission is regime‐dependent and time‐varying, highlighting the importance of uncertainty‐specific and adaptive strategies to support China's low‐carbon transition.

papers.title: Emissions Performance as a Capability‐Based Organizational Outcome: Evidence From Interpretable Machine Learning in Hospitality and Tourism
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Reducing corporate greenhouse gas emissions has become a central strategic challenge for firms, yet substantial heterogeneity persists in emissions performance even among organizations facing similar regulatory and market conditions. Existing research has largely attributed emissions outcomes to governance mechanisms, ESG initiatives, or financial capacity, often assuming linear and additive effects. This study advances a capability‐based perspective by conceptualizing firm‐level emissions performance not as a capability in itself, but as an emergent organizational outcome reflecting how effectively firms deploy and coordinate capability‐related workforce, operational, and managerial systems. Using firm‐level ESG and financial data from 110 publicly listed hospitality and tourism firms over the period 2015–2024, we apply ensemble machine learning techniques, bagging, random forest, and boosting, to model emissions performance. Boosting models consistently outperform alternative approaches and are analyzed using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and partial dependence plots (PDP) to ensure interpretability and theory development. Across four progressively enriched model specifications, the results show that workforce quality, resource‐use efficiency, and managerial effectiveness, the empirical proxies for underlying organizational capabilities, are the most influential and stable predictors of emissions performance. Governance mechanisms and financial performance display patterns consistent with conditioning rather than substitutive roles, being associated with the effectiveness of capability‐related systems without independently determining emissions outcomes. The analysis identifies nonlinear relationships, asymmetric predictive patterns associated with weak capability‐related organizational indicators, and joint partial‐dependence patterns consistent with complementarity among organizational systems, suggesting that emissions‐related performance may be sensitive to organizational deficiencies and the alignment of related practices. By focusing on the hospitality and tourism industry, where emissions are embedded in continuous service operations, the study highlights the central role of organizational execution in shaping environmental outcomes. The findings contribute to sustainability and strategic management research by explaining emissions performance as an observable outcome of capability deployment, coordination, and complementarity rather than as the direct product of isolated ESG policies, governance structures, or financial resources.

papers.title: From Entrepreneurial Orientation to Environmental Performance: Dynamic Capabilities and Institutional Weaknesses in an Emerging Economy
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines how entrepreneurial orientation is associated with environmental performance in manufacturing firms, focusing on the mediating roles of dynamic managerial capabilities and dynamic technological capabilities and the conditioning role of institutional weaknesses. Drawing on dynamic capabilities theory and institutional theory, the study adopts a capability‐based and context‐sensitive perspective to explain how entrepreneurial strategies translate into environmental outcomes in an emerging economy. Survey data were collected from 320 manufacturing firms located predominantly within Ghana's Southern industrial zone and analysed using a two‐step approach involving confirmatory factor analysis and regression‐based bootstrapped estimation of direct, indirect and conditional indirect associations. The results show that entrepreneurial orientation is positively associated with environmental performance, primarily through dynamic managerial and technological capabilities. Moreover, the indirect associations are stronger under higher levels of institutional weakness, indicating that internal capabilities become more salient in challenging institutional environments. The study contributes to the entrepreneurship and sustainability literature by demonstrating that entrepreneurial orientation is associated with environmental performance mainly through capability‐based mechanisms and that institutional context shapes the strength of these mechanisms. The findings offer context‐specific insights for managers and policymakers seeking to enhance environmental performance among manufacturing firms operating in weak institutional settings, although the geographic concentration of the sample requires caution in generalising the results to less industrialized and resource‐constrained regions.

papers.title: Organizational Rootedness, Territorial Dynamic Capabilities and Environmental Priorities: Evidence From European Regional Firms
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines organizational rootedness as the degree of territorial integration that differentiates environmental priorities in regional firms. Although its constitutive function in shaping environmental engagement is recognized, its ordering function in determining which initiatives become more salient is less clear. We examine whether higher‐ and lower‐rooted regional firm patterns prioritize environmental initiatives differently, how their priorities vary under social and economic pressures, and how these pressures are associated with eco‐innovation orientation in higher‐rooted patterns. The conceptual framework integrates organizational embeddedness with territorial dynamic capabilities: the first conceptualizes the different degrees of firms' territorial integration, whereas the second explains how this integration supports readaptation processes and eco‐innovative development under pressures. Using a novel database from 145 EU regions, we identify distinct priorities in environmental initiatives, reordered under contextual pressures. Furthermore, in higher‐rooted patterns, eco‐innovation orientation tends to be stronger under economic than social pressures. The findings suggest that managers should treat environmental sustainability as a territorially ordered portfolio of initiatives.

papers.title: Leader humility and employee psychological well-being: the roles of relational age and supervisor gender
papers.abstract: Purpose The study aims to apply the social information processing (SIP) theory to examine the three-way interaction of leader humility, supervisor-subordinate relational age and supervisor gender on hospitality employees’ psychological well-being (PWB) through job crafting. Design/methodology/approach Data were gathered from 235 US hospitality employees through a time-lagged, multiwave survey design. Confirmatory factor analysis was used to validate the measurement model and PROCESS analyses were used to examine the hypothesized mediation and moderation effects. Findings Leader humility is positively associated with hospitality employees’ PWB directly and indirectly through job crafting. Leader humility, relational age and supervisor gender interact to impact employees’ job crafting and PWB. The positive association between leader humility and job crafting was strengthened for female supervisors across both relational age conditions. The positive relationship between leader humility and PWB was strengthened for female supervisors regardless of relational age. The indirect effect of leader humility on PWB via job crafting was positive when employees perceived female supervisors as younger or similar in age or male supervisors as older. Research limitations/implications The study extends SIP theory by showing that leader humility is interpreted through the combined social information signaled by supervisor gender and relational age. These social cues jointly influence the effects of leader humility on hospitality employees’ job crafting and PWB. Originality/value To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this study is among the first to investigate the joint moderating roles of supervisor gender and relational age in the effects of leader humility and to examine their conditional indirect effect on PWB via job crafting.
papers.journal_name: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management

papers.title: Perceived authenticity in ethnic and cultural restaurants: a systematic review and meta-analysis
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to address fragmented evidence on perceived authenticity in restaurant contexts by developing an integrated understanding of its key antecedents and customer outcomes in ethnic and cultural dining settings. Design/methodology/approach A systematic literature review identified 100 studies, with 50 meeting the inclusion criteria for meta-analytic synthesis. Effect sizes were synthesized using random-effects models, and moderator analyses were performed to examine the roles of culture, age and gender. Findings Perceived authenticity is strongly shaped by tangible cues, particularly brand image and food quality. In turn, authenticity exerts robust positive effects on customer satisfaction, revisit intention and word of mouth. Moderator analyses further show that individualism strengthens the authenticity–positive emotion relationship, that older consumers place greater emphasis on authenticity in forming memorable dining experiences and that female customers are more sensitive to interpersonal cues. Practical implications The findings provide guidance for restaurant managers on developing and communicating authentic dining experiences in ways that support favorable customer responses. They also highlight the value of considering cultural and demographic differences when designing and delivering authenticity-related experiences. Originality/value This study clarifies how key antecedents differentially shape perceived authenticity and how authenticity influences customer outcomes. It also identifies boundary conditions across cultural and demographic contexts.

papers.title: Consumer misbehavior in tourism and hospitality contexts: a framework-based systematic review and future agenda
papers.abstract: Purpose This paper aims to synthesize the fragmented literature and develop an integrative framework to advance understanding of the emergence, consequences and management of consumer misbehavior in tourism and hospitality. Design/methodology/approach A framework-based systematic review is conducted. Drawing on 83 peer-reviewed articles retrieved from Scopus and Web of Science, this paper uses an Antecedents–Enactments–Consequences–Interventions (AECI) framework to synthesize the literature. Findings Consumer misbehavior is primarily shaped by external situational factors and consumers’ psychological catalysts. Negative feelings, defensive regulation and threat evaluation emerge as key enactment mechanisms linking antecedents, consumer misbehavior and stakeholder responses. Consumer misbehavior generates consequences for employees, other consumers and residents. These individual-level impacts may lead to organization- and destination-level outcomes. Research on interventions has focused more heavily on precautionary strategies than on coping strategies. In particular, coping strategies addressing the impacts of consumer misbehavior on employees and residents remain largely overlooked. This review identifies theoretical fragmentation and under-researched areas, including contagion effects and post-incident recovery for employees and residents. Practical implications Effective management of consumer misbehavior requires both precautionary and coping strategies. Managers should tailor interventions to the severity and context of misbehavior. Organizations and destinations should also provide active post-incident management and immediate psychological support to facilitate employee and resident recovery. Originality/value This paper offers a comprehensive synthesis of consumer misbehavior in tourism and hospitality using an AECI framework. This paper clarifies conceptual ambiguity, integrates dispersed evidence and proposes a future research agenda.

papers.title: Mindful eating and sustainable dining behaviors: a psychological resources perspective
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine the psychological mechanisms linking mindful eating (ME) with sustainable dining behaviors in restaurant contexts. Drawing on Hunecke’s psychological resources perspective for sustainable lifestyles, the study explains how self- and other-focused psychological resources are associated with green restaurant selection and dining-out leftover prevention across pre- and post-consumption stages. Design/methodology/approach A dual-pathway sequential mediation model was developed and tested using data from 611 Taiwanese consumers who had dined out within the previous three months. Structural equation modeling was used to examine the hypothesized paths and mediating relationships. Findings The findings support two sequential pathways linking ME to sustainable dining outcomes. The self-focused pathway operates through self-compassion and subjective vitality, whereas the other-focused pathway operates through altruistic values and food gratitude. Together, these complementary psychological resources connect ME with green restaurant selection and dining-out leftover prevention across pre- and post-consumption stages. Research limitations/implications The findings advance sustainable hospitality research by highlighting psychological resources as mechanisms through which ME is associated with sustainable dining behaviors. From a practical perspective, mindful dining experiences may encourage self-focused resources, while appreciative communication may strengthen altruistic concern and food gratitude. Originality/value This study extends Hunecke’s psychological resources perspective to hospitality by specifying complementary self- and other-focused pathways. It advances research on the intention–behavior gap and broadens ME as a dining-specific antecedent associated with sustainable decisions through downstream psychological resources.

papers.title: Cognitive Offloading to Generative AI: A Theoretical Framework for Memory, Metacognition, and Consumer Decision-Making
papers.abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (Gen-AI) increasingly mediates product search, evaluation, and choice, consumer cognition is becoming distributed across human–AI systems. This shift challenges a largely unexamined assumption in advertising theory: that persuasion operates through cognitive elaboration within the individual consumer. Drawing on cognitive offloading research from cognitive psychology, we develop the CogOffload framework to explain when consumers delegate cognitive work to Gen-AI and what consequences follow. A seven-stage delegation continuum maps increasing levels of offloading, and a value-based cost-benefit framework identifies its antecedents and the moderators that shape how consumers weigh them. We propose three clusters of outcomes. First, offloading weakens memory for brands and product attributes while strengthening memory for AI-generated summaries. Second, it inflates metacognitive self-esteem and decision confidence, producing AI-induced overconfidence that reduces further information-seeking. Third, effects on decision quality depend on AI reliability: when AI is unreliable, verifying AI recommendations imposes cognitive and emotional costs but can restore impaired memory and recalibrate inflated confidence. Seven propositions and three long-term conjectures extend these effects to consumer autonomy, competence erosion, and brand loyalty. Together, the CogOffload framework positions advertising in the era of Gen-AI as operating within a distributed system of human and artificial cognition.
