Electricity supply reliability and firm productivity: A dual perspective on spatial reallocation and within-industry differentiation
A Monetary Model with Money and Safe Assets
Institutional Shocks and Capability Revaluation: Labor-Market Disequilibrium and Endogenous Institutional Adjustment
The corporate effects of environmental governance policy in Chinese A-share listed firms
Influence of Digital Resources and Information Sharing on Supply Chain Sustainability
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Although supply chain digitalization has received considerable research attention, the mechanisms through which digital resources contribute to sustainability outcomes are not fully understood. This study examines how digital technologies, particularly big data analytics (BDA), support sustainability practices and performance in supply chains through information sharing. Building on the resource‐based view (RBV) and the dynamic capabilities perspective, a conceptual framework is developed and empirically tested using cross‐industry survey data from Finland and partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS‐SEM). The results show that digital resources and BDA indirectly contribute to supply chain sustainability by enhancing information sharing among supply chain partners. More effective information sharing improves transparency and coordination across the supply chain, thereby supporting the achievement of sustainability goals. This study makes two contributions. First, from an RBV perspective, it shows that information sharing is a key resource through which digitalization translates into sustainability outcomes. Second, from a dynamic capabilities perspective, it extends the emerging literature by showing how digitally enabled capabilities support sustainability transitions in supply chains.

papers.title: How Green SMEs Combine Resources for Financial Performance and Environmental Action: Multiple Pathways in Weak Institutional Contexts
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT This study explores the key determinants of green small‐ and medium‐sized enterprise (SME) performance in economies that have performed inadequately concerning global sustainability goals. Drawing on the dynamic capabilities view (DCV) as a theoretical lens and utilizing qualitative comparative analysis (QCA), we examined which configurations of resources are associated with higher financial performance and environmental action intensity. Our analysis identified financial, technical, human, and institutional resources that combine in complex ways and are associated with high financial performance in four equifinal configurations: (1) a knowledge‐intensive pathway that combines technical know‐how with private sector support, (2) an institutionally supported pathway that leverages technical know‐how with public sector support, (3) a human capital‐centered pathway that emphasizes green workers with financial resources, and (4) a comprehensive pathway that integrates all resource types. For high environmental action intensity, three configurations are sufficient, with public‐ and private‐sector support jointly associated with broad adoption of energy and waste routines even when internal assets are limited. The study advances beyond “why” entrepreneurs pursue green opportunities to examine “how” these configurations are associated with higher financial performance and environmental action intensity. These findings are also significant to policy and SME managers for highlighting strategic sustainability approaches that enable pathways to competitive advantage through environmental performance while strengthening business resilience in resource‐sensitive and competitive environments.

papers.title: Binding the present and orchestrating the future: accounting as a technology of government in water sustainability
papers.abstract: Purpose The paper explains how water sustainability becomes governable in fragmented hybrid settings. It shows how accounting and accountability hold together diverse actors, competing obligations and different rationalities, enabling sustainability aspirations to translate into coordinated action. The paper illuminates the fragile character of this process, showing how accounting and accountability partially stabilise tensions without resolving them. Design/methodology/approach The study adopts an interpretive case study of an Italian water utility undergoing regulatory and organisational changes. It applies Dean's analytics of government framework to analyse data from interviews, sustainability reports and publicly available documents. Findings The study identifies four regimes of practice through which water sustainability was rendered governable. Across these regimes, accounting and accountability perform “binding” and “orchestrating” roles in governing water sustainability. These practices establish norms, responsibilities and incentives (binding) and align actors and activities (orchestrating), thereby stabilising but not resolving inter-regime tensions. Practical implications The study helps multiple actors, such as managers, policymakers and stakeholders, to understand how accounting and accountability can support the organisation of collective responsibility for water sustainability. Social implications The study shows how accounting and accountability redistribute responsibility for water sustainability across organisations and communities in hybrid public–private settings. In doing so, they can promote collective responsibility for water conservation but may also normalise particular ways of valuing water. Originality/value The paper introduces the concepts of binding and orchestrating to explain how accounting and accountability render sustainability governable in fragmented hybrid settings. Its value lies in showing how accounting enables collective action while leaving unresolved tensions among economic, public-service and environmental commitments visible.

papers.title: Strategic Revenue Model Choice of a Video-Sharing Platform: Content Provision and Welfare Implications
Regulatory Rationales in the Face of Emerging Technologies: A Systematic Review
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Technology is evolving, and so is the discussion of regulation theory among academics. Taking a unique approach to legal research, this paper utilizes the systematic literature review methodology to uncover quantitative evidence on the current consensus among academics on regulation theory, in particular, regulatory rationales. This paper seeks to determine whether the narrative assumptions that social solidarity‐based regulatory rationales have become more prevalent as technology has evolved are correct. Based on the data gathered, this article asserts that the discussion of regulatory rationales is facing a tonal shift as a result of artificial intelligence. Academics are shifting away from a traditional economic view of regulation toward discussion of regulatory rationales based on protecting the common good. This should be welcome. Social solidarity should serve as a foundational principle of good technology regulation. Through applying the principles of social solidarity, regulators can better balance the risks and benefits of modern technology.

papers.title: Settlement, wealth inequality and witchcraft
Research progress and prospect of thermo−hydro−mechanical−chemical−sand multi−field coupling evolution in natural gas hydrate reservoirs
Identification of highly representative safety-oriented battery features in real-world electric vehicles via a novel statistical method
Coupled capacity-scheduling optimization of hybrid renewable hydrogen systems under multi-year resource variability
Global Steel Decarbonization under Policy, Technology, and Resource Constraints: A Process-Unit Agent-Based Model
papers.abstract: Abstract Deep decarbonization of steel requires low-emission technologies to be deployed through a long-lived and heterogeneous asset fleet without disrupting steel supply. We developed a country-resolved agent-based model that follows global steel process units annually from 2023 to 2060. Units choose among continued operation, renewal, retrofit, conversion, retirement, and new construction, subject to construction time, linked upstream capacity, national production pathways, and annual supplies of scrap, hydrogen, natural gas, and pellets. Four scenarios distinguish stronger climate policy from improved technology and resource availability. Global process-chain CO2 emissions decline by 67–79% by 2060, reaching 0.476–0.737 Gt. The integrated case achieves the lowest emissions, but the two-component interventions do not independently outperform the reference case. Stronger policy changes when assets enter a finite transition queue, whereas technology and material conditions determine whether replacement routes can be built and operated at that time. By 2060, Scrap-EAF supplies 74–80% of crude steel, but residual unabated blast furnaces and coal-based direct reduction keep national steel pathways above their allocated levels in many countries. Deep decarbonization, therefore, depends on coordinating asset turnover, construction, and complementary material systems, rather than on technology availability or carbon-price pressure alone.

papers.title: Aspects of sustainable plant and project management in the Polish tanning industry
Operationalising a territorial nature-based solutions model: an indicator-based case study of URBAN GreenUP Valladolid
A Comparative Machine Learning Assessment for Urban Flood Susceptibility Modeling and Future Flood Susceptibility Projections in Dhaka Metropolitan Area (DMA), Bangladesh
Voyage-level optimal scheduling of the gas management system in liquefied natural gas carriers based on heat ingress profiles from actual voyages
Critical mineral supply chain readiness for commercial fusion energy: A framework with applications to the ARC and EU-DEMO tokamaks
papers.abstract: Private fusion energy companies are targeting commercial electricity generation within the next two decades, yet the material supply chains required to build and operate these reactors have received limited systematic assessment. This paper develops and applies a Supply Chain Readiness Level (SCRL) framework to evaluate 13 materials for the ARC compact tokamak, arguably the most detailed publicly documented commercial fusion design. The framework assesses each material across three dimensions: demand (bottom-up engineering estimates from published design parameters), supply chain maturity (geographic concentration, volume adequacy, and specification gap), and timeline criticality (investment lead times measured against deployment scenarios). The analysis uses the Hillesheim et al. (2026) Version 3A engineering baseline as the primary reference case, the Sorbom et al. (2015) original concept as a historical comparator, and the published EU-DEMO material assessment as a cross-design benchmark. Five materials essential to the ARC design score Critical. Four share a single failure mode, fusion-grade production that has not yet been established at any scale: enriched lithium-6 for tritium breeding, REBCO superconducting tape, FLiBe molten salt, and vanadium alloy V-4Cr-4Ti. The fifth, beryllium, is Critical on volume grounds, with single-reactor demand approaching 40% of global annual production. The specification gap between the commodity form and the fusion-grade product, rather than raw material scarcity or geographic concentration, is the dominant constraint across the material set. Under deployment timelines stated by leading private developers, decision windows for several critical materials are already closed or closing. Industry survey evidence from the Fusion Industry Association's 2026 supply chain report independently confirms both rising materials concern among developers and the coordination failure between developers and suppliers that prevents timely investment. The SCRL framework provides the quantified, material-specific demand signals needed to bridge this gap.

papers.title: Performance investigation of a novel valve-integrated ejector-enhanced CO2 cycle for heating and cooling

papers.title: Balancing ecological benefits and feasibility in large-scale restoration planning: A multi-objective optimization decision-support framework
papers.abstract: Ecosystem restoration requires decision-support tools capable of balancing ecological benefits under limited resources while explicitly accounting for the long-term likelihood of restoration success. Despite its recognized importance, ecological feasibility has rarely been formulated as an optimization objective in spatial planning, typically being treated only as a constraint or biophysical filter. Here, we present a multi-objective optimization framework for large-scale restoration planning that explicitly incorporates ecological feasibility alongside biodiversity and ecosystem service objectives. The framework is grounded in Systematic Conservation Planning and formulated as a Mixed-Integer Linear Programming model. We jointly optimize four criteria—extinction risk reduction, carbon storage, water provision, and ecological feasibility—under a fixed restoration area budget and land suitability constraints. Optimization proceeds in two steps: single-objective benchmark solutions are first obtained to define aspiration levels, which are then integrated using Goal Programming to generate balanced compromise solutions and characterize trade-offs. Ecological feasibility is modeled as a socio-ecological property linked to recurrent disturbance regimes, operationalized through spatial proxies of wildfire frequency, anthropogenic pressure, and invasive species richness. Applied to continental Chile using 812,910 units at 1 km² resolution, incorporating feasibility leads to significant spatial reconfiguration: approximately 16.6% of selected units (under a 30% restoration target aligned with Target 2 of the Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework) are replaced relative to solutions that ignore feasibility. This shift preserves total restored area while increasing feasibility performance by 11.1 percentage points, with minimal reductions (below 5%) in the remaining objectives (−4.1 for carbon storage and −2.4 for water provision). Spatial diagnostics based on selection frequency reveal that compromise solutions are anchored in a "backbone" of multipurpose planning units (˃ 80% of selected units), complemented by specialized units that resolve localized trade-offs. Overall, the proposed framework provides a transparent and transferable approach for integrating ecological feasibility into spatial restoration planning, enabling more robust and policy-relevant decision-making.

Advancing acid and metalliferous drainage characterisation, prediction, and monitoring in mine waste systems using electrical methods: Challenges and future directions
papers.abstract: Acid and metalliferous drainage (AMD) is one of the most persistent environmental liabilities faced by the mining industry, owing to its potential to cause long-term contamination. AMD encompasses acidic to neutral, metal-rich waters generated by the oxidation of sulfide minerals upon exposure to oxygen and water. With the energy transition, the volume of mine wastes stored in large-scale facilities is projected to increase, and the magnitude and complexity of AMD-related risks are likely to intensify. Consequently, early assessment and effective monitoring of the geochemical stability of mine wastes are critical for mitigating environmental impacts, avoiding unforeseen closure and remediation costs over the mine life cycle. At present, AMD assessment and monitoring largely rely on conventional geochemical testing methods, which are constrained by inherent uncertainties and provide point-scale data with limited spatial representativeness across heterogeneous mine waste structures. In this context, geophysical techniques, particularly electrical methods, offer a complementary, non-invasive, spatially continuous, and cost-effective alternative for the assessment of AMD potential. This review critically synthesises current knowledge on the application of electrical resistivity tomography (ERT) and induced polarisation (IP) methods for AMD investigations in mine waste systems. The review highlights the predominance of qualitative investigations and key barriers that limit the transition to quantitative and predictive AMD assessments, including the lack of validated petrophysical relationships and limited field-scale calibrations. By identifying critical knowledge gaps and future research priorities, the review provides a framework for advancing quantitative AMD prediction, monitoring, and risk-based mine waste management using electrical methods.

Forward Return Expectations
papers.abstract: Abstract We measure investors’ short- and long-term stock-return expectations using both options and survey data. These expectations at different horizons reveal what investors think their own short-term expectations will be in the future, or forward return expectations. Across data sources, investors’ forward return expectations are countercyclical, especially when measured as forward risk premiums. This countercyclical variation is, however, excessive, as changes in forward return expectations are too large relative to subsequent realized short-term expectations. The excess variation in forward return expectations can help account for a meaningful share of the stock-price declines during the global financial crisis and the COVID-19 crisis. (JEL G10, G12, G40)

papers.title: Middlemen as an exchange technology in international production networks
Pork, Infrastructure and Growth: Evidence from the Italian Railway Expansion,
papers.abstract: Abstract We study the political economy of transport infrastructure placement and its long-term impact, exploiting quasi-random variation in political factors. Using unique data from XIX-century Italy and deploying a regression discontinuity design, we focus on close races to show that towns in marginal districts supporting winning candidates were more likely to be reached by a railway. Using alignment with the government as a natural instrument for infrastructure placement, we then show that over the following century, services - rather than manufacturing - grew faster in connected municipalities. Our results also indicate that political allegiances likely helped towns with lower growth prospects.

papers.title: Consistency and convergence rate bounds of initial sequence type variance estimators for reversible Markov chains
ASYMPTOTIC PROPERTIES OF APPROXIMATE MAXIMUM LIKELIHOOD ESTIMATOR IN MARKOV-SWITCHING STATE-SPACE MODELS
papers.abstract: For Markov-switching state-space models, it is practically infeasible to compute the likelihood function through the Kalman filter because of the path dependence on regimes. A widely applied approximation algorithm uses a collapsing step to average out the most dated regime and truncates the regime path. This algorithm’s performance, however, has not been examined analytically. This study fills the gap. We characterize the parameters that affect the approximation error, derive the upper bounds of the errors in likelihood computation and latent variable inference, and investigate the asymptotic properties of the approximate maximum likelihood estimator. We also provide a practical procedure for measuring approximation errors and selecting the number of regime periods to keep in the truncated path. All the analysis is based on our new collapsing step, which removes a nonlinear adjustment term in the existing method to facilitate theoretical derivations.

papers.title: Equity equilibrium for cooperative games
Life‐Cycle Wage Growth and Firm Productivity in Developed and Developing Economies
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Life‐cycle wage growth varies substantially across countries. We study the firm productivity distribution's role in a random‐search model with learning and labor‐market frictions, estimated for Brazil, Colombia, and the United States. Brazil has a long left tail of low‐paying firms, and Colombia has a highly compressed firm ladder. Replacing each country's firm distribution with that of the United States closes most of the cross‐country gap in wage growth, raising Brazil's relative wage growth from 73 to 103 percent and Colombia's from 52 to 115 percent. The results are robust to alternative distributional assumptions and additional sensitivity checks.

papers.title: Energy shocks and the climate transition
papers.abstract: We present a two-sector growth model in which a representative agent invests in fossil fuel-based energy and renewable energy. These differ in capital intensity and project duration: fossil fuel investments require lower upfront investment and have shorter duration, whereas renewables are more capital-intensive with longer-lived assets. We show that a negative economic shock (such as an energy supply shock or recession) leads to both cuts in total investment and to a shift in the composition of the remaining investment toward fossil fuel projects. This delays the clean energy transition, even if renewable energy is cost-effective on a levelised cost basis, implying a role for policies to sustain clean investment during recessions. We discuss how this mechanism can be amplified by higher interest rates, pro-cyclical climate policies, perceived risk, and financial frictions, and we relate our findings to recent empirical episodes (e.g. the 2022-23 energy crisis and post-2008 recession).
papers.journal_name: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management

papers.title: Polycrisis and labour agency in global production networks: evidence from Bangladesh’s apparel industry
papers.abstract: Abstract This article explains how temporally uneven polycrisis reshapes labour agency within apparel production networks. Developing a spatial–temporal analytical framework, it shows how interactions, amplification, and acceleration across crises reconfigure workers’ opportunity structures through legitimacy, profitability, and social reproduction pressures. This qualitative case study of Bangladesh’s apparel industry examines how the Rana Plaza accident, COVID-19, and the climate crisis interacted to produce cumulative effects that enabled openings and constrained mobilization, shifting labour agency across associational, coalitional, and micro-practices over time. The study advances labour regime analysis by demonstrating the temporal contingency and spatial situatedness of labour agency during polycrisis.

papers.title: The impact of geographical and technological proximity on knowledge spillovers from formal standards
papers.abstract: Abstract Proximity is traditionally viewed as crucial for overcoming the search and transfer costs associated with imperfectly codified knowledge. But does proximity still matter when formal standard publication jointly enhances the codification, certainty, and accessibility of technical knowledge? Evidence from the U.S. Information and Communication Technology industry shows that technological proximity drives substantial spillover gains, largely irrespective of location. Conversely, geographical proximity confers a compensating advantage when technological proximity is low. We reveal a nuanced interplay of proximity in knowledge spillovers: while formal standardization effectively flattens the world for the technologically proximate, co-location remains vital for their less proximate counterparts.

papers.title: Does the Salience of Climate-Related Risk Affect Asset Prices?
papers.abstract: Abstract Using regression discontinuity and difference-in-differences designs to compare prices of California homes across a new wildfire risk zone boundary, I identify null effects in the immediate vicinity of the new risk zone boundary. In contrast, prices of homes newly assigned to a riskier zone drop by 5.7% further away from the new risk zone boundary. These findings suggest that households do not respond to the risk salience triggered by the new risk zone assignment. Instead, they update their risk beliefs in response to rezoning in a way that is consistent with the actual wildfire risk.
papers.journal_name: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis

papers.title: Does Climate Change Affect Firm Sales? Identifying Supply Effects
papers.abstract: Abstract We estimate the supply-side effects of climate change on firm sales by exploiting variation in local average temperature across suppliers of the same client. A 1°C increase in temperature leads to a 2.5% decline in annual sales. This effect is nonlinear, with stronger effects among suppliers in regions with the largest temperature increases and in cooler regions. Manufacturing and heat-sensitive industries are more affected, consistent with a reduction in labor productivity and labor supply when local temperatures rise. Nondiversified and financially constrained firms are also more affected, supporting the importance of operational and financial flexibility in adapting to climate change.

Sorting, training, and careers: public and private universities as complementary providers of doctoral education
papers.abstract: The growth of private providers has increased heterogeneity in doctoral education, raising questions about how university types contribute to advanced skill formation. Using linked administrative labour-market data on PhD graduates in economics and business studies in Germany, we analyse how pre-doctoral employment histories relate to the choice between public and private universities and how careers unfold during and after the doctorate. We find strong sorting: candidates with stable private-sector employment disproportionately enroll in private universities, while those embedded in academic workplaces select public universities. Many private-university candidates complete the doctorate alongside non-academic employment, whereas public-university candidates typically hold academic positions during training. After graduation, public-university graduates are more likely to remain in academia and sustain research activity, whereas private-university graduates more often advance into high-income and leadership positions outside academia. Public and private universities thus operate as organizational complements, serving distinct segments of a heterogeneous doctoral population.

papers.title: Local Returns and Beliefs about the Stock Market
On the optimal location of public charging stations in a monocentric city
papers.abstract: This study examines how the location of public charging stations (PCS) shapes the spatial equilibrium of a monocentric urban economy. We develop a linear urban model in which commuters endogenously choose vehicle type (conventional or electric), charging mode (public or home), and residential location. We show that the PCS location affects these choices, which in turn determine urban spatial structure, traffic-related emissions, and social welfare. We find that placing the PCS in non-ideal locations may exacerbate urban sprawl, reduce electric vehicle adoption, and lower social welfare. We derive closed-form solutions for the optimal PCS location under alternative policy objectives and quantitatively illustrate how deviations from the optimum affect equilibrium outcomes.

papers.title: EXPRESS: When Marketers Get the Top Job: How Marketing CEOs Influence Firms’ Product-Market Strategy
papers.abstract: Research on upper echelons in marketing has primarily focused on the CMO, yet the CEO ultimately bears responsibility for key strategic decisions, including those related to marketing. This study examines how CEOs with marketing experience (i.e., “marketing CEOs”) influence firm stock market performance by shaping product portfolio decisions. Drawing on upper echelon theory and in-depth interviews with business practitioners, we argue that marketing CEOs are more effective at selecting customer segments and implementing competitive strategies, leading to more differentiated portfolios and, consequently, higher shareholder returns. Our analysis of the main research question combines a qualitative study, a natural experiment involving CEO turnovers, large-scale panel data analysis, and an experiment with executives. Our results show that marketing CEOs positively impact shareholder returns through portfolio differentiation. Furthermore, the positive effect of marketing CEOs on portfolio differentiation is strengthened by their larger professional networks and a strong customer orientation within the firm but is diminished by CEO overconfidence and high firm financial leverage. Our findings highlight the distinctive value of CEOs with marketing experience and provide insight into the conditions that enhance or constrain their ability to generate firm value.

papers.title: From Slack to Staff: Managers' Allocation of Slack Resources to Hiring
papers.abstract: Abstract Prior research views cash holdings, or high‐discretionary slack, as a buffer against shocks or a catalyst for strategic change. Drawing on stakeholder salience theory, we argue that cash can also reshape managers' interpretation and prioritization of employee hiring‐related claims, thereby increasing hiring, and that this effect is more pronounced when structural influences heighten the salience of those claims. Study 1, a large‐scale field study of Belgian firms, finds a positive but diminishing relationship between cash and hiring. This relationship strengthens under conditions of greater firm dependence on specific employee groups or following an exogenous legal reform, both of which are hypothesized to make the salience of specific employee groups more apparent. In Study 2, a vignette experiment offers causal support for the hypothesized mechanism, with employee salience cues strengthening how managers translate cash into hiring allocations. Combined, our findings contribute to research on slack resources and stakeholder salience by showing that managers use high‐discretionary cash not only for buffering or strategic change but also to respond to salient stakeholders.

papers.title: EXPRESS: Impatient for Impact: Intertemporal Preferences for Earlier Donation Impact Timing
papers.abstract: Impatience when choosing for oneself has been widely documented, but are people also impatient when making prosocial decisions about benefits to unknown others? The authors study whether and why people care about a donation’s “impact timing,” the time when the benefits of the donation would reach the beneficiaries. In seven pre-registered experiments (N = 2,462) and an analysis of GoFundMe secondary data, they show that people consistently prefer to donate to a charitable program with an earlier impact timing, across different causes, donation amounts, timeframes, charity sizes and tradeoffs between impact timing and other considerations (impact magnitude, number of prior donors, remaining cost to complete, quality rating, and overhead). They find that decreased perceived benefits of delayed donation impact provides an incomplete explanation of the impact timing preference. Beyond less discounting of less delayed benefits, people also infer greater donation efficacy-based trust from earlier impact timing, increasing donation preferences. Together, the strong preference for earlier impact timing is an important and largely overlooked aspect of prosocial decision-making, with implications for building trust in prosocial organizations.

papers.title: National Audit Oversight and Foreign Investment
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Public audit oversight bodies have become ubiquitous following the establishment of the U.S. PCAOB in 2002. However, despite their cost and prominence, little is known of their economic implications, if any. We examine the relation between establishment of public audit oversight bodies (POBs) and cross-border investment. Using a difference-in-differences design, we find that after a country establishes a POB, the country attracts more foreign capital. Our results suggest that total foreign portfolio investment (FPI) increases by approximately $11 billion for the average country that establishes a POB. The impact of POBs on foreign investment is dependent on the effectiveness of the POB in improving audit quality and the strength of a country’s existing institutional environment. Our study provides evidence of real economic effects of public audit oversight around the world, which adds to the literature on auditor oversight and to the broader literature on economic consequences of regulation. Data Availability: Data are available from the public sources cited in the text. JEL Classifications: M42; M48; F21; L51; G15; G18.

papers.title: The Cost of Regulatory Inaction: Evidence from IFRS Nonadoption
papers.abstract: A growing literature has examined the benefits and costs of implementing new disclosure regulations. However, little is known about the consequences when regulators fail to take action. Using IFRS adoption in 2005 as the setting, we examine the costs of regulatory inactions among non-adopting countries. We find that firms located in non-adopting countries with a higher overlap of common investors with firms in IFRS-adopting countries experience a significant decline in liquidity. Employing a within-firm-time design, we further demonstrate that analysts and institutional investors shift their attention from non-IFRS firms when other firms in their portfolios adopt IFRS. Moreover, the decline in liquidity and the associated reduction in information production by analysts and institutional investors are particularly pronounced in non-adopting countries with weak reporting enforcement actions and increasing accounting distance from IFRS standards. Overall, our findings highlight the potential costs of regulatory inaction. Valuable information production resources are diverted to the new regime, resulting in a worsened information environment for companies in the old regime.

papers.title: Accounting Comparability and Common Owners
papers.abstract: Abstract We examine the relationship between accounting comparability and common ownership. Accounting comparability can reduce information asymmetry between firms and investors by lowering information acquisition and processing costs. At the same time, greater comparability can reduce the private information advantages that sophisticated investors, such as common owners, exploit. Which of these opposing forces dominates is ultimately an empirical question. Using a sample of US firms for 1999–2021, we find that accounting comparability is positively associated with common ownership, particularly non‐transient common ownership. Further analyses indicate that this relation is driven by a reduction in information asymmetry and is significantly stronger among firms with weaker information environments.

papers.title: The Recycling Illusion: How the Mobius Loop Fuels Greenwashing
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Globally used labelling systems regulated by governments can inadvertently greenwash packaging. We show that the Mobius loop and plastic resin identification numbers are misleading consumers about recyclability. This is because not all plastic packaging can be recycled. Across three experiments, we demonstrate that the Mobius loop system is inadvertently greenwashing packaging for consumers as it signals recyclability irrespective of other messaging. Packaging displaying the Mobius loop was consistently rated positively and perceived as recyclable and environmentally friendly, even when it was not. The symbol also enhanced brand image. This occurred irrespective of the color of the Mobius loop and product category used. This system will perpetuate the plastic waste problem even though it is not intended. We extend the greenwashing concept by presenting evidence that regulation can greenwash.

papers.title: When leaders prioritize health: Investigating when and how health-oriented leadership shapes employee in-role and extra-role behaviors
I can handle robot errors! Robot error learning and industry turnover intentions
Horizontal emotional pathways: A path-dependent perspective on guest evaluation in online reviews
More Than a Bind That Ties—Introducing the Family Meta-Logic in Single-Family Offices When Navigating Financial and Social Welfare Logics
papers.abstract: Single-family offices (SFOs) must balance financial, social welfare, and family logics. Drawing on institutional logics research, this multi-case study of German SFOs examines how the family logic shapes the relationship between financial and social welfare logics in investment decisions. We find that the family logic acts as a meta-logic. Depending on power distribution, value alignment, and governance design, it enables centrality, compatibility, or pseudo-compatibility of the two logics, and it works as an exit barrier that keeps tensions from escalating. We contribute by conceptualizing the family meta-logic and by showing how power dynamics and generational differences shape decision-making in SFOs.

papers.title: More AI, better coordination? Comparing AI incorporation and institutionalized project management practices in project work
Beyond the bottle: decoding the wine list architecture and ordering decisions
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine the wine lists’ influence on restaurant customers’ ordering decisions and the role of wine ordering in shaping the overall dining experience. Design/methodology/approach Based on 27 in-depth interviews with restaurant patrons who ordered wine from a wine list, this study employed a grounded theory methodology (GTM) to analyze data. Findings The findings reveal three core categories influencing wine ordering experiences: wine list architecture, wine ordering process and wine-centric experiences. Within the wine list category, wine attributes, menu designscape and cognitive navigability emerged as key subcategories shaping wine list architecture. The wine ordering process is shaped by wine-specific factors, restaurant-related factors, personal factors and food-wine pairing. Notably, a wine-centric experience, characterized by wine fascination, culinary enhancement and relational enjoyment, significantly impacts the overall dining experience. Practical implications These findings inform restaurant managers about the complex wine-ordering process. To optimize diners’ decision experience, managers should prioritize key wine attributes, such as grape variety, price, type, serving size, region, taste profiles and the wine list’s design. Originality/value This study provides an exploratory conceptualization of the wine list as a decision-making interface that shapes consumers’ wine-ordering decisions in restaurant settings, offering conceptual insights with implications for research and practice.
papers.journal_name: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management

papers.title: Designing employee wellness programs in hotels: a prioritized resource framework
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how employee wellness programs (EWPs) function in high-demand service environments, addressing the limitation that prior research assumes wellness resources automatically improve employee well-being. Design/methodology/approach A four-stage mixed-methods design was adopted, including literature review, expert content validation, Fuzzy Delphi analysis with 28 experts and a survey of 507 hotel employees analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling. Findings A six-dimensional EWP framework comprising 26 validated indicators was confirmed. The results show that EWP dimensions are not functionally equivalent but operate within a structured system. Organizational resources, particularly healthcare support and health management policies, play a foundational role, while other dimensions contribute to recovery and longer-term development. The findings suggest that the effectiveness of wellness initiatives depends on employees’ capacity to use available resources. Research limitations/implications By integrating conservation of resources theory with the well-being-as-capability perspective, this study reframes EWPs as a capability-enabling system that emphasizes resource usability rather than mere provision. Practically, hotels should prioritize foundational organizational resources before expanding other wellness initiatives, using the proposed three-stage implementation roadmap to guide strategic investment and promote sustainable employee well-being. Originality/value This study provides a mechanism-based explanation of how wellness resources function in practice, offering a more nuanced framework for understanding employee well-being in the hospitality industry.
papers.journal_name: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management

papers.title: Unveiling the dark side of workplace community: knowledge hiding in frontline hospitality
papers.abstract: Purpose Grounded in Deutsch’s theory of cooperation and competition, this study aims to explain the paradoxical effect of psychological sense of community at work (PSCW) on knowledge hiding (KH) in frontline hospitality. It tests knowledge-based psychological ownership (KBPO) as the explanatory mechanism and prosocial motivation (PSM) as a motivational contingency. Design/methodology/approach Time-lagged data were gathered in three waves from frontline hospitality employees in Pakistan, yielding 632 usable responses. The hypothesized moderated mediation model was tested using covariance-based structural equation modeling with bias-corrected bootstrapping. Findings Contrary to the prevailing assumption that positive workplace social contexts suppress KH, PSCW was positively associated with KBPO and KBPO with KH, producing a significant indirect effect. PSM dampened the PSCW–KBPO link, weakening the indirect pathway among more prosocially motivated employees. Research limitations/implications The study extends KH theory by conceptualizing PSCW as an integrative antecedent, identifying KBPO as the mechanism explaining why KH persists within cohesive workplace communities and specifying PSM’s moderating role in this pathway, thereby questioning the view that positive workplace dynamics necessarily curbs KH. Practical implications Hospitality managers should pair efforts to strengthen workplace community with practices that frame knowledge as a collective rather than a personal resource, such as cross-training, team-based rewards and promotion criteria that recognize knowledge contribution over exclusive expertise and should recruit and develop prosocially motivated employees. Originality/value The study offers three contributions to KH research. It positions PSCW as a theoretically integrative antecedent, moving beyond the fragmented relational constructs of prior work; provides time-lagged evidence that strong workplace community can give rise to ownership-driven KH, revealing its dark side; and shows PSM to be the motivational contingency that determines when workplace community reduces protective hiding in frontline hospitality.
papers.journal_name: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management

papers.title: A supply chain life cycle framework using social exchange theory
papers.abstract: Purpose The purpose of this research is to develop supply chain life cycle theory using the concepts of supply chain uncertainty, supply chain orientation and social exchange theory. Design/methodology/approach This research employs conceptual research methodology to develop theoretical propositions of the relationships that are fundamental to supply chain processes, while following established theory-building guidelines in supply chain management. Findings Supply chain processes must be examined longitudinally, sequentially and as multiple cycles of events and conditions of multiple firms. Doing so can provide theoretical insights into the birth, continuance and dissolution of supply chains. Originality/value This research offers a temporal, process explanation of how supply chain uncertainty may generate supply chain orientation and supply chain management responses, how those responses subsequently alter uncertainty and how this recursive process may help explain the emergence, continuation, adaptation and dissolution of SCM activities and supply chains.

papers.title: Political risk insurance in the digital age: How CPA moderates negative investor reactions following head of government attacks on social media
From financial constraints to performance via innovation: Evidence from Indigenous‑owned SMEs
papers.abstract: Conventional wisdom suggests that financial constraints hinder innovation and firm performance, yet emerging research hints at a more complex relationship. Building on Indigenous entrepreneurship and cultural entrepreneurship theory, we examine how and why financial constraints translate into innovation, and subsequent consequences for firm performance. Drawing on a nationally representative sample of 1,101 Indigenous-owned SMEs in Canada and matching with mediation analysis, we find that financial constraints are associated with weaker firm performance, yet are simultaneously associated with a higher likelihood of product and process innovation. Innovation, in turn, offsets up to 32% of the negative association between constraints and performance. We explain this pattern through the notion of culturally purposeful innovation—which channels scarcity into market‑ and mission‑relevant solutions. In Indigenous entrepreneurship contexts characterized by structural constraints and strong cultural logics, innovation emerges as a culturally grounded mechanism linking adversity to sustained performance outcomes. We contribute to strength-based Indigenous entrepreneurship, cultural entrepreneurship, and financial constraint literature. We also offer implications for entrepreneurship practice.

papers.title: Decoding the influence of the reviewer's country of origin on eWOM adoption: a transnational perspective
papers.abstract: Purpose Prominent travel platforms like Booking, TripAdvisor and Hotels.com increasingly publish electronic word of mouth (eWOM) worldwide, with reviewers' information including country of origin (COO). However, research that analyzes the role of culture in the context of e-WOM remains scarce. Our study addresses this gap by investigating the effects of reviewers' COO and the country stereotypes evoked – based on the degree of a nation's development and culture – on eWOM adoption. Design/methodology/approach Two quantitative studies were conducted using a 3X2 between-subjects factorial design. The manipulated factors were reviewer category according to country-of-origin (COO) culture and level of development (same nationality, developed country with a different culture, developing country with a different culture) and positive or negative eWOM valence. In Study 1, 323 American participants were randomly assigned to one of the experimental conditions. Study 2 extends Study 1 by examining the moderating role of national identification with a sample of 303 British participants. Findings Across both studies, the results demonstrate that for reviewers from other countries, COO positively influences perceptions of reviewer competence when the latter is from a developed country and is perceived as an outgroup member, thereby increasing eWOM adoption. Additionally, Study 2 shows that at higher levels of national identification, ingroup members are perceived as more competent than outgroup members from developed countries. These findings offer valuable insights for both marketing researchers and practitioners. Originality/value To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this study is the first to empirically examine how COO stereotypes shape perceptions of reviewer competence and eWOM adoption. It also breaks new ground by investigating the moderating role of national identification in shaping perceptions of reviewer competence.

papers.title: Decision inertia in emergencies: Reasons to be cheerful ten years on
papers.abstract: Abstract A decade on from the publication of Decision inertia: Deciding between least worst outcomes in emergency responses to disasters , this commentary reflects on the paper's contribution to understanding decision‐making in high‐stakes environments and its subsequent theoretical, methodological and practical impact. The original paper identified decision inertia as a cognitively active form of indecision, where decision makers in critical incidents get trapped in redundant deliberation rather than committing to a least‐worst course of action. Since its publication, research has advanced understanding of the cognitive, behavioural, affective, social and contextual factors that contribute to decision inertia, while methodological developments have provided increasingly more sophisticated and ecologically valid approaches for studying complex operational settings beyond the practitioner community. However, important questions remain regarding how decision inertia should be measured and how its antecedents and mechanisms can be integrated into a comprehensive multi‐dimensional theoretical model. Moreover, despite advances in the science and recognition in policy, translation into operational practice has been comparatively limited. We argue that greater collaboration and co‐production between researchers and practitioners would ensure that advances in understanding decision inertia lead to meaningful, evidence‐based changes on the ground. Ten years on, there are reasons to be cheerful, but the challenge for the next decade is to translate what we now know into better decision‐making on the ground.

papers.title: How Does Board Composition Shape Tax Effectiveness?
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT We investigate whether having various nationalities represented on a board of directors is associated with effective tax planning at the firm. We rely on upper echelons theory, which argues that an individual’s experiences, values, and personalities influence their interpretations of the situations they face and their decisions. We use a new tax effectiveness measure developed in prior literature that gauges a firm’s tax effectiveness using tax and non-tax costs. We find a positive association between board nationality heterogeneity and tax effectiveness, consistent with our hypothesis and the proposed role of board scrutiny in tax-relevant business decisions. Our study extends the research on board composition, tax-related decision-making, and how tax outcomes are determined. Data Availability: All data used in this manuscript are publicly available.

Crafting Persuasive Environmental Messages for Virtual Influencers: The Role of Anthropomorphic Conversational Style, Persuasion Appeal, and Behavioral Context
papers.abstract: The use of virtual influencers (VIs) has emerged as an alternative to human influencers for marketing initiatives. Prior studies have focused primarily on the visual characteristics of VIs and their use in advertising settings, with limited attention given to their capacity to drive pro-environmental behaviors (PEBs). We have developed an integrated persuasive framework, grounded in the Elaboration Likelihood Model and Congruity Theory, that links VI characteristics, message appeals, and behavioral context to persuasion outcomes. Study 1 examined VI message strategies and found that competence (vs. warmth) anthropomorphic conversational style and influencing (vs. de-influencing) appeal enhanced message persuasiveness. Study 2 explored the effectiveness of VIs in promoting plastic waste reduction behaviors across different behavioral contexts and found that messages pertaining to difficult (vs. easy) and private (vs. public) behaviors significantly enhanced message persuasiveness, but that messages promoting easy and private behaviors generated stronger behavioral intentions. The insights from these studies can provide valuable guidance to businesses, marketers, and environmental advocates on effective VI message strategies for addressing challenges related to climate change.

papers.title: Buyer green innovation volatility and the supplier bullwhip effect: a signalling theory perspective
papers.abstract: Purpose Buyers' green innovation does not remain confined within the firm; its volatility may ripple upstream and reshape suppliers' operations. Drawing on signalling theory, we examine how buyers' green innovation volatility (GIV) affects the supplier bullwhip effect (SBE), and how buyers' green supplier management (GSM) and inventory utilisation efficiency (IUE) moderate this effect. Design/methodology/approach We construct a dyadic dataset covering 436 Chinese buyer firms and 871 global suppliers from 2012 to 2022, and employ fixed-effects models to test our hypotheses. Findings There is a U-shaped GIV–SBE relationship: compared with both low and high levels of GIV, moderate GIV leads suppliers to adjust production more cautiously in response to unstable demand, resulting in lower SBE. When buyers' green innovation is on an overall downward trend, GSM helps suppliers interpret demand and operational changes more accurately, curbing GIV-induced increases in SBE. Higher IUE enables suppliers to detect GIV-related requirement changes more promptly, prompting stronger production responses and widening the SBE gap between moderate and low or high GIV. Originality/value By introducing GIV, our study identifies a novel antecedent of SBE and provides insights into how buyers can help suppliers accurately interpret GIV and calibrate their operational responses.

The virtue paradox: how perceived organizational social responsibility and organizational shame fuel resistance to change among motivated public servants
papers.abstract: Public organizations increasingly adopt corporate social responsibility frameworks, yet little is known about how employees react emotionally when their organization falls short of its professed standards. Drawing on appraisal theories of moral emotion, we examine whether organizational shame links perceived organizational social responsibility (OSR) to resistance to change, and whether public service motivation (PSM) moderates this process. Three-wave data from 113 French local government employees show that lower perceived OSR is associated with greater shame, especially among high-PSM employees, and that shame relates to greater resistance to change. Paradoxically, responsibility initiatives may fuel resistance among the most committed public servants.

papers.title: Towards more impactful co-design: insights from a systematic review of food loss and waste solutions
papers.abstract: Co-design, as a component of broader co-production processes, has gained attention in public policy as a means of addressing complex policy challenges. Yet comparative research remains limited on what occurs under participatory and design-led approaches labelled co-design, what policy solutions these processes produce, and how they are expected to generate change. We address this gap through a PRISMA-guided systematic literature review of 38 studies on food loss and waste (FLW). Findings indicate that co-design labels inconsistently reflect participatory and iterative design practices; creative engagement methods remain underutilized. Co-designed outputs remain at ideation and prototyping stages, while interventions often lack a clear theory of change. We introduce a coding scheme to document co-design implementation and propose CIMO (Context, Intervention, Mechanism, Outcome) as an ex ante evaluation heuristic to articulate the theory of change of co-designed interventions. We conclude with a research agenda emphasizing enhanced reporting practice, theory-building, and implementation-focused research.

papers.title: Beyond Convergence and Model Fit: Structural Guidance in CFA, EFA, ESEM-T, and Penalized SEM
papers.abstract: This study examines how alternative forms of structural guidance shape latent-variable solutions under dense-loading conditions in which all indicators have systematically nonzero cross-loadings. Near-population analyses (N = 1,000,000) compared exact restrictions, empirical rotation, target-guided rotation, and penalization while minimizing sampling fluctuation. CFA produced increasing distortion as departures from independent-clusters structure increased. EFA recovery depended strongly on the rotation criterion, with Geomin ε = 0.50 performing consistently well across both populations. Exploratory structural equation modeling with target rotation recovered the generating structure accurately when targets were sufficiently aligned and remained highly accessible. Penalized structural equation modeling recovery likewise depended on structural alignment, although accurate retained solutions could be difficult to access across starting values. Supplementary repeated-sampling analyses at N = 500 and 2,000 showed that numerical convergence and excellent fit did not guarantee corresponding factor orientations. Overall, the form and alignment of structural guidance jointly shaped admissibility, accessibility, recovery, and orientation stability, with important implications for practice.

papers.title: ‘Like going out at night without pepper spray’: responses to cyber-victimization among LGBTQIA+college students in the United States
papers.abstract: The internet has reshaped the nature of social interactions, providing new environments for people to connect in both prosocial and, too often, antisocial ways. The lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, questioning, intersex, asexual, and associated (LGBTQIA+) communities are among those who studies reveal are most at risk for cyber-victimization. For young people, already the most vulnerable to being targeted, being openly LGBTQIA + serves to compound the likelihood of online harassment. This study reports on three focus groups conducted with LGBTQIA + college students at a mid-sized university in the United States northeast, who discussed their experiences with cyber-victimization. The findings indicate a lack of faith in systemic platform-based responses, and a consensus that young LGBTQIA + people are forced to take personal responsibility for their own online safety. This includes curating their online profiles and feeds, as well as (to a lesser extent) taking direct action to combat anti-LGBTQIA + abuse.

Does a maternal history of childhood maltreatment influence prevention program impact on child outcomes? Exploratory findings from a randomized controlled trial in British Columbia, Canada
papers.abstract: Background Nurse-home visiting programs starting prenatally are a promising approach for preventing child maltreatment including injuries. Understanding which families benefit the most can inform policies to ensure greater impact and efficiency. Objective We investigated whether maternal history of childhood maltreatment (CM) moderated Nurse-Family Partnership (NFP) impact on child outcomes. Participants and setting We utilized secondary data from the Canadian NFP randomized controlled trial (RCT) involving 739 mothers aged 14–24 years and their 737 children in British Columbia (data collected 2013–2019). Methods Baseline data, including maternal CM history, were collected during pregnancy and before random assignment to existing services or NFP plus existing services. Data on main child outcome indicators: injuries (emergency department events), problem behaviour and language (maternal report) and language and cognition (in-home observations) were collected at age two years. Results Many maternal participants reported CM exposure (73.1%), including 57% medium-to-severe and 41.8% severe thresholds. CM history significantly moderated NFP impacts on selected child outcomes including injuries (adjusted differences in rate differences =102.92, 95% CI: 15.18, 193.45) and language via maternal report (adjusted differences in mean differences = −82.52, 95% CI: −150.77, −14.27). Conclusions A maternal history of CM moderated NFP impacts on injuries and language, but not all child outcomes examined. Researchers are encouraged to harness existing RCT data to learn how prevention program outcomes vary across populations. Policymakers may then apply this nuanced guidance to inform the refinement of prevention programs for families with unmet needs, fulfilling the ethical obligation to ensure that programs are effective for all.

Delegating Digital Policing: The Evolution of China’s Security-Industrial Complex
papers.abstract: Abstract How did China build its formidable digital policing apparatus so rapidly? While prevailing narratives emphasize top-down state direction, this statist perspective obscures critical local dynamics. This article argues that China’s security-industrial complex actually emerged from decentralized administrative pressures. Burdened by unfunded, time-sensitive central security mandates, resource-strapped local security agencies abandoned state-led technological development and outsourced to the private sector. Drawing on extensive field interviews (2017–2022) and policy analysis, this study traces the complex’s evolution through three interrelated mechanisms: the decentralization of internal security politics, the formation of hybrid public–private partnerships, and the varied transactional behaviour exhibited by capitalists, as well as between government and business, in a multi-layered system. By demonstrating how localized security projects inadvertently catalysed technological innovation, this research reveals the hidden market-driven roots of China’s security-industrial complex. It offers a novel framework for understanding how the party-state adaptively leverages capital for building a digital security state.

papers.title: Enacting and negotiating institutional rules in participatory budgeting: how institutional rules shape inclusion and exclusion in democratic innovations
papers.abstract: Local governments increasingly experiment with democratic innovations to strengthen local democracy and decision-making power of residents. This article examines how the institutional rules of a specific democratic innovation – participatory budgeting – shape who is included or excluded. Participatory budgeting holds the potential to empower and emancipate underprivileged citizens through firsthand knowledge and experience with decision-making practices, but it can also reinforce existing inequalities and power disparities. Drawing on institutional theory through a public encounters lens, this study analyzes how rules regarding position, boundary, scope and authority affect the emancipatory potential of participatory budgeting in practice. Particular attention is given to how participants in different positions engage with and shape these rules, as to understand how decision-making within participatory budgeting works. The findings show that institutional rules are continuously contested and that rules intended to empower disadvantaged participants often, in practice, benefit those who already have a dominant position.

Carbon Source Diversity Shapes DOM Chemodiversity and Antibiotic Resistome in Earthworm Casts
papers.abstract: Abstract The earthworm gut acts as a hotspot for reprocessing ingested organic matter, thereby altering carbon availability. These changes reshape microbial communities and competitive interactions, potentially affecting the dissemination of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) in the gut. Beyond substrate amount, substrate diversity shapes these processes, yet its role remains unknown. We established microcosm experiments with a substrate-diversity gradient, combining FT-ICR MS and metagenomics to investigate dissolved organic matter (DOM) chemistry, microbial traits and ARGs in earthworm guts. Higher substrate diversity enriched carbon-centered metabolic genes and increased gut DOM availability, possibly through the proliferation of polysaccharide-degrading microorganisms with larger genomes. However, higher carbon availability may have increased microbial nutrient demand, accompanied by reductions in CHON-containing compounds and stronger microbial competition. ARG enrichment was associated with greater potential for microbial competition, as indicated by stronger negative microbial interactions and higher competition indices derived from genome scale metabolic models. In vitro monoculture of gut-derived pathogenic Klebsiella pneumoniae showed that substrate diversity enriched multidrug- and β-lactam-resistance genes and reshaped the resistome. Collectively, these findings suggest that increased substrate diversity modifies earthworm-driven carbon reprocessing, may reshape microbial resource competition and promote ARG enrichment, providing insights into the linkage between organic matter processing and resistome in soil fauna.

papers.title: Mitochondrial-Endocrine Axis Dysfunction Mediates Diet-Dependent Susceptibility to Nanoplastic Ovarian Toxicity and PCOS Risk
papers.abstract: Abstract Nanoplastics (NPs) pollution represents an emerging threat to reproductive health, yet how dietary habits modulate this toxicity remains largely unexplored. Here, mice were assigned to a control (CD), high-fat (HFD), or high-fiber (HFib) diet and received oral doses of deuterated polystyrene nanoparticles at 0, 5, or 25 mg/kg/day over an eight-week period. Ovarian NP accumulation was dose-dependent under CD, reaching 23.33 ± 5.39 μg/g tissue at the highest dose. HFD markedly elevated this burden to 96.87 ± 13.44 μg/g, whereas HFib significantly reduced it to 7.77 ± 1.32 μg/g. Functionally, HFD synergized with NPs to disrupt estrous cyclicity (only 13% regular cycles), suppress anti-Müllerian hormone by 74%, and increase follicular atresia rate, while HFib maintained near-normal ovarian physiology. Transcriptomics identified steroid hormone biosynthesis and oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) as core pathways convergently dysregulated by NPs across all diets. Mechanistically, HFD amplified NP-induced ovarian oxidative stress, inflammation, and mitochondrial OXPHOS impairment, culminating in hyperandrogenism and profound estradiol deficiency. Conversely, HFib preserved aromatase expression and mitochondrial respiratory capacity, thereby restoring steroidogenic homeostasis. Mendelian randomization further linked human orthologues of these dysregulated genes, including UQCR10 and COX4I1 encoding mitochondrial complex III and IV subunits, to elevated polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) risk, highlighting the central role of OXPHOS disruption. These findings establish a diet-NP interaction pattern with implications for reproductive health guidance in populations.

papers.title: Environmental Mechanochemistry: From Force-Induced Reactivity to Aqueous Reaction Platforms
papers.abstract: Abstract Mechanochemistry is increasingly used in environmental research, but is still commonly treated as a material synthesis or pretreatment step rather than a mode of driving reactions that directly affects pathways relevant to pollution control and resource recovery. This Perspective argues that its environmental significance is most evident when force not only changes material properties before use, but also alters how reactions proceed during operation. We compare how force becomes chemically effective in inorganic and organic systems and classify environmental applications according to its primary role. Using zerovalent iron (ZVI) as a representative example, we show that mechanochemistry can simultaneously alleviate multiple bottlenecks in ZVI preparation, storage, and application. Earlier studies have shown that force can regulate ZVI lattice structure, surface state, and interfacial charge transfer. The wet-milling mechanochemical reactor (MCR) extends these effects into aqueous operation by applying force during rather than before reaction. This intensifies solid–liquid contact, accelerates heterogeneous kinetics, and, in some systems, shifts target transformation from surface-confined pathways toward subsurface redistribution and lattice-associated capture. Future advances should identify systems in which force can strengthen reactions sufficiently to open pathways that conventional treatment processes do not readily access.

papers.title: Implementation Gap in Global Power Capacity Expansion to meet Paris Agreement Climate Targets
papers.abstract: Abstract Meeting the Paris Agreement’s climate targets demands an unprecedented expansion of renewable energy. Despite global commitments, significant implementation gaps persist due to economic, policy, and technical uncertainties. Here, we develop a Global Power Capacity Dynamics Framework, integrating facility-level data, machine learning and transition modeling to assess the feasibility of global power expansion. Analyzing 215,849 power plant units across five status modes (operating, planned, canceled, standby, retired), the framework explicitly incorporates the likelihood of planned capacity realization and the conversion of existing fossil assets. We find that by 2030, only 51% [40%–61%] of announced planned capacity is expected to become operational, while 26% [19%–36%] is likely to be canceled, with fossil fuel projects, especially coal, facing a cancellation rate of about 35%. Global operational capacity is projected to reach 9727 GW [9626–9848], including 178 GW [159–198] of existing fossil units requiring conversion or replacement (e.g., coal-to-gas, fossil-to-biomass). Although renewables dominate the planned pipeline, they are projected to constitute only 52% of the global energy mix by 2030, well below levels needed to meet climate goals. Regional disparities are pronounced: Asia, despite its relatively low cancellation rate, faces the world’s largest implementation gap, requiring an additional 2488 GW of solar and contending with 523 GW of stranded coal capacity to remain on a 1.5 °C pathway. This study provides the first probabilistic, facility-level assessment of global power capacity trajectories, revealing critical shortfalls in planned deployment and underscoring the urgency of aligning capacity expansion with climate targets.
