Is Informed Short Selling Concentrated in Family Firms? Evidence from a Reinvestigation
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT We reinvestigate Anderson, Reeb, and Zhao's findings that informed short selling is unique to family firms and driven by information leakage from internal disputes. Using the same firm sample and more comprehensive short‐selling data, we find that short selling predicts future returns in both family and nonfamily firms. We also find no significant difference in abnormal short selling before negative earnings announcements. In extended sample periods, short selling continues to predict returns for nonfamily firms under both ownership‐based and familial‐link definitions. Overall, our evidence suggests that short sellers are broadly informed and that family firms are not uniquely vulnerable.

papers.title: China Walls
Increasing healthcare usage among the homeless: Evidence from Mobile Street Clinics in Brazil
The Political Economy of Propaganda: Evidence from US Newspapers,
papers.abstract: Abstract This study examines whether racial outrage in the media can result from the incentives of elites who seek to divide society for political gain, focusing on the late 19th century Southern United States. At this time, the Democratic Party had strong political incentives to incite racial outrage, and local Democratic elites exercised considerable influence over newspapers, the only mass media at the time. Using high-frequency historical newspaper data and difference-in-differences and triple-difference estimation strategies, we find evidence consistent with Democratic elites orchestrating a racist propaganda campaign to sway white voters. Supporting analyses are consistent with Democrats benefiting from anti-Black propaganda in the subsequent elections.
papers.journal_name: Journal of the European Economic Association

papers.title: The price of geoeconomic dependence: Sanction intensity and corporate credit spreads
Local Crime and Prosocial Behaviours: Evidence from Charitable Donations
papers.abstract: Abstract We study the relationship between local crime and residents’ charitable donations and explore the mechanisms underlying this relationship. The analysis combines longitudinal postcode-level data on charitable donations made through a UK giving portal with publicly available data on local crime and neighbourhood characteristics. Our main results suggest that an increase in local crime corresponds to a significant rise in the size of unscheduled charitable donations. This pattern is primarily driven by the donation choices of female and gender-unclassified donors. The strength of the relationship between local crime and donation amounts also varies with postcode-specific population characteristics, such as religiosity, age, and mental health.

papers.title: Marital sorting, household inequality and selection
papers.abstract: Using CPS data for 1976 to 2025, we explore how wage inequality has evolved for married couples with both spouses working full time full year, and its impact on household income inequality. We also investigate how marriage sorting patterns have changed over this period. To determine the factors driving income inequality we estimate a model explaining the joint distribution of couples’ wages that accounts for spouses’ employment decisions. This requires a multivariate distribution regression model that incorporates a double selection rule. We find that income inequality has increased for these households and increased wage sorting has exacerbated the inequality resulting from individual wage growth. We find that positive sorting partially reflects the correlation across unobservables influencing the wages of both members of the marriage. We decompose the changes in sorting patterns over the 50-year sample into structural, composition and selection effects and find that the increase in positive sorting primarily reflects the increased skill premia for both observed and unobserved characteristics.

papers.title: Two-stage least squares with treatment-covariate interactions for treatment effect heterogeneity
Agricultural Trade and Industrial Development
Anchoring and Cost Vector Design in Discrete Choice Experiments:Testing Rational Choice, Coherent Arbitrariness, and Discovered Preferences
papers.abstract: This study revisits and extends the discussion by Bateman et al. (2008) regarding potential deviations from Rational Choice Theory, focusing on two hypotheses – Coherent Arbitrariness (CAH) and Discovered Preferences (DPH) – and their manifestations in Discrete Choice Experiments (DCEs). Using data from 5,917 Polish respondents, we implemented multiple treatments varying the cost vector, choice set size, priming techniques, and the placement of a contingent valuation Willingness To Pay (WTP) question either before or after the DCE. Our findings show that the design of the cost vector systematically influences stated preferences and that attempts to mitigate this anchoring effect (e.g., by presenting an open-ended WTP question prior to the DCE) were unsuccessful. The persistence of cost vector effects over time aligns with CAH, while the lack of any discernible preference refinement challenges DPH. Further analyses reveal systematic variations in cost sensitivity and show that excluding respondents who violated the Weak and Strong Axioms of Revealed Preferences did not reduce cost vector effects. In light of these results, we recommend using diverse cost vectors to verify the robustness of DCE-based welfare estimates and call for further research into the broader impacts of heuristic behaviors in stated preference methods.
papers.journal_name: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management

papers.title: Urban densification to support climate adaptation: balancing costs and agglomeration benefits in the Netherlands
papers.abstract: Abstract Where should we build new housing under growing climate hazards? This study develops a framework that balances the economic benefits of density against the geographically varying costs of climate adaptation. We apply it to the Netherlands, where demand for new housing is high, but much of the land lies in floodplains or subsidence-prone areas. Agglomeration benefits are proxied by land values, while adaptation costs are derived from engineering estimates of flood protection and soil subsidence. Combining these data allows us to map spatial trade-offs and identify where development remains welfare-enhancing. Our findings show that dense cities continue to generate strong net welfare gains, even in places with high costs, while low-density settlements generate a welfare loss for new housing. We identify density thresholds above which housing development becomes feasible. Many medium-sized Dutch cities already exceed these thresholds, making densification more beneficial than peripheral expansion. Climate adaptation thus strengthens—rather than weakens—the case for urban densification.

papers.title: Towards an Ambivalence framework: decision-making on skills and training in global reproduction networks
Policy Making with an Informed Opposition
Housing Yields
papers.abstract: Abstract We build a granular data set of residential property yields using rental and sale listings from a major German real estate platform. With more than 1.5 million property-level rent-to-price ratios, we document a novel heterogeneity puzzle. About two-fifths of yield dispersion remains unexplained after controlling for extensive observable property characteristics and postal code-level time-varying factors using fixed effects. When we absorb finer neighborhood amenities through richer fixed effects, the unexplained share remains close to one-third. This evidence points to the importance of investors’ beliefs and preferences—rather than several alternative explanations we test—as sources of heterogeneity in risk premia.

papers.title: Economic Fundamentals and Short-Run Exchange Rate Prediction: A Machine-Learning Perspective
papers.abstract: Abstract The exchange rate predictability puzzle—that fundamentals fail to forecast short-horizon exchange rate movements out of sample—has long resisted resolution. We show that fundamentals do matter, but their effects vary with global financial conditions. Using a rich set of country characteristics interacted with global state variables and machine-learning techniques to handle the high-dimensional data, we document that interactions between country characteristics and foreign exchange market volatility are particularly important, consistent with a “flight to fundamentals” during periods of financial stress. Our forecasts deliver substantial economic value and offer new insight into the carry trade.

papers.title: The Effects of Prohibiting Marriage Bars: The Case of U.S. Teachers
papers.abstract: Married women in the early twentieth-century United States faced “marriage bars,” a form of employer discrimination that barred them from paid employment. However, because the end of marriage bar use coincided with shifting social norms and labor market conditions, it is unclear how the end of marriage bars affected women’s employment. We study the effects of the state-level prohibition of marriage bars in teaching during the 1930s. A difference-in-differences design shows that the prohibitions increased the share of white married women teachers by 4.1 p.p. (26 percent), with no effect on Black teachers.

papers.title: Information in the First Globalization: News Agencies and Trade
papers.abstract: This paper documents the effect of information frictions on trade using a historical large-scale improvement in the transmission of news: the emergence of global news agencies. The information available to potential traders became more abundant, was delivered faster and at a cheaper price between countries covered by a news agency. By exploiting differences in the timing of telegraph openings and news agency coverage across pairs of countries, we are able to disentangle the pure effect of information from the effect of a reduction in communication costs. Panel gravity estimates reveal that bilateral trade increased by 30% more for pairs of countries covered by a news agency and connected by a telegraph than for pairs of countries simply connected by a telegraph.

papers.title: Incentives and strategic behaviour: an experiment
papers.abstract: Abstract How do incentive levels affect strategic behaviour? We address this with an experiment that separately identifies own- and opponent-incentive effects in two dominance-solvable games that differ in strategic complexity. Higher own incentives favour more strategically sophisticated actions and increase best responding to stated beliefs. Beliefs shift in a parallel direction and participants expect more sophisticated opponent actions. Furthermore, although higher own incentives increase belief accuracy, opponents with higher incentives are harder to predict. Higher incentives also increase response times, and longer response times are associated with better performance and more sophisticated actions and beliefs. Taken together, the evidence suggests that incentives affect strategic behaviour through two main channels: by reducing payoff-dependent mistakes and by increasing the effort devoted to reasoning, with the returns to that effort shaped by strategic complexity of the environment.

papers.title: Echoes of hyperinflation: The link between past exposure and formation of expectations
The behavioral structure of one-shot cooperation in small and large groups
papers.abstract: Cooperation is essential for realizing collective benefits in both small and large groups. In modern societies, many interactions are one-shot and differ in the magnitude of collective benefits. This paper identifies the unified behavioral structure underlying one-shot cooperation. Using online public goods games (N=2,136) and two versions of the strategy method, we examine how attitudes toward cooperation—the causal relationship between one’s own cooperation and others’—and beliefs about others’ cooperation explain cooperative behavior across group sizes (3, 9, and 30) and collective returns (low vs. high). Our ABC framework (Attitudes and Beliefs explain Cooperation) reveals a consistent structure: average attitudes toward cooperation are equally conditionally cooperative across all settings, while beliefs increase with the collective benefit of cooperation but not with group size, although beliefs become more important the larger the group. These results suggest that the ABC framework provides a parsimonious behavioral foundation for understanding one-shot cooperation.

papers.title: Do commodity prices signal inflation under quantitative easing? Evidence from interest rate co-movements
papers.abstract: This paper examines the dynamic relationship between real commodity price changes and interest rate changes during the U.S. Federal Reserve’s quantitative easing (QE) and COVID-19-era policies. Employing wavelet coherency and phase difference analysis over the period from January 2003 to December 2025, we provide a time–frequency characterisation of how these variables co-move under unconventional monetary regimes. We find robust short-term positive correlations between interest rate changes and real price changes across metals, energy, agriculture, and food commodities during both the QE and COVID-19 periods. Precious metals exhibit negative correlations during the subprime crisis, reflecting demand for value preservation. Critically, real price changes in hard-to-store commodities frequently lead interest rate changes, consistent with commodity prices anticipating monetary policy actions. To distinguish inflation-related channels from broader confounders, we implement partial wavelet coherency conditioned on money growth and core inflation. The significant attenuation of correlations under these conditions supports the quantity theory of money and the Fisher effect, indicating that the observed co-movements are substantially linked to inflation expectations. Our findings carry a direct policy implication: when the zero lower bound stifles conventional interest rate channels, commodity prices act as high-frequency barometers of evolving inflation expectations. This necessitates that policymakers treat energy, metals, and food markets as primary leading indicators during episodes of unconventional monetary policy. Complementing this policy insight, we introduce a wavelet-based methodology that significantly advances the literature by exposing the nonlinear, time-varying dynamics that standard econometric approaches systematically suppress.
papers.journal_name: Journal of International Financial Markets, Institutions and Money

papers.title: Are dairy cows replaced too early? Evidence from a structural model and cow‐level data
papers.abstract: Abstract In past analyses of animal replacement decisions, studies have claimed that dairy farms often replace dairy cows too early to be maximizing profits. I estimate a structural model of asset replacement to determine the motives behind early replacement of dairy cows. I specifically test whether the costs from premature removal, an event where cows are removed off‐schedule due to health problems, explain replacement ages on dairy farms that are considered by previous studies to be unprofitable. Using data from over 1000 Wisconsin dairy farms, I find that a cow prematurely leaving the herd costs $2300 per removal, totaling $75 million in lost profit over the sample period. This cost is larger than what has been previously assumed, especially for dairies with less than 200 cows, suggesting that replacement rates appear unprofitable because previous analyses underestimated these costs. Dairy farms may benefit from prioritizing cow longevity and health over productivity to both cut costs and address environmental externalities from dairy. These results highlight the economic damages from poor cattle health on US dairy farms and the extent to which there may be cost savings from increasing cattle resilience to conditions that cause unexpected removal.

papers.title: The effect of extreme wildfire exposure on energy poverty: Evidence from Australia's Black Saturday bushfires
papers.abstract: Abstract This study assesses the effects of the 2009 Black Saturday Bushfires (BSB), which primarily occurred in rural regions of Victoria and represent the deadliest bushfire event in Australia's history, on household energy poverty. Using a linear panel event‐study, an entropy‐balanced event‐study, and a staggered difference‐in‐differences (DiD) design, applied to matched longitudinal household and geographical data, our results suggest a significant increase in the likelihood of experiencing energy poverty among households residing within 15 km of wildfire areas. Specifically, we find that for households directly affected by the fires, the likelihood of being in energy poverty increases by 9.9–11.3 percentage points in 2010 and by 13.2–16.7 percentage points in 2011 across specifications, compared to 2005–2007, which is the reference period. We find that the data are statistically consistent with life satisfaction, perceived safety and quality of life fully mediating the effect of BSB exposure on energy poverty in 2010, and with perceived safety fully mediating the relationship in 2011. We also find that adopting longer‐term financial planning mitigated the adverse effects of BSB exposure on energy poverty.

papers.title: Contextualization of Numbers in Earnings Conference Calls
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Prior research generally finds that using numbers in financial disclosure is beneficial. However, numbers can also be strategically proffered due to their perceived precision and informativeness. We find the use of undercontextualized numbers in earnings conference calls is associated with short‐term benefits but negative longer‐term consequences. Specifically, undercontextualization is associated with a short‐term positive market return, positive analyst forecast revisions, and a more positive tone in analysts’ questions. Furthermore, we find undercontextualization is associated with a longer‐term negative market return, a decrease in year‐over‐year earnings, and a higher incidence of restatements. In additional analyses, we find evidence consistent with the intentional use of undercontextualization, as it is associated with conference call casting, insider trading, and internal information quality. Given the uniqueness of our measure, we provide evidence of its validity by documenting its association with analyst scrutiny and other proxies for strategic call behavior. Finally, we examine a mechanism underlying our results and find evidence that undercontextualized numbers have a greater influence on retail investors.

papers.title: Assessing the common ownership hypothesis in the US banking industry
Demand‐Driven Propagation of Job Losses: Evidence from the Great Recession a
papers.abstract: Abstract This paper presents evidence for the demand‐driven propagation of job losses in the context of the United States during the Great Recession. Using county‐level tradable job losses driven by aggregate shocks as an instrument, it shows that retail and restaurant (R&R) employment fell by 0.37% for every 1% of job loss in the rest of the county's economy. The finding is not driven by the house price decline or by credit supply problems. Moreover, the spillover is more severe for R&R industries that are most affected by consumer demand shocks during the Great Recession, which strengthens the argument for the demand‐driven propagation of job losses.

papers.title: A Conditional Shrinkage Method for Portfolio Selection
papers.abstract: Abstract We develop a conditional shrinkage method for portfolio selection. Our approach builds on a decomposition of the mean-variance portfolio into the 1/N portfolio and an alpha component that offers large efficiency gains but is exposed to substantial estimation risk. We show that a linear shrinkage covariance matrix determines the portfolio’s relative exposure to these components, and our framework allows the shrinkage intensity to depend on a state variable that predicts their relative performance. We implement the method using investor sentiment and find that the estimated relation predominantly leads to greater shrinkage toward 1/N when sentiment is low, improving mean-variance efficiency while maintaining low turnover. JEL Classification: G11, G12.

papers.title: Neighborhood mismatch and visits
Trust in Financial Services
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT We examine how generalized trust relates to investing, building on previous literature by simultaneously considering different accounts, assets, and the use of financial advice. We find that account ownership and financial advice are positively correlated with trust. For types of assets, we find mixed results: a positive relationship for assets that involve delegation of decision making; no relationship for cryptocurrency; and a negative relationship for precious metals. We find a positive relationship with having a financial professional take action on your behalf. Our results are consistent with a model where nontrusting investors perceive greater risk of loss. JEL Classification: D14, G11, Z13

papers.title: Beyond Leaderism: Recentering Leadership Science Towards Relationships in Action
papers.abstract: Abstract The historical origins of ‘Great Man’ theories of leadership, and their contemporary offshoots, have produced an accumulated literature in which the leader's behaviours are the focal unit of analysis. This Point article surfaces five theoretical assumptions underlying the leader behavioural paradigm: leaderism, individualistic attribution, behavioural universalism, democratization of leadership, and individual‐level ontology. We discuss theoretical counterfactuals to each assumption and call for a shift in the scene of scholarly conversation, from individual leaders to relationships that incorporate context and stakeholders. This shift in the focal unit of analysis from individual leader behaviour to relationships represents a foundational theoretical pivot built on multidisciplinary foundations, attention to levels of analysis, and a deep grounding in context. By questioning the assumptions underlying 85 years of leader behaviour research, we argue that the science (episteme), skill development (techné), and contextual judgement (phronesis) of leadership could be more tightly coupled by directing the spotlight towards relationships in context rather than individual leaders. In doing so, we move the focus from leaders in action to leadership as relationships in action .

papers.title: Learning‐by‐twinning: Organizational digital twins and the future of search
papers.abstract: Abstract Research Summary Entrepreneurs and managers often need to evaluate strategic choices, such as redesigning an incentive plan or entering an unfamiliar market, before committing scarce resources. Existing offline search tools, including mental models, analogical reasoning, model building, and simulation, allow managers to weigh alternatives without acting, but each is limited by what a single decision maker can specify, recall, or imagine. We argue that advances in generative AI, combined with the growing availability of firm‐specific digital trace data, are transforming this tradeoff. We introduce the organizational digital twin (ODT), an infrastructure combining firm‐specific data, AI‐based behavioral simulation models, and governance rules which facilitates a new form of offline search that we call learning‐by‐twinning: search conducted by observing how a strategic choice unfolds within a digital replica of the firm. We identify three mechanisms through which learning‐by‐twinning creates value, namely expanded search, safer experimentation, and richer system‐level feedback as well as specify certain conditions under which these benefits may attenuate. Managerial Summary Strategic entrepreneurship depends on discovering and refining opportunities through search and experimentation under uncertainty. Enabled by advances in generative artificial intelligence and organizational data infrastructures, we theorize that a new form of entrepreneurial search—learning‐by‐twinning—allows managers to conduct systematic virtual experimentation prior to real‐world implementation. We introduce the concept of the organizational digital twin (ODT) as the technological infrastructure that makes this search and experimentation possible: an evolving simulation environment built from firm‐specific digital trace data and multi‐agent AI models capable of reproducing organizational routines, interactions, and decision processes. We argue that learning‐by‐twinning alters the traditional tradeoffs of offline search by expanding the set of alternatives managers can explore, enabling low‐risk experimentation, and revealing second‐order organizational consequences before strategic commitments are made.

papers.title: The Emergence of Sustainability Reporting in a Family Firm: A Case Study in the Luxury Fashion Industry
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines the emergence of sustainability reporting in a family‐owned luxury fashion firm. Using a qualitative case study and drawing on socioemotional wealth theory, it focuses on the preparation of a firm's first sustainability report. Findings show that reporting is not initiated as a technical compliance exercise but as a sustainability conceptualization process involving the translation of longstanding values and practices into a communicable, formal structure. This process unfolds through interrelated stages, with a specific configuration of socioemotional wealth dimensions shaping its development. The family influences this development through concerns for authenticity, control, and continuity. Sustainability reporting evolves through negotiation between internal identity and external expectations, supported by a governance core and cross‐functional collaboration. Rather than using disclosure instrumentally, the firm adopts a cautious and value‐driven approach, gradually moving toward selective transparency. In a context dominated by quantitative research, this study offers qualitative, process‐based insights into the micro‐dynamics through which sustainability reporting emerges in a family firm.

papers.title: Greenhushing and Reputational Threat: Theory and Evidence
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Motivated by the importance of credible sustainability disclosure and concerns about reputational risk, this study investigates greenhushing—the deliberate under‐communication of strong corporate sustainability performance. As stakeholders increasingly demand transparent and reliable ESG disclosures, firms face a strategic dilemma: how to communicate progress without triggering skepticism, regulatory scrutiny, or accusations of greenwashing. We develop a theoretical framework that extends voluntary disclosure theory by incorporating uncertainty about the outcomes of external scrutiny, explaining why highly active firms may greenhush. Using a panel dataset of 17,012 firm‐year observations from 2003 to 2022, we analyze the relationship between internal and external sustainability actions and find an inverted U‐shaped pattern. Companies initially increase sustainability disclosure as internal efforts rise, but those with the most intensive sustainability activities reduce reporting—consistent with greenhushing. Moreover, high‐reputation firms face heightened scrutiny, leading to greater perceived risks and lower thresholds for greenhushing. These insights reveal that regulatory pressure and fear of misinterpretation can distort corporate transparency.

papers.title: Green Marketing Orientations and Differentiation Advantage in Hospitality: Mediating Effects of Supply Chain Collaboration and Green Product Innovation
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Green marketing is increasingly central to hospitality strategy, yet how different orientations translate into competitive advantage remains unclear. The study examines how strategic, tactical, and internal green marketing orientations, green supply chain collaboration, and innovative green product development affect competitive differentiation advantage in the hospitality industry. The study collected data from 412 hotels, including 198 in the US and 214 in Saudi Arabia, using convenience sampling. Results indicate that strategic green marketing influences innovative green product development but not supply chain collaboration. Tactical green marketing influences innovative green product development but not green supply chain collaboration. Internal green marketing orientations influence green supply chain collaboration and innovative green product development. Innovative green product creation and green supply chain collaboration boost competitive distinctiveness. Innovative green product development links all three green marketing approaches to competitive differentiation. In contrast, green supply chain collaboration merely links internal green marketing orientations to competitive differentiation. Green supply chain collaboration does not mediate the links between strategic and tactical green marketing orientations and competitive differentiation benefits. This study advances the green marketing and hospitality literature by demonstrating that internal execution and innovation are necessary for competitive advantage.

papers.title: Scaling Sustainability: A Process Eco‐Innovation Model for Food Waste Reduction
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines how foodservice management companies respond to sustainability pressures through process eco‐innovation (PEI) in food waste management. Using interview data from mid‐ to senior‐level managers, we develop a PEI model leveraging institutional theory. The model explains how institutional directives, including the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, drive organizational change. The findings reveal that institutional learning, compliance monitoring, and stakeholder engagement are key mechanisms that translate global directives into operational improvements. This study further identifies adaptive sourcing, whereby organizations dynamically reconfigure the boundary between external technology partnerships and internal solution development as legitimacy expectations and operational fit evolve. Financial, cultural, and operational barriers further shape PEI implementation and scaling. By linking institutional pressures with organizational adaptation, the PEI model contributes to understanding how service‐intensive firms can embed sustainability into core processes while maintaining legitimacy. The results offer actionable guidance for advancing sustainability in on‐site foodservice management.

papers.title: Corporate Biodiversity Disclosure Under SDG 15: The Role of Internal and External Governance in Emerging Asian Economies
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines how internal (corporate) and external (country‐level) governance mechanisms jointly influence corporate biodiversity disclosure under SDG 15 (CBD_SDG15) in emerging Asian economies. Drawing on stakeholder theory and institutional theory, the study conceptualises internal and external governance as complementary governance mechanisms operating across organisational and national levels. Using a balanced panel of 1800 firm‐year observations from five emerging Asian economies over 2016–2017 to 2021–2022, CBD_SDG15 is measured through manual content analysis based on GRI‐2016 biodiversity indicators aligned with SDG 15 targets. The findings reveal an increasing trend in biodiversity disclosure over the study period. Panel Tobit estimation, supported by robustness analyses using fractional logit, IV‐2SLS and System GMM estimators, indicates that both corporate governance and country‐level governance positively influence biodiversity disclosure. Furthermore, stronger country‐level governance enhances the effectiveness of corporate governance, whereas additional sectoral analysis shows that the influence of corporate governance is particularly pronounced among environmentally sensitive firms. The study contributes to the biodiversity disclosure literature by demonstrating that the effectiveness of corporate governance depends on the surrounding institutional environment and the environmental context in which firms operate, offering practical insights for policymakers and firms seeking to advance SDG 15 through improved biodiversity disclosure.

papers.title: The Survival Signalling Paradox: How Financially Constrained Firms Defend ESG Under Climate Stress
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Does climate pressure lead financially constrained firms to cut environmental, social and governance (ESG) performance or to defend it? Using 28,439 firm‐year observations from 44 countries over 2005–2023, we show that the answer depends on the firm's dependence on external capital. Managerial climate salience, measured from earnings calls, is associated with lower ESG performance on average, but the penalty is borne by unconstrained firms and reverses among constrained ones, a pattern we call the survival signalling paradox. We argue that capital dependence is a boundary condition separating two established logics: where ESG decisions are private, slack‐resource theory applies and stress produces retrenchment; where lenders observe them, withdrawing the visible ESG flow is read as evidence about viability, so the firms least able to afford ESG have the strongest reason to maintain it. Three results support this reading. Constrained firms retrench selectively, shielding ESG while cutting research and development. Among constrained firms, ESG performance under climate salience is associated with debt access in the same year. The constraint gradient also appears when climate pressure is measured by the frequency of recorded country‐level weather disasters, though not by their severity. Institutional quality and market flexibility temper the penalty but do not reproduce the firm‐level reversal. The climate–ESG relationship therefore depends on how the firm is financed.

papers.title: Standardization with nuance: Selective cultural buffering in Michelin-starred luxury dining
Stop honeying me: Endearing language works in human service recovery but backfires for (machine-like) robots
When Do Family Firms “Walk the Talk” in Sustainability? The Role of Socioemotional Wealth
papers.abstract: A central debate concerns under which conditions sustainability orientation—a firm’s attitudinal disposition toward creating social and environmental value alongside economic value—translates into concrete environmental practices in some family firms but not others. Drawing on socioemotional wealth (SEW) theory, we argue that specific socioemotional priorities shape whether family firms “walk the talk” in their environmental practices. Using survey data from 182 Turkish family firms, we find that sustainability orientation is more strongly associated with environmental practices when owning families emphasize preserving the business across generations (renewal of family bonds), but not when they show stronger emotional attachment to the firm.

papers.title: Multiple Family Offices and Stock Price Crash Risk
papers.abstract: Drawing on principal–principal agency theory, we examine how multiple family offices (MFOs) affect stock crash risk of family firms owned and managed by at least two founding families or family lineages. In a study of publicly listed Korean firms where principal–principal agency conflicts are prevalent due to substantial control by family owner-managers, we find that MFOs help reduce stock crash risk by enhancing governance mechanisms that facilitate the alignment of divergent principal interests, especially in non-business-group-affiliated family firms and those facing unfavorable investment environments. Overall, we contribute toward the understanding of the governance function of family offices.

papers.title: Family Management Control and Trade Credit Utilization: The Influence of Financial Constraints and Supplier Monitoring
papers.abstract: We examine how family management control affects trade credit utilization. We find that firms with family management control use significantly lower trade credit, reflecting both lower financial constraints and a stronger preference to preserve control. More importantly, we show that the effect varies across family firms, becoming stronger with deeper family involvement and under first-generation control. We also note that institutional ownership and competitive environment encourage greater trade credit utilization, whereas independent directors and nonfamily Chief Executive Officers (CEOs) exert limited influence. Overall, our findings indicate that substantive family control matters more than formal governance structures in shaping family firms’ short-term financing decisions.

papers.title: Trust gained, trust lost: how service robot anthropomorphism shapes consumer trust in tight and loose cultures
papers.abstract: Purpose This paper aimed to examine the dual pathways through which service-robot (SR) anthropomorphism shapes consumer trust in service robots (CTSR), specifically the positive serial mediating effect of perceived warmth (WA) and perceived competence (CO) and the negative serial mediating effect of perceived identity threat (TH) and discomfort (DI). It further explored cross-cultural differences in consumer attitudes and their underlying reasons from the perspective of cultural tightness-looseness. Design/methodology/approach Five scenario experiments were conducted across three sets of SR picture stimuli, two service settings (hotel and hospital) and two cultures (China and the United States). Findings Both study 1 and study 2 found that anthropomorphism had a double-edged sword effect on CTSR across different sets of SR picture stimuli, service settings and cultures. An exploratory analysis in study 1 further revealed that among Chinese consumers, CTSR and its antecedents did not show significant differences across different service settings. Study 2 results further indicated that Chinese (versus. American) consumers had higher WA, CO and CTSR, along with lower TH and DI and that region-level cultural tightness influenced CTSR and its antecedents, potentially explaining these cross-cultural differences. Practical implications For hospitality managers, this paper offers insights on how to deploy anthropomorphic SRs across different cultural contexts. Originality/value This study developed a dialectical framework that integrates cognitive and affective serial mediation pathways and considers both the country- and region-level effects of cultural tightness on attitudes toward SRs.
papers.journal_name: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management

papers.title: Ethical signals attract job seekers when backed by representative leadership
papers.abstract: Purpose Labor shortages in the hospitality industry have intensified reliance on online recruitment strategies, making diversity cues a critical signal to potential employees. This study aims to examine how diversity cues in hospitality recruitment influence applicants’ intent to apply. Design/methodology/approach This study adopts an exploratory mixed-methods design across three studies. Study 1 used focus groups with 12 job seekers to explore perceptions of diversity cues. Study 2 (n = 291) examined relationships among diversity beliefs, endorsed diversity rationales and applicant intentions using survey data. Study 3 (n = 187) experimentally manipulated leadership diversity levels (3%, 23%, 53%) and message rationale (moral vs instrumental). Findings Job seekers preferred morally framed diversity cues over instrumental ones and perceived superficial messaging as insincere. Although endorsing an instrumental rationale was unexpectedly associated with higher application intentions in the survey study, experimental results showed that moral messaging paired with higher leadership diversity increased organizational attractiveness, whereas instrumental messaging reduced perceived mobility as leadership diversity increased. Practical implications Hospitality organizations should prioritize authentic, morally grounded diversity communications to strengthen employer attractiveness and perceived advancement opportunities. Superficial or instrumental messaging may undermine organizational attractiveness and limit application intentions. Originality/value This study advances hospitality recruitment research by integrating signaling theory with organizational legitimacy theory to show how diversity cues shape applicants’ perceptions and behavioral intentions. It provides a multi-method examination of authenticity in diversity signaling, offering insights into how organizations can effectively signal inclusivity in competitive hospitality labor markets.
papers.journal_name: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management

papers.title: The symbolic divide: how human and robotic service rituals shape perception of brand symbolism
papers.abstract: Purpose The rapid adoption of service robots in tourism and hospitality raises questions about their ability to generate brand-related meaning compared to human-led service rituals. Drawing on interaction ritual theory, this study aims to examine how human and robotic service rituals influence perception of brand symbolism through emotional energy and memory and how these effects differ for customers with varying levels of social phobia. Design/methodology/approach Using a multistudy design, this research uses five experiments across airports, hotels and restaurants to test the hypotheses. The inclusion of both Asian and Western respondents across varying service contexts provides preliminary evidence regarding the generalizability of the findings. Findings Human-led service rituals create a stronger perception of brand symbolism than robot-led rituals, with emotional energy and memory as sequential mediators. For high-social-phobia customers, perception of brand symbolism did not differ significantly between the two ritual types, although human-led rituals generated higher emotional energy; for low-social-phobia customers, human-led rituals produced greater perception of brand symbolism and higher emotional energy. Originality/value This study contrasts human and robotic service rituals, identifies sequential mechanisms (emotional energy and memory) and extends interaction ritual theory by specifying when the symbolic outcomes of robot-led rituals do not significantly differ from human-led rituals. The findings also guide managers in designing inclusive rituals that balance emotional richness and social comfort.
papers.journal_name: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management

papers.title: Sensing through simulation: Alt-Text descriptive granularity and digital embodiment for visually impaired consumers
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how alternative text (Alt-text) descriptive granularity influences purchase intention among visually impaired consumers in digital restaurant environments. This study further investigates the roles of message framing, health consciousness, restaurant trust and perceived healthfulness through the lens of digital embodiment. Design/methodology/approach A qualitative pretest with 18 visually impaired participants informed stimulus development, followed by four between-subjects experiments (n = 868). The studies manipulated Alt-text descriptive granularity and promotion- versus prevention-focused framing, while health consciousness was measured in Studies 2–4. Studies 3 and 4 tested restaurant trust and perceived healthfulness as mediating mechanisms. Findings Highly descriptive Alt-text increases purchase intention. The effect is stronger under promotion-focused framing and becomes stronger as health consciousness increases. Restaurant trust and perceived healthfulness emerge as complementary relationship- and product-oriented mediating mechanisms. The overall pattern is consistent with an embodied-cognition account of accessible descriptive information. Originality/value This research extends digital accessibility beyond technical compliance by conceptualizing descriptive Alt-text as a basis for digital embodiment. It also shows that accessibility quality can shape both persuasive communication and consumer evaluations of service providers and menu items.
papers.journal_name: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management

papers.title: The future of interaction, relationships and networks: Reshaping interdependencies in a changing world
Modern slavery governance, digital transformation and financial distress risk: evidence from legally grounded text-based accounting measures
papers.abstract: Purpose This paper aims to develop and validate a legally grounded accounting measurement framework for modern-slavery governance and examines whether the resulting governance measures are associated with firms' financial distress risk. Existing research predominantly relies on ESG ratings, disclosure proxies, or qualitative assessments that do not clearly distinguish externally specified governance obligations from firms' disclosed governance architecture. We address this measurement gap by translating mandatory modern-slavery governance requirements into reproducible firm-level accounting measures and evaluating their informational relevance for accounting-based risk assessment. Design/methodology/approach This research adopts a two-corpus measurement framework. The first corpus comprises mandatory modern-slavery legislation and internationally recognised institutional frameworks issued between 1930 and 2024, including the Tariff Act (1930), California Transparency in Supply Chains Act, UK Modern Slavery Act, French Duty of Vigilance Law, Australian Modern Slavery Act, German Supply Chain Due Diligence Act, Norwegian Transparency Act, the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD), the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD), and complementary institutional frameworks including the ILO, OECD, PRI, and the United Nations Guiding Principles. Rather than serving as institutional background, these sources are used to define the governance construct by identifying legally codified organisational obligations and harmonising them into a unified governance ontology representing implementation-oriented governance mechanisms.The second corpus comprises more than 5,000 annual reports of S&P 500 firms covering the period 2010–2022. Artificial intelligence (AI), natural language processing (NLP), and supervised machine-learning techniques operationalise the predefined governance ontology to identify disclosed evidence of implementation-oriented governance mechanisms within corporate reports, thereby generating firm-year Modern Slavery Index (MSI) measures. A complementary Digital Transformation Index (DTI) captures disclosed digital capability. The empirical design combines firm and year fixed-effects estimation with 2SLS endogeneity-sensitivity analysis and additional tests addressing disclosure intensity and boilerplate reporting, institutional validity, digital-capability interactions, competing explanations and potential mechanisms. Findings The findings show that firms disclosing stronger implementation-oriented modern-slavery governance mechanisms exhibit lower financial distress risk, although the strength of this association varies across the underlying institutional architectures. Among the four governance measures, the California-based MSI2 provides the strongest evidence, indicating that disclosed governance mechanisms centred on supplier verification, monitoring, accountability, and supply-chain oversight are associated with lower financial distress risk. Digital transformation, by contrast, does not independently reduce financial distress risk and is associated with lower Altman Z-scores in several specifications, a pattern consistent with – but not establishing – the organisational costs and implementation challenges that may accompany technological transformation. Importantly, digital capability also conditions the association between disclosed modern-slavery governance and financial distress risk, with the positive MSI4 × DTI interaction indicating that the financial relevance of governance disclosure varies with firms' digital capabilities under particular institutional arrangements. Overall, the findings indicate that legally grounded measures of disclosed modern-slavery governance contain economically relevant information for financial-distress assessment, while their associations vary across governance architectures and according to firms' digital capabilities. Originality/value This paper makes four contributions to the accounting literature. First, it develops four transparent, legally grounded, and fully reproducible Modern Slavery Indices (MSI1–MSI4), each derived from distinct regulatory and institutional governance frameworks, providing researchers, practitioners, managers, auditors, and policymakers with standardised accounting measures of implementation-oriented modern-slavery governance. Second, it introduces a novel two-corpus measurement framework that explicitly separates construct definition from empirical observation by deriving the governance construct from mandatory legislation and internationally recognised frameworks before operationalising it through AI-enabled textual analysis of corporate reports. Third, it demonstrates how artificial intelligence, natural language processing, and supervised machine-learning techniques can operationalise externally defined governance obligations into scalable firm-level accounting information while preserving construct validity. Finally, it provides evidence that these legally grounded accounting measures contain decision-useful information for accounting-based risk assessment, advancing research on non-financial accounting measurement, governance architecture, disclosure credibility, internal control systems, and corporate resilience under emerging mandatory reporting regimes.

papers.title: Ethics and climate litigation: from case law to knowledge networks
papers.abstract: Purpose This article examines how climate litigation has evolved from a policy instrument into a legal mechanism for enforcing ethical obligations, positioning climate change as an ethical issue and identifying human rights as a litigation outcome. Design/methodology/approach Adopting the design of an integrative literature review, the study combines bibliometric mapping of Web of Science citation data, processed using Bibliometrix and Biblioshiny, with conceptual and doctrinal analysis of key climate litigation case law. Findings Climate change litigation is maturing not only in scope but in ethical grounding, with human rights emerging as a strategic outcome courts increasingly pursue. Using bibliometric analysis, this article maps the intersection of climate litigation and ethics, identifying five research areas: greenhouse gases as pollutants, duty of care, climate science, global climate policy and intercountry equity. Cross-jurisdictional themes show that judicial decisions do more than resolve individual disputes – they shape, legitimize and accelerate transnational governance responses to climate change, positioning courts as meaningful actors in addressing climate change as an ethical imperative. Social implications This study maps the acceptance of ethics within legal spheres as part of the climate debate. Originality/value The article is among the first to integrate bibliometric mapping with doctrinal and ethical analysis of climate litigation, and proposes a tiered research agenda that addresses the interplay between government objectives and the interests of litigants.

papers.title: Firms’ carbon disclosure and low-carbon product sales: A perspective from the three-factor theory of customer satisfaction
Neither elevating nor degrading? Technology, job characteristics, and workers' role in manufacturing production
A Perfect Time to Recalibrate Frontlines Research
papers.abstract: Technology continues to transform firm-customer interactions, creating increasingly complex configurations of human and machine interfaces. Orchestrating the actions of widely distributed actors and systems has proven difficult. Agentic commerce, involving interactions between autonomous machines, will add complexity, shift points of marketing influence, and require new tactics. The frontlines have changed faster than scholars’ approaches to studying them, and the gap is widening precisely when decision makers need guidance. Closing this gap requires four imperatives: adopt empirics-first thinking, provide more credible evidence, lead practice – inform decisions, and be prescient.

papers.title: Rethinking Customer Service Digitalization: Incongruent Frames and Alignment Mechanisms in Retailing
papers.abstract: This multilevel study investigates customer service digitalization (CSD), the customer-facing transformation of service processes through digital technologies, in retailing through fifty-two expert interviews with twenty-seven headquarters (HQ) managers, eleven store managers (SMs), and fourteen frontline employees (FLEs). Grounded in a theories-in-use approach and guided by Technology Framing Theory (TFT), the study identifies systematic framing differences between HQ and stores. While HQ managers frame CSD as digitalization, human augmentation, and a continuous “journey,” FLEs perceive CSD as digitization, human substitution, and a fixed “destination.” As boundary spanners between HQ and FLEs, SMs can reinforce these frames and are seen as either enablers or barriers. The study introduces four collective congruence framing mechanisms (CCFMs), namely Ba, Psychological Safety, Redundancies, and Nudging, that buffer the negative consequences of frame incongruence on CSD success and, ultimately, customer service interaction quality; SM boundary spanning strengthens their effectiveness. These findings extend TFT to a multi-actor, multilevel service context. For managers, they suggest diagnosing frame incongruence before rollout, deploying CCFM instantiations such as HQ store days or temporary redundancies, and developing SMs as translators between HQ strategy and frontline practice.

papers.title: Do Disclosures of Corporate Transformative Service Initiatives Signal Enhanced Financial Outcomes? Moderating Roles of Firm-Level Factors
papers.abstract: Corporate transformative service initiatives (CTSIs) are service-led initiatives by for-profit firms that serve communities experiencing vulnerability and articulate an explicit well-being intent. When disclosed, as with other corporate disclosures, they can function as market-facing signals of firms’ enacted service-oriented societal engagement. However, it remains unclear whether such signaling improves financial outcomes and whether firm-level factors moderate this effect. To address this gap, this study examines the impact of CTSIs disclosures on firms’ financial outcomes and the moderating roles of chief marketing officer (CMO) presence, relative firm size, and firm type. A systematic automated content analysis of sustainability reports, cross-checked with annual reports from 2010 to 2019 for U.S. S&P 500 firms, identifies three main forms of CTSIs disclosures: corporate commitment, corporate giving, and employee volunteering. Dynamic panel analyses show that CTSIs disclosures and their components positively impact firms’ financial outcomes (Total q , return on equity), with stronger effects when a CMO is present. Relative firm size matters, with firms with greater relative asset size benefiting more strongly when a CMO is present, and smaller firms showing broader gains across CTSIs disclosure dimensions. The signaling effects of CTSIs disclosures are consistent across service and non-service firms, suggesting that market responses are driven by the communication of service-oriented transformative initiatives rather than by industry boundaries. These findings extend transformative service research and signaling theory by showing how CTSIs disclosures can position service-led initiatives as financially relevant market signals, with implications for managerial disclosure practice.

papers.title: Generative AI Identity Duality: The Mediating Effects of AI Connection versus AI Resistance on Generative AI Acceptance
Guidelines for Employing Large Language Models in Information Systems Research
Toward an “Identity Turn” in Public Service Motivation Theory: A Problematizing Review and Research Agenda
papers.abstract: Abstract Since its inception, Public Service Motivation (PSM) has been recognized as a key driver of behavior in public institutions. Despite its prominence, skepticism has emerged. In response, research has primarily focused on empirical analysis and measurement refinement rather than on conceptual development. This conceptual path dependency has become problematic as mixed empirical results increasingly challenge core theoretical propositions of PSM theory. We argue that one potential cause lies in a dominant assumption shaping the field: its positioning within motivation theory. To address this, we conducted a problematizing review across concepts and disciplines, comparing how PSM is understood in Public Administration with related concepts–such as motivation, altruism, and identity–in Management, Psychology, Sociology, and Economics. Based on this analysis, we propose a novel theoretical framework that reconceptualizes PSM as a social identity. In doing so, we outline a research agenda that (i) revises PSM’s core conceptual features and develops a new measurement approach informed by identity theory; (ii) introduces new ways of understanding PSM's functioning through identity work theory; and (iii) situates PSM theory within the broader debate on the “identity turn” in motivation research, highlighting its potential contribution to this multidisciplinary discourse.
papers.journal_name: Journal of Public Administration Research and Theory

papers.title: Looking the Part? How Candidates’ Race and Attire Shape Employers’ Hiring Decisions in a Low-Wage Labor Market
papers.abstract: Racial disparities in employment persist in the United States, particularly in low-wage labor markets in which employers frequently cite self-presentation, especially attire, as a basis for hiring decisions. Yet, whether improving professional attire yields equal returns across racial groups remains largely unexamined. Drawing on status characteristics theory, we argue that professional attire functions as an ambiguous proxy for unobservable traits such as motivation and reliability, making it susceptible to racialized interpretations. We predict that professional attire will yield weaker hiring returns for Black candidates than for their White counterparts and that perceived professionalism mediates this gap. We test these arguments using data from a gig-staffing platform comprising over 1 million job applications with profile photos, supplemented by a preregistered experiment that manipulates attire within candidates, using two photos of each candidate: one in professional attire, one in casual. The results converge across field and experimental data. Professional attire improves hiring prospects overall but yields substantially smaller returns for Black candidates. Moderated mediation tests confirm that perceived professionalism drives this disparity, such that race discounts how attire translates into perceived professionalism and how perceived professionalism translates into hiring. The racial gap attenuates in customer-facing roles in which appearance is task relevant. These findings challenge supply-side accounts of hiring inequality and reveal how a demand-side interpretation of equivalent signals perpetuates racial disadvantages.

papers.title: Cardiometabolic dysfunction and age at natural menopause: a prospective study
Estimating Marginal Effects on Survival Outcomes for Clinical Interpretations and Decision Making
papers.abstract: The Cox regression model is the most widely used method in survival analysis, but the hazard ratio has limited clinical interpretability. Survival or cumulative incidence curves are often used to illustrate treatment effects, yet there is no consensus on the most appropriate methods for generating these curves, particularly in the presence of confounding and competing risks. We reviewed original research articles published in a general medical journal in 2025, identified limitations in common practices, and describe a marginal effects framework to generate adjusted cumulative incidence curves that are coherent with the analysis model, anchored in absolute risk estimates, and adaptable to competing risks and clustered data. The framework targets the population-average difference in cumulative incidence between exposure groups, under the assumptions of no unmeasured confounding, positivity, and non-informative censoring. As a demonstration, we applied the framework to real-world data from Yek et al. (2025) and showed that it produced clinically interpretable estimates of hospital-acquired antimicrobial resistance risk that a single hazard ratio could not convey. To facilitate implementation, we describe each analytic step in detail, discuss available software, and share an R program with core routines written in C for computational efficiency.

papers.title: Exposure, constraint, and repair: How child abuse pediatrics fellows navigate strain and restore purpose
papers.abstract: Background Child Abuse Pediatrics (CAP) fellows train in a subspecialty marked by repeated exposure to child maltreatment and high-stakes clinical and legal demands. Objective This qualitative study examined how CAP fellows describe and make meaning of emotional strain and restorative experiences during training. Participants and setting Participants were 13 fellows enrolled in U.S. CAP fellowship programs, all practicing in urban settings. Methods Semi-structured interviews were conducted via Zoom between May and August 2024 and analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis. Vicarious resilience sensitized the analysis to restorative experiences; the job demands-resources model informed interpretation after themes were constructed. Results Three themes were constructed. Carrying What Cannot Be Left Behind described secondary traumatic stress as an accumulating presence that affected relationships and prompted protective silence. Procedural Continuity, Eroding Presence captured accounts of emotional numbing, constrained agency, and cumulative exposure that strained emotional presence even as fellows described continuing clinical tasks. When the Work Gives Back described how children's recovery, family recognition, and perceived accountability renewed meaning. Conclusions Fellows linked strain and restoration to exposure, supervision, and opportunities for recovery. Their accounts identify workload organization and supervisory support as areas for evaluation alongside individual coping.

papers.title: Symptom trajectories in head and neck cancer from diagnosis to long-term survivorship
papers.abstract: Abstract Purpose Patients with head and neck cancer (HNC) experience substantial symptom burden related to both disease and intensive treatments. Understanding long-term symptom patterns may help identify patients at risk for persistent emotional and physical symptom burden. This study evaluated symptom trajectories of anxiety, depression, fear of cancer recurrence (FCR), and oral pain among patients with HNC from diagnosis through long-term survivorship. Methods This secondary analysis included 5411 patients with HNC from the Head and Neck 5000 study in the UK. Latent class growth analysis (LCGA) and growth mixture modeling (GMM) were used to examine changes in symptoms, predictors of class membership, and within-class variability. Results The majority of patients were classified into a mild symptom class for depression (58%), anxiety (48%), and oral pain (62%), whereas the largest FCR class (44%) represented moderate symptoms. Anxiety, FCR, and oral pain followed recovery trajectories characterized by symptom improvement, while depression demonstrated a distinct pattern of worsening symptoms. Across symptoms, nearly 20% of patients belonged to an elevated symptom trajectory. These patients were more likely to be younger in age, have lower income, and report greater weekly alcohol consumption. Patients with HPV-positive HNC experienced faster reductions in anxiety and FCR but greater increases in depression over time. Conclusions Distinct symptom trajectories were observed into long-term survivorship among patients with HNC. Although most patients experienced mild-to-moderate symptoms, a clinically important subgroup remained at elevated risk for persistent symptoms. Implications for Cancer Survivors Early identification of patients at risk for persistent symptoms may facilitate targeted supportive care and behavioral interventions to improve long-term survivorship outcomes.

papers.title: Visual Sexual Health Communication Assisted by AI: The Case of Synthetic Menstruation Images
papers.abstract: Abstract Public communication about sexual and reproductive health and rights (SRHR) relies on both text and images. A recent development is the proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI) image generators, which enable rapid, cost-effective, and highly customizable images with appealing aesthetics based on textual requests (prompts). To examine the opportunities and challenges of AI-generated images in SRHR communication, we used the topic of menstruation and developed six research questions (RQs) anchored in the current state of research on AI-supported visual health communication. These questions addressed key areas of concern, such as unsuccessful image creation (RQ1), objective image flaws (RQ2), lack of diversity of human representation (RQ3), stereotypical portrayals of women (RQ4), use of visual symbols (RQ5), and image valence (RQ6). Our study applied 15 AI image generators, 2 user accounts per generator, 5 menstruation-related prompts, 2 prompt languages, and 2 images per prompt, resulting in a sample of N = 600 AI outputs generated in Autumn 2025. All outputs were manually coded using a reliability-tested codebook developed through both deductive and inductive approaches. In 20.0% of cases, menstruation prompts did not produce the requested image but only text output (RQ1). When images were generated, they often (78.1%) exhibited visual and/or textual flaws (RQ2). The images showed a lack of diversity in some human attributes (e.g., body type) but not in others (e.g., skin tone; RQ3). Stereotypical depictions of women were observed but not predominant (RQ4). Common menstruation-related visual symbols (e.g., blood, pain) were identified (RQ5), but most images did not convey a negative portrayal and instead a neutral or positive portrayal of menstruation (RQ6). While results show that initial outputs from AI image generators are often not directly suitable for visual sexual health communication, they might work with targeted refinement. Further research is required to examine the production, characteristics, consumption, and effects of AI-generated images in SRHR communication.

papers.title: Post-Soviet Brides in the China Dream: Migration, Marriage, and Geopolitics Across Borders Elena Barabantseva. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2026. 244 pp. £95.00 (hbk). ISBN 9781009600170
Safeguarding online panel surveys from LLM pollution: evidence from Canadian federal survey contracts
papers.abstract: Bots and large language model (LLM) agents can now complete online surveys convincingly enough to pass as real respondents, a risk long flagged in other fields but rarely addressed in public management research. Drawing on disheartening empirical findings from previous efforts to validate responses to online panel surveys, this research note offers a portrait of efforts to ensure the integrity of data collected by firms that survey citizens on behalf of Canadian federal departments and ministries, a case study likely representative of the challenges facing online survey practices across countries and levels of governments.

papers.title: Optimization of power allocation scheduling and component sizing in battery-assisted electrolyser systems
papers.abstract: This paper presents a co-design optimization framework for battery-assisted electrolyser systems aimed at improving the cost-effectiveness of green hydrogen production. As renewable energy sources (RES) increasingly strain electricity grids, decentralized power-to-hydrogen (P2H) production can mitigate grid imbalance while supplying a clean energy carrier, yet its financial viability remains uncertain. The proposed framework integrates models of battery energy storage systems (BESS), electrolysers, RES, and grid connections, and optimizes them on two levels: Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) determines the operational strategy that maximizes operating profit, while Bayesian Optimization (BO) selects the component sizing that maximizes net present value (NPV) over a continuous three-year horizon. The framework is applied to two real-world cases: a grid-limited 2 MW solar site (case A) and a more balanced solar–wind site (case B). For case A the optimal design pairs a 964 kW electrolyser with a 220 kWh battery, whereas case B favors a 475 kW electrolyser without a battery, showing that battery storage is decisive only when the grid connection is small. At a hydrogen price of €8/kg both systems are near break-even (NPV €−0.1 to €−0.9 million) and become clearly profitable at €16/kg (NPV €3.9–4.3 million); a sensitivity analysis shows they remain firmly loss-making across the €3–5/kg range projected for 2030. The electrolyser operates with an average efficiency of about 80% (HHV), at a levelized cost of hydrogen of about €10/kg. These results quantify how hydrogen price, grid capacity, and component sizing jointly govern the techno-economic feasibility of P2H systems, and provide a transferable framework for their cost-effective design.

papers.title: Unlocking flexibility in buildings through batteries: a case study of the Netherlands
papers.abstract: Residential buildings account for a significant share of energy consumption and emissions, and heating electrification and rooftop photovoltaic (PV) generation create new challenges for distribution grids: import peaks from heat pumps and export peaks from PV surpluses. Battery energy storage systems (BESSs) can reduce peak demand and increase self-consumption. We report a multi-objective optimization of BESS sizing and dispatch in a 58-apartment positive-energy building in Utrecht, using a full year of measured smart-meter data. A linear-programming model with a Wöhler-based degradation cost trades off peak shaving and self-consumption across a capacity sweep, under two scenarios: a hypothetical configuration in which all 58 apartments and the facilities share one ± 110.4 kW connection instead of their individual connections (Scenario 1), and the current configuration, in which the BESSs serve only the facilities (Scenario 2). Consolidation rather than operational savings dominates the economics: once the BESS dispatch eliminates the 122 hours of PV export violation (the summed apartment exports exceeding the shared connection, purely from aggregation), the avoided cost of the 58 individual connections becomes accessible. The installed 70 kWh BESS crosses this threshold, with a payback of 0.55 years; the economic optimum lies near 280 kWh. Scenario 1 is notional: its economics depend on contractual and regulatory consolidation of the 58 connections, which is not addressed in this study. In Scenario 2, where peak-shaving has no value, the BESS adds modest self-consumption gains. The results show the value of measured multi-apartment data and of institutional drivers alongside technological ones in residential storage economics.

papers.title: Shipping big data informed maritime decarbonisation strategies for green and digital shipping corridors
A network-aware combinatorial auction mechanism for local multi-energy markets with coupled conversion
Distributionally robust configuration optimization of climate-resilient active distribution networks for enhancing flexibility dispatchability
Comparative field deployment of model-based reinforcement learning and model predictive control for residential HVAC
A hypergraph-based constrained reinforcement learning method for electric vehicle charging navigation in coupled power-transportation networks
Vulnerability assessment of buildings-power distribution networks under compound heatwaves and power outages
A model-uncertainty-aware fault location method for active distribution networks with high-penetration renewable energy sources
The heterogeneous transmission of geopolitical energy shocks: A structural framework
Social acceptance of a green ammonia hub in a remote coastal community – the case of Ísafjörður in Iceland
papers.abstract: The International Maritime Organisation targets net-zero greenhouse gas emissions from international shipping by 2050, considering green ammonia to be a promising fuel for decarbonisation. However, development and deployment of this fuel is contingent not only on aspects such as techno-economic feasibility and supportive policy frameworks, but also on social acceptance (SA). This study examines the community-level SA of a potential green ammonia hub for maritime uses in Ísafjörður, Iceland, a remote coastal settlement with a strong maritime history. Based on sixteen semi-structured interviews with local stakeholders, the study identifies the key drivers and barriers influencing SA. It reveals that perceived benefits such as job creation and environmental protection function as drivers, while barriers stem from perceived concerns regarding safety, cost, and lack of clear governance. Guided by a community-adapted corporate sustainability classification and a PESTLE lens, identified themes are mapped across political, economic, social, technological, legal and environmental dimensions. The findings indicate that political and governance conditions function as an important enabling condition for SA, particularly through the perceived need for clear legislative frameworks and government incentives. Rather than operating independently, these political conditions were closely intertwined with economic and technological considerations, influencing investment risk, infrastructure development, affordability, safety, and equitable benefit distribution. The study concludes that for a just maritime energy transition to succeed, national policymakers must prioritise the implementation of robust incentive mechanisms and strategic roadmaps that satisfactorily address local socio-economic realities and contexts.

papers.title: Life cycle assessment of floating offshore wind anchors: A state-of-the-art review
papers.abstract: Floating offshore wind (FOW) is moving from demonstration projects towards commercial-scale deployment, but the lifecycle greenhouse-gas implications of its anchoring systems remain poorly resolved. This paper presents a state-of-the-art review of how FOW anchors are represented in life cycle assessment (LCA) studies, focusing on system boundaries, functional units, lifecycle-stage coverage, anchor disaggregation, and the links between environmental impacts and engineering function. The review shows that anchor-related emissions are controlled by coupled drivers: material demand, fabrication route, installation-vessel logistics, mooring configuration, load direction, soil conditions, and end-of-life treatment. These drivers are often hidden in current LCAs because anchors are aggregated with mooring lines, foundations, substructures, or farm-level inventories and are commonly normalised by electricity production. To address this mismatch, the paper proposes a complementary component-level functional unit, the provision of 1 MN of holding capacity under stated reference conditions, and an associated capacity-normalised carbon-intensity indicator expressed in tCO 2 eq/MN. The indicator is meaningful only when reference conditions are stated, including soil class, load inclination, static or cyclic capacity basis, capacity definition, and lifecycle boundary. Applied to the four studies in the review that report both anchor-level emissions and holding capacity, the indicator can preserve material- and installation-related trends. This quantitative base is, however, too narrow to rank anchor technologies, and the demonstration is presented as a proof of concept rather than as a benchmarking result. The paper concludes with a practical reporting framework intended to support transparent anchor-level benchmarking and low-carbon anchor selection in future FOW projects.

papers.title: Assessing 50 Years of Salt Effects in Heterogeneous Photocatalysis
papers.abstract: Abstract Heterogeneous photocatalysis has been studied for the treatment of recalcitrant compounds for half a century, but one of the severe limitations for practical oxidation treatment continues to be the inhibitory effect of salt found in real water matrices. The negative impact of Na+, K+, Cl–, and other ionic species is rarely quantified, as there has been no systematic way to discuss salt effects, making the evaluation of photocatalysis performance across studies difficult and imprecise. In analyzing 50 years of literature for this review, we identified >1,200 publications on heterogeneous photocatalysis in different water types, such as seawater, brackish water, and industrial brines. Just 84 studies reported degradation rates in deionized and salt-containing water, with nearly all involving TiO2 as the photocatalyst composition and charged dye compounds as the model contaminant class. To analyze the kinetic data extracted from these studies, we introduce the photocatalysis salt-effect (PSE) metric as calculated through the relative salt-effectiveness evaluation (RSEE) method, quantifying the percent change in degradation rate when the water matrix contains a salt species. We identified an unexpected correlation between PSE and ionic strength (IS), irrespective of the contaminant, at solution pH values less than the TiO2 point-of-zero-charge (PZC), which is the plausible result of salt-induced particle aggregation at high ionic strengths during photocatalyst testing. While most published results showed salt inhibition of photocatalysis (−100% < PSE < −5%), there is evidence for salt promotion (PSE > +5%) and salt tolerance (−5% < PSE < +5%), which challenges the notion that salinity is always detrimental to photocatalytic activity. These findings highlight the opportunity to study fully and systematically the relationships among contaminant structure, photocatalyst PZC, solution pH, IS, and salt type. The PSE-based framework would be critical in understanding the effects of more complex water matrices and in ultimately developing salt-tolerant and salt-promoted heterogeneous photocatalysis for practical water treatment.

papers.title: Mild Oxidant Regulation of *H Coverage Promotes Electrocatalytic Nitrate Reduction to N2 in Low-Conductivity Media
