Overall Evaluation Criteria for A/B Tests: A Meta-Analytic Approach
papers.abstract: This paper discusses meta-analytic methods for estimating the value of marketing interventions given a database of historical A/B tests with multiple outcome variables.

papers.title: Knowledge‐Based Institutional Work in the Circular Economy
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT The circular economy ( CE ) literature has primarily focused on incremental additions to the linear economy, whereas understanding of institutional change towards the CE remains limited. This study explores knowledge‐based institutional work in small born‐circular businesses that possess advanced CE applications and fundamentally aim to drive change. Drawing on 28 interviews and extensive secondary data from the clothing and apparel industry in Northwest Europe, the study identifies three forms of knowledge‐based institutional work: operational, engagement‐based and altruistic institutional work. Creating CE solutions under operational institutional work creates the foundation of the other identified forms of institutional work, whereas acknowledgement of the businesses' CE expertise enables their further development. The study concludes that, in the CE , (1) knowledge intertwines institutional work and business operations, (2) knowledge‐based institutional work blurs the boundaries between businesses and their surroundings and (3) views of knowledge help explain the mechanisms and motivations underlying institutional work.

papers.title: Organizational Capabilities for Sustainability‐Oriented Innovation in Multi‐Stakeholder Networks: An Integrative Framework and Future Research Agenda
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Organizational capabilities have become imperative for stakeholders to realize sustainability‐oriented innovation in multi‐stakeholder networks, where diverse stakeholders collaborate to address complex sustainability challenges. Yet, the literature remains fragmented, lacking a clear and integrative understanding of which organizational capabilities are required and how they jointly support sustainability‐oriented innovation. To address this fragmentation, we conduct a systematic literature review of 54 articles and synthesize existing literature into an integrative multilevel framework drawing on the dynamic capabilities and ecosystem perspectives. The framework conceptualizes 17 capabilities across macro‐, meso‐, and micro‐levels and across the higher‐order dynamic capability categories of sensing, seizing, and reconfiguring. Our analysis particularly highlights network orchestration capabilities at the macro‐level, collaboration capabilities at the meso‐level, and knowledge management capabilities at the micro‐level. The study further proposes a future research agenda focused on system‐level capability interdependencies and identifies four specific domains through which these interdependencies can be examined.

papers.title: Sustainability as a Mediating Construct: Connection, Evaluative Openness, and the Risk of Capture
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Similar sustainability commitments can become organizationally consequential in markedly different ways, yet the relational architecture producing this variation remains under‐theorized. This conceptual paper theorizes sustainability as a mediating construct through representational, projective, and organizing forms. Recursive translation explains how changes within one form feed back into the others, generating varying degrees of connection. Because connection does not determine which sustainability claims retain capacity to challenge and revise mediation, the framework introduces evaluative openness as a second, analytically independent dimension. Their intersection yields four configurations: symbolic, exploratory, embedded, and captured sustainability. The embedded–captured distinction reveals the central implication: strongly connected mediation can sustain coordinated action while the range of values, actors, evidence, and possible futures capable of redirecting that mediation progressively narrows. By separating connection from evaluative openness, the framework extends research on decoupling, hybrid organizing, and performativity and explains why organizational incorporation alone does not establish transformative capacity.

papers.title: AI‐Driven Marketing Strategy as a Catalyst for Circular Economy Participation
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines how sustainable marketing communication and AI‐driven marketing personalization influence circular economy participation through marketing automation maturity, carbon‐aware digital infrastructure, and willingness to purchase low‐carbon products. Drawing on dynamic capabilities theory, it explains the capability‐building mechanisms underlying digitally enabled sustainability. We collected data from 3253 middle‐ and senior‐level marketing and advertising managers across five countries. We tested the proposed model using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS‐SEM). We also used Jeffreys's Amazing Statistics Program (JASP) to run machine learning analyses, including support vector machine regression, regularized linear regression, and random forest regression, to assess predictive performance. Marketing automation maturity and carbon‐aware digital infrastructure significantly mediate the relationship between sustainable marketing communication and circular economy participation. Low‐carbon product willingness to purchase emerged as the strongest market‐level mechanism, whereas AI‐driven marketing personalization primarily influenced circular economy participation through sequential capability pathways. Random forest regression demonstrated superior predictive performance and confirmed the dominant importance of willingness to purchase low‐carbon products. By integrating explanatory and predictive analytics, this study extends dynamic capabilities theory by demonstrating that circular economy participation stems from sequential development of digital capabilities rather than direct marketing effects, offering actionable implications for organizations pursuing AI‐enabled sustainability and circular transformation. JEL Classification: M31, Q56, O33

papers.title: Shocks, recovery, and labour dynamics: Evidence from the accommodation sector
papers.abstract: This study examines the long-term relationship between tourism demand and employment in Spain's accommodation sector during the Great Recession and the COVID-19 pandemic. Using a dynamic System GMM panel model across fifty provinces over two decades, the analysis captures employment persistence and regime-specific responses to tourism demand. Findings reveal significant employment inertia, particularly for permanent contracts, while temporary employment acts as the primary adjustment margin. Employment sensitivity to tourism demand weakened during the Great Recession but rose during COVID-19, reflecting a shift in the margin of adjustment under Spain's furlough scheme. Disaggregated results highlight pronounced heterogeneity: temporary and male employment adjust rapidly to demand shifts, while permanent and female employment adjust more gradually. Long-run results suggest that employment growth tracks sustained tourism expansion, though female employment adjusts more rigidly, possibly reflecting occupational segregation. These findings underscore the need for labour policies promoting stability and gender equity to strengthen sectoral resilience against future shocks.

papers.title: Aligning institutions and organizations for sustainable supply chains: the role of digital transformation and low-carbon practices
papers.abstract: Purpose The transition toward carbon neutrality has become a global strategic priority for achieving sustainable development and a green economy. Despite growing interest in digital transformation among scholars and practitioners, achieving a balance between green supply chain performance and carbon performance within the context of carbon neutrality remains underexplored. Drawing on the technology acceptance model and change management theory, this research aims to provide solutions for achieving the zero-carbon target in 2060 through holistic digital transformation, and how institutional pressure and organizational readiness influence green supply chain and carbon performance through digital transformation, low-carbon operations management practices (LCOMP) and the moderating role of environmental proactivity. Design/methodology/approach Data from 442 Chinese manufacturing firms were analyzed using Smart PLS v4 to test the research hypotheses. Findings The results indicate that all three dimensions of LCOMP mediate the relationship between digital transformation, green supply chain and carbon performance. In addition, environmental proactivity strengthens the influence of digital transformation on the three dimensions of LCOMP. Originality/value The findings contribute to the literature by addressing a key gap in sustainable supply chain and digital transformation research, which has largely examined these relationships in isolation without fully explaining the mediating mechanisms and boundary conditions.
papers.journal_name: Supply Chain Management: An International Journal

papers.title: How can generative AI's conversational affordances drive firm performance? A service-dominant logic perspective
Conceptualising and designing experiential consumer logistics: a literature synthesis towards a value-based framework
papers.abstract: Purpose The value of last-mile delivery is no longer confined to functional performance but increasingly involves consumers' experiences. Despite growing recognition of experiential value, research in this area remains fragmented and underdeveloped. Thus, this study aims to develop a value-based conceptualisation of experiential consumer logistics (ECL) through a synthesised literature review. Design/methodology/approach A two-study literature review design was employed. Study 1 synthesises the logistics literature to conceptualise the value configurations and experiential mechanisms underlying ECL. Building on this conceptualisation, Study 2 integrates insights from the service design literature to examine how experiential value can be systematically reinforced. Findings Study 1 conceptualises ECL based on two analytical dimensions, value proposition (high-touch vs high-tech) and value appreciation (individualised vs networked), leading to four principal value configurations labelled as: traditional, technology-based, ethical and platform-enabled logistics. Furthermore, Study 2 identifies two complementary service design approaches for reinforcing experiential value: accommodating (relationship building and design for invisibility) and empowering (design for visibility and community building), each aligned with distinct configurations of ECL. Originality/value By consolidating dispersed literature, this review proposes an initial conceptualisation of ECL that explains how experiential value is proposed, appreciated and reinforced through service design. The findings provide an integrated theoretical foundation for understanding experiential mechanisms in last-mile logistics, offer practical guidance for designing logistics services and identify directions for future research.
papers.journal_name: International Journal of Physical Distribution & Logistics Management

papers.title: Does access to credit improve labour productivity?
papers.abstract: Abstract If credit rationing justifies public intervention in credit markets, it should be the case that unconstrained firms should result in higher productivity. In this paper, we use a longitudinal SME dataset for the UK to empirically test whether this is true. Our findings are nuanced and show that SMEs subject to quantity rationing suffer from productivity declines of up to 40%, which is more important than full rationing in the determination of labour productivity. We suggest that partial rationing forces firms to undertake second-best investment projects that limits their ability to become more productive. This implies that the returns to capital would increase if small firms that are of sufficient quality to pass banks screening tests received all the funds they applied for. This suggests that loan guarantee schemes may play a fundamental role in removing quantity rationing barriers for SMEs. We also find that discouragement can have a positive effect on productivity, and this suggests that firms reconfigure their capital structure by retaining more cash to avoid engaging with debt markets.

papers.title: Compressed work week – predictors and outcomes: a systematic review using text mining
papers.journal_name: The International Journal of Human Resource Management

papers.title: Explaining and mitigating hiring discrimination against transgender women: evidence from India
papers.abstract: Despite legal and organizational recognition of transgender rights in India, transgender people continue to face exclusion from professional jobs. Prior research suggests that such exclusion is often framed in ostensibly job-relevant terms rather than explicit prejudice. Drawing on the Justification-Suppression Model (JSM), we argued that when overt discrimination is normatively constrained, cisgender hiring managers rely on stereotype-based justifications to rationalize unequal treatment. Integrating the JSM and the Stereotype Content Model (SCM), we proposed that diverse rejection rationales converge on a core evaluative structure: perceptions of low warmth and low competence. Using a between-participants in-basket experimental design with Indian professionals, we examined evaluations of a transgender woman and a cisgender woman applicant for a nursing role. In the no-individuating information condition, the transgender woman applicant received significantly lower hireability ratings than the cisgender woman applicant. When counterstereotypical individuating information indicating high warmth and high competence was provided, this disparity was eliminated. These findings demonstrate that discrimination operates through stereotype-based justifications grounded in warmth and competence and that bias attenuates when the justificatory basis is weakened. The study advances theory by empirically grounding JSM in a transgender woman professional hiring context and specifying low warmth and low competence as a potential justification factor through SCM.
papers.journal_name: The International Journal of Human Resource Management

papers.title: Management control across complexity and dynamism: A synthesis of contingency-based research
papers.abstract: More than five decades of contingency-based research have generated extensive evidence on how management control (MC) practices vary with organisational context, yet the diversity of contingency factors examined makes it unclear what cumulative knowledge the field has produced. This paper synthesises 1844 empirical associations from 266 studies published from 1969 to 2022, using a conceptual framework that relates contingency factors to two sources of uncertainty, complexity and dynamism, and to the distinct control problems they impose. Firms facing greater complexity or dynamism rely less on direct supervision and more on a common set of MC practices, including formal strategic planning, diagnostic measurement use, performance-based pay, decentralisation, lateral coordination, and personnel controls. Uncertainty is therefore associated not with less control, but with reliance on a wider range of MC practices. Complexity is associated with a control pattern termed distributed bureaucracy, in which formalised accountability structures are combined with delegation and lateral coordination to support integration. Dynamism is associated with bounded autonomy, in which formal controls guide and evaluate responses to changing conditions while preserving the local discretion needed for adaptation. The more limited evidence on contexts high in both complexity and dynamism suggests that firms combine the two patterns rather than prioritising one. The paper concludes by outlining priorities for advancing MC contingency theory through research on the functions and interdependencies of MC practices, the implications of digital technologies, and the evolution of MC over time.

papers.title: Developing agile teams from the inside out: The role of team and individual psychological capital
Avoiding the AI knowledge trap: A simulation-based forecast of entry-level automation, talent pipelines, and innovation capacity
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly capable of automating professional tasks traditionally performed by entry-level staff. While such automation may drive short-term efficiency and profitability, it risks disrupting the experience-based learning pipeline essential for developing a firm's long-term innovation capacity. This paper introduces the Knowledge Trap: a structural condition where immediate gains from AI adoption lead to the gradual degradation of the tacit knowledge and adaptive search capabilities required for future performance. Using an NK agent-based simulation model, the study examines how different sectors and governance horizons influence this risk. The model distinguishes between three adoption strategies - substitutive, hybrid, and complementary - to track their long-term effects on a firm's experience pool and innovation fitness. The findings demonstrate that the Knowledge Trap is most severe under substitutive adoption, particularly in sectors with high task interdependency. Conversely, adopting AI in a complementary mode can substantially mitigate these capability losses. This research contributes a forecasting framework to help organisations and policymakers identify structural risks and develop AI implementation strategies that protect the human talent pipeline.

papers.title: The economics of bundling in casino markets: Theory and evidence from U.S. gaming destinations
When AI does too much: Generative AI vs agentic AI and traveller empowerment in travel planning
Rethinking the Anatomy of Passion: A Biopsychosocial Configurational Perspective on Antecedents of Work and Entrepreneurial Passion
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Despite over two decades of passion research, our understanding of how passion is construed remains fragmented and dominated by additive approaches that treat antecedents as isolated predictors (both theoretically and empirically). Drawing on the biopsychosocial (BPS) framework, we challenge prior research by reconceptualizing passion as a configurational phenomenon emerging through interdependent BPS conditions which combine in complex ways to form equifinal pathways to passion. In doing so, we comparatively analyze configurations associated with harmonious and obsessive passion across the two most frequently studied domains in the management literature: work and entrepreneurship. To empirically examine this configurational perspective, we employ fuzzy set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA), which is well equipped to test the equifinal, compensatory, and interdependent nature of configural constructs. Using two time‐lagged samples of employees and entrepreneurs, we identify multiple distinct configurations that not only differentiate harmonious from obsessive passion but also distinguish passion across the work and entrepreneurial domains. Our results demonstrate that passion is largely domain‐contingent, such that work and entrepreneurial passion are each associated with mostly unique BPS configurations rather than universally operating antecedents. Our study advances passion research by shifting attention from isolated net effects toward a holistic view of passion as a system of interdependent BPS predictors.

papers.title: Data Breach Risks of Adopting Interorganizational Data Exchange Systems: Evidence from Health Information Exchange Adoption
Pricing the Priceless? How Communities Challenge the Marketization of Public Goods and Services
Acts, Threats, and Regime Shifts: U.S. Policy Uncertainty, Global Geopolitical Risk, and Korean Sectoral Stock Returns
How Does Green Transformation Shapes Corporate Investment: The Conditional Role of Green Finance
How Digital Governance Reshapes Corporate Fixed Asset Investment: Evidence from the Data Security Law
Ripple in Green: The Supply Chain Spillover Effects of Green Finance
Selective industrial policy for the EU open strategic autonomy: The role of products' relatedness
papers.abstract: The European Union has adopted the concept of Open Strategic Autonomy (OSA) to reduce strategic dependencies while preserving openness to international trade. An important policy question is therefore which countries are best positioned to develop new trade advantages in strategic products. Building on the literature on relatedness and export diversification, we address this question by complementing the standard notion of product distance, measuring how close a country is to a product compared to other countries, and how close a product is to a country's productive structure compared to other products. We term these concepts absolute and relative distance advantages. We argue that relative distance advantages reflect countries' incentives to diversify into a product, whereas absolute distance advantages capture their ability to successfully develop new trade advantage in that product. Using trade data for EU countries, we show that both dimensions significantly predict the emergence of new export specializations in products identified by the EU as strategic.

papers.title: Digging Into the Subsoil: Considering and Theorizing Human Services Delivery at the Sub‐Micro‐Level of the Public Service Ecosystem
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Public services are often delivered in partnership with families and communities, yet these relationships receive limited attention within public service ecosystem (PSE) theory. Responding to call to develop the sub‐micro‐level of the PSE, we introduce the concept of subsoil sensitivity to foreground the family and community ecosystems that underpin public service value creation. These informal systems are active sites of value creation and destruction with sensitivities arising from their alignment or misalignment with public services. We propose legislative and policy nodes as connectors that translate macrolevel policy into microlevel practice. Drawing on child protection vignettes, we show how nodes create the conditions for interaction, while subsoil dynamics influence whether value is cocreated or codestroyed amid power asymmetries and differing belief systems. The paper extends the sub‐micro‐level of the PSE and offers a framework for examining family and community ecosystems in public service delivery.

papers.title: The difficulties of reducing administrative burden via the nonprofit sector: how sedimented governance stifles care coordination
papers.abstract: Care coordination services are designed to reduce administrative burden. However, they may not always achieve this aim. This paper, which draws from care coordination service user experiences, provides insights concerning why policies designed to reduce administrative burden may struggle when embedded in existing institutional systems, and how they might inadvertently contribute to new costs. We thematically analyse a multi-modal dataset concerning dementia care navigation services provided by non-profits in two English counties and find that stakeholders’ efforts to deal with administrative burden-related costs may be unsuccessful and potentially counterproductive: attempts to maximize information provision, reduce psychological costs and avoid compliance costs may obscure the role of a care coordination service so that learning costs remain high or even increase. We show that while studies have argued that non-profits in pluralist, networked governance models can reduce burdens, the ways they interact with sedimented governance logics can stifle such efforts.

papers.title: The only game in town: NPM’s resilience and depoliticizing effects in (r)urban sustainability transition
papers.abstract: This article explains the resilience of New Public Management (NPM) by conceptualizing it as a ‘mobile assemblage’ of flexible ideas and practices translated across contexts. Drawing on a qualitative study of four Swedish municipalities undergoing (r)urban sustainability transition, we demonstrate how NPM is mobilized as a set of flexible resources – managerial tools, entrepreneurial identities, market-making devices, legitimizing discursive resources, and behaviour-prescribing scripts – to organize transition initiatives. NPM thus becomes raw material for four governing arrangements – temporary projects, consultant collaboration, municipally owned companies, and public-private partnerships. Through these arrangements, NPM embeds market and management logics into local governance, fostering silent depoliticization.

papers.title: Assessing mediation of sexual orientation disparities in miscarriage by age at pregnancy, gravidity, and use of medically assisted reproduction in four national cohorts
papers.abstract: Recent research has documented a higher miscarriage risk among sexual minority individuals than heterosexual individuals. These disparities may be partly mediated by age at pregnancy, gravidity, and use of medically assisted reproduction (MAR). We used data from four cohorts (Nurses' Health Study 2 and 3, Growing Up Today Study, and National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health) to estimate randomized interventional analogues of mediational direct and indirect effects of sexual orientation on miscarriage (pure natural direct effects [rPNDE], total natural indirect effects [rTNIE], and proportions mediated [rPM]). We found that pregnancies to sexual minority individuals were more likely to end in a miscarriage than those to heterosexual individuals. We found weak mediation of this effect by age (rPNDE: 1.23, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.15-1.32; rTNIE: 1.02, 95% CI: 1.01-1.03; rPM: 12%, 95% CI: 5%-19%), but not gravidity (rPM: 2%, 95% CI: -1%-6%) and MAR use (rPM: -1%, 95% CI: -4%-3%). While these factors impact miscarriage risk, our findings suggest that sexual orientation disparities in miscarriage are only minimally explained by age, and not explained by gravidity and use of MAR, contributing to the understanding of the role of pregnancy-related factors vs. structural factors in sexual orientation disparities in miscarriage.

papers.title: Neighborhood deprivation and the risk of stillbirth in New York
papers.abstract: Stillbirth (fetal death ≥ 20 weeks gestation) occurs in approximately 21,000 births each year in the United States. Previous studies have observed associations between neighborhood deprivation and adverse perinatal outcomes. We estimated associations between neighborhood deprivation and singleton stillbirth in New York. We performed a cross-sectional study of stillbirths and live births from hospital claims data from the Statewide Planning and Research Cooperative System (2022-2024). Neighborhood deprivation index (NDI) at the census tract level was assigned to geocoded addresses at delivery. Risk ratios (RR) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated using a generalized estimating equations model adjusted for individual-level maternal variables of age at delivery, race/ethnicity, marital status, and primary health insurance payer. Our analysis included 3,128 stillbirths and 552,361 live births. The NDI quartiles were associated with stillbirth, with higher levels of deprivation corresponding to increased risk compared to the least deprived quartiles. We observed the highest risk of stillbirth among women in the most deprived quartile (RR 1.42; 95% CI 1.25-1.61). The association of NDI quartile on the risk of stillbirth did not differ by race/ethnicity. Our findings highlight that women residing in the most deprived NDI quartile could benefit from enhanced prenatal services and support.

papers.title: Identification and dating of pregnancies in administrative healthcare claims databases: An updated, transparent, and transportable algorithm
papers.abstract: Studies using routinely collected healthcare data are essential for understanding the benefit-risk profile of medications in pregnancy. However, reproducibility is limited by the lack of shared pregnancy identification algorithms, and generalizability is constrained by their development primarily in commercial insurance databases. A previously developed pregnancy identification algorithm was updated for ICD-10-CM and translated into a standardized format to support transport across diverse databases. Algorithm implementation characteristics were evaluated in three US health insurance claims databases (2000-2025), including commercially and publicly insured populations. Overall, 5.8 million and 3.0 million pregnancies were identified in two commercial databases (Merative™ and Optum) and 2.3 million pregnancies in Merative™ MarketScan® Multi-State Medicaid Database (MDCD). Across databases, live birth prevalence ranged from 76-83%, miscarriage/abortion 15-23%, ectopic pregnancy 1%, and stillbirth ≤0.5%, with a higher proportion of live births in MDCD. Pregnancy dating methods varied substantially across coding eras: use of gestational age records increased from 4-9% in the ICD-9-CM era to 87-92% during the ICD-10-CM era, with greater use in MDCD. Using a standardized algorithm, this study demonstrates how database characteristics and coding transitions influence pregnancy identification and dating in healthcare data, highlighting methodological considerations for reproducible pregnancy research across data sources.

papers.title: A recipe for population-based doubly robust estimation via weighting, regression, calibration, and standardization
papers.abstract: A large class of doubly robust estimators can be viewed as regression standardization augmented by a bias correction based on inverse probability of treatment weights. These estimators are often justified as solutions to augmented inverse probability weighted (AIPW) estimating equations. When regression standardization is based on a canonical-link generalized linear model fit via maximum likelihood estimation to an inverse probability of treatment weighted sample (IPTW-GLM), double robustness holds without any explicit bias correction. These estimators have usually targeted causal effects within a population represented by the study sample. Here, we present a unification and extension of these doubly robust estimators in terms of constructing a weighted pseudosample that represents a flexible target population with randomized exposures. This allows the bias correction to be understood and operationalized as calibrating the outcome model to match the group means within the balanced pseudosample, illuminating the connection between IPTW-GLM and other AIPW estimators. It also allows the straightforward construction of estimators that are doubly robust for target populations other than the study sample, which is useful when data come from studies where enrollment depends on exposure (e.g., observational cohort studies).

papers.title: Compulsive Sexual Behaviour vs Problematic Pornography Use: Converging Evidence of Distinct Constructs from GGM, EGA and Bayesian Networks
How Frequent is Sexual Exploitation Among Passengers of Ridehailing, Robotaxis, and Taxis? Prevalence, Relative Risk, and Comparison with Industry Disclosures
Burden of Disease Attributable to Violence in Childhood in the United Kingdom
papers.abstract: Childhood exposure to violence is widespread in the UK and leads to significant long-term mental, behavioural, and physical health problems. While some violence types are recognised in the Global Burden of Disease (GBD) framework, many remain overlooked, and the complete burden in the UK had not been previously quantified. This study estimated the disease burden attributable to various forms of violence-including physical, emotional, and sexual abuse, neglect, domestic violence, bullying, and community violence-experienced before age 18. Using UK and Australian data, population attributable fractions (PAFs) were calculated for conditions like depression, anxiety, alcohol use disorder, smoking, and self-harm, and applied to 2021 GBD UK figures. Results showed that 7.9% of total Disability Adjusted Life Years (DALYs) were attributable to childhood violence, with men bearing a higher burden, particularly for smoking and self-harm, and women for depression and anxiety. These findings highlight the urgent need for stronger violence prevention and trauma-informed approaches in the UK.

papers.title: Supernatural explanations and norm enforcement in nine societies
papers.abstract: Historical and ethnographic evidence suggests that people around the world use supernatural beliefs to explain misfortune. The cross-cultural prevalence of this pattern may arise from our expectations that norm violations lead to sanctioning. In cases where an outcome seems punitive yet lacks an identifiable cause, individuals, motivated to fill this explanatory gap, may rely on beliefs in supernatural punishment to make sense of what has happened. If true, supernatural explanations for misfortunes should be more common when a victim is believed to have not cooperated in the past (i.e., in cases where misfortunes might be unexplained but otherwise appear deserved). Using a vignette experiment across nine diverse populations ( N = 714), including African hunter-gatherers and Melanesian horticulturalists, we tested if knowledge of past bad actions increased participants' endorsements of supernatural causes for misfortune. Across all populations, participants rated a misfortune as more likely to be supernaturally caused when the victim was known to have failed to reciprocate a favour or engage in generous actions towards others in the past. This was slightly increased when the behaviour was additionally labelled normative. Responses to open-ended free-listing questions provide additional evidence that when the victim was known to be uncooperative, participants were more likely to propose supernatural causes for misfortune as well as supernatural solutions. Additional normative labelling had only a small effect. Together, these findings suggest that when misfortunes lack clear causes, people's motivation to explain interacts with moral evaluations, leading them to invoke supernatural beliefs most commonly when misfortune appears deserved.

papers.title: Framing Service-Learning Experiences: Evidence From a Survey Experiment Engaging Prosocial and Pre-Professional Identities
papers.abstract: Universities are increasingly expected to integrate civic and social goals into their curricula, yet it remains unclear how to engage students whose motivations are primarily professional. Service-learning experiences (SLEs), which combine academic study with community service, are one strategy, but student self-selection complicates design and evaluation. Because SLEs help cultivate the voluntary sector’s future volunteers and donors, who gains access is a question for the sector, not only for educators. This study examines how prosocial and pre-professional identities shape students’ interest in SLEs and whether course framing influences engagement. In a preregistered survey experiment, students evaluated SLEs framed as descriptive, volunteer-focused, or career-focused. Altruistic values and pre-professional identity modestly but significantly predicted interest; volunteer identity did not. Course framing had no effect. These findings suggest civic and professional orientations may be more compatible than assumed, and engagement depends less on framing than on integration within broader curricular and developmental pathways.

papers.title: Public policy and political trust within unequal societies: evidence from India
papers.abstract: Deeply entrenched socioeconomic inequalities complicate public service delivery, especially for local governments in developing countries. In jurisdictions characterized by deep economic cleavages, it can be exceedingly difficult for local governments to fund and deliver public works that satisfy most citizens’ needs in a timely and efficient manner. However, one of the tragic consequences of extreme inequality is that it reduces people’s trust in their government. Here, we hypothesize that policy interventions that encourage the co-production of local public works, such as bottom-up, demand-driven rural development programs, help neutralize the negative effect of inequalities on trust in local governance institutions by improving perceptions of state responsiveness and building social capital. Using quasi-experimental methods, large-N panel data, and the case of the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA) – the world’s largest rural employment guarantee initiative – our analysis finds support for these expectations.

papers.title: Co-optimization of intraday and frequency containment reserve bids for battery energy storage
papers.abstract: As renewable energy integration increases supply variability, battery energy storage systems (BESS) present a viable solution for balancing supply and demand. This paper proposes a joint bidding strategy that combines participation in the primary frequency reserve market with continuous trading in the intraday market, addressing a gap in the extant literature that typically considers these markets in isolation and simplifies the continuous nature of intraday trading. Our approach utilizes a mixed integer linear programming implementation of the rolling intrinsic algorithm for intraday decisions and state of charge recovery, alongside a learned classifier strategy (LCS) that determines optimal day-ahead capacity allocation between markets. A comprehensive out-of-sample backtest over more than one year of tick level historical German market data validates our approach: The LCS increases overall profits by over 4\% compared to the best-performing static strategy and by more than 3\% over a naive dynamic benchmark. Crucially, our method closes the gap to a theoretical perfect foresight strategy to just 4\%, demonstrating the effectiveness of dynamic, learning-based allocation in a complex, multi-market environment.

papers.title: Data center cooling in the AI era: cross-scale challenges and system-level outlook
Capacity design in district energy systems with thermal energy storage – a new planning paradigm
papers.abstract: Planning future district energy systems is increasingly challenged by uncertainties in demand growth and spatial development. Conventional planning resolves this by oversizing infrastructure to meet projected peak demand – tying up capital in assets used only a fraction of the year, with reactive upgrades still required where demand develops beyond projections. The result is a persistent trade-off between cost, emissions, and resiliency. This study proposes a new paradigm for capacity design that treats thermal energy storage (TES) – and particularly strategically placed decentralized TES (DecTES) – as an integrated design element that adds a degree of freedom to the capacity design problem. While centralized TES reduces peak production requirements, DecTES additionally resolves transmission bottlenecks by absorbing peak demand locally, adding a spatial dimension to system flexibility. The approach is demonstrated on district cooling and heating systems at Stanford, California, and Aalborg, Denmark. At Stanford, existing TES reduces OPEX by ~12% and CO₂ emissions by ~7% annually; doubling TES potentially adds ~2% OPEX and ~1.5% CO₂ savings, and DecTES enables 20-23% local demand growth without infrastructure expansion. In Aalborg, existing TES delivers ~10% OPEX savings and ~17% CO₂ reductions; DecTES enables 20-28% local demand growth at baseline and 54-62% under adaptive operation, potentially adds ~2.5% OPEX and ~5% CO₂ savings, and phases out decentralized fossil peak production. The analyses also indicate derived electricity-grid benefits, with connection capacity reducible by 24% and 39% respectively. Unlike conventional peak capacity, TES delivers year-round value from day one – reducing planning risk regardless of how demand unfolds.

papers.title: Accelerating wind-farm AEP evaluation by exploiting near-low-rank wake structure
Two-stage robust coordinated scheduling of port integrated energy systems for resilience enhancement with flexible resource collaboration
Long-term stochastic modelling and economic assessment of a centralised CCU network
Advances in sorption-based thermochemical energy storage: from material properties to prototype-level performance
Arrow's shadow over climate governance
papers.abstract: For thirty years, climate negotiations have failed to produce a stable and widely accepted rule for distributing mitigation burdens, even as finance, technology, and loss and damage have advanced. Political will, free-riding, and domestic constraints explain part of that, but not why the deadlock persists. This paper contends that the challenge is structural. It uses Arrow's voting paradox to diagnose the burden-sharing track of the climate negotiations and to draw the institutional consequences. Burden-sharing constitutes a preference-aggregation problem involving incompatible fairness principles. Arrow's impossibility theorem elucidates both the nature and direction of this difficulty: no procedure can transform divergent rankings of historical responsibility, capability, and equal per capita claims into a single, stable, and broadly accepted formula. Although the theorem does not establish formal impossibility within a treaty context or explain any specific negotiation breakdown, it highlights a constraint that neither improved analysis nor increased commitment has overcome.Because the constraint is structural and unsolvable, agreement proceeds by working around the aggregation problem. Issue linkage relaxes Arrow’s independence condition, while the Paris Agreement shifts aggregation from an ex ante distribution to self-differentiation, focal points, and an ex post stocktake of collective progress. Sen’s comparative justice helps explain why this works: parties need not agree on a fair allocation to agree that some outcomes are worse than others. The deeper threat to cooperation is therefore not disagreement over shares within the shared frame, but rejection of the frame itself.

papers.title: Who owns the land after regime collapse? Shifting land claims and tenure governance in post-2021 Afghanistan
papers.abstract: In Afghanistan, land ownership has long shifted with political power. Successive regime changes have reshaped who is recognised as an owner, who can occupy property, and how territorial resources are redistributed. The Taliban’s return in 2021 did not produce formal land reform, but it reopened a familiar pattern in which political transition unsettles property relations and enables new forms of control. Drawing on qualitative interviews with Afghan landowners now living in exile, this article examines how ownership moves between informal occupation and formal recognition. Houses, plots, and commercial spaces often remain legally tied to former owners while authority is renegotiated on the ground. In some cases, occupation becomes institutionalised through administrative approval, new documentation, or policy measures that regularise access for politically aligned actors. Property change therefore unfolds less as a single act of confiscation than as a layered process through which possession, mediation, and emerging governance practices redefine ownership. The analysis shows how struggles over land operate as a mechanism for reassembling political order. Ownership becomes increasingly difficult to exercise across distance, producing conditions in which property may persist on paper or be reassigned through governmental decree, while recognition and effective control shift in practice. By foregrounding absent owners and unsettled claims, the article contributes to land use policy debates on restitution, return, and post-conflict land administration, with implications for other fragile political environments.

papers.title: From urban greenbelt to peri-urban ecological zone: A counterfactual evaluation of nature-based solutions under the Park City strategy
Quantitative analysis of public perception regarding nuclear waste in Türkiye: Knowledge level, risk perception, and trust indicators
Do international critical mineral prices influence energy access? Evidence from developing countries
Electric vehicle–integrated sustainable community microgrids: A review of control strategies, challenges, opportunities and pathways toward SDG 7
papers.abstract: The demand for electricity continues to increase with economic growth and increasing end-use electrification, particularly in the transport sector. Despite ongoing progress, achieving Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 7 by 2030, which aims to provide affordable and clean energy for all, remains uneven and structurally constrained. Electric vehicle (EV)-integrated community microgrids (MGs), operating in grid-connected or islanded modes are a promising solution that combines distributed energy resources, local electricity generation options and mobile energy storage systems (ESSs) through EV fleets. However, the high penetration of renewable energy resources, EVs and battery ESSs introduces significant challenges to system stability, power flow and operational reliability. This review provides a comprehensive assessment of recent developments in EV-integrated community MGs, energy management, decentralized EV fleet coordination and bidirectional EV charging/discharging into the electricity network. It also provides a framework for integrating MGs, EVs, and renewables, including grid-to-vehicle (G2V) charging, bidirectional vehicle-to-grid (V2G) and vehicle-to-everything (V2X) applications, to enhance grid flexibility and ancillary services. It further discusses the optimization mechanisms, control frameworks and their applications within the MG environment. In addition, the review evaluates the contribution of EV-integrated community MGs toward achieving SDG 7 in sustainable community energy systems. The analysis also addresses existing technical, economic, social acceptance and regulatory challenges that hinder large-scale deployments. The study outlines future research directions and proposes a conceptual framework for researchers and policymakers, offering actionable pathways to accelerate the global clean energy transition and support the achievement of the UN 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development.

papers.title: Towards reducing the environmental impact of the healthcare industry through circular economy strategies
Correction to “Application of the Biological Toxicity Effect Ratio (BER) Method for Advancing Water Quality Criteria Derivation”
Nanoconfinement Drives Non-Monotonic Methane Density in Shale Nanopores: Direct Observation of Competitive Water–Gas Exchange
papers.abstract: Abstract The efficiency of unconventional gas recovery is fundamentally governed by the nanoscale partitioning and competitive exchange between methane and water in shale reservoirs, yet direct experimental insight into their coupled behavior under in situ conditions (pressure and temperature) remains elusive. Here, we integrate a first-of-its-kind approach, combining contrast-matching ultra- and small-angle neutron scattering (USANS/SANS) at 50 MPa with vapor sorption, cryo-microscopy, and molecular simulations, to achieve unprecedented direct visualization of methane–water distribution across the multiscale pore–fracture network of the Longmaxi Shale. We report a fundamental revision to classical models, discovering that methane density exhibits a non-monotonic dependence on pore size, increasing with nanoconfinement but peaking sharply at ≈2 nm before declining in sub-2 nm pores. Mechanistically, water forms continuous films on hydrophilic quartz surfaces but aggregates into distinct clusters on organic kerogen. The stronger affinity of water for quartz and its increasing interaction with kerogen at higher saturations enable it to displace adsorbed methane competitively, thereby directly controlling local gas saturation. Furthermore, we reveal that microfractures are the dominant pathways for early water flowback and subsequent gas migration, with pore–fracture connectivity dictating fluid accessibility and phase exchange efficiency. These results establish a mechanistic link between interfacial nanophysics and macro-scale reservoir performance, providing a scientific foundation for optimizing hydraulic fracturing and maximizing resource recovery in deep sedimentary systems.

papers.title: Slippery Amphiphilic Antifouling Loose Nanofiltration Membrane with “Double-Defense” Functionalities for High-Salinity Organic Wastewater Sustainable Management
papers.abstract: Abstract Loose nanofiltration (LNF) holds potential for sustainable management of high-salinity organic wastewater through precise organics/salts fractionation, but practical application is constrained by severe organic–inorganic combined fouling. Herein, we propose a “double-defense” antifouling strategy and develop a slippery amphiphilic LNF membrane via facile stepwise surface modification. A hydrophilic branched polyethylenimine (PEI) network was first cross-linked onto a polyamide (PA) substrate to form a fouling-resistant protection layer, followed by covalent grafting of liquid-like polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) brushes to confer a slippery, fouling-release surface. The PEI layer acts as a hydration and electrostatic barrier to repel organic-cation complexes and scale precursors, while the slippery PDMS layer with high mobility and low surface energy minimizes interfacial interactions and strengthens hydraulic shear responsiveness. During the concentration of authentic leachate membrane bioreactor (MBR) effluent, the optimized membrane showed superior antifouling performance: low flux decline ratio (FDR) of 41.6% and high flux recovery ratio (FRR) of 98.1%, outperforming a commercial PA membrane (FDR 91.2%, FRR 78.4%). It also delivered an organics/salts fractionation selectivity 7.8 times that of the commercial membrane, demonstrating multiple cycles stability. This rationally designed architecture offers a practical solution for challenging wastewater and is extensible to other PA-based membrane systems in environmental applications.

papers.title: From Nontargeted Analysis to Toxicity: Revealing the Disinfection Byproduct Exposome
papers.abstract: Abstract Chemical disinfection is essential for ensuring the microbiological safety of drinking water, but it inevitably generates disinfection byproducts (DBPs), introducing a complex and largely unresolved chemical burden. Trihalomethanes (THMs) and haloacetic acids (HAAs) have long underpinned DBP regulation, shaping monitoring and treatment strategies. However, recent analytical advances have fundamentally reshaped our understanding of DBPs. In this perspective, we examine how high-resolution mass spectrometry (HRMS)-based nontargeted analysis (NTA) has expanded the detectable DBP chemical space, while revealing key limitations that hinder translation from detection to identification. We then highlight emerging mass spectrometry and computational approaches as key pathways toward scalable DBP discovery and identification. We further examine the disconnect between rapid DBP discovery and limited toxicological understanding, highlighting key limitations of current toxicity assessments, including high-dose testing paradigms, fragmented end points, and overlooked mixture effects. To address these challenges, we propose an exposome-oriented framework as a conceptual model that integrates comprehensive chemical characterization with toxicity assessment, highlighting the need for future computational tools and prioritization strategies. Bridging chemical diversity to health relevance will be critical for prioritizing DBPs of concern and supporting risk-informed water quality management and public health protection.

papers.title: Investigations of New Particle Formation Mechanisms in North China Plain during the Spring Campaign Based on Observations and Simulations
papers.abstract: Abstract New particle formation (NPF) plays a critical role in atmospheric aerosol loading, yet the mechanisms controlling NPF under high-pollution conditions remain poorly understood. Ground-based measurements and GEOS-Chem-APM simulations were combined to investigate the factors governing NPF in a typical industrial city over North China Plain. During the spring campaign (3 May-2 June 2016), 10 NPF days were identified, each preceded by nighttime northwesterly ventilation and occurring under dry daytime conditions. The model reproduced 6 of 10 observed NPF events, whereas the remaining 4 showed substantially weaker simulated nucleation. Well-simulated events were generally associated with low relative humidity (RH) and condensation sink (CS) environment. NH3 remained in large excess throughout the campaign. In our test, increasing H2SO4 by up to a factor of 3 substantially enhanced nucleation rate (J) but did not fully reproduce the observed particle evolution, while replacing modeled RH and aerosol surface area with observations only moderately adjusted J. The model underestimated growth rates by 51% and 75% on well-simulated and poorly simulated days. These results indicate that nighttime ventilation reduces surface area and CS of pre-existing aerosol loading, favoring NPF, while successful reproduction of observed NPF depends jointly on diverse precursor-driven nucleation, aerosol scavenging, and subsequent particle growth.

papers.title: Cross-Level Responses of Freshwater Zooplankton to Micro/Nanoplastics: A Meta-Analysis Integrating Individual- to Community-Level Evidence
papers.abstract: Abstract Despite the known threats of micro/nanoplastics (MNPs) to freshwater ecosystems, their risks to zooplankton remain poorly resolved because existing evidence is fragmented across biological levels. Consequently, associations between lower-level responses and population- and community-level outcomes remain unclear. Here, we synthesized 3042 research cases from controlled experiments worldwide covering 12 response categories. We found significant overall negative effects of MNPs in systems without predators, with predators, and with predator-conditioned medium. Although molecular-level evidence remains limited, a consistent hierarchical response pattern emerged under predator-absent conditions. We therefore propose a conceptual hierarchical effect pathway (HEP) framework integrating effect sizes and cross-level associations. Within this framework, MNPs exposure was associated with increased ingestion of MNPs, physiological damage, feeding impairment, and reduced activity and defense. These responses formed an upstream tier associated with life-history impairments, including impaired growth and development, reduced reproductive capacity, and reduced survival, although these associations do not establish temporal ordering or causation. Under predator-present conditions, negative population- and community-level effects were also observed. Effect magnitudes also varied with MNPs characteristics, exposure duration, and zooplankton group. Together, the HEP framework clarifies cross-level associations and helps identify informative endpoints and incorporate food-web context into risk assessment of MNPs.

papers.title: Global Potential of No-Tillage in Enhancing Soil Carbon and Reducing Greenhouse Gas Emissions While Sustaining Crop Yields
papers.abstract: Abstract Pursuing the balance between environmental sustainability and agricultural productivity remains a critical challenge for achieving global sustainable development goals. No-tillage (NT), as a key measure of sustainable conservation and climate-smart agriculture, offers a promising approach to addressing this challenge. However, its comprehensive effects on soil carbon accumulation, greenhouse gas emissions, and crop yields remain unquantified at the global scale, limiting our ability to optimize both environmental and agronomic outcomes. Here, we conducted such a global synthesis by combining a meta-analysis of 8,303 paired observations from 1,371 studies with a random forest model to assess the influence of site conditions and management on NT effects. Our meta-analysis demonstrates integrated benefits of NT in enhancing soil organic carbon (SOC) stocks in 0–30 cm layer by 11.0% and mitigating greenhouse gas (the sum of CO2, CH4, and N2O in CO2-equivalent) emissions by 13.5%, without a significant impact on crop yields (−0.6% ± 1.5%). The integrated benefits are stronger in drier climates and coarser-textured soils, and they exhibit significant time-dependent patterns. Our prediction identifies 44% of global croplands as being optimal for NT’s integrated benefits, mainly in Africa, South Asia, and North America. Adopting NT in these areas would result in a 4.8% increase in major food-crop yields, a 15.2% increase in 0–30 cm SOC stocks, and a 6.4% reduction in global cropland emissions, respectively. These findings underscore the relevance of implementing NT in suitable regions by adopting it into Good Agricultural Practice Guidelines.

papers.title: Pollutant Release and Transfer Registers (PRTRs) as a Cornerstone of Global Chemicals Management: Current Gaps and Future Directions
papers.abstract: Abstract Pollutant Release and Transfer Register (PRTR) systems in different countries are key tools for global chemicals management and an important data source for measuring progress toward achieving Sustainable Development Goal 12 of sustainable consumption and production patterns. However, current implementations face several structural and functional limitations that hinder the broad applicability of the PRTR reporting data. These limitations can be categorized into two main aspects: within-system issues and between-system inconsistencies. Within systems, data gaps can result from limited monitoring of nonpoint sources, incomplete reporting, exemptions due to thresholds and confidentiality agreements, and other similar factors, while data inaccuracies can be caused by estimation errors, duplicated counts, and other related issues. Between systems, differences in chemical lists, threshold settings, emission source types, reporting methods, and other discrepancies can hinder data comparability and integration, limiting the effectiveness of global chemicals management. Addressing these issues, through unified pollutant lists, harmonized reporting methodologies, expanded source coverage, and improved data verification, can significantly strengthen the utility of PRTR systems, advancing an integrated and evidence-based global sound management of chemicals.

papers.title: Direct Upcycling of Rare Earth Hyperaccumulator Biomass into Luminescent CaS:Ce Phosphors
papers.abstract: Abstract Rare earth elements (REEs) are essential to high-tech industries and sustainable development, but traditional mining poses significant environmental challenges. Phytomining, which uses hyperaccumulators to recover REEs from soils or low-grade mines, has emerged as a sustainable alternative; however, the high cost and low efficiency of extracting and purifying REEs from harvested biomass remain major barriers to its practical application. Here, we propose a novel in situ doping strategy to directly convert cerium (Ce)-enriched hyperaccumulator biomass into color-tunable CaS:Ce phosphors and value-added syngas, bypassing complex separation of Ca and REEs. The results show that Ce, Ca, and S could be selectively enriched from hyperaccumulator biomass to the resulting char through solvothermal pretreatment with sulfuric acid and ethanol. Subsequent steam gasification of the char produces Ce-doped CaS phosphors with broad, green-yellow emission and high photoluminescence quantum yields of 18.5–37.4%. Our approach reduces energy use by 33.6%, carbon emissions by 22.4%, and costs by \$2.62 kg–1 biomass, outperforming conventional REE recovery in both environmental and economic sustainability. This strategy provides an environmentally sustainable and economically viable route for high-value utilization of REE-rich biomass, addressing a critical bottleneck in phytomining and advancing its development as a green REE recovery technology.

papers.title: Fe(II) Speciation Regulates Microbial Metabolic Reprogramming and Phototrophic Fe(II) Mineralization in Rhodopseudomonas palustris SX2
papers.abstract: Abstract Phototrophic iron mineralization (PIM) is a keystone biogeochemical process linking anoxic iron redox transformations to carbon sequestration. Although PIM is widely documented, how Fe(II) speciation impacts cell physiology and thus causes divergent mineralization phenotypes remains poorly understood. In this study, we systematically investigated the physiological, mineralogical, and molecular responses of a newly isolated photoferrotroph, Rhodopseudomonas palustris SX2, exposed to uncomplexed Fe(II) [Fe(II) without OM] versus organically complexed Fe(II) [Fe(II)-OM] under anoxic and illuminated conditions. We demonstrate that distinct Fe(II) speciation drives divergent metabolic reprogramming for rapid metabolic adaptation and phototrophic biomineralization phenotypes. Fe(II) without OM triggered cell-surface encrustation and activated stress-mitigation and metal-efflux systems, whereas Fe(II)-OM stimulated the formation of discrete intracellular iron nanoparticles while upregulating photosynthetic light harvesting and autotrophic CO2 fixation. Furthermore, genetic knockout and complementation confirmed that the pioABC operon constitutes the indispensable electron conduit driving Fe(II) oxidation across both speciation regimes, with organic complexation significantly enhancing its transcriptional activation. Our findings reveal how metabolic adaptation driven by Fe(II) speciation dictates the spatial distribution of biogenic iron minerals and regulates the efficiency of coupled carbon sequestration in anoxic ecosystems.

papers.title: Wastewater Treatment Plants as Anchor Infrastructure for Geothermal Energy in Cold Regions
papers.abstract: Abstract Thermal constraints in cold regions suppress biological treatment, increase energy demand, and elevate greenhouse gas emissions of existing wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs), and remain a major barrier to the deployment of adequate sanitation infrastructure in many cold-region communities. Where geothermal resources exist, low-enthalpy hydrothermal heat is well matched to this energy gap. Yet, WWTPs are underrecognized anchors for broader geothermal deployment, providing a continuous, weather-independent thermal offtake through which subsurface CAPEX can be amortized. We reframe geothermal-WWTP integration as a system-level enabler that benefits both parts. Using three cascaded configurations for a full-scale WWTP, a rapid techno-economic analysis identifies three trends: energy and carbon savings/revenues alone are insufficient under realistic policy stacks, whereas crediting the upgrade-deferral value of geothermally enhanced treatment makes the project economically favorable across most policy scenarios. Globally, this triple intersection encompasses ∼11,600 catalogued WWTPs serving ∼280 million people, with a further estimate of ∼48 million people in the same regions beyond current service radii. The opportunity is greatest in cold, remote, and underserved communities, where local geothermal resources, treatment intensification, and community-scale demand together carry a case that no single driver could sustain alone.

papers.title: Multi-Omics Gut Microbiome Species Communities and Functional Modules Linking Metal Exposures to Children’s Neurodevelopmental Health in a Canadian Birth Cohort
papers.abstract: Abstract Early life metal exposure has been associated with adverse neurodevelopment, with gut microbiome disruption proposed as a potential pathway. However, most studies have focused on individual taxa or pathways, despite microbes functioning within ecological communities and coordinated functional networks. Here, we integrated stool metal measurements, shotgun metagenomics, metatranscriptomics, and neurodevelopmental assessments in 116 children aged 8–12 years from the GESTE birth cohort in Sherbrooke, Canada. Nineteen metals were quantified in stool samples, and neurodevelopment was assessed using parent-reported behavioral scales, attention performance testing, and resting-state fMRI. Using network-based community detection, we identified 10 co-occurring species communities (SCs) from metagenomic data and 16 coexpressed functional modules (FMs) from metatranscriptomic data and evaluated their associations with metal exposures and neurodevelopmental outcomes. Higher levels of lead, cadmium, aluminum, zinc, copper, and magnesium were associated with lower abundance of Streptococcus- and Veillonella-dominated SCs, while multiple metals were associated with lower abundance of amino acid metabolism and carbohydrate degradation FMs. Exploratory mediation analyses suggested potential indirect associations between stool metals and parent-reported ADHD-related traits througha methionine cycle-related FM or sequentially through a Clostridium spp. SC and a Factor 420 biosynthesis FM. These findings suggest that stool metal concentrations are associated with community-level variations in gut microbial composition and function, some of which were further associated with parent-reported ADHD-related traits.

Energy and carbon routing in hydrothermal conversion of lignocellulosic biomass: An uncertainty-aware machine-learning framework
papers.abstract: Reliable assessment of hydrothermal lignocellulosic biomass conversion requires quantitative prediction of how feedstock mass, chemical energy, and carbon partition among bio-oil, solid residues, aqueous products, and gases under heterogeneous feedstock, solvent, catalyst, and severity conditions. We constructed a harmonized database of 3,693 HTL/HTC experiments from 187 scientific papers and 433 different biomass samples, with temperatures up to ∼ 600 ◦C and maximum residence times of up to 1,200 min. From this literature-scale dataset, we developed an uncertainty-aware machine-learning framework for predicting mass partitioning, energy and carbon allocation, and higher heating value (HHV) of condensed phases. Among the tree-ensemble regression methods examined, Random Forest (RF) provided the most stable cross-target compromise, with test R2 values for product yields around 0.8, energy/carbon allocation metrics between 0.8 and 0.9, and bio-oil HHV around 0.7 with root-mean-squared error ∼ 2–3 MJkg−1. The model recovers established severity, solvent, and composition trends while identifying regions where predictions are well supported or weakly constrained. SHAP attributions are interpreted as model-conditional associations: liquid-phase outcomes depend strongly on solvent and operating conditions, whereas solid-phase HHVs are more associated with feedstock carbon and ash content. Ensemble and conformal uncertainty methods distinguish relative epistemic uncertainty from calibrated scenario bounds. The framework is intended for uncertainty-aware process screening, scenario bounding, and experimental prioritization rather than unqualified point optimization in poorly represented regimes.

Who gets to govern local food? Knowledge, power, and participation in a post-socialist urban food system
papers.abstract: Urban areas face intersecting challenges related to environmental sustainability, food security, and climate resilience, raising questions about who has the authority to define food-related problems and translate them into urban policy action. This study examines a community-led participatory governance process in Kraków (Poland) and explores how multi-stakeholder dialogue makes local food governable through unequal forms of knowledge, authority, and institutional positioning. Drawing on three structured workshops (February-May 2025) involving farmers, market organizers, municipal officers, public institutions, NGOs, and researchers, we ask: (1) What themes and priorities emerge from multi-stakeholder discussions on local food markets and urban environmental governance? and (2) How do stakeholder groups’ institutional positions, resource dependencies, and claims to legitimate knowledge shape the priorities they articulate and the governance options they treat as feasible? Using Framework Analysis, we identify six thematic frames – market infrastructure, institutional governance, consumer awareness, economic viability, promotion, and quality assurance/certification – and analyse how their salience differs across stakeholder groups according to actors’ institutional mandates, resource dependencies, exposure to risks, and claims to legitimate knowledge. The findings show that participatory food governance does not simply aggregate diverse priorities. It reveals how actors differently positioned within the food system seek to make their risks, responsibilities, and knowledge claims visible, while uneven authority shapes which problems appear actionable, which forms of expertise are recognised, and which governance options remain marginal or invisible. The Kraków case contributes to urban food governance debates by showing how general dynamics of participatory governance under capitalism intersect with post-socialist conditions of fragmented mandates, uneven trust in collective organisation, and weakly institutionalised food policy.

papers.title: Community‐Managed Systems as Nature‐Based Solutions: Effects of Elevation and Size on Floral Richness and Carbon Stock of Sacred Groves in Kerala, India
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Limiting global warming to 1.5°C–2°C requires rapid reductions in atmospheric carbon, highlighting the need to conserve ecosystems with high carbon stock potential. Sacred groves are culturally protected forest fragments maintained through traditional practices and represent community‐managed landscapes with significant potential as nature‐based solutions. This study evaluated the influence of elevation and grove size on plant species richness, carbon stock and soil properties in 55 sacred groves (31 lowland, 19 midland and 5 highland; ranging from 0.025 to 20.2 ha and from 3 to 906 m above mean sea level) across different physiographic regions of Kerala, India. Aboveground biomass carbon was estimated using allometric equations, and soil organic carbon was quantified by wet digestion; these components were combined to estimate total carbon stock. Species richness, carbon stock and soil properties were analysed across elevation and grove‐size categories using one‐way ANOVA, Kruskal–Wallis tests and multiple linear regression. Total carbon stock ranged from 30.46 to 318 Mg ha −1 (mean 113 Mg ha −1 ) but showed no significant relationship with elevation or grove size. In contrast, plant species richness (5–177 species) varied significantly across both factors (elevation: p = 0.005, grove size: p < 0.001). Sacred groves in the midland region supported the highest mean species richness (70 species) among elevation classes, compared with 56 in highland and 37 in lowland groves, while larger groves harboured more species (71) than medium (67) and small (30) groves. Multiple regression identified soil nitrogen as the strongest predictor of species richness (adjusted R 2 = 0.19), with grove area showing a consistent positive but marginal effect, whereas total carbon stock was best explained by exchangeable potassium (adjusted R 2 = 0.13). Soil properties, particularly exchangeable potassium (highest in midland groves, 0.004%) and bulk density (highest in highland groves, 1.76 g cm −3 ), exhibited distinct physiographic patterns. The results demonstrate that sacred groves consistently store substantial carbon irrespective of size or elevation, whereas biodiversity conservation is strongly influenced by grove extent and elevation. These findings underscore the role of sacred groves as effective nature‐based solutions, where traditional stewardship supports both biodiversity conservation and climate change mitigation in human‐dominated landscapes. Integrating systematic management and ecological restoration practices into existing conservation frameworks, with active community participation, is recommended.

papers.title: Quantifying uncertainty in deep learning models for urban safety perception: An MC Dropout approach
papers.abstract: Deep learning models have revolutionized the automated analysis of urban perception. However, these models typically provide point predictions without associated uncertainty estimates, limiting their application in critical urban planning and policy decisions. This research explores the implementation of Monte Carlo Dropout (MC Dropout) as a method for quantifying uncertainty in deep learning models for urban safety perception. Using ResNet-based convolutional neural networks, we evaluated this approach on both global urban datasets (PlacePulse 2.0) and a specific case study of Santiago, Chile, focusing specifically on the safety dimension of urban perception. Our findings reveal that MC Dropout yields per-image uncertainty estimates without requiring significant architectural modifications, alongside a modest improvement in predictive accuracy (from 66.81% to 67.64%). We show that these estimates vary systematically with urban characteristics, with distinct patterns observed between different urban districts, and that the MC Dropout spread is systematically narrower than the discrepancy between the stochastic and deterministic predictions. We are explicit about what the study does not establish: none of our analyses tests the uncertainty estimates against predictive error, so we do not claim that they are calibrated or that they rank predictions by reliability, and we specify in detail the risk–coverage protocol and pairwise proper scoring rule that such a validation would require. The potential implications for urban analytics—triage of cases for human verification, mapping the spatial distribution of predictive dispersion within cities, and improved interpretability of model decision-making—are presented as prospective applications conditional on that validation. The methodological framework established here can be adopted and extended for future studies and practical applications in urban environments.
