papers.title: The Economic Sustainability of Intangible Cultural Heritage in the Platform Age With Global Evidence and Implications for Xinjiang
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Digital platforms lower market access costs for intangible cultural heritage but can concentrate visibility, weaken community control, and disconnect revenue from cultural reproduction. This global survey integrates platform and cultural economics with research on authenticity, intellectual property, and heritage governance. Its Platform Frictions, Cultural Rents, and Intergenerational Reproduction framework distinguishes living practices from their commercial products, recordings, and experiences. Economic sustainability requires four minimum conditions that cannot substitute for one another. These comprise adequate net market access, viable cultural reproduction, a sufficient practitioner value share, and meaningful community control. The framework distinguishes these conditions from the mechanisms through which platforms affect them. Rankings, provenance labels, copyright, and certification can improve discovery and bargaining while concentrating demand, excluding legitimate variants, or burdening small producers. Community authorization requires representation, reviewable delegation, and effective appeal. Distributional assessment separates individual earnings, collective transfers, unpaid contributions, and investment in transmission. Applications to Xinjiang differentiate crafts, performances, foodways, and community events by economic object and institutional responsibility. Longitudinal indicators of apprentice retention, repertoire in use, and contextual participation distinguish authorized adaptation from commercial hollowing. Platform growth sustains living heritage when returns support practitioners, learning, and community authority.

papers.title: Exchange Rates and International Tourism Demand with Endogenous Prices and Capacity Constraints
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Why does destination depreciation sometimes expand tourism and sometimes leave demand almost unchanged? We develop a two‐destination equilibrium model with endogenous supplier prices, imported‐cost exposure, currency risk, and capacity constraints. Five propositions separate price transmission, destination reallocation, additional trips, and welfare. Depreciation expands demand only when its conversion benefit exceeds the associated increase in supplier costs. A binding capacity constraint absorbs further cost relief into scarcity rents and creates unequal quantity responses to favorable and adverse shocks. Destination gains can arise entirely from reallocation when total international travel is fixed. Risk protection raises demand only when its certainty‐equivalent benefit exceeds its price. These analytical results organize a critical synthesis of tourism‐demand evidence. A documented literature verification and a paired comparison of Mauritian studies distinguish measurement differences from changes in samples and estimators. Booking‐horizon alignment remains a theoretical implication requiring direct testing. The analysis identifies the observations needed to distinguish the mechanisms behind conflicting exchange‐rate estimates.

papers.title: Natural Capital Measurement and Applications in Economic and Financial Analysis1
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Natural capital refers to environmental assets that produce economic goods or services used in production or consumption. Today, the concepts of natural capital and the associated ecosystem service flows are being applied beyond their traditional applications in cost‐benefit analysis to a range of topic areas in economics and finance. These broader applications include assessment of physical risks to real estate, insurance, and supply chains, and advancements in modelling economic growth, productivity, and financial risk. These developments have the potential to shift perspectives on economic measurement to include more comprehensive concepts of output and consumption, increase the accuracy of measured productivity and risks, and add precision to our understanding of tradeoffs in resource allocation. We provide an overview of the economic theory underlying natural capital valuation and recent initiatives in natural capital measurement and discuss how new data sources, modeling advances, and frameworks are broadening the application of natural capital concepts and metrics. We include open questions integrated throughout to inform or prompt future scholarly research, model development, and economic measurement.

papers.title: Fisher Dynamics, Monetary Policy, and Household Indebtedness
papers.abstract: Abstract Growth in household debt‐to‐income ratios reflects nominal debt changes or “Fisher dynamics” due to interest income and expenses, real income growth, and inflation. Using two decades of microdata on all Norwegian households, we decompose these channels' roles in how debt‐to‐income evolves over time and in response to monetary policy shocks. On average, debt changes outsize Fisher dynamics, except among highly leveraged households. After interest rate hikes, the channels pull in opposite directions, but the debt changes dominate, so debt‐to‐income ratios decline. This holds across subgroups, including highly indebted households, recent movers, and those facing liquidity constraints or high unemployment risk.

papers.title: Water‐Conscious Governance: The Role of Co‐Opted Members in Water Withdrawal
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT This study investigates the impact of co‐opted board directors on water withdrawal. Based on a U.S. sample of 4194 firm‐year observations between 2008 and 2022, we find that the presence, independence and tenure of co‐opted directors reduce firm water withdrawals. Co‐opted directors can play a constructive role in improving corporate water management by aligning with the CEO environmental initiatives, responding to legitimacy pressures, and supporting strategies that balance profit with stakeholder concerns. Additional analyses reveal that this relationship is stronger when the CEO and board chair roles are separated and in firms with strong corporate governance and environmental performance, as well as in firms that link executive compensation to CSR performance. Also, we show that the effect is prevalent in firms with CSR and nomination committees. Our findings offer new insights for regulators and managers seeking to address water management issues and encourage firms to improve their board structure by increasing board co‐option to better align board decisions with CEO water management policies.

papers.title: Sustainable Innovation Management: From Knowledge Creation to Resource Efficiency
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT This study aims to uncover the internal organizational mechanisms driving sustainable innovation and to develop a unified conceptual framework. To address the theoretical fragmentation in current research, a systematic review of 128 recent empirical articles was conducted, combining conceptual mapping of keyword co‐occurrences with qualitative thematic synthesis. The findings reveal a sequential organizational architecture comprising four interdependent pillars: cognitive foundations, strategic orchestration (driven by dynamic capabilities and strategic agility), technological amplification, and sustainable materialization, all supported by a transversal human and relational substrate. Based on these insights, the study proposes the capability‐based sustainable innovation (CBSI) framework. By integrating the resource‐based view, the knowledge‐based view, and the dynamic capabilities framework, the model explicates the operational sequence required to execute the twin transformation and achieve verifiable circular economy and environmental performance. The framework provides a structured agenda for future research and offers managers a practical blueprint for appropriately aligning human capital with digital investments.

papers.title: Does the Facial Trustworthiness of Hosting Staff Lead to Forecast Bias? Evidence from Analysts’ Site Visits
papers.abstract: We use unique data about corporate site visits in China to examine whether face‐to‐face interactions introduce bias in analyst forecasts. We find that analysts tend to issue more optimistic forecasts when accompanied by hosting staff with high facial trustworthiness, indicating a cognitive bias. This effect is amplified when firms convey more positive information during visits, but is attenuated for firms with high disclosure quality, for experienced and star analysts, for analysts with science, technology, engineering, and mathematics backgrounds, and for analysts visiting industry peers concurrently. Furthermore, the bias is stronger for sole‐visiting analysts but diminishes over time as additional information becomes available or with repeated interactions. Additional analyses show that forecast accuracy also declines, but the effect of facial trustworthiness does not extend to analysts’ stock recommendations or market reactions. Overall, our findings highlight that even sophisticated analysts are susceptible to cognitive bias in face‐to‐face interactions, while alternative information sources, professional experience, and repeated engagement help mitigate such bias.

papers.title: Regional Service Trade Agreements and Manufacturing Global Value Chains: Evidence from 60 Economies
papers.abstract: This study uses the data of 60 countries (regions) from 2000 to 2018 to test the impact of regional service trade agreements on the participation of a country (region) in the global value chain of manufacturing. (1) Overall, signing regional service trade agreements can promote the forward participation of a country’s (regional) value chain, and enhance the division of labour status of a country’s (regional) manufacturing GVCs. (2) After a series of robustness tests, the results remain consistent with the benchmark results. The impact of signing regional service trade agreements on the participation of a country’s (regional) manufacturing GVCs division of labour varies due to the heterogeneity of the country (region), income level and multilateral resistance. (3) The signing of regional service trade agreements between countries (regions) enhances the participation of a country (region) in the GVCs division of manufacturing industry. (4) Trade network status and dynamic evolution process.

papers.title: “Planning” Or Decentralization? Strategic Choices for Business Groups Under Economic Policy Uncertainty
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the impact of EPU on the allocation of decision rights among business groups. We find that when EPU increases, business groups encourage decentralization in order to leverage information from lower-level managers. Furthermore, when the top managers of business groups have an information advantage, the negative relationship between EPU and business group centralization is less pronounced. Moreover, group decentralization promotes corporate innovation and technology acquisition propensity when EPU increases, which enhances firm value. Overall, the findings of this study empirically support traditional decentralization theory while also establishing a trade-off relationship between top managers' and decentralized information advantage.

papers.title: Sovereign Risk Mitigation Mechanism in Emerging Markets
papers.abstract: This paper explores a mechanism for mitigating sovereign risk in emerging markets without risks mutualization. The mechanism involves pooling diversified portfolios of sovereign bonds and issuing them in tranches, with the senior tranche offering low-risk payoffs protected by the subordination of the junior tranches. We argue that this mechanism is feasible for emerging markets. The senior bonds issued by the securitization vehicle attain the properties of a safe asset. The risk level of the junior bonds depends on the structure of the underlying sovereign bonds portfolio. Nevertheless, the properties of the synthetic bonds are, arguably, acceptable for the practical application of the proposed mechanism in promoting the development of financial markets in emerging markets and for practical tasks such as intergovernmental aid or lending.

papers.title: Trade Tariffs and Corporate Greenwashing: Evidence from Chinese A-Share Listed Firms
papers.abstract: Using data on Chinese A-share firms from 2009 to 2023, we examine how import tariff exposure is related to corporate greenwashing. We combine tariff and customs data with annual reports and environmental penalty records. Greenwashing is measured by the gap between environmental disclosure and penalties relative to peers. Random-effects logit estimates show that lower tariff exposure is associated with a higher likelihood of this gap. This relationship varies with media attention, managerial incentives, and fund occupation. The findings do not prove that firms intend to mislead or that tariffs improve the environment.

Scaling up to the cloud: Cloud technology use and growth rates in small and large firms
papers.abstract: Using a unique combination of micro-level data sources on French firms, this paper explores the relationship between cloud technologies and firm growth. Whereas digital technologies have generally been found to disproportionately benefit larger firms, we document that cloud use is positively associated with firm growth, and this association is significantly stronger for smaller firms. Distinguishing cloud services between Infrastructure-as-a-Service (IaaS) and Software-as-a-Service (SaaS), we find that the size-contingent association is driven entirely by SaaS. Crucially, this small firm advantage is conditional on complementary assets as it emerges only among firms endowed with ICT capabilities. Our results are robust across a range of specifications, including instrumental variable strategies. SaaS cloud use is further associated with internal workforce reorganisation toward ICT, managerial, and intermediate occupations and away from manual and clerical ones, particularly among smaller firms, consistent with SaaS cloud operating as an organisational innovation enabling digitalisation and scaling. Finally, we present descriptive sectoral evidence of a negative correlation between cloud and market concentration.

Who Goes Toxic? Understanding Political Toxicity on Social Media Across Individuals and Contexts
papers.abstract: As political toxicity has become widespread on social media, scholars have sought to understand what drives it. While studies often emphasize platform-level explanations, such as algorithmic amplification, they offer limited insight into which users are more likely to produce toxic content. Even less is known about how the relationship between individual-level factors and toxicity varies across political contexts. Using data from 184,354 randomly sampled U.S. Twitter (now X) users, their original tweets (25M), and the accounts they follow, we link users’ inferred characteristics and political context to their real-life toxic behavior. Results show that Republican, male, and older users are consistently more likely to post both impolite and intolerant content, whereas education shows no clear association. We also find that state-level electoral competitiveness increases overall toxicity and, in some cases, conditions individual-level relationships. The age gap in impolite behavior significantly narrows in more competitive states, while the corresponding moderation for intolerance is only marginally significant. There is also some indication that partisan differences in impoliteness become larger in more competitive states, but this moderation is only marginally significant. Together, these results demonstrate that political toxicity is shaped jointly by users’ individual characteristics and the political contexts in which they operate.

Genetic Background and Metabolic Influence on Long-Term Lithium Bioaccumulation in Mytilus Mussels and Their Hybrids
papers.abstract: Abstract Marine mussels are widely used as sentinel organisms in coastal biomonitoring, yet the biological mechanisms controlling the bioaccumulation of emerging metals remain poorly constrained. Climate change and anthropogenic disturbances are reshaping species distributions and contact zones, promoting mussel hybridization that may alter physiological traits and contaminant-handling capacities. Lithium (Li) remains largely overlooked despite its potential toxicity and rapidly increasing global demand. Here, we investigate the influence of critical factors on Li bioaccumulation by mussels combining genetic background and isotopic approaches. Progenies of two Mytilus species and their hybrids were transplanted to the same Atlantic coastal site for 12 months. Over this in situ exposure period, Li concentrations show comparable temporal trends across all progeny groups, with an initial uptake-dominated phase followed by biodilution. Lithium isotope ratios (δ7Li) display a coherent temporal trend across all groups (decrease at early exposure, increase during later growth), and the magnitude of the shift differs slightly among genetic backgrounds. Across samples, δ7Li is coupled to growth-related metrics (dry weight) and inversely related to Li concentrations, indicating a metabolic control on Li isotope compositions of these organisms. Li concentrations are also positively correlated with lithogenic-associated elements (e.g., aluminum), consistent with the influence of particle associated Li. A simplified biodynamic modeling including Li isotopes data further indicates a more efficient Li depuration after 5 months, combined with a relatively stronger contribution from dissolved Li. Overall, growth-related factors emerged as the primary biological drivers of Li concentration and isotope variability, with the relative contributions of dissolved and particulate exposure pathways varying in association with physiological growth. Hybridization may modulate Li bioaccumulation and δ7Li values, but its influence appears secondary and does not compromise the use of Mytilus mussels as bioindicators in established frameworks such as “Mussel Watch”.

papers.title: Building-Stock Turnover Reshapes Mitigation Priorities in China’s Building Sector
papers.abstract: Abstract China’s building sector is pivotal to the 2060 carbon-neutrality ambition, yet prospective assessments often insufficiently capture regional heterogeneity and life-cycle emission dynamics. Here, we develop a provincial-level dynamic framework integrating material flow analysis, life-cycle assessment, and machine-learning-informed parameter trajectories to project emissions through 2060. Under a business-as-usual (BAU) scenario, China’s building life-cycle emissions are projected to peak in 2031–2033, while carbon neutrality remains challenged by persistent pressures from both material use and building operations. These pressures arise from the existing stock, whose continued use sustains energy demand while increasing building retirements shift construction from stock growth to the replacement of retired buildings. Implementing a high-efficiency scenario with regionally differentiated deployment of material- and energy-efficiency strategies could reduce China’s building-sector life-cycle emissions by 90% in 2060 relative to the BAU scenario. Provincial analysis further reveals that similar overall mitigation potential masks substantial differences in the composition of effective mitigation portfolios, reflecting local building-stock and energy-use characteristics. To close the remaining gap, deeper operational decarbonization should be coupled with stock-management strategies that extend building lifetimes, avoid premature demolition, and prioritize renovation and reuse.

papers.title: Can the Spatial Planning of Livestock Production Tackle Future Nitrogen Pollution in China?
papers.abstract: Abstract Nitrogen (N) pollution from livestock production significantly threatens China’s air and water quality, necessitating innovative solutions to balance food security and environmental sustainability. Studies have mostly overlooked the spatial heterogeneity of N-related environmental impacts and the trade-offs between reducing ammonia (NH3) emissions and N concentrations in water. This study develops a spatially explicit multiscale model system encompassing 13,000 polygons across China to assess soil N balance, NH3 emission intensity, and N concentrations in surface water, aiming to explore integrated spatial-planning (SP) strategies that maximize synergy and minimize trade-offs. Our findings reveal that single-purpose SP scenarios (e.g., reducing NH3 emissions or instream N concentrations) can effectively address one N-related issue but produce substantial trade-offs, leaving >50% of China’s population exposed to at least another N-related problem. However, an integrated SP approach could reduce harmful N exposures for 90% of China’s population while ensuring food security. This approach involves reallocating 14% of livestock production, reducing livestock numbers by one-third relative to the 2050 baseline, and implementing advanced technologies to mitigate N pollution hotspots. Thus, our findings emphasize the importance of spatially explicit N boundaries and multicriteria planning to tackle N pollution in air and water simultaneously, supporting cross-media N management policy-making and region-specific strategies.

Layered double hydroxides functionalized electrospun recycled polyamide 6 from fishing nets: structure–property relationships for antimicrobial non-woven fabrics
papers.abstract: Plastic pollution, particularly marine plastic waste from discarded fishing nets, represents a significant environmental challenge and highlights the need for effective strategies to recover and valorize end-of-life polymers. Polyamide 6 (PA6) fishing nets are an underexploited source for the development of high-value functional materials. This work develops antimicrobial non-woven fabrics (NWFs) from recycled PA6 (rPA6) incorporating organo-modified Mg/Al layered double hydroxides (LDHs) intercalated with antimicrobial anions, namely ascorbate (ASA), ferulate (FER), salicylate (SAL), and citrate (CA), into rPA6, followed by electrospinning. The resulting nanofibrous NWFs were characterized by Field Emission Scanning Electron Microscopy (FESEM), Fourier Transformed Infrared Spectroscopy (FTIR), Wide Angle/Small Angle X-ray Scattering with micro-beam (μWAXS/μSAXS), thermal analysis and tested against Escherichia coli and Staphylococcus aureus . Homogeneous nanofibers were obtained and LDH incorporation preserved rPA6 chemical structure while reducing crystallinity. rPA6/LDH-FER, rPA6/LDH-ASA, and rPA6/LDH-CA, showed 96.7 to 99.9% bacterial mortality. After thermal aging at 115 °C, LDH-containing NWFs exhibited improved structural stability. These results demonstrate the feasibility of converting recycled PA6 fishing-nets into functional antimicrobial nanofibrous fabrics through LDH functionalization and electrospinning, supporting circular and sustainable applications of marine recycled polyamides.

papers.title: Multi‐Objective Spatial Optimization of Cropland Layouts in Highly Urbanized Regions: Evidence From Dongguan, China
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Cropland protection in highly urbanized regions requires reconciling stable quantitative‐qualitative targets with the functional optimization of extremely fragmented spatial structures. This study develops a patch‐level multi‐objective spatial reconfiguration framework of cropland layouts based on the Non‐dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm‐II (NSGA‐II) to balance fragmentation mitigation and land conversion costs under constraints of quantity balance, cropland quality non‐degradation, spatial feasibility, and adjustment priorities. The method integrates multi‐scenario cropland adjustment scales with three patch‐level adjustment modes, that is, internal filling, edge expansion, and patch connection. Validation in Dongguan, a representative highly urbanized city in China, demonstrates the framework's effectiveness in generating spatially realistic layouts through a well‐distributed Pareto front. Results indicate that while larger adjustment scales substantially improve landscape aggregation, land conversion costs escalate non‐linearly; the highest‐intensity scenario incurred costs over six times those of the smallest. Across all scenarios, edge expansion served as the primary cost‐effective pathway for consolidation, while internal filling contributed to resolving patch perforations and stabilizing core areas. Patch connection remained indispensable for bridging isolated fragments and ensuring systemic landscape integrity. However, sensitivity analysis showed that optimization outcomes were more responsive to the connection distance than to the relative cost coefficients, and increasing the connection distance did not necessarily improve the overall landscape structure. These findings emphasize that coupling patch‐level mechanisms with multi‐objective optimization provides a robust, actionable tool for precise spatial planning and targeted cropland policy in high‐density urban environments.

Skill certifications and migrant labor market integration: Experimental evidence from Colombia
papers.abstract: This paper studies whether government-issued skill certification improves labor market integration when workers skills are hard to verify. We evaluate a randomized offer of access to an occupation-specific certification program in Colombia to locals and migrants, two groups with different ex ante signaling capacity. The program certifies existing skills rather than providing training. Among locals, the offer increases employment by reducing inactivity and raises hours worked. The effects persist unevenly over time and are robust to attrition bounds and alternative outcome measures. Among migrants, estimates are less precise and provide no evidence of effects in employment, hours, or wages. The results show that a common skill certification generates different patterns of labor market adjustment among locals and migrants.

FDI spillovers in history: Interwar Japanese “Zaikabo” investment in China's cotton spinning industry
papers.abstract: We estimate productivity spillovers from Japanese cotton-spinning firms in China (known as Zaikabo) to local Chinese cotton-spinning mills based on plant-level data for 1925 to 1938. In order to capture the important role of distance in facilitating such spillovers we geo-localised the plants. Our results provide clear evidence for positive spillovers from Zaikabo to local Chinese mills, which go hand-in-hand with an upgrade in production technology towards greater use of capital. Spillovers are very localised, being strongest within a radius of up to 10 km around the Zaikabo and particularly strong for mills in Shanghai. Exploiting information on the workforce composition of the Japanese affiliates, we find suggestive evidence of a skilled-labour channel: spillovers tend to be larger from Zaikabo employing higher shares of skilled labour. We also find some evidence in line with the idea that these gains are larger for Chinese mills with higher initial productivity, consistent with a role for absorptive capacity. Our paper is the first to document FDI productivity spillovers in a historical context and to characterise the channels through which they operate.

Inflation and price dispersion: New cross-sectoral and international evidence
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the relationship between price dispersion and inflation, shedding light on one major source of the cost of high inflation. By analyzing novel product-level web-scraped data from over 60,000 restaurants and supermarkets across 18 countries facing high and low inflation periods, I uncover new evidence of a significant positive correlation between inflation and price dispersion. My findings reveal that average annualized inflation, ranging between 0 and 20 percentage points across countries within a condensed time frame, is significantly associated with higher price dispersion in both the restaurant and the supermarket sectors. The estimates indicate that the marginal effect of suboptimal inflation on product-level distortions is positive, economically significant in all inflation environments and heterogeneous across sectors. Cross-sectionally, I find that as annualized inflation rises from 0% to 10% inefficient price dispersion is about 46% higher for supermarkets and 73% higher for restaurants. Lastly, the relationship between inflation and price dispersion does not flatten much at higher inflation, so that the marginal cost of additional inflation does not vanish as inflation rises – a pattern standard menu-cost models do not generate. This indicates a sustained impact of inflation on price dispersion, implying that accommodating higher inflation levels incurs substantial welfare costs.

Spillover effects of foreign currency loans: The role of the bank lending channel
papers.abstract: Local currency borrowers are statistically significantly affected by exchange rate fluctuations due to the bank lending chan‐ nel. Using microdata on borrowers from Hungary, this study examines the spillover effects of foreign currency loans on local currency borrowers following an unexpected appreciation of the Swiss franc (CHF) in January 2015. CHF corporate loans are considered unhedged since the majority of the borrowers did not have income in CHF. Our analysis indicates that banks holding a larger portion of unhedged CHF corporate loans reduced their lending in local currency corporate loans after the shock. This relationship is robust across both extensive (loans terminated by a given bank and no new loans at a bank or banks different from the account holder bank or banks) and intensive (no new loans at its current bank or banks) margins. Further investigation into the mechanisms reveals that banks with more unhedged CHF corporate loans experience an increase in non‐performing CHF loans post‐shock, reducing their capital adequacy. Furthermore, the evidence in our paper suggests that reductions in banks’ local currency lending due to exchange rate shocks adversely affect the investment activity of small firms and increase their likelihood of default.

papers.abstract: I argue that household heterogeneity plays a key role in the transmission of aggregate shocks in emerging market economies. Using Mexico's 1995 crisis as a case study, I first document empirically that working in the tradable versus non-tradable sector is a crucial determinant of the income and consumption losses of different types of households. Specifically, households in the non-tradable sector suffered much larger income and consumption losses regardless of other household characteristics. To account for the effect of this observation on macroeconomic dynamics, I construct a New Keynesian small open economy model with household heterogeneity along two dimensions: uninsurable sector-specific income and limited financial-market participation. I find that the propagation of shocks in this economy is affected by both dimensions of heterogeneity, with uninsurable sector-specific income playing a quantitatively larger role. In terms of policy, a managed exchange rate policy is more costly overall when households are heterogeneous; however, households in the non-tradable sector benefit from it.

Examples illustrate the scope and implications of our findings.

Information design in smooth games
papers.abstract: We study information design in games where players choose from a continuum of actions and have continuously differentiable payoffs. We show that an information structure is optimal when the equilibrium it induces can also be implemented in a principal–agent contracting problem. Building on this result, we characterize optimal information structures in symmetric linear‐quadratic games. With common values, targeted disclosure is robustly optimal across all priors. With interdependent and normally distributed values, linear disclosure is uniquely optimal. We illustrate our findings with applications in venture capital, Bayesian polarization, and price competition.

papers.title: Optimal auction design with contingent payments and costly verification
papers.abstract: We study the design of an auction for an income‐generating asset such as an intellectual property license. Each bidder has a signal about his future income from acquiring the asset. After the asset is allocated, the winner's income from the asset is realized privately. The principal can audit the winner, at a cost, and then charge a payment contingent on the winner's realized income. We solve for an auction that maximizes the principal's revenue, net of auditing costs. The winning bidder is charged linear royalties up to a cap, beyond which there is no auditing. A higher bidder pays more in cash upfront and faces a lower royalty cap.

papers.title: Repeated games with many players
papers.abstract: Motivated by the problem of sustaining cooperation in large groups with limited information, we analyze the relationship between group size, monitoring precision, and discounting in repeated games with independent, player‐level noise. The viability of cooperation under independent noise is linked to the per‐capita channel capacity of the stage‐game monitoring structure. We show that cooperation is impossible if the per‐capita channel capacity is much smaller than the discount rate. A folk theorem under a novel identification condition provides a near converse. If attention is restricted to co‐linear equilibria (a generalization of strongly symmetric equilibria), cooperation is possible only under much more severe parameter restrictions.

papers.title: Informed communication equilibrium
papers.abstract: We consider a privately informed principal selecting a communication device to influence players' actions. In contrast to standard information design, the principal cannot commit ex ante, and the device must elicit information from all players. We define an informed communication equilibrium (informed CE) as a perfect Bayesian equilibrium outcome of this informed communication design game. We show that the set of informed CE is the subset of communication equilibria (CE) that yield principal payoff vectors bounded below by an equilibrium payoff vector of the silent game, under some consistent interim beliefs. The ex ante optimal CE may fail to be an informed CE. We provide sufficient conditions for a CE to be an informed CE and identify classes of games in which CE and informed CE coincide.

papers.title: Strategic experimentation with privately observed payoffs
papers.abstract: We study a strategic experimentation game with exponential bandits in which experiment outcomes are private. The equilibrium amount of experimentation is always weakly higher than with public outcomes. Moreover, in pure equilibria, experimentation is never significantly below the socially optimal level and may be strictly higher. We provide a tight bound on the extent of over‐experimentation. The analysis rests on a novel encouragement effect.

papers.title: Belief in mean reversion and the law of small numbers
papers.abstract: Studies find that people systematically underestimate the likelihood of streaks in a random sequence. In a canonical coin‐tossing environment, this paper shows that the evidence can be explained by a belief in mean reversion. Such beliefs are represented as if the bias of the coin is history‐dependent and “self‐correcting.” In a Bayesian inference setting, a belief in mean reversion ensures that the agent never rules out the true parameter.

papers.title: Semistability in roommate problems
papers.abstract: We study the roommate problem allowing for preferences with indifferences and agents remaining single. A stable outcome need not exist. We introduce semi‐stability, a novel notion that guarantees existence and restores stability through minimal policy or group interventions. We build an equilibrium foundation for semistability by showing its equivalence to a newly proposed choice‐based equilibrium concept. We show that undominated semistable outcomes are Pareto optimal and under strict preferences, every semistable outcome is Pareto optimal. Nevertheless, standard structural properties, such as the rural hospital theorem and the lattice properties, fail for semistable outcomes. We also discuss possible applications.

papers.title: Contract terms monotonicity in matching markets
papers.abstract:
We study doctor–hospital matching markets with contracts, in which hospitals can offer a range of contract terms to doctors. We show that introducing new terms can reduce doctors' welfare, whereas withdrawing terms may generate a Pareto improvement. We establish the preference domains under which welfare is preserved and show that only
 agent‐lexicographic preferences
 for all agents ensure that no doctor is worse off when additional terms are introduced. Since this condition is rarely satisfied in practice, our results imply that most real‐world markets are vulnerable to welfare losses when the set of contract terms expands.

papers.title: Frontmatter of Theoretical Economics Vol. 21 Iss. 4
Selling information for bilateral trade
papers.abstract: We study the design and pricing of information by independent information providers for a buyer engaged in a trading relationship with a seller, and examine their welfare implications. While competitive information firms would sell full information about the value of the good, a monopolist supplies limited information in a particularly simple form—often resulting in higher total surplus than under full information, by influencing the seller's pricing decision. If only a single information structure can be offered, it takes a binary threshold form. If the provider can offer a menu of priced information structures before the seller sets a price, he offers a continuum of thresholds, inducing a unit‐elastic demand function for the seller. In both scenarios, the information firm increases total welfare when the seller's production cost is high but reduces it when the cost is low.

papers.title: Collaboration between and within groups
Combinator dynamics: Multidimensional evolutionary learning
papers.abstract: In complex strategic settings with multiple dimensions, players often simplify decisions by breaking them down into separate dimensions. In contrast to standard replicator dynamics, which assume perfect multidimensional coordination, our combinator dynamics model captures cases in which players revise actions dimension by dimension, imitate successful traits in each dimension, and then combine the selected traits into a new action. We analyze key properties of these dynamics—monotonicity, stationarity, and stability. We then extend the model to heterogeneous settings, where some players imitate entire multidimensional actions while others combine traits imitated separately in each dimension. We apply the framework to organizational decision‐making, where decentralized adoption of practices can generate coordination failures, persistent performance differences, and a trade‐off between specialized and versatile organizational traits.

papers.title: Stochastic Commitment in Repeated Games
Obvious strategy-proofness with respect to a partition
papers.abstract: We define and study obvious strategy-proofness with respect to a partition of the set of agents. It encompasses strategy-proofness as a special case when the partition is the coarsest one and obvious strategy-proofness when the partition is the finest. For any partition, it falls between these two extremes. We establish two general properties of this new notion and apply it to the simple anonymous voting problem with two alternatives and strict preferences.

papers.title: Secure and efficient networks
papers.abstract: This study aims to understand efficient network formation and optimal defensive resource distribution in the presence of an intelligent attacker. We present a two-player dynamic framework in which the Defender and the Attacker compete in a network formation and defence game with heterogeneous vertices’ values. Such a model allows for studying the trade-off between network efficiency and security. Contrary to the literature, we find that a centrally protected star network does not yield the maximum payoff for the defending side in most circumstances, even being the most secure network formation. Additionally, it reveals a new type of network that often arises in an equilibrium of the games with limited defensive resources—a maxi-core network.

papers.title: Experience-based pairwise comparison dynamics
Single and multi-winner auctions with performance obligation
Risk, time, and diet quality: Evidence from a general population survey
papers.abstract: This paper explores the relationships between overall diet quality and attitudes toward risk and time using a general population survey. We combine a food frequency questionnaire and a choice-based preference module to elicit individual risk and time preferences. The online questionnaire was administered to a socioeconomic panel representative of the French population. We show that risk and time preferences are associated with individual heterogeneity in key aspects of diet quality, a result that holds across a wide range of robustness checks. Using a hierarchical Bayes framework, we jointly estimate individual risk aversion and impatience parameters and show that associations hold for both model-free and structural estimates of risk and time preferences. We further show that these associations account for a substantial share of the heterogeneity in dietary outcomes beyond sociodemographic controls. Risk and time preferences contribute to both the income-diet-quality and education-diet-quality gradients, but in opposite directions, resulting in a limited net contribution to explaining socioeconomic inequalities in diet quality.

papers.title: In sickness and in health insurance: Gender in household benefit plan choice
papers.abstract: I document that households in the United States are more likely to choose health plans offered by the husband's employer than the wife's. This gap may reflect gender disparities in employment status, plan quality, or an inherent gender effect. Using a novel identification strategy that holds employment status and plan quality fixed, I find that the gender effect increases the probability of selecting the husband's plan by 6.3 percentage points.

papers.title: The rise and fall (and rise) of the Affordable Care Act: Varying impacts on coverage over time and place
Recent minimum wage policy and its impacts on birth outcomes
papers.abstract: After a pause in statutory minimum wage increases during the Great Recession, several states increased their minimum wages, including increases as large as 60% over just a few years. Using a triple difference-in-differences framework and data on the universe of births from 2010 to 2019, this study investigates how recent minimum wage hikes affected birth outcomes. We first document sizeable negative impacts of minimum wage policy on the labor supply and economic well-being of females aged 16-44. We then document small adverse effects on birth outcomes, estimating that minimum wage increases led to lower birthweight, fewer normal birthweight births, and more small for gestational age births. These findings generally contrast with an earlier literature relying primarily on much smaller minimum wage increases which showed more evidence of positive impacts on birth outcomes.

papers.title: Beyond targeting women: Intrahousehold contexts and the effectiveness of food vouchers
papers.abstract: Many transfer programs target women based on evidence that mothers are more likely than fathers to allocate resources toward child welfare. However, findings on gendered impacts remain mixed-likely because parental knowledge, preferences, and household decision-making roles differ across contexts. In this study, we experimentally vary the intrahousehold informational context itself through a randomized controlled trial in rural Ethiopia. Specifically, employing a factorial design, we cross-randomize two key dimensions: (1) which parent receives nutrition behavior change communication (BCC) - neither, mother only, or both; and (2) which parent receives a household food voucher - mother or father. We find that, pooled across settings in which fathers do not receive BCC, vouchers assigned to mothers generate larger improvements in child-feeding practices than vouchers assigned to fathers. The largest effects occur when mothers receive both BCC and the voucher. This maternal advantage attenuates and is no longer detectable when fathers also receive BCC. We provide suggestive evidence that when mothers have both a knowledge advantage and control over resources, they are better able to mobilize greater intrahousehold support. These findings highlight the importance of accounting for intrahousehold contexts, not just recipient gender, when designing nutrition interventions.

papers.title: Labor unions and deaths of despair: Evidence from right-to-work laws
papers.abstract: This paper examines the relationship between union membership and deaths of despair. Using state-level variation in the timing of the adoption of right-to-work laws as a natural experiment, I show that right-to-work laws are associated with a decline in union membership and an increase in deaths of despair. Two-way fixed-effects (TWFE) difference-in-differences (DiD) estimates suggest that the adoption of a right-to-work law is associated with a 2.6 percentage point reduction in union membership and an increase in deaths of despair mortality of 13 additional persons per 100,000, implying there are approximately 7.5 additional deaths of despair for every 1,000 workers who lose union membership. An analysis of mechanisms suggests the increase in mortality is largely driven by increased opioid usage and a concomitant increase in overdose deaths. I support the TWFE results with estimates from two alternative estimators robust to concerns about treatment effect heterogeneity and variation in treatment timing. Estimates from the Callaway and Sant'Anna (2021) estimator and the Borusyak et al. (2024) estimator support the TWFE findings: right-to-work laws reduce union membership and increase deaths of despair.

papers.title: The effect of online sales bans on e-cigarette use
The adverse effects of weight reports in schools
papers.abstract: Using rich survey data for England, we investigate whether providing parents with information about the weight status of their children reduces children's weight and improves health behaviors, or whether it has adverse effects. We exploit the timing of survey interview compared to the timing of sending out weight reports to parents in a difference-in-differences framework. Our analysis does not reveal the intended effects on body weight or health behaviors. Instead, we find adverse effects for children with overweight that are concentrated in disadvantaged families and driven by increases in breakfast skipping and feeling tired and unhappy at school.

papers.title: Do Higher-Cost Settings Deliver Better Outcomes? Post-Acute Care Efficiency in Medicare Skilled Nursing Facilities and Home Health Agencies
papers.abstract: Determining the value of different post-acute care settings for clinically similar patients is important for providers and payers. This study examines the causal effect of post-acute care (PAC) setting on Medicare spending and short-term patient outcomes among beneficiaries discharged from hospitals following treatment for stroke or congestive heart failure (CHF). Using 2013-2017 Medicare claims data, we implement an instrumental variable strategy that exploits daily variation in skilled nursing facility (SNF) bed occupancy at the hospital service area level to estimate the local average treatment effect of SNF versus home health agency (HHA) care. Our findings reveal no significant differences, on average, in 30-day mortality or rehospitalization rates between SNF and HHA care among stroke and CHF patients. However, the 95% confidence intervals do not exclude clinically meaningful reductions in 30-day mortality. Meanwhile, SNF care is associated with approximately $4700 more in Medicare spending per PAC episode. The spending gap is larger in markets with more constrained SNF capacity, particularly in states with Certificate of Need regulations, rural areas, and low-income neighborhoods. However, we do not detect statistically significant differences in short-term health outcomes across these markets on average, suggesting that supply constraints may amplify the spending implications of SNF use while the relationship between PAC setting and short-term clinical outcomes remains uncertain. These findings highlight the importance of aligning PAC discharge decisions with both clinical needs and local capacity considerations, particularly under value-based payment models.

papers.title: Is bitcoin a hedge against central banking? Evidence from AI-driven monetary policy expectations
papers.abstract: This study investigates the transmission of monetary policy narratives to Bitcoin prices, distinguishing policy expectations from realized policy implementation. We introduce a weekly Monetary Policy Expectations (MPE) index derived from the Large Language Model (LLM)-based classification of 118,000+ market messages, providing a granular measure of hawkish and dovish monetary policy discourse. We demonstrate that changes in the MPE index provide evidence of significant linear predictive information for Bitcoin returns at short-to-medium horizons, with significant Granger causality at multiple lags. A Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) framework combined with SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) further identifies nonlinear and regime-dependent relationships between monetary-policy expectations and Bitcoin returns, indicating that Bitcoin functions as a sensitive barometer of central bank signaling. In particular, hawkish monetary-policy narratives are associated with negative price responses that are not accounted for by contemporaneous Federal Funds Rate adjustments. These findings highlight Bitcoin's structural sensitivity to global monetary discourse, establishing LLM-derived monetary-policy sentiment as a high-frequency measure of central-bank communication and as an informative leading macroeconomic indicator for the digital asset landscape.

papers.title: Forecasting the price of carbon with macroeconomic and financial variables
papers.abstract: We tackle the issue of producing point, sign, and density forecasts for the monthly real price of carbon in the European Union Emissions Trading System (EU ETS). We show that Bayesian Vector Autoregressive (BVAR) models augmented with factors based on macroeconomic and financial variables yield improvements in point and density forecasting performance, with the largest point-forecast gains emerging at intermediate and longer horizons. In particular, the one-factor BVAR model provides lowest values at six and nine months ahead, while the baseline BVAR performs best at the one-year horizon. By contrast, a large BVAR including all predictors individually does not improve point forecast accuracy, supporting the use of parsimonious model specifications. Simple forecast pooling delivers modest gains from medium horizons onward, but does not mitigate the time variation in relative forecast performance. We also provide a qualitative comparison of model-based forecasts with survey expectations and forecasts released by data providers, which further highlights that relative forecast performance varies over time. Moreover, we consider verified emissions and show that stochastic volatility improves point forecasts, with reductions of about 6.5 to 7.1% at the one-year horizon. Lastly, we use model-based forecasts to construct market monitoring tools that track demand and price pressure in the EU ETS.

A conditional probability hierarchy for stochastic choice
papers.abstract: We introduce point conditional probability spaces (PCPSs) as primitive building blocks for stochastic choice. This concept goes back to R\'enyi (1955), who proposed conditional probability spaces (CPSs) as a basis for probability theory. Luce (1959) noted the connection between CPSs and stochastic choice, and Cerreia-Vioglio et al. (2021) have developed the connection further. A PCPS is a CPS each of whose component probability measures concentrates on a singleton selection. We build a four-level PCPS-based hierarchy of families of stochastic choice rules. Level 1 consists of PCPSs, Level 2 is made up of finitely additive"conditionally consistent"mixtures of PCPSs, Level 3 comprises all finitely additive probabilistic mixtures of PCPSs, and Level 4 consists of all finitely additive signed probabilistic mixtures of PCPSs. We construct our hierarchy at a general measure-theoretic level that encompasses infinite choice sets. We also connect each level of our hierarchy to well-known axioms for stochastic choice, namely, the Weak Axiom of Stochastic Revealed Preference, Independence of Irrelevant Alternatives, and no Dutch book. We establish the relationship between total orders and PCPSs and demonstrate a sense in which PCPSs can be a more parsimonious representation of choice.

papers.abstract: Consider the problem of designing a revenue-optimal auction mechanism when two heterogeneous items are sold to a single buyer having independent valuations over the items. The distributions of the buyer's valuation for the items are assumed to have densities that are positive, nondecreasing, and continuously differentiable on their support sets $[c_i,c_i+b_i]$ in the positive axis. I prove that the optimal mechanism is deterministic if at least one of the minimum valuations (i.e., either $c_1$ or $c_2$) is sufficiently high. I provide a method to calculate the threshold of $(c_1,c_2)$ beyond which the optimal mechanism is deterministic. I also provide a sufficient condition on the distributions of buyer's valuations for which the individual sale mechanism is optimal. I show that when $c_1$ is low and $c_2$ is high, it is optimal for the seller to sell item $2$ at the minimum valuation $c_2$, thus effectively reducing the problem to finding the optimal mechanism in the one-dimensional setting only for item $1$. I conjecture with promising preliminary results that this result can be extended to the three-item setting. Specifically, I conjecture that when $c_1$ and $c_2$ are low but $c_3$ is high, it is optimal for the seller to sell item $3$ at the minimum valuation $c_3$, thus effectively reducing the problem to finding the optimal mechanism in the two-dimensional setting for items $1$ and $2$.

Interregional trade, structural changes and regional inequality
papers.abstract: . This paper investigates the drivers of structural change stemming from the reallocation of economic activity across sectors and regions in Brazil. Using interregional input-output analysis, we decompose structural change into contributions from technology, domestic and foreign trade, and consumption. We find that final expenditure (income level) are the dominant force behind structural transformation and the reducing regional inequality. However, domestic trade reinforces regional disparities by shifting growth gains toward more developed areas. Interregional linkages act as shock absorbers, dampening regional convergence and amplifying income leakages from poorer regions. Shifts in technical and preference coefficients toward value-added-intensive sectors supported growth in lagging regions. Foreign trade also contributed to reducing regional inequality. Our findings underscore the critical role of input-output linkages and domestic trade patterns in shaping structural change and regional disparities—highlighting the often-overlooked importance of interregional trade.

papers.title: Shock spillovers and international financial (dis)integration
papers.abstract: Global shocks - ranging from climate-related disasters and geopolitical con-(cid:135)icts to pandemics - transmit rapidly across borders and shape (cid:133)nancial market co-movements. This paper develops a two-country general equilibrium model to study how cross-border shock spillovers a⁄ect optimal international portfolio holdings and the degree of (cid:133)nancial (dis)integration. The analysis highlights that both the magnitude and heterogeneity of spillovers across income sources (capital versus labour income) play a central role in determining international risk-sharing opportunities. When spillovers mainly a⁄ect capital income, countries reduce their foreign asset positions and markets become more segmented. By contrast, when labour-income spillovers dominate, (cid:133)nancial integration strengthens. The model generates empirical implications regarding the relation between global shocks, international portfolio rebalancing, and time-varying degrees of (cid:133)nancial integration, providing a structural framework that can help interpret recent episodes of global (cid:133)nancial fragmentation.

Convergence to collusion in algorithmic pricing
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence algorithms are increasingly used by firms to set prices. Previous research shows that they can learn to collude, but how quickly and reliably they can do so has remained an open question. I study average-reward soft actor-critic algorithms that set continuous prices in the workhorse environment of this literature: a repeated Bertrand duopoly with symmetric firms, deterministic logit demand, and constant marginal costs, where agents observe only market prices and their own profits. The algorithms can converge to a collusive outcome within 50,000 periods, and in 36% of simulations learned punishments make one-period deviations unprofitable, so that high prices are mutual best responses. Successful simulations show cooperative behaviour supported by reward-punishment schemes that discourage deviations. When high prices are not supported by punishments, profitable deviations are typically on the order of hundredths of a percent.

Work-from-home and wage convergence across cities: An exploration
papers.abstract: This paper provides evidence on a WFH-related hypothesis that has not previously been tested empirically. The hypothesis is that the presence of fully remote workers, for whom residence and work locations are decoupled, should create a tendency toward wage convergence across cities within teleworkable occupations. The reason is that, since fully remote workers can work anywhere, local wages must match those available in other cities for employers to attract any of these workers. By combining occupational wage data with data on which occupations are teleworkable, the paper attempts to test the wage-convergence hypothesis. The results are mixed, but some evidence does emerge in favor of the hypothesis.

The Asymmetric Nature of Social Hierarchies: Unpacking the Dynamic Relationship Between Power and Status
papers.abstract: Scholars and practitioners alike have long presumed that power and status, two foundational bases of social hierarchy, share a symmetric, mutually reinforcing relationship. However, support for this presumption has largely taken the form of theoretical accounts due to the prevalence of static research designs and a dearth of dynamic methodology in organizational research. Drawing on the Dual Perspective Model, we propose that one’s status is more likely to drive changes in one’s power than vice versa because status has a stronger connection to communion—an important component of interpersonal evaluations—than does power, and communality is an important predictor of both power and status. Using data from two studies involving project teams and a contemporary methodology from developmental psychology for modeling dynamic relationships (bivariate dual change score models), we illustrate that there is indeed a mutually reinforcing relationship between power and status over time, but this relationship is asymmetric. In three additional experiments, we find that perceptions of communality explain this asymmetry. We also find similar effects whether power is formal—attached to a position or role—or involves control over informal resources. Across all studies, we find that the path from status to changes in power is stronger than the path from power to changes in status.

Agency mechanisms in foreign affiliate divestment: The roles of corporate restructuring and ownership type
papers.abstract: Why do multinational enterprises (MNEs) delay or avoid divesting foreign affiliates even when exit appears warranted? We argue that divestment is a visible strategic action that prompts renewed principal scrutiny of prior investment decisions and ongoing stewardship, increasing the evaluative exposure of the corporate management function. Drawing on agency theory, we examine how ownership commitment, headquarters involvement, and performance-based discretion shape divestment. Using longitudinal data on foreign affiliates in Korea (2007 – 2019), we find that ownership commitment and performance-based discretion reduce divestment likelihood, that restructuring weakens these effects, and that relational ownership moderates the effect of headquarters involvement. Divestment thus reflects governance and attribution processes, not merely economic considerations.

The role of gender norms within independent financial advice
papers.abstract: Financial advice has gained importance in asset-based welfare systems, yet it continues to operate within professional cultures shaped by masculine-coded practices. While existing scholarship has documented occupational segregation and gendered outcomes in financial advice, it often treats gender and gender capital as fixed attributes, underestimating how advisors can navigate and reshape gendered habitus. This paper moves beyond such framings by demonstrating how financial advice is not merely a site where gendered inequalities are reproduced but also one where they are negotiated and, at times, transformed. Drawing on 30 semi-structured interviews with independent financial advisors, the study develops an analytical framework that integrates Bourdieu ’ s concept of habitus with a ‘doing/undoing gender ’ lens and recent theorizing on variegated subjectivities. The analysis demonstrates that advisors employ differentiated strategies, seeking to transform gendered habitus through four different approaches, even as industry logics constrain these efforts. By conceptualizing habitus as fragmented, evolving, and mediated through individualized and socialized subjectivities, the paper advances debates on gender and finance, offering insights into how professional practices simultaneously challenge and reinforce gendered inequalities.
